In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

Commentary on Surat an-Nisa'

In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. May God bless our master and patron Muhammad (ﷺ), and his family and companions, and grant them abundant peace.

This surah is Madani, except for one verse which was revealed in Makkah in the year of the Conquest concerning 'Uthman ibn Talha, and it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa': 58]. An-Naqqash said: It has also been said that the surah was revealed at the time of the Prophet's (ﷺ) emigration from Makkah to the illuminated city of Madinah.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Some people have said that the words of God, Exalted is He, ﴿O people﴾ (yā ayyuhā al-nās), wherever they occur, are Makkan. So it is likely that the beginning of this surah is Makkan, and whatever was revealed after the emigration is Madani, even if it was revealed in Makkah or during one of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) journeys. An-Nahhas said: This surah is Makkan.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

There is no disagreement that it contains what was revealed in Madinah. In al-Bukhari, the last verse revealed was: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning the kalala﴾ [an-Nisa': 176]. He mentioned it in the commentary on Surat [Bara'a] on the authority of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib. In al-Bukhari, it is narrated from 'A'isha that she said: "Surat an-Nisa' was not revealed except while I was with the Messenger of God (ﷺ)," meaning: he had consummated the marriage with her.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿O people, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate, and from the two of them spread forth many men and women. And fear God, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed, God is ever Watchful over you﴾

(p. 460) Ya is a particle of address, ayyu is a singular vocative noun, ha is an attention marker, and al-nas is an epithet (na't) of ayyu, or a complement (silah) according to the view of Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash. Rabb means the owner. The verse contains a reminder of the Creator and of the beginning of existence. It also contains an urging to maintain kinship because of the sanctity of this relationship, however distant it may be. He said wāḥidatin (feminine) in agreement with the feminine form of the word nafs (soul). This is like the saying of the poet:

Your father was a successor, whom another woman bore, and you are a successor, that is perfection.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read min nafsin wāḥidin without the feminine ending, and this is in consideration of the meaning, since by nafs is meant Adam (ﷺ). This was said by Mujahid, Qatada and others.

Khalq (creation) in the verse means origination (ikhtira'). By His saying zawjahā He means Eve (Hawwa'). In Arabic usage, zawj means a man's wife, and it is also said zawja. From this is the verse of Abu Firas:

And indeed the one who strives to corrupt my wife is like one who runs to the lions of the thicket to take her from them.

As for His saying minhā (from it), Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Qatada said: God, Exalted is He, created Adam as a wild creature in the Garden alone. Then he slept, and God removed one of his short ribs from his left side, and it was also said from his right side, and from it He created Eve. This view is supported by the authentic hadith in which he (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, woman was created from a rib. If you try to straighten her you will break her, and breaking her is divorcing her." Some of them said: the meaning of minhā is "of her kind," and the word encompasses both meanings. Or it may be that her flesh and substance are from his rib, and her soul is of the same kind as his soul.

Baththa (He spread) means: he dispersed, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'a: 4], meaning: spread out. The restriction of their offspring to two kinds, men and women, implies that the hermaphrodite (khunthā) is not a kind. And even if we assume that his apparent state is ambiguous to us, he has a reality which returns him to one of these two kinds. The repetition of the command to fear God contains emphasis and an alert to the souls of those addressed.

Alladhi is in the accusative position as an epithet, and tasa'alūn means: you appeal to one another by Him, so one of you says: "I ask you by God to do such-and-such," and the like. A group said its meaning is: you ask for your rights by Him, and you make Him a means of claiming them. Its original form is tatasā'alūn, the second tā' was changed to sīn and assimilated into the sīn. This is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ibn 'Amr, according to one transmission from him. The rest read tasā'alūn with a light sīn, because they dropped the second tā' for ease. So this tā' of tatafā'alūn is assimilated in one dialect and dropped in another, due to the coming together of close letters. Abu 'Ali said: When close letters come together, they are lightened by deletion, assimilation and substitution, as they said ṭasṭ (basin), where they changed one of the two sīns into a tā', since the original form is ṭassun. Al-'Ajjaj said:

If she had appeared to a monk of Ayboli, shaggy-headed and in his cell, dressed in hair...

He yearned for her like the yearning of a basin...

Ibn Mas'ud said: tasalūn, lightly, without an alif. Wal-arḥāma (and the wombs) is in the accusative by coordination with the place of bihi (by Him), because its place is in the accusative. The more apparent view is that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, whose meaning is: and fear the wombs, lest you sever them. This is the reading of the seven readers except Hamza, and Ibn 'Abbas and others interpreted it accordingly. 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid read wal-arḥāmu with a nominative ending, as an inchoative (mubtada') with an implied predicate, meaning: and the wombs are deserving of being joined. Hamza and a group of scholars read wal-arḥāmi with a genitive ending, coordinated with the pronoun. Its meaning for them is: they are asked by, just as a man says: "I ask you by God and by the womb." This is how al-Hasan, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Mujahid explained it. This reading is not permitted according to the leading grammarians of Basra, because they do not allow a noun phrase to be coordinated with a pronoun in the genitive. Al-Zajjaj reported from al-Mazini: Because the coordinated and the thing coordinated upon are partners, each of which can occupy the position of the other, just as one cannot say "marartu bi-Zaydin wa-ka" (I passed by Zayd and you), so one cannot say "marartu bika wa-Zaydin" (I passed by you and Zayd). As for Sibawayh, it is in his view ugly and not permitted except in poetry, as he said:

Today you have been mocking us and insulting us, so go; what is with you and the days of wonder?

And as he said:

We hang our swords on pillars like these, and between them and the heel is a wide and uneven terrain.

Some grammarians considered it easy. Abu 'Ali said: That is weak according to analogy.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

A genitive pronoun is not separable, so it is like a letter within the word, and one does not coordinate on a letter. In my view, there are two meaning-based objections to this reading. The first is that mentioning "the wombs" among the things by which one asks has no meaning in urging the fear of God, and there is no benefit in it beyond informing that the wombs are asked by, and this is a dispersal of the meaning of the sentence and a diminishing of its eloquence. Eloquence lies in the mention of the wombs having an independent benefit. The second objection is that mentioning them in this way affirms asking by them and swearing by their sanctity, and the authentic hadith rejects that in his (peace be upon him) saying: "Whoever is swearing, let him swear by God or keep silent." Some said that wal-arḥāmi was put in the genitive by way of an oath from God by what He singled out for Himself, there is no god but He, from swearing by His creatures, and what is sworn to would be in what follows: "Indeed, God is ever Watchful over you." This is a statement which the structure and flow of the speech reject, even if the meaning allows it.

The kāna (was) in this verse is not only for limiting the past, but the meaning is: He was and He is. Raqib is the form of the active participle from raqaba, yarqubu, when one fixes one's gaze with the eye or with insight upon a matter in order to verify it as it is, and this is accompanied by protection, observation and knowledge of what results from the watching. In His saying "over you" there is a kind of warning, and He did not say "for you," to avoid the sharing that would arise from the idea that He watches for them what others do. From what we have mentioned, the one who watches the emergence of the arrow from the notch of the divider in the arrow-lots (qidah) is called raqib, because he watches for that. From this is the saying of Abu Dawud:

Like the seats of the watchmen for the clumps of... their hands are ready to strike.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 2–3:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not consume their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is a great sin.﴾ ﴿And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphan girls, then marry what seems good to you of women, two or three or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then only one, or what your right hands possess.﴾

Yatama (orphans): the plural of yatim (orphan boy) and yatima (orphan girl). In the speech of the Arabs, the yatim is one who has lost his father before reaching puberty. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no orphanhood after puberty." Among animals, it refers to the loss of the mother in the state of youth. It is also related that the yatim among humans is (defined) by way of the mother.

Ibn Zayd said: this address is for those whose custom among the Arabs was that the young child among the offspring does not inherit alongside the adult. So it was said to them: give them their property as inheritance, and do not, O adults, leave your shares, which are lawful and good, while taking the whole thing wrongfully and unlawfully, bad. Your doing that would then be a substitution. Another group said: this address is to the guardians of the orphans, and the meaning is: when they reach maturity and right judgment is perceived in them. He called them orphans though they had reached maturity, out of continuing the earlier state of orphanhood that had been established for them.

﴿"And do not substitute"﴾ It was said: what is meant is what some of them used to do, namely replacing a fat sheep from the orphan's property with a lean one from their own property, and a good dirham with a counterfeit one from their own property. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak. It was also said: what is meant is: do not consume their property, which is bad, and leave your property, which is good. And it was said: its meaning is: do not hasten to consume the bad from their property, and abandon waiting for lawful provision from Allah. This was said by Mujahid and Abu Salih. The bad and the good here are only in terms of what is permitted and what is forbidden.

It is related from Ibn Muhaysin that he recited "tabaddalu" with the assimilation of the taʾ into the taʾ. The joining of two sukuns was permissible in this, because one of them is a letter of prolongation and softness that resembles a vowel movement.

(p-464) As for His saying: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾, the orphans are equal in the prohibition against consuming "their property", whether they were heirs prevented from inheritance or under guardianship. The verse is explicit in targeting the property of the orphan for consumption and appropriation in all its forms. It is related from Mujahid that he said: the verse forbids mixing in expenditure, for the Arabs used to mix their expenses with the expenses of their orphans, so they were forbidden from that. Then the prohibition was abrogated (naskh) from it by His saying: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. This has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah. Ibn Furak said, from al-Hasan: people understood from this verse the prohibition of mixing, so they avoided it on their own account, and so it was lightened for them in the verse of al-Baqarah. Another group of later scholars said: "ila" (to) is in the sense of "ma'a" (with), but this is not a good view. It is related from Mujahid that the meaning of the verse is: do not consume their property with your property.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an approximation of the meaning, not that he intended that one particle has the meaning of the other.

The skilled scholars said:

"Ila" remains in its own sense, and it implies an addition. The estimated meaning: do not add their property to your property in consumption, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52], i.e., who will be added to Allah in my support?

The pronoun in "innahu" refers to the consumption implied by the explicit verb. "Hub" means sin. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and others. You say: "hab al-rajul yahubu hububan wa habaan" when he sinned. Umayya ibn al-Askar said:

"And indeed two emigrants who surrounded him, on that morning, they had erred and sinned."

al-Hasan recited "hawban" with a fatha on the ha', and this is the dialect of Banu Tamim. It was also said that with a fatha it is the verbal noun, and with a damma it is the noun. "Tahawwaba al-rajul" means when a man casts off sin from himself. Likewise "tahannatha", "ta'athtama" and "taharraja" are of this type, for these four are different from the whole "tafa''ala" pattern, since tafa''ala means entering into a thing, like "ta'abbada" and "takassaba" and what resembles them. Added to these four is "tafakkahuna" in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Had We willed, We would have made it crumbled debris, and you would have remained astonished﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65], i.e., you would cast off amusement from yourselves, as evidenced by His saying after that: ﴿Indeed, we are in debt﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 66] ﴿Rather, we are deprived﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 67], i.e., they say that. His saying "kabiran" (great) is explicit that consuming the property of an orphan is among the major sins.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphans﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "khiftum" here means "ayqantum" (you are certain), and he cited the verse of the poet:

"So I said to them: fear! with two thousand armored men..."

What he said is not correct; fear never means certainty in any respect. It is rather among the verbs of expectation, except that the assumption may incline toward one of the two sides. As for reaching the level of certainty, it does not. "Tuqsitu" means "ta'dilu" (you act justly). It is said: "aqsata al-rajul" when he acted justly, and "qasata" when he acted unjustly. Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i recited "alla taqsitu" with a fatha on the ta', from "qasata", on the assumption that "la" is extra, as if he said: and if you fear that you will act unjustly.

There is disagreement about the interpretation of the verse. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

It was revealed concerning the guardians of orphans who were impressed by the beauty of their female wards, and wished to underpay them in the bridal gift because of their guardianship over them. So it was said to them: act justly regarding their bridal gifts. Whoever fears that he will not act justly, let him marry what is good for him of other women who will bargain over their rights. Rabi'a also said this.

'Ikrima said: it was revealed concerning Quraysh, because a man among them would marry ten or more or fewer, and when his wealth ran short he would turn to the property of his orphan and marry from it. So it was said to them: if you fear that your means will fall short so that you act unjustly toward orphans, then restrict yourselves.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas said: the Arabs used to be scrupulous regarding the property of orphans, but were not scrupulous about justice among women. They used to marry ten or more, so the verse was revealed concerning that, meaning: just as you fear that you will not act justly with orphans, so be scrupulous regarding women, and marry within this limit which keeps injustice far away.

Mujahid said: the verse is only a warning against fornication and a deterrent from it, meaning: just as you are scrupulous regarding the property of orphans, so be scrupulous about fornication, and marry within what has been set for you. Al-Hasan, Abu Malik and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "ma taba" means "ma halla" (what is lawful).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because the forbidden women are many.

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "man taba" with reference to rational beings. Some people related that "ma" in this verse is temporal, meaning "as long as you find marriage agreeable."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this line of argument there is weakness. He said "ma" and not "man" because he did not intend to specify rational beings, but rather intended the category which is good in terms of what is lawful. It is as if he said: marry what is good. This command to marry is a recommendation for some people and a permission for others, according to the circumstances of the person. Marriage in general and for the most part is recommended. He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever among you is able to bear the expenses of marriage, let him marry."

As for "masna wa thulatha waruba'": their place in grammar is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "ma taba". They are indefinite nouns that are not declined because they are both derived from a different form (ma'dul) and adjectival. So said Abu 'Ali. Others said: they are derived in form and in meaning, and also they are derived and plural, and also they are derived and feminine. Al-Tabari said: they are definite because the definite article does not enter them. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view. They are derived from "two", "three" and "four", except that they imply the repetition of the number up to the limit of the counted thing. Al-Zajjaj cited a poet:

"But my family are in a valley whose companions are wolves, roaming among people, two by two and singly."

Its meaning is: two by two, and one by one. Likewise your saying: "the men came in twos and threes," its meaning is: two by two, and three by three.

Yahya ibn Wathhab and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited "wa rubaʿ" without the alif, and this is a dialect whose purpose is lightening, as the poet said, in the voice of the lizard:

"I do not desire to approach except for 'arad 'arid..."

"And silyan barid, and 'anakith multabid."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿But if you fear that you will not act justly, then only one, or what your right hands possess﴾. Al-Dahhak and others said:

The meaning: that you will not be equitable in inclination, love, intercourse and companionship among the four, the three, or the two. And on the view of the one who said that it was revealed concerning one who fears that he will spend the property of orphans on his marriages, the meaning would be: that you will not be just in marrying the four and the three, so that you spend on them the property of your orphans; that is, marry one with your own property, or take concubines from among them.

"Wahida" (one) is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: then marry one. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hurmuz and al-Hasan recited "fa-wahidatun" with a nominative, as an inchoative, and the predicate is estimated: then one is sufficient, or something similar. This reading is also reported from Abu 'Amr.

"What your right hands possess" means by it the slave-women. The meaning: if he fears that he will not act justly in the companionship of one, then what his right hand possesses. The ownership is ascribed to the right hand because it is a description of praise, and the right hand is specially characterized by good qualities for its firmness. Do you not see that it is the one that spends, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "until his left hand does not know what his right hand spends." It is also the one that makes covenants and pledges, and by it the oath was named "yamin." It is the one that receives the book of salvation and the banners of glory. The Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade using it for istinja' (cleansing after excretion) and commanded a person to eat with it.

Marriage in general and for the most part is recommended. He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever among you is able to bear the expenses of marriage, let him marry."

As for "masna wa thulatha waruba'": their place in grammar is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "ma taba". They are indefinite nouns that are not declined because they are both derived from a different form (ma'dul) and adjectival. So said Abu 'Ali. Others said: they are derived in form and in meaning, and also they are derived and plural, and also they are derived and feminine. Al-Tabari said: they are definite because the definite article does not enter them. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view. They are derived from "two", "three" and "four", except that they imply the repetition of the number up to the limit of the counted thing. Al-Zajjaj cited a poet:

"But my family are in a valley whose companions are wolves, roaming among people, two by two and singly."

Its meaning is: two by two, and one by one. Likewise your saying: "the men came in twos and threes," its meaning is: two by two, and three by three.

Yahya ibn Wathhab and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited "wa rubaʿ" without the alif, and this is a dialect whose purpose is lightening, as the poet said, in the voice of the lizard:

"I do not desire to approach except for 'arad 'arid..."

"And silyan barid, and 'anakith multabid."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿But if you fear that you will not act justly, then only one, or what your right hands possess﴾. Al-Dahhak and others said:

The meaning: that you will not be equitable in inclination, love, intercourse and companionship among the four, the three, or the two. And on the view of the one who said that it was revealed concerning one who fears that he will spend the property of orphans on his marriages, the meaning would be: that you will not be just in marrying the four and the three, so that you spend on them the property of your orphans; that is, marry one with your own property, or take concubines from among them.

"Wahida" (one) is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: then marry one. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hurmuz and al-Hasan recited "fa-wahidatun" with a nominative, as an inchoative, and the predicate is estimated: then one is sufficient, or something similar. This reading is also reported from Abu 'Amr.

"What your right hands possess" means by it the slave-women. The meaning: if he fears that he will not act justly in the companionship of one, then what his right hand possesses. The ownership is ascribed to the right hand because it is a description of praise, and the right hand is specially characterized by good qualities for its firmness. Do you not see that it is the one that spends, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "until his left hand does not know what his right hand spends." It is also the one that makes covenants and pledges, and by it the oath was named "yamin." It is the one that receives the book of salvation and the banners of glory. The Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade using it for istinja' (cleansing after excretion) and commanded a person to eat with it.

(p-468) His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿That is nearer to ensuring that you do not deviate from justice.﴾ [An-Nisa: 3] ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift. But if they willingly give you something of it, then consume it with enjoyment and satisfaction.﴾ ﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it, clothe them, and speak to them with kind words.﴾

"Adna" means "aqrab" (nearer), and it is derived from "dunuww." The place of "an" in i'rab (grammatical analysis) is in the accusative, with the preposition dropped. The governing element is the sense of the verb contained in "adna." The estimated reading is: "That is nearer to [ila] ensuring that you do not deviate." "Ta'ulu" means "tamilu" (you incline or deviate). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Abu Malik, al-Suddi, and others. It is said: "'ala al-rajulu ya'ulu" when he inclines and acts unjustly. From this is the verse of Abu Talib about the Prophet (ﷺ):

"With a scale of justice that does not cheat by a grain of barley, and a balance of truth whose weight does not deviate [ghayr 'a'il]."

He means "ghayr ma'il" (not inclining). From this is the saying of 'Uthman to the people of Kufa when he wrote to them: "I am not a scale that deviates (la a'ul)." The verse of Abu Talib is also narrated as: "For him is a witness from himself, not deviating [ghayr 'a'il]." "A'ala, yu'ilu" means "iftaqara" (became poor) and so became a dependent (ʿala). A group including Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn Zayd, and al-Shafi'i said that its meaning is: "That is nearer to ensuring that your dependents do not multiply." Ibn al-A'rabi related that the Arabs say: "'ala al-rajulu ya'ulu" when his dependents increase. Al-Zajjaj and others criticized this, arguing that Allah has permitted the multiplication of concubines, and that this entails an increase in dependents, so how could it be nearer to not multiplying?

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This criticism is not sound, because concubines are only property that may be disposed of by sale, whereas the heavy burden of dependents is the free wives, who have binding rights.

As for His words: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, and Ibn Jurayj said: the address in this verse is to the husbands, and Allah commanded them to voluntarily give the dowries to their wives as a gift from them. Abu Salih said: the address is to the guardians of the women, because it was a custom among some Arabs that a woman's guardian would consume her dowry; Allah removed this with Islam and commanded that it be given to them. Al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman said, on the authority of his father: "A Hadrami claimed that the verse refers to those who engage in shighar (exchange marriages), who would marry one woman in exchange for another, so they were commanded to give dowries." [p. 469]

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse encompasses all three of these groups.

Most of the people and the Seven readers read "sadaqatihinna" with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal. Musa ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Fayyad ibn Ghazwan, and others read "sudaqatihinna" with a damma on the sad and the dal. Qatada and others read "sudqatihinna" with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal. Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i read "sudqatahunna" in the singular, with a damma on the sad and a damma on the dal. The singular of all of these is "sadaqa" and "sudaqa." As for "nihla," its meaning is "nihlatan minkum lahunna," i.e., a gift (ʿaṭiyya). It was also said that the estimated reading is: "from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to them," because Allah made the dowry obligatory upon men and did not make anything obligatory upon women. It was also said that "nihla" means "shir'a" (a law), derived from "al-nahl," as one says: "fulan yantahilu din kadha" (so-and-so adopts the religion of such-and-such). This is appropriate if the address is to the guardians, and it is also acceptable if it is to others. Its accusative status, if it is from the husbands, is by implying a verb from its own root, the estimated reading being: "ankaluhunna nihlatan" (give them as a gift). It is permissible for the apparent verb to govern it even if it is not from the same root, because it is semantically appropriate to "nihla." Its accusative status, if it is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is by implying a verb from the same root, and nothing other than this is valid; and also if it is a law that is itself from Allah.

As for His words: ﴿But if they willingly give you something of it, then consume it with enjoyment and satisfaction.﴾ The address, as previously mentioned, is subject to the disagreement regarding the husbands and the guardians. The meaning is: if they give, not under compulsion, with their souls content. The pronoun in "minhu" refers to the dowry, and this is what 'Ikrima and others said; or it refers to the giving. Hadrami said: the reason for the verse is that some people were scrupulous about any portion of what they had paid to their wives returning to them. "Nafsan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). According to Sibawayh, it is not permissible for it to precede its governing element except in poetic necessity, with the governing element being inflected, while others permit it in ordinary speech. From this is the verse of the poet:

"... and she who was not content with the separation [nafsan]."

And "min" here implies the category, which is why it is permissible to give the entire dowry. If "min" were taken as partitive, that would not be permissible. It was read "haniyyan mariyyan" without hamza, which is the reading of al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and al-Zuhri. Al-Tabari said: "From the hana' of the camel is that it gives healing."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. Rather, the linguists said: "Food that is hani' is that which is palatable, praiseworthy, and whose outcome is good; and likewise mari'." The linguists say: "hana'ani al-ta'amu wa mara'ani" as a following construction (ittiba'), and when they use them separately they say: "amra'ani," on the pattern of "af'ala." Abu 'Ali [al-Farisi] said: this is like what came in the hadith: "Return, [women], burdened with sins, not rewarded." The waw in "mawzurat" was altered only by following the form of "majurat," so likewise "mara'ani" follows "hana'ani." A man entered upon 'Alqama while he was eating something that his wife had given him from her dowry, and he said to him: "Eat of the hani' mari'." Sibawayh said: "Haniyyan mariyyan" are two adjectives that they put in the accusative as masdars invoked by an unexpressed verb, which is omitted, the meaning being understood from the speech, as if they said: "that is established as haniyyan mariyyan."

As for His words: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property...﴾ the verse. The interpreters differed about the intended meaning of "al-sufaha' (the foolish)." Ibn Mas'ud, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, and others said: it was revealed concerning a man's young children and his wife. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed concerning those under guardianship who are foolish. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning women specifically. It is narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar that a woman with an ostentatious appearance passed by him, and he said to her: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property...﴾ the verse. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, al-Tabari, and others said: it was revealed concerning everyone who possesses the characteristic of foolishness that Allah stipulated, whoever they may be. The view of those who restricted it to women is weak in terms of the plural form, because the Arabs only pluralize "fa'ila" as "fa'a'il" or "fa'ilat."

As for His words: "amwalakum" (your property), it means the property of those addressed. This is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it means the property of the foolish, and it is attributed to those addressed to make them covet the property, meaning: it belongs to them when they are in need, like your property which protects your honor, preserves you, and elevates your status. From this is the similar verse: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [An-Nisa: 29] and what is similar to it.

[p. 471] Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i read "al-lati" (the ones which). "Al-amwal" is a plural for inanimate things, so the more correct reading is that of the majority.

"Qiyaman" is the plural of "qima," like "dima" and "diyam," but it is anomalous in returning to the ya', just as the saying "jiyad" as the plural of "jawad" is anomalous, and as the Banu Dabba said: "tawil" and "tiyal," and similar forms. "Qiwaman," "qiwaman," and "qiyaman" mean steadiness in a good state and continuance in that. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "qiyaman" without an alif. It is narrated that Abu 'Amr opened the qaf in "qawaman" and "qiyaman," which was originally "qiwaman," but the kasra of the qaf changed the waw into a ya' for harmony. Ibn Mujahid mentioned this without attributing it, and this is the reading of Abu 'Amr and al-Hasan. The rest read "qiyaman," and a group read "qiwaman."

As for His words: ﴿And provide for them from it, and clothe them﴾, it was said: its meaning is concerning those whose maintenance and clothing a man is obligated to provide, namely his wife and his young children. It was also said: it concerns those under guardianship with regard to their property. As for "ma'rufan" (kind), it was said: its meaning is to invoke for them: "May Allah bless you, protect you, and provide for you." It was also said: its meaning is to promise them a good promise, i.e., if you become mature, we will hand over your property to you. The meaning of the word is: every speech that people recognize, find comforting, and that the Sharia requires.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 6:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Then if you perceive in them sound judgment, release their property to them. And do not consume it extravagantly and hastily, [anticipating] that they will grow up. And whoever is wealthy - let him abstain; and whoever is poor - let him eat according to what is acceptable. And when you release their property to them, have witnesses over them; and sufficient is Allah as Reckoner.﴾

This is an address to all, and the meaning restricts the handling of this matter to the guardians (awsiya', sing. wasiyy). Al-ibtila' (testing) is al-ikhtibar (examination). "Balaghu al-nikah" (reach marriageable age) means they reach the stage of men, by wet dream and menstruation, or what is equivalent to it. Its meaning is: test their intellects, their discernment, and their conduct. "Anastum" (perceive) means you know, sense, and become aware, as the poet said:

؎ She perceived a sound, and the lances frightened her, at the time of afternoon, when evening had approached.

Ibn Mas'ud read "ahastum" with the ha' and a sukun on the sin, on the pattern of "fa'altum." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Abu al-Sammal, Ibn Mas'ud, and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "rashadan" with a fatha on the ra' and the shin, and the meaning is the same. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that both conditions must be met: maturity and tested sound judgment; and then the property is released. Abu Hanifa holds that the property may be released on the single condition [of maturity] so long as he has not kept any provision for him, just as the tasriyah (a form of sale) is permitted on a single condition; but the Book of Allah has restricted it by the absence of ability to marry and the fear of sin (al-'anat), and other examples, such as the oath and its breaking, after which expiation becomes obligatory, though it is permissible before breaking.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view, the comparison regarding releasing property by the events of the two conditions is not correct. That is because maturity is not placed by the verse in the context of a condition; rather, it is the state in which the intellects of the sons of Adam generally become complete. It is therefore the time when the condition of sound judgment is considered only in it. So He said: when that time arrives, let him look to the condition, which is sound judgment at that point. The eloquence of the speech indicates this, because the stipulation of maturity came with "idha" (when), while the conditional clause came with "in" (if), which is the basic conditional particle. And "idha" is not a conditional particle for the occurrence of what follows it. Sibawayh permitted that it be used as a conditional in poetry, and he said: they did that out of necessity; it was used conditionally because it requires an answer, and because a verb follows it, explicit or implicit. Al-Khalil argued against its being a conditional particle by the occurrence of what follows it: do you not see that you say, "I will come to you when the unripe dates turn red," and do not say, "if the unripe dates turn red"?

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: sound judgment (rushd) is in intellect and religion. Ibn 'Abbas said: rather, it is in intellect and managing property only, and this is the opinion of Ibn al-Qasim in our school. The other narration, that it is in intellect and religion, is attributed to Malik.

A group said: the guardian's release of property to the ward requires that he raise the matter to the ruler and that his sound judgment be established before him, or that he be one whom the judge trusts in such matters. Another group said: this is left to the guardian's own discretion, without needing to refer it to the ruler.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view regarding the guardians of our time is that the matter should not be deferred beyond referring it to the ruler and establishing sound judgment before him, because of what has been preserved of the collusion of guardians to declare the guardian sound of mind and the ward cleared, despite the ward's foolishness and poor management at that time.

As for His saying, "And do not consume it..." — the verse is a prohibition from Allah, Exalted, to the guardians against consuming the property of orphans beyond what is obligatory or permissible for them. Al-israf is excess in action, and al-saraf is error in the places of spending. From this is the poet's saying:

؎ ................. ∗∗∗.... ∗∗∗ there is in their giving neither reproach nor excess.

That is, they do not err in the places of giving. "Bidaran": its meaning is hastening their growing up, i.e., the guardian takes advantage of his ward's property, eating and saying, "I hasten his growing up, lest he become of sound judgment and take his property." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. "An yakbaru" is governed by "bidaran," and it is also possible that the sense is: for fear that. As for His saying, "And whoever is wealthy - let him abstain..." — it is said: 'affa a man from a thing and ista'affa, when he refrained. So He commanded the wealthy to refrain from the property of the orphan, and Allah permitted the poor guardian to eat from his orphan's property according to what is acceptable.

The scholars differed on the limit of what is acceptable. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ubayda, Ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, and Abu al-'Aliya said: that is a loan, that he borrows from his orphan's property and repays when he becomes well off, and he does not borrow more than his need.

Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did 'Ikrima, al-Suddi, and 'Ata': it is narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I have been placed in the position of the guardian of the orphan with respect to Allah's property: if I am wealthy, I abstain; if I am in need, I eat according to what is acceptable; and when I become well off, I repay."

It is narrated from Ibrahim, 'Ata', and others that there is no repayment obligation on the poor guardian for what he eats according to what is acceptable. Al-Hasan said: it is a sustenance from Allah for him, namely that he eat what sustains him, eating with the tips of the fingers, and not clothe himself from it in any way. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Makhul said: "He eats what sustains him, and clothes himself with what covers his nakedness, and does not wear linen or fine garments."

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Hasan, and al-Sha'bi said: "The guardian eats according to what is acceptable only when he drinks of the milk and eats of the fruit, to the extent that he soothes the mangy camels, smears the trough, harvests the fruit, and what is similar to that."

A group said: what is acceptable is that he should have a wage in proportion to his work and service.

Al-Hasan ibn Hayy said: if he is the guardian appointed by a father, then he may eat according to what is acceptable; but if he is the guardian appointed by a judge, then he has no claim whatsoever to the property.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Nakha'i said: the intended meaning is that the guardian eats according to what is acceptable from his own property, so that he does not need to take from the orphan's property.

Rabi'a ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman said: the intended meaning is orphans in both states, i.e., whoever among them is wealthy, let him be kept chaste by his own wealth, and whoever is poor, let him be provided for in moderation according to what is acceptable and with economy.

As for His saying, "And when you release..." — the verse is a command from Allah to caution and prudence. This is the basis for taking witnesses in all transfers, when withholding them at first is acceptable. A group said: taking witnesses here is obligatory; another group said: it is a recommendation to prudence. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn Jubayra narrated that this refers to the repayment of what a poor guardian borrows when he becomes well off, and the wording covers this and other things. "Al-Hasib" here means "al-muhsib," i.e., He is sufficient as a reckoner, so said al-Tabari; and the more evident view is that "hasiban" means reckoning your deeds and recompensing you for them. In this is a warning to everyone who denies a right.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 7–9:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and the near relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and the near relatives leave, whether it is little or much, a share ordained.﴾ ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives, orphans, and the needy, provide for them from it and speak to them kind words.﴾ ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them; so let them fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾

God, may He be exalted and glorified, called the father "wālid" (parent) because the child comes from him and from the mother, as the poet said:

﴿Where the crow hatches its eggs﴾ (a line of poetry)

because the egg comes from the female and the male.

Qatada, ʿIkrima and Ibn Zayd said: the occasion of this verse is that some of the Arabs did not give inheritance to women, saying: "None inherits except one who thrusts with the spear and fights with the sword." So this verse was revealed.

ʿIkrima said: its occasion was the report of Umm Kahla. Her husband, Aws ibn Suwayd, died and left her a daughter. The paternal uncle of his sons went about to deprive her of inheritance. She went to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the uncle said: "O Messenger of Allah, she does not fight, does not bear burdens, and gains are made through her while she earns nothing." The name of the uncle, as he mentioned, was Thaʿlaba.

As for "a share ordained" (naṣīban mafrūḍan), it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl). So said Makki, but it is in fact a noun put in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) is put in the accusative in the position of a circumstantial. Its sense is "obligatory" (farḍan). That is why its accusative is permissible. As you say: "For you upon me is such-and-such, a binding right (ḥaqqan wājiban)." Were it not for the sense of the verbal noun contained in it, this accusative would not be permissible for a noun that is not a verbal noun, and its proper case would have been the nominative.

As for His saying: ﴿And when the division is attended...﴾ — the verse. The commentators differed about who is addressed by this verse, on two views. One is that it is addressed to the heirs, and the meaning is: when those three categories attend the division of the estate of your deceased, provide for them from it. Then those who held this view differed. Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Malik, al-Ḍaḥḥak and Ibn ʿAbbas, as related from him by al-Mahdawi, said: this was abrogated by the verses of inheritance. This was a division before the inheritance laws; then God gave each entitled person his right after that, and the bequest was made for those who are not heirs. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shaʿbi, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: it is muḥkam (established) and was not abrogated.

Ibn Jubayr said: "People have neglected this verse." Al-Ḥasan said: "But people are stingy." A group of the Successors (tābiʿūn), ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr and others, acted upon it, and Abu Musa al-Ashʿari commanded it.

Those who held that it is established (muḥkam) differed. One group said: it is an obligation (farḍ and wujūb) that the heirs give these categories what is reasonable and what their souls are content with, such as household utensils, a worn garment, and what is light like the chest (tābūt), and what cannot be divided. Ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan said: it is recommended (nadb), so whoever leaves it there is no blame upon him. This view was disputed concerning the case where the heir is a minor who does not manage his own property. Saʿid ibn Jubayr and others said: this is only in the way of kindness (maʿrūf), spoken by the guardian of the heir, not a gift that is executed; another group said: rather, the guardian of the minor heir gives from the property of his ward as much as he sees fit.

The second view concerning who is addressed: the address is to the dying persons who divide their wealth by bequest. The meaning: when death attends you, O believers, and you divide your wealth by bequest, and there attend you those who do not inherit from the near relatives and orphans, provide for them from it. Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Zayd said: they used to say to the executor (waṣī): "So-and-so is dividing his property." The meaning of "attend" (ḥaḍara) is "witness," except that the description of weakness, orphanhood and need indicates that this is the reason for provision, so wherever these qualities are found they are provided for, even if they did not attend the division.

"Ūlū" is a plural noun with no singular from its own form, and it is never used except in construct, because of the indefiniteness within it; its singular sometimes occurs without the word "dhū."

Yutm means solitude, and yatīm means a single one; thus whoever loses his father is called yatīm for being alone. ʿUbayda and Muhammad ibn Sirin held that the provision in this verse means that food is prepared for them to eat, and they did so: they slaughtered a sheep from the estate.

The pronoun in His saying "fa-arzuqūhum" (provide for them) and in "lahum" (to them) refers to the three categories. Other than that, distinguishing the two pronouns' referents, as al-Ṭabarī maintained, is arbitrary. "Qawl maʿrūf" (kind speech) is everything by which one is comforted, whether supplication, a promise, or other than that.

His saying "wa-l-yakhsha" is in the jussive by the imperative lām. According to Sibawayh it is not permissible to omit this lām analogically to the prepositions except in poetic necessity, and from it the poet's saying:

﴿Muhammad, let yourself be ransomed by every soul, if you fear any calamity⦆ (a line of poetry)

Abu Ḥaywa, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and al-Ḥasan and al-Zuhri read the imperative lāms in this verse with kasra.

The discussion of the word "dhurriyyatan" has already passed in Surat Āl ʿImrān. The object of "yakhsha" is omitted, as the context indicates it, and its omission is good because the fear may be understood as fear of God, and fear of the consequence in this world, so each interpreter looks according to what is more important to him.

Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥman, Abu Ḥaywa, al-Zuhri, Ibn Muḥayṣin and ʿĀʾisha read "ḍuʿafāʾ" with madd and damm of the ḍād, and it is related from Ibn Muḥayṣin "ḍuʿufan" with damm of the ḍād and ʿayn and tanwīn of the fāʾ. Ḥamza inclined "ḍiʿāfan," and inclined "khāfū." The reason for the inclination of "khāfū" is the kasra in the past tense "khiftu," so that it indicates it. "Khāfū" is the answer of "law" (if); its estimated form is: "if they had left, they would have feared." It is permissible to omit the lām in the answer of "law," as you say: "law qāma Zayd qāma ʿAmr" and "law qāma Zayd qāma ʿAmr."

It has been disputed: who is meant by this verse? Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḍaḥḥak and Mujahid said: it means whoever attends a dying person when he makes his bequest, and says to him: "Advance for yourself, and give to so-and-so and so-and-so," harming the heirs by it. So it is as if the verse says to them: just as you feared for your heirs and offspring after you, so fear for the heirs of others and their offspring, and do not drive him to squander his property and leave them destitute. Miqsam and Ḥaḍramī said: it was revealed about the opposite of that, namely that one says to the dying: "Hold back for your heirs, and leave for your child," and forbids him from bequest, so that he harms thereby the near relatives and everyone who deserves to be bequeathed to. It was said to them: just as you feared for your offspring and were pleased that they be well treated, so likewise speak rightly concerning the needy and orphans, and fear God regarding their harm.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

These two views do not apply uniformly to all people; rather, people are of two kinds: one of the two statements suits one kind, and the second statement suits the other. For when a man leaves heirs who are independent and wealthy, it is good that he be encouraged to make a bequest and be inclined to advance for himself. When he leaves weak and poor heirs, it is good that he be encouraged to leave for them and to take precaution, for his reward in intending that is like his reward for the needy. The consideration is indeed weakness, so one must incline with it.

Ibn ʿAbbas also said: the verse refers to the guardians of orphans. The meaning: treat them well, speak rightly to them, and fear God regarding the consumption of their property, just as you fear that your offspring be treated otherwise.

Another group said: rather, the verse refers to all people. The meaning: He commanded them to fear God regarding orphans and the children of others even if they are not in their care, and to speak rightly to them, as each person wishes to be done to his child after him.

From this is what al-Shaybani related, who said: "We were at Constantinople in the army of Maslama ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. One day we sat in a company of people of knowledge, among them al-Daylami. They discussed the terrors of the last age. I said to him: 'O Abu Busr, I wish I had no child.' He said to me: 'What is the matter with you? No soul that God has decreed to come forth from a man comes forth except that it comes forth, loved or hated. But if you want to be safe regarding them, then fear God regarding others'," and then he recited this verse.

Al-sadīd (rightly/appropriate) means: that which hits the truth. From it is the poet's saying:

﴿I teach him archery every day, but when his arm grew firm, he shot me﴾ (a line of poetry)

Its meaning: when he matched the targets at which he aims.

Abu Ḥaywa, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and al-Ḥasan and al-Zuhri read the imperative lāms in this verse with kasra.

The discussion of the word "dhurriyyatan" has already passed in Surat Āl ʿImrān. The object of "yakhsha" is omitted, as the context indicates it, and its omission is good because the fear may be understood as fear of God, and fear of the consequence in this world, so each interpreter looks according to what is more important to him.

Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥman, Abu Ḥaywa, al-Zuhri, Ibn Muḥayṣin and ʿĀʾisha read "ḍuʿafāʾ" with madd and damm of the ḍād, and it is related from Ibn Muḥayṣin "ḍuʿufan" with damm of the ḍād and ʿayn and tanwīn of the fāʾ. Ḥamza inclined "ḍiʿāfan," and inclined "khāfū." The reason for the inclination of "khāfū" is the kasra in the past tense "khiftu," so that it indicates it. "Khāfū" is the answer of "law" (if); its estimated form is: "if they had left, they would have feared." It is permissible to omit the lām in the answer of "law," as you say: "law qāma Zayd qāma ʿAmr" and "law qāma Zayd qāma ʿAmr."

It has been disputed: who is meant by this verse? Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḍaḥḥak and Mujahid said: it means whoever attends a dying person when he makes his bequest, and says to him: "Advance for yourself, and give to so-and-so and so-and-so," harming the heirs by it. So it is as if the verse says to them: just as you feared for your heirs and offspring after you, so fear for the heirs of others and their offspring, and do not drive him to squander his property and leave them destitute. Miqsam and Ḥaḍramī said: it was revealed about the opposite of that, namely that one says to the dying: "Hold back for your heirs, and leave for your child," and forbids him from bequest, so that he harms thereby the near relatives and everyone who deserves to be bequeathed to. It was said to them: just as you feared for your offspring and were pleased that they be well treated, so likewise speak rightly concerning the needy and orphans, and fear God regarding their harm.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

These two views do not apply uniformly to all people; rather, people are of two kinds: one of the two statements suits one kind, and the second statement suits the other. For when a man leaves heirs who are independent and wealthy, it is good that he be encouraged to make a bequest and be inclined to advance for himself. When he leaves weak and poor heirs, it is good that he be encouraged to leave for them and to take precaution, for his reward in intending that is like his reward for the needy. The consideration is indeed weakness, so one must incline with it.

Ibn ʿAbbas also said: the verse refers to the guardians of orphans. The meaning: treat them well, speak rightly to them, and fear God regarding the consumption of their property, just as you fear that your offspring be treated otherwise.

Another group said: rather, the verse refers to all people. The meaning: He commanded them to fear God regarding orphans and the children of others even if they are not in their care, and to speak rightly to them, as each person wishes to be done to his child after him.

From this is what al-Shaybani related, who said: "We were at Constantinople in the army of Maslama ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. One day we sat in a company of people of knowledge, among them al-Daylami. They discussed the terrors of the last age. I said to him: 'O Abu Busr, I wish I had no child.' He said to me: 'What is the matter with you? No soul that God has decreed to come forth from a man comes forth except that it comes forth, loved or hated. But if you want to be safe regarding them, then fear God regarding others'," and then he recited this verse.

Al-sadīd (rightly/appropriate) means: that which hits the truth. From it is the poet's saying:

﴿I teach him archery every day, but when his arm grew firm, he shot me﴾ (a line of poetry)

Its meaning: when he matched the targets at which he aims.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 10–11 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:
﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will [soon] enter a Blaze.﴾ ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females. And if there are [only] daughters, two or more, for them is two thirds of what he has left.﴾

Ibn Zayd said: It was revealed concerning the disbelievers who would not give inheritance to women and children, and would consume their property. Most people said: It was revealed concerning the guardians who consume what is not permitted to them from the property of the orphan. It encompasses every consumer, even if he is not a guardian. The taker of property in all its forms is called a "consumer," since the aim is consumption, and most destruction of things comes through it. In its wording "into their bellies" there is an eloquence that exposes their deficiency and censures them with the opposite of noble character: the greed caused by the belly, which is the lowest and basest of causes, so that they fall under the threat of the Fire.

And "unjustly" means: exceeding what is customary, while the guardian is poor. Some people said: the meaning is that since their consuming of property ultimately leads to their entering the Fire, they are called "consuming fire." Another group said: rather, it is literal, that they will be fed fire, and there are hadiths on this. Among them is the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Prophet ﷺ narrated to us about the night he was taken on the Night Journey, saying: "I saw people who had lips like the lips of camels, and an angel had been assigned to them who would take hold of their lips, then place in their mouths stones of fire which would come out from their lower parts. I said: O Jibril, who are these? He said: They are those who consume the property of orphans unjustly."

The majority of readers read "wa-sa-yaṣlawna" with the verb attributed to them. Ibn 'Amir read it with a dammah on the yā', and there is a difference from 'Asim. Abu Haywa read "wa-sa-yuṣallūna" with the verb in the passive, with a dammah on the yā' and the lām, a fatḥah on the ṣād, and a shaddah on the lām for intensification. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-sa-yuṣlūna" with a dammah on the yā' and the lām, and this is weak. The first is more correct, because it is so in the Qur'an in His saying: ﴿He who denied and turned away﴾ [al-Layl: 16], and in His saying: ﴿the burning of Hellfire﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 163]. Ṣalā (to be scorched) means being heated by nearness to a fire or by direct contact with it, and from it is the saying of al-Harith ibn 'Abbad:

"I was not among its [the war's] instigators, God knows, yet I am today scorched by its heat."

One who is burned up by the burning does not remain scorched except at the beginning of his affair, whereas the people of Hell are not consumed; they remain in it burning. And saʻīr means the kindled blazing embers.

This is one of the verses of threat. What the people of the Sunnah believe is that this is enforced upon some of the disobedient, lest the report contradict its reporter, and it is dropped by the Will for some of them. The summary of the discussion on this question: the promise is concerning good, and the threat concerning evil; this is their customary usage when they are mentioned without qualification. The promise may also be used for evil when qualified by it, as He, exalted, said: ﴿The Fire—Allah has promised it to those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 72]. The Mu'tazilah said: all verses of promise are concerning the repentant and the obedient, and verses of threat concerning polytheists and those disobedient through major sins, and some of them said: and minor sins. The Murji'ah said: all verses of promise concern whoever is characterized by faith, which is affirmation, whether he be a sinner or an obedient one. We, the People of the Sunnah and the Community, say: verses of promise concern the believing obedient ones and whoever the Will encompasses among the disobedient, and verses of threat concern the polytheists and whoever enforcement encompasses among the disobedient. The verse that decides in accordance with what we have said is His saying, exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. If the Mu'tazilah say: "for whom He wills" means the repentant, it is answered that the benefit of the distinction would be nullified, since polytheism too is forgiven for the one who repents; and this is decisive by the ruling of His saying "for whom He wills" that there are those forgiven and those not forgiven. The Sunni position is thereby established.

His saying, exalted: "Allah instructs you" (yūṣīkum) includes obligation and necessity, as the word "commanded" (amara) does in all its inflections. As for the form of command apart from this word, there is the difference that will come in its proper place, if Allah wills. Similar to this verse is His saying, exalted: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. That is what He has enjoined upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 151].

It has been said: this verse was revealed concerning the daughters of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi'. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the daughters of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Thabit, brother of Hassan ibn Thabit. And it has been said: concerning Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited him during his illness. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: and he mentioned that the people of the Jahiliyyah would not give inheritance except to one who fought wars and fought the enemy, so the verses were revealed clarifying that every female and child has their share. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the reason for the revelation of this was that property belonged to the child and the bequest to the parents, so this was abrogated (nusikha) by these verses.

"Mithl" (equal to) is in the nominative by being the subject or by being an attribute; its estimated form is: a share equal to the share of. Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla read: "fī awlādikum anna lil-dhakar."

His saying, exalted: ﴿And if there are [only] daughters...﴾ The verse. "Awlad" (children) is a word that comprises males and females. When this verse intended to single out females by mentioning their ruling, it made the verb feminine according to the meaning. Had it followed the wording of "awlad," it would have said "kānū." The subject of "kāna" is a pronoun. Some grammarians of Basra said: its estimated form is: "and if the ones left behind are women."

His saying: "fawqa ithnatayn" means: two and what is above them, the strength of the speech requires this. As for holding to the wording, the text concerning the two would fall away with it, and the two-thirds would be established for them by the consensus which the regions and the eras have agreed upon, and no dissent has been preserved concerning it, except what is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas that he holds that they receive half. It is also established for them by analogy with the two sisters, who are specified in the text, and it is established for them by the hadith which al-Tirmidhi mentioned: "that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ruled for the two daughters with two-thirds." Whoever says "fawqa" is superfluous and argues with His saying: "fawqa al-a'nāq" (above the necks), meaning: strike from them the necks, his statement is an error, because adverbs and all nouns may be used in the speech of the Arabs without meaning. And because His saying "fawqa al-a'nāq" is the eloquent form; and "fawqa" is not superfluous but has a firm meaning, since the striking of the neck must be above the bones at the joint, not at the brain, as Durayd ibn al-Simma said: "Lower [the blow] away from the brain and raise it above the bone; thus I used to strike the necks of heroes."

Their taking two-thirds has been argued for by other than this, and all of it is contested. Isma'il al-Qadi said: if the daughter takes a third together with her brother when he stands alone, then it is more fitting that she take that together with her sister. Another said: just as the ruling for two or more of the uterine siblings is one (a single third), so too for daughters.

Al-Nahhas said: the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad is: "al-thuluth" and "al-rubu'" up to "al-'ushr," and al-Hasan read all of these with the middle letter sukun, and al-A'raj read it so. The view of al-Zajjaj is that it is one dialect, and that the sukun of the 'ayn is a lightening.

If the daughters of the loins take two-thirds, nothing remains after that for the daughters of a son, unless there is a brother for them or a son of a brother, in which case it is returned to them. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud does not hold that they receive anything even if there is a brother or a son of a brother, and he holds that the whole estate belongs to the male alone, to the exclusion of them.

**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And if [the deceased] was a woman with no children and has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if there are more than two, they share a third.﴾

The seven readers other than Nafi' read "wāḥidatan" in the accusative as the predicate of "kāna"; Nafi' read "wāḥidatun" in the nominative, taking "kāna" in the sense of "occurred" and "was present." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "al-nuṣf" with a dammah on the nūn, and so did 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Zayd ibn Thabit throughout the Qur'an.

His saying: "walad" (child) means a male or a female, one or a group, of the loins or of a son who is male. Whenever that occurs, it makes the father's share a sixth, and even if he takes a half in his inheritance, he takes it by way of 'asabah (residuary).

His saying, exalted: ﴿But if there is no child for him...﴾ The verse. The meaning: if he has no child, nor a child's child, male or female. His saying: ﴿and his parents inherit him﴾ requires by the strength of the speech that the two of them stand alone apart from all the sharers, whether child or other. On this basis, his saying "and his parents inherit him" is a ruling granting them the estate; when after that the share of one of them is mentioned alone, the other takes the other share, just as you say to two men: "This property is between you two," then you say to one of them: "You, so-and-so, have a third of it," so you have specified for the other two-thirds by the text of your speech.

And on the basis that their share is free of child and others, comes the statement of most people: that the mother, when alone, takes a third of the whole estate; if a spouse is with them, the mother takes a sixth, which is a third in relation to the father. And on the basis that the share is free of child only, comes the statement of Shurayh and Ibn 'Abbas: that when the share is free of a child, the mother takes a third of the whole estate together with the spouse, and what remains is for the father. And on this basis is His saying: "and his parents inherit him," alone or together with others.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "fa-li-immihi" with a kasrah on the hamzah, a dialect related by Sibawayh; likewise they made the hamzah kasrah in His saying: ﴿in the wombs of your mothers﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], "wa-fī immihā" and "fī umm al-kitāb" (in the Mother of the Book). All this is when they connect (in recitation), following the kasrah or the yā' that precedes the hamzah. The rest read all of this with a dammah on the hamzah. Hamza kasrahed the mīm of "immahātikum," following the kasrah of the hamzah. Whenever there is no connection and no yā' or kasrah, the dammah is by agreement.

His saying, exalted: ﴿But if he has brothers, then for his mother is a sixth﴾. The brothers reduce the mother to a sixth and do not take it themselves, whether they are full brothers, paternal, or maternal. Someone whose view is not counted except as an anomaly said: they reduce her and take what they reduce for themselves together with the father; this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and there is narrated from him the opposite of the view of the sixth, which they block the mother from. Qatadah said: the father took it to the exclusion of them, because he maintains them, takes charge of their marriage, and bears their expenses; this is in the majority of cases. And they are unanimous that two brothers or more block the mother from it, except what is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: that two brothers are in the ruling of one, and the mother is not blocked except by three. All of them argue that the least plural is two, because duality is the joining of a thing to its like, so the meaning requires that it be a plural. The exegetes mentioned that the Arabs may use the plural form while meaning the dual, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And [mention] David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field, when the sheep of the people pastured in it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78], and as in His saying about the litigants: ﴿when they climbed over the wall of the prayer chamber﴾ [Sad: 21], ﴿when they entered﴾ [al-Hijr: 52], and as in His saying: "and the extremities of the day." They argued by all of this that the word "brothers" includes two brothers.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These verses offer no proof, in my view, for this position, because in each of them the meaning has been made clear by the text itself that the intended number is two. That permits a figurative usage, so that the plural form is used afterwards: in the first verse there is "yahkumani" (the two of them judge), and in the second "inna hadha akhi" (indeed this is my brother). Moreover, judgment may be attributed to the judge and the litigants, and others may join the litigant, so they become a group. As for "al-nahar" (the day) in the third verse, the alif and lam in it are for the genus (li-l-jins), so what is meant is the two ends of each day. When the plural form occurs and nothing accompanies it that clarifies the intended meaning, it is taken as plural and is not taken as dual, because the word governs the meaning and the morphological form has its own right. Some of those who argued for the view of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas mentioned that the dual form indicates the genus and the number just as the singular form does, while the plural form indicates the genus but does not indicate the number; therefore it is not correct for this to be applied to that.

Ibn 'Amir... [note: the reading list follows] Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yuwassa" (p-484) with a fathah on the sad and with shaddah, and this applies in both places. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fathah in the first place and with a kasrah in the second.

This verse was intended only to place these two actions before the inheritance, and it was not intended to fix their order relative to one another. For this reason the bequest was mentioned first in wording, while the debt takes precedence over the bequest by consensus. What I say on this is that he put the bequest first because it is less binding than the debt, out of concern for it and as an encouragement toward it, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It leaves out nothing, small or great﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. Also, he put it first because it includes the bequest, which is like something necessary for every deceased person, since the Law has urged it. He delayed the debt because of its rarity, since it may occur or may not occur, so he began with what is unavoidable and then joined with it what may happen at times. This is reinforced by the fact that the conjunction is "aw" (or); had the debt been a regular matter, the conjunction would have been "wa" (and). The bequest was also put first because it is the portion of the needy and the weak, while the debt was delayed because it is the portion of a creditor who demands it forcefully, and he has a right in it, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, the one who holds a right has a right to speak." The scholars agreed that no one may bequeath more than one-third, and many of them recommended that it not reach one-third, and that people reduce it to one-quarter.
