**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And if [the deceased] was a woman with no children and has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if there are more than two, they share a third.﴾

The seven readers other than Nafi' read "wāḥidatan" in the accusative as the predicate of "kāna"; Nafi' read "wāḥidatun" in the nominative, taking "kāna" in the sense of "occurred" and "was present." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "al-nuṣf" with a dammah on the nūn, and so did 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Zayd ibn Thabit throughout the Qur'an.

His saying: "walad" (child) means a male or a female, one or a group, of the loins or of a son who is male. Whenever that occurs, it makes the father's share a sixth, and even if he takes a half in his inheritance, he takes it by way of 'asabah (residuary).

His saying, exalted: ﴿But if there is no child for him...﴾ The verse. The meaning: if he has no child, nor a child's child, male or female. His saying: ﴿and his parents inherit him﴾ requires by the strength of the speech that the two of them stand alone apart from all the sharers, whether child or other. On this basis, his saying "and his parents inherit him" is a ruling granting them the estate; when after that the share of one of them is mentioned alone, the other takes the other share, just as you say to two men: "This property is between you two," then you say to one of them: "You, so-and-so, have a third of it," so you have specified for the other two-thirds by the text of your speech.

And on the basis that their share is free of child and others, comes the statement of most people: that the mother, when alone, takes a third of the whole estate; if a spouse is with them, the mother takes a sixth, which is a third in relation to the father. And on the basis that the share is free of child only, comes the statement of Shurayh and Ibn 'Abbas: that when the share is free of a child, the mother takes a third of the whole estate together with the spouse, and what remains is for the father. And on this basis is His saying: "and his parents inherit him," alone or together with others.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "fa-li-immihi" with a kasrah on the hamzah, a dialect related by Sibawayh; likewise they made the hamzah kasrah in His saying: ﴿in the wombs of your mothers﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], "wa-fī immihā" and "fī umm al-kitāb" (in the Mother of the Book). All this is when they connect (in recitation), following the kasrah or the yā' that precedes the hamzah. The rest read all of this with a dammah on the hamzah. Hamza kasrahed the mīm of "immahātikum," following the kasrah of the hamzah. Whenever there is no connection and no yā' or kasrah, the dammah is by agreement.

His saying, exalted: ﴿But if he has brothers, then for his mother is a sixth﴾. The brothers reduce the mother to a sixth and do not take it themselves, whether they are full brothers, paternal, or maternal. Someone whose view is not counted except as an anomaly said: they reduce her and take what they reduce for themselves together with the father; this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and there is narrated from him the opposite of the view of the sixth, which they block the mother from. Qatadah said: the father took it to the exclusion of them, because he maintains them, takes charge of their marriage, and bears their expenses; this is in the majority of cases. And they are unanimous that two brothers or more block the mother from it, except what is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: that two brothers are in the ruling of one, and the mother is not blocked except by three. All of them argue that the least plural is two, because duality is the joining of a thing to its like, so the meaning requires that it be a plural. The exegetes mentioned that the Arabs may use the plural form while meaning the dual, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And [mention] David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field, when the sheep of the people pastured in it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78], and as in His saying about the litigants: ﴿when they climbed over the wall of the prayer chamber﴾ [Sad: 21], ﴿when they entered﴾ [al-Hijr: 52], and as in His saying: "and the extremities of the day." They argued by all of this that the word "brothers" includes two brothers.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These verses offer no proof, in my view, for this position, because in each of them the meaning has been made clear by the text itself that the intended number is two. That permits a figurative usage, so that the plural form is used afterwards: in the first verse there is "yahkumani" (the two of them judge), and in the second "inna hadha akhi" (indeed this is my brother). Moreover, judgment may be attributed to the judge and the litigants, and others may join the litigant, so they become a group. As for "al-nahar" (the day) in the third verse, the alif and lam in it are for the genus (li-l-jins), so what is meant is the two ends of each day. When the plural form occurs and nothing accompanies it that clarifies the intended meaning, it is taken as plural and is not taken as dual, because the word governs the meaning and the morphological form has its own right. Some of those who argued for the view of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas mentioned that the dual form indicates the genus and the number just as the singular form does, while the plural form indicates the genus but does not indicate the number; therefore it is not correct for this to be applied to that.

Ibn 'Amir... [note: the reading list follows] Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yuwassa" (p-484) with a fathah on the sad and with shaddah, and this applies in both places. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fathah in the first place and with a kasrah in the second.

This verse was intended only to place these two actions before the inheritance, and it was not intended to fix their order relative to one another. For this reason the bequest was mentioned first in wording, while the debt takes precedence over the bequest by consensus. What I say on this is that he put the bequest first because it is less binding than the debt, out of concern for it and as an encouragement toward it, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It leaves out nothing, small or great﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. Also, he put it first because it includes the bequest, which is like something necessary for every deceased person, since the Law has urged it. He delayed the debt because of its rarity, since it may occur or may not occur, so he began with what is unavoidable and then joined with it what may happen at times. This is reinforced by the fact that the conjunction is "aw" (or); had the debt been a regular matter, the conjunction would have been "wa" (and). The bequest was also put first because it is the portion of the needy and the weak, while the debt was delayed because it is the portion of a creditor who demands it forcefully, and he has a right in it, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, the one who holds a right has a right to speak." The scholars agreed that no one may bequeath more than one-third, and many of them recommended that it not reach one-third, and that people reduce it to one-quarter.

"Ābāʾukum wa-abnāʾukum lā tadrūna ayyuhum aqrabu lakum nafʿan farīḍatan mina Llāh inna Llāha kāna ʿalīman ḥakīman" (Qur'an 4:11) and "Wa-lakum niṣfu mā taraka azwājukum in lam yakun lahunna waladun fa-in kāna lahunna waladun fa-lakumu l-rubʿu mimmā taraknā min baʿdi waṣiyyatin yūṣīna bihā aw dayn" (4:12).

"Ābāʾukum wa-abnāʾukum" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtadaʾ, "the subject of a nominal sentence"), and its predicate (khabar) is implied. Its estimated sense is: "they are those among whom it is divided and those who are given." This is a presentation of the wisdom behind it, and a reassurance to the Arabs who used to distribute inheritance on a different basis. "Lā tadrūna" functions as a governing verb in meaning for the clause, and is suspended from acting on the wording because of the interrogative that follows, since an interrogative is not governed by what precedes it (ʿāmil muʿallaq). As for "nafʿan" (benefit), Mujāhid, al-Suddī and Ibn Sīrīn said: its meaning is "in this world," i.e., when one is compelled to spend on them out of need; al-Zajjāj inclined to this view, though people may also spend without compulsion. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan said: "in the Hereafter," i.e., through the intercession of the superior for the inferior. Ibn Zayd said: it applies to both; and the wording allows this.

"Farīḍatan" is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar muʾakkad), since the sense of "yūṣīkum" is "yafriḍu ʿalaykum" (prescribes for you). Makkī and others said it is an emphatic circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), but this is weak. The governing verb is "yūṣīkum." "Kāna" is the defective (nāqiṣa) verb. Sībawayh said: when they saw knowledge and wisdom, it was said to them: God has always been thus. The form "kāna" conveys only past time, and from the meaning there is a remoteness that is understood to mean that God, exalted is He, was so, and He still is; this is not derived from the wording of the verse. Some said "kāna" means "found" or "occurred," and "ʿalīman" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); but this is weak. Whoever says "kāna" is superfluous (zāʾida) has spoken erroneously.

As for the Most High's words: "Wa-lakum niṣfu mā taraka azwājukum" ... the verse: the address is to men, and "walad" here means the children of the loins and the sons of their male descendants, however far down they go, males and females, one or more; this is by consensus of the scholars.

Qur'an 4:12 continues: "Wa-lahunna l-rubʿu mimmā taraktum in lam yakun lakum waladun fa-in kāna lakum waladun fa-lahunna l-thumunu mimmā taraktum min baʿdi waṣiyyatin tūṣūna bihā aw dayn. Wa-in kāna rajulun yūrathu kalālatan aw imraʾatun wa-lahu akhun aw ukhtun fa-li-kulli wāḥidin minhumā l-sudusu fa-in kānū akthara min dhālika fa-hum shurakāʾu fī l-thuluth."

The word "walad" in this verse has the same meaning as in the preceding verse. "Al-thumun" (the eighth) is for the wife or wives, among whom they share by consensus; and "al-ʿawl" (proportional reduction) applies to the shares of husband and wife just as it applies to all the other fixed shares. Only Ibn ʿAbbās differed: he said they receive their share without ʿawl.

"Al-kalāla" is derived from "takallala al-nasab," meaning it surrounded: because when a man leaves neither parent nor child, his two sides are cut off, and what remains is that he is inherited by those whose kinship encircles him, i.e., surrounds him on all sides like a crown (iklīl), and like a plant when it surrounds a thing. From this comes "rawḍun mukallalun bi-l-zahr" (a meadow crowned with flowers). "Al-iklīl" is also a lunar mansion surrounded by stars. From "al-kalāla" is the verse of the poet:

"Fa-inna abā l-marʾi aḥmā lahu / wa-mawlā l-kalāla lā yaghḍabu"
(Indeed a man's father is more protective of him, and the kinsman of the kalāla does not become angry.)

Thus the father and the son are the two pillars of lineage, and the rest of the relatives are the surrounding (mukallilūn). Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ibn ʿAbbās, Salīm ibn ʿUbayd, Qatāda, al-Ḥakam, Ibn Zayd, al-Zuhrī and Abū Isḥāq al-Subayʿī said: "al-kalāla" is the deceased's lacking of a child and a parent; and this is the correct view. Another group said it is the deceased's lacking of a child only; this was narrated from Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq and ʿUmar, then they both retracted it, and it was also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās. This is inferred from his words concerning siblings alongside the parents: that they reduce the mother's share and take what the mother loses.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is how al-Ṭabarī related it. It follows from Ibn ʿAbbās's view, when he gave them inheritance, that the Qur'an's specification that the heirs are "kalāla" means that he gives them the third by explicit text. Another group, including al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUtayba, said: "al-kalāla" is the lacking of a parent. These two views are weak, because whoever has a living parent or child is inherited by a definite blood relation, not by encircling. The community now agrees that siblings do not inherit alongside a son or a father, and on this the regions and the eras have proceeded.

The majority of readers recited "yūrathu" with a fatḥa on the rāʾ. Al-Aʿmash and Abū Rajāʾ recited "yuwarrithu" with a kasra and shadda on the rāʾ. Abū l-Fatḥ Ibn Jinnī said: al-Ḥasan recited "yūrithu" from awratha, and ʿĪsā recited "yuwarrithu" with a shadda on the rāʾ from warratha; the two objects in both readings are omitted, the estimate being: "yūrithu wārithuhu mālahu kalālatan" (his heir inherits his property as kalāla), and "kalālatan" is accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl).

They differed regarding what "al-kalāla" refers to in this verse. ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās said: "al-kalāla" is the deceased who is inherited when he has no father, and its accusative is as the predicate of "kāna." Ibn Zayd said: "al-kalāla" is the heirs as a whole; the deceased and the living are all kalāla, and its accusative is as a circumstantial or as an adjective to an omitted verbal noun whose estimate is: "wirāthan kalālatan" (an inheritance of kalāla); on this view "kāna" may be complete, meaning "occurred," or defective with "yūrathu" as its predicate. ʿAṭāʾ said: "al-kalāla" is the wealth, and it is accusative as the second object.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The derivation of the meaning of kalāla invalidates naming wealth by it.

Another group said: "al-kalāla" means the heirs, and this is consistent with the reading "yūrithu" with a kasra on the rāʾ, so that "kalāla" is accusative as an object. These relied on the hadith of Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, when the Messenger of God ﷺ visited him and he said: "O Messenger of God, only a kalāla inherits from me; may I bequeath all my wealth?" Some related that "kalāla" may mean the heirs, with its accusative as the predicate of "kāna," by omitting a modified noun whose estimate is: "dhā kalālatin" (one who has kalāla). All the other interpretations are consistent with a kasra on the rāʾ.

As for the Most High's words: "Wa-lahu akhun aw ukhtun" ... the verse: the pronoun in "lahu" refers to the man, and it is sufficient to refer to him rather than the woman, since the meaning is the same in both, and the ruling has been fixed by the first conjunction. The original of "ukht" is "ukhwa," just as the original of "bint" is "binya"; the initial of "ukht" is vowelled with a ḍamma because the omitted letter is a wāw, and the initial of "bint" is vowelled with a kasra because the omitted letter is a yāʾ. This omission and the explanation are not by regular analogy.

The scholars agreed that the siblings in this verse are uterine siblings (siblings through the mother), because their ruling is explicitly stated in this verse with a particular attribute, and the ruling for the other siblings differs from it, which is the one in the kalāla at the end of the sūra.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ recited: "Wa-lahu akhun aw ukhtun li-ummihi" (and he has a brother or sister from his mother). The female and the male are equal in this case, and their sharing of the third is equal even if they are many; this is a consensus. If a woman dies and leaves a husband, a mother and full siblings, then the husband has half, the mother has a sixth, and what remains goes to the siblings. If they are uterine only, they have the third. If the deceased woman leaves a husband, a mother, two uterine siblings and full siblings, this is the "Ḥimāriyya" case. Some said: in it the uterine siblings have the third, and the full siblings have nothing, just as if a man died and left two uterine brothers and a hundred full brothers: the two receive the third and the hundred receive two-thirds, so the two are preferred over them with the third. Others said: the mother is one, so suppose their father was a donkey (ḥimār), and they share the third among them; they also named it "al-Mushtaraka" (the shared case).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This case does not hold if the deceased were a man, because then something remains for the full siblings, and whenever something remains for them, they have only what remains, while the third belongs to the uterine siblings.

(p-488) Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿After any bequest he may have bequeathed or debt, without causing harm. This is a commandment from Allah, and Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing.﴾ [An-Nisa: 12] ﴿These are the limits of Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him into the Fire, abiding therein forever, and for him is a humiliating punishment.﴾

"غَيْرَ مُضارٍّ" (ghayra mudarrin, "without causing harm") is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), and its governing verb is "يُوصى" (yūṣā, "is bequeathed"). "وَصِيَّةً" (waṣiyyatan) is in the accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun) in the position of a ḥāl, and its governing verb is "يُوصِيكُمُ" (yūṣīkum, "He commands you"). It has also been said that it is in the accusative by way of a departure (khurūj) from the statement ﴿فَلِكُلِّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما السُدُسُ﴾ [An-Nisa: 11] ("then for each one of them is a sixth"), or from the statement ﴿فَهم شُرَكاءُ في الثُلُثِ﴾ [An-Nisa: 12] ("then they are partners in the third").

It is also valid that "مُضارٍّ" (mudarrin) governs "وَصِيَّةً" (waṣiyyatan), and the meaning would then be that the harm falls upon the bequest and through it, so the harm is attributed to it by way of metonymy (tajawwuz). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "غَيْرَ مُضارِّ وصِيَّةٍ" with the genitive construction (idafa), as one says "shujā'u ḥarbin" (a warrior of war), "midrahu ḥarbin" (a champion of war), and "baḍḍatu al-mutajarrid" (the smooth flesh of the one who strips himself), in the verse of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd. The meaning, according to what we have mentioned, is by way of metonymy in the wording, for the sake of the soundness of the meaning.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Causing harm in a bequest is among the major sins." He narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Hurayra narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever causes harm in a bequest, Allah will cast him into a valley in Hell."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The forms of causing harm are numerous and cannot be confined, and all of them are prohibited: acknowledging a debt that is not owed, bequeathing more than a third, or bequeathing to an heir, or bequeathing a third in order to flee from a needy heir, and other such things. The well-known position of the school of Malik and Ibn al-Qasim is that the testator's act is not considered harm as long as it is within the third. If he harms the heirs within his third, that stands. Within the school there is also the opinion that harm is rejected even if it is within the third, when it is known through an admission or a circumstantial indication. This is supported by the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But whoever fears from a testator an error or sin and reconciles between them...﴾ [Al-Baqara: 182] ... the verse.

(p-489) ﴿These are the limits of Allah...﴾ ... the verse. "تِلْكَ" (tilka, "these") refers to the division mentioned previously concerning inheritance. The ḥadd (limit) is a barrier that prevents one thing from entering upon another, or another entering upon it. From this comes the saying about the doorkeeper: "ḥaddād," because he prevents. From it also comes "iḥdād" for a woman, which is her abstaining from adornment. This is the meaning of ḥadd in this verse.

His statement "مِن تَحْتِها" (min taḥtihā, "beneath them") means beneath its buildings and its trees, for which it was named a garden (jannah), because the rivers of Paradise are on the surface of its ground, not in trenches.

Al-Tabari related that the ḥudūd (limits) here, according to al-Suddi, are the conditions of Allah; according to Ibn 'Abbas, the obedience to Allah; according to some, the sunna of Allah; and according to some, the obligations (farā'iḍ) of Allah. All of this is one meaning with different expressions.

"خالِدِينَ" (khālidīn, "abiding"): al-Zajjaj said it is a ḥāl of estimation (taqdīr), meaning "destined to abide therein." "خالِدِينَ" is in the plural in accordance with the meaning of "مَن" (man, "whoever") after the singular had preceded, observing the wording of "مَن." The reverse of this is not permissible.

His statement ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger...﴾ ... the verse: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "نُدْخِلُهُ" (nudkhiluhu) with the royal plural "nūn" (nūn al-'aẓama), while the rest read "يُدْخِلُهُ" (yudkhiluhu) with "yā'" in both places. These are two verses of promise and threat, and brevity in this has preceded. Allah the Exalted made hope conditional upon adherence to these limits in the division of inheritance, and threatened disobedience concerning them, in accordance with the Arabs' rejection of this division. The Prophet (ﷺ) had spoken with 'Uyayna ibn Hisn and others about it.

His statement ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger...﴾ ... the verse: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "نُدْخِلُهُ" (nudkhiluhu) with the royal plural "nūn" (nūn al-'aẓama), while the rest read "يُدْخِلُهُ" (yudkhiluhu) with "yā'" in both places. These are two verses of promise and threat, and brevity in this has preceded. Allah the Exalted made hope conditional upon adherence to these limits in the division of inheritance, and threatened disobedience concerning them, in accordance with the Arabs' rejection of this division. The Prophet (ﷺ) had spoken with 'Uyayna ibn Hisn and others about it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah an-Nisa', verses 15–16**

The Exalted and Majestic One said:

﴿As for those of your women who commit lewdness, call four witnesses from among you against them. If they testify, then confine them to the houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way.﴾ ﴿And if two of you commit it, then punish them both. If they repent and amend, then leave them alone. Indeed Allah is ever Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾

His words, "*wa-l-lati*" (﴿واللاتِي﴾): this is a plural form of "*allati*" (the feminine relative pronoun, "those who"). It is also pluralized as "*al-lawati*", and it is said "*al-la'i*" with a *ya'*. "*Al-fahisha*" (﴿الفاحِشَةَ﴾) in this place means fornication (*zina*) and every gross sin. However, the *alif* and *lam* here are for definiteness (*'ahd*, a known referent). Ibn Mas'ud read "*bil-fahisha*" with the *jarr* (genitive) construction.

His words, "*min nisa'ikum*" (﴿مِن نِسائِكُمْ﴾): this is an idafa (possessive construction) implying Islam, because a non-Muslim woman may be among the women of Muslims by lineage, and this ruling does not apply to her. Allah made the testimony for fornication specifically require four witnesses, to be complete, as a severe measure against the accuser (*al-mudda'i*) and as a concealment for the servants (of Allah). Some people said: this is so that two witnesses would be established against each of the two fornicators.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. This was the first punishment for fornicators: confinement in the houses. 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it was abrogated (*nusikha*, the technical term *naskh*, meaning abrogation by a later ruling) by the harm (*adha*) that follows it, then this was abrogated by the verse of Surat an-Nur and by stoning for the married (*thayyib*). A group said: rather, the harm was first, then it was abrogated by confinement, but the recitation came later and earlier. This was mentioned by Ibn Furak. The word "*sabilan*" (﴿سَبِيلًا﴾) means a way out (*makhraj*) by one of the commands of the Shari'a. Hittan ibn 'Abdullah al-Raqashi narrated from 'Imran ibn Husayn that he said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), when revelation descended upon him. Then it ceased, and his face was reddened. He said: 'Allah has made for them a way: the virgin (*bikr*) with the virgin, one hundred lashes and a year's exile; and the married with the married, one hundred lashes and stoning.'"

His words, "*wa-l-lazani*" (﴿واللَذانِ﴾): this is the dual of "*al-ladhi*" (the masculine relative pronoun). The analogical form would have been "*al-ladhayani*", like "*rahayani*". Sibawayh said: the *ya'* was deleted to distinguish between declinable nouns and indeclinable (*mubhamat*) nouns. Abu 'Ali said: the *ya'* was deleted for lightness, since confusion is safe from occurring in "*al-lazani*", because the *nun* does not drop. The dual *nun* in declinable nouns may drop with an idafa, as in "*rahayaka*" and "*mustafaya al-qawm*". So if the *ya'* were deleted, the singular would be confused with the dual. Ibn Kathir read "*al-lazanni*" with a doubled *nun*, and that is a substitute for the deleted *ya'*. Likewise he read "*hadhanni*", "*fadhanika*", and "*hatayanni*", with shadda (doubling) in all of them. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read all of these with a single *nun*. Abu 'Amr doubled "*fadhanika*" alone and did not double the others.

"*Wa-l-lazani*" is in the nominative case by being the subject of a sentence (*raf'* bil-ibtida'). It is also said that it is in the sense of: "in what is recited to you, the two (*al-lazani*)."

There is disagreement about the harm (*adha*). 'Ubada and al-Suddi said: it is rebuke and reproach. A group said: it is abuse and harshness without reproach. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is striking with the tongue and the hand, and beating with sandals and the like.

Mujahid and others said: the first verse concerns women generally, both married and unmarried. The second verse concerns men, and by the dual form it specifies the two categories of men, those who are married and those who are not. So the punishment of women is confinement, and the punishment of men is harm. This is an opinion that the wording requires, and the text covers all categories of fornicators with it. The wording supports it: in the first verse there is "*min nisa'ikum*" (of your women), and in the second verse "*minkum*" (from among you). Al-Suddi, Qatada and others said: the first verse concerns married women, meaning that men who are married are included with them in meaning. The second verse concerns the virgin man and the virgin woman.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of this view is complete, except that the wording of the verse is at odds with it. Al-Tabari preferred it. Ibn Mas'ud read: "*wa-lladhina yaf'alunahu minkum*" (and those among you who do it).

The scholars agreed (*ajma'a*) that these two verses are abrogated by the verse of flogging in Surat an-Nur. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and others, except those who said that the harm and reproach remain alongside the flogging, because they do not contradict each other but can both be borne by one person. As for confinement, it is abrogated by consensus. The verse of flogging is general concerning fornicators, both married and unmarried. Likewise the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) generalized it in the hadith of Hittan ibn 'Abdullah al-Raqashi that I mentioned just now. Although it is in Sahih Muslim, it is a *khabar al-ahad* (a solitary report, which does not reach the level of mass transmission). Then there came the *khabar al-mutawatir* (a mass-transmitted report, the highest level of reliability): "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned and did not flog." So whoever says that mutawatir Sunna abrogates the Qur'an makes the Prophet's stoning without flogging abrogate the flogging of the married. This is the view on which the leading scholars rest: that mutawatir Sunna abrogates the Qur'an, since both are revelation from Allah, and both require knowledge and action. They differ only in that the Sunna lacks the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the Qur'an. This is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the report of Ma'iz, in the hadith of the woman of al-Ghamidiyya, and in the hadith of the woman to whom he sent Unays. Whoever says that mutawatir Sunna does not abrogate the Qur'an says: the ruling of the Qur'an is only certain, and then the Sunna comes as a new ruling without involving abrogation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an imagined view that does not hold, because we find that the Sunna lifts by its ruling what was established in the ruling of the Qur'an in the manner of abrogation, and no examination rejects that, nor does any principle break down because of it. As for whether this particular incident can be argued in this way, in my view it may be said about it that the abrogating text for the ruling of flogging is the Qur'an, whose wording is agreed to be lifted while its ruling remains, in His saying, the Exalted: "*The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely*." This is explicit about stoning. 'Umar confirmed it from the pulpit in the presence of the Companions, and mentioned that they had recited it during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). The full hadith is in Muslim. Also, what supports that this is from the Qur'an is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the one who said to him: "Judge between us, O Messenger of Allah, by the Book of Allah." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "I will certainly judge between you both by the Book of Allah," then he ordered Unays to stone the woman if she confessed. This apparent meaning shows that stoning was in the Qur'an, and the community agreed on the lifting of its wording. And these two verses, I mean flogging and stoning, if there had been no explanation from the Messenger, it would not be required that one of them abrogate the other, since it is permissible for both to apply to one person. The hadith of 'Ubada mentioned above strengthens both of them. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, acted on it regarding Shurahah: he flogged her and then stoned her, and said: "I flog her by the Book of Allah and I stone her by the Sunna of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." This was also the view of al-Hasan and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh. But when the Messenger explained with stoning without flogging, his act was like his word with this verse: "Stone and do not flog." So the Qur'an is the abrogating text and the Sunna is the explaining one. It is valid to object to whoever says abrogation by Sunna in this case, and we say: a condition of the abrogating text is that it be independent in explanation by itself. If it is not independent, it is not abrogating. The verse of stoning, after its authenticity is granted, is not independent in abrogating by itself, but is linked with flogging and combined with it, as the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit contains. But the Messenger's dropping of flogging is what abrogates, because his act in this is in the position of his word: "Do not flog the married." As for the virgin, there is no disagreement that he is flogged. There is disagreement about exiling him. The four rightly-guided Caliphs, Ibn 'Umar, Malik, al-Shafi'i and a group said: there is no exile today. A group said: he is exiled. It was also said: his exile is his imprisonment. A woman or a slave is not exiled. This is the view of Malik and a group of scholars.

His words, "*fa-a'ridu 'anhuma*" (﴿فَأعْرِضُوا عنهُما﴾): this punishment of confinement and harm was intended so that the fornicators would repent, and repentance means turning back from fornication and persisting in it. So Allah, the Exalted, commanded the believers that when the two fornicators repent and amend the rest of their deeds, harm must be withheld from them. The command to withhold this harm came as "*a'ridu*" (turn away, leave alone). In the force of the wording there is a note of contempt for the fornicators even if they repent, because leaving them alone is only a turning away. Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: "*And turn away from the ignorant*" (Al-A'raf: 199)? Turning away in the two verses is not a command to shun (*hijra*), but is leaving alone one who has turned away. In that there is a demeaning of them according to the earlier sin, and according to the ignorance mentioned in the other verse. Allah, the Exalted, is *Tawwab*, that is: He returns His servants from sins to abandoning them and to adhering to obedience.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 17–18:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Repentance with Allah is only for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after. Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment.﴾

Innama (إنَّما) is restrictive (حاصِرَةٌ), and this is always the intent of the one who uses it. Sometimes the meaning it conveys is one in which reason requires restriction, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is only One God﴾ [an-Nisa': 171]. Sometimes the meaning it conveys is one in which reason does not require restriction, as in the saying: "Innama al-shuja' 'Antara" (the brave man is only 'Antara). In that case the restriction remains within the intent of the one praising, and through it every listener achieves confirmation of this attribute for the one described, with emphasis.

This verse is one that requires consideration, in that it restricts repentance. In the usage of the Shari'ah, repentance (tawba) is the return from evil to good. Its definition is: regret over a past act insofar as it is a disobedience of Allah, exalted and mighty is He. If the regret is because that act harmed the body or property, it is not repentance. If the act is one that this penitent is able to do again in the future, then among the conditions of repentance is the resolve to abandon that act in the future; otherwise there is persistence (إصرار), with which there is no repentance. If the act is one that he is not able to do, such as one who repents from fornication and is then rendered impotent as a result, or the like, then this does not require the condition of resolving to abandon it. Repentance is obligatory upon the believers by the consensus of the Community (ijma'), and the consensus is the indicator by which His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you﴾ [an-Nur: 31], is understood as obligatory. Repentance from one sin is valid while persisting in another of a different kind, contrary to the Mu'tazila in their saying: "One who persists in a sin is not a penitent." Repentance is also valid even if the penitent later breaks it by returning to the sin, for the first repentance was an act of obedience that has ended and is valid, and he then needs, after committing the sin, a fresh and new repentance. The faith of the disbeliever is not itself his repentance; rather his repentance is his regret over his past disbelief.

His saying, exalted is He, "with Allah" (عَلى اللهِ), contains an elided noun (حذف مضاف), its estimate being: "upon the bounty of Allah and His mercy toward His servants." This is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "O Mu'adh, do you know what the right of Allah upon the servants is?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "That they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him." Then he was silent for a little while, then said: "O Mu'adh, do you know what the right of the servants upon Allah is?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "That He admits them to Paradise." So all of this means only: what is their right by the bounty and mercy of Allah. The creed is that nothing is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, by reason ('aql). Yet His informing, exalted is He, about things He made obligatory upon Himself necessitates the obligation of those things by revelation (sam'). Among these is the eternal punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire, and among these is the acceptance of the faith of the disbeliever. As for repentance, it is not obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, to accept it by reason. As for revelation, its apparent meaning is the acceptance of the penitent's repentance. Abu al-Ma'ali and others said: "These apparent texts only give a probable opinion (غَلَبَةَ ظَنٍّ), not a certainty, regarding Allah's acceptance of repentance."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu al-Ma'ali and others have been opposed in this matter. If we suppose a man who has repented a sincere repentance (توبة نصوحا) complete in its conditions, then the saying of Abu al-Ma'ali is: it is predominantly probable (يَغْلِبُ عَلى الظَنِّ) that his repentance is accepted. Others said: it is certain regarding Allah, exalted is He, that his repentance is accepted, as He informed about Himself, mighty and majestic is He.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

My father, may Allah's mercy be upon him, inclined to this latter view and preferred it, and I say the same. Allah, exalted is He, is more merciful to His servants than that the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He is the One who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [ash-Shura: 25], and His saying, ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving toward one who repents and believes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82], be violated concerning this obligated penitent. The "evil" (السوء) in this verse encompasses both disbelief and sins.

His saying, exalted is He, "in ignorance" (بِجَهالَةٍ), means: with foolishness and lack of deliberation that led to disobedience. The meaning is not that the ignorance is that the act is a disobedience, because one who deliberately commits sins would then be excluded from repentance, and this is invalid by consensus. It is with this explanation of ignorance that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke. Abu al-'Aliya reported this from them. Qatada said: "The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ agreed that every act of disobedience is in ignorance, whether intentional or from lack of knowledge." This was also said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi. It is narrated from Mujahid and al-Dahhak that both said: "Ignorance here means deliberate intent." 'Ikrima said: "All worldly affairs are ignorance."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means by this the particular ignorance that takes one out of obedience to Allah. This meaning, in my view, is consistent with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The life of this world is only play and amusement﴾ [Muhammad: 36]. Some have interpreted the saying of 'Ikrima as meaning: those who do evil in the world.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So it is as if ignorance is a name for the life of this world. This, in my view, is weak. It was also said: "in ignorance" means: one does not know the reality of the punishment. This too is weak; Ibn Fawrak mentioned it and it was refuted.

The interpreters differed regarding His saying, exalted is He, "soon after" (مِن قَرِيبٍ). Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: its meaning is before sickness and death. Abu Mijlaz, Muhammad ibn Qays, al-Dahhak, 'Ikrima, Ibn Zayd and others said: its meaning is before witnessing the angels and the driving, and before a person is overcome by his own soul. Abu Qilaba narrated: "When Allah created Adam, Iblis saw him hollow. Then what happened happened to him, and he was cursed and given respite. He said: 'By Your might, I will not leave his heart as long as the spirit is in him.' Allah, exalted is He, said: 'By My might, I will not withhold repentance from him as long as the spirit is in him.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned the best times for repentance, while the majority set the last limit of its time. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: it was said: "Repentance is open to one of you as long as he has not been seized by his throat." Bashir ibn Ka'b and al-Hasan narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not begun the death rattle (يُغَرْغِرْ) and has not been overcome in his intellect."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because hope remains in him, and regret and resolve to abandon the act in the future are still valid for him. When he is overcome, repentance is impossible due to the absence of regret and resolve to abandon.

His saying, exalted is He, "soon after," means only: soon after the time of the sin. The entire duration of life is "soon," and the one who hastens in health is more excellent and more worthy of his hope than one who acts righteously. The complete distance is death, and from this is the saying of Malik ibn al-Rayb:

"......... and where is the place of distance except my own place?"

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ means: Knowing of who repents, and He facilitates repentance for him; Wise in what He executes of that, and in delaying whoever is delayed until he perishes.

Then, by His saying, exalted is He, "And repentance is not..." to the end of the verse, He negated that one who is present at his death and has come into the realm of despair enters the ruling of the penitents. The presence of death is like the condition of Pharaoh when he came into the overwhelming water and drowning, so what he showed of faith did not benefit him. With this said Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and a group of the exegetes.

Al-Rabi' said: the first verse, "Repentance with Allah is only..." concerns the believers, and the second verse, "And repentance is not..." was revealed concerning the Muslims, then abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa': 48]. Thus He decreed that He would not forgive the disbeliever, and He deferred the believers to His will, not despairing them of forgiveness.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some people objected to this view, saying that the verse is a report (خَبَر), and reports are not abrogated. This is not necessary, because the verse is in the form of a report but its meaning is the establishment of a legal ruling. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will hold you accountable for it﴾ [al-Baqara: 284], and like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If there are among you twenty patient ones, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 65]. The view of abrogation is weak only insofar as the two verses are interdependent and there is no need to establish an abrogation, because this verse does not deny that one who did not repent soon may be forgiven. So we would not need to say that His saying, ﴿and He forgives what is less than that﴾ [an-Nisa': 48], abrogated it. Rather this verse only negates that one is a penitent if he repents only at the presence of death. So the creed in my view regarding these verses is: whoever repents soon after has the ruling of the penitent, and it is predominantly probable that he will be blessed and not punished. This is the position of Abu al-Ma'ali and others. Others said: rather he is certainly forgiven, because Allah, exalted is He, has informed of that. Abu al-Ma'ali makes those reports apparent texts conditioned by the will (of Allah). As for one who does not repent until death is present, he is not in the ruling of the penitents. If he was a disbeliever, he will abide eternally. If he was a believer, he is a sinner subject to the divine will, but fear predominates over him, and the probability of his punishment is strong. Yet it is established by revelation that among this category are those whom Allah forgives out of His grace and does not punish.

Allah, exalted is He, also informed that those who die while they are disbelievers have no chance to make amends and no repentance in the Hereafter.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those, We have prepared a painful punishment﴾: if the reference (الإشارة) is only to those who die while disbelievers, then the punishment is an eternal punishment. If the reference includes them and those upon whom the threat is executed, from among the sinners who do not repent except at the presence of death, then he falls under this category: a punishment without eternity with it. "A'tadna" means: We made ready and brought forth. The apparent meaning of this verse is that the Fire is already created.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 17–18:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Repentance with Allah is only for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after. Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment.﴾

Innama (إنَّما) is restrictive (حاصِرَةٌ), and this is always the intent of the one who uses it. Sometimes the meaning it conveys is one in which reason requires restriction, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is only One God﴾ [an-Nisa': 171]. Sometimes the meaning it conveys is one in which reason does not require restriction, as in the saying: "Innama al-shuja' 'Antara" (the brave man is only 'Antara). In that case the restriction remains within the intent of the one praising, and through it every listener achieves confirmation of this attribute for the one described, with emphasis.

This verse is one that requires consideration, in that it restricts repentance. In the usage of the Shari'ah, repentance (tawba) is the return from evil to good. Its definition is: regret over a past act insofar as it is a disobedience of Allah, exalted and mighty is He. If the regret is because that act harmed the body or property, it is not repentance. If the act is one that this penitent is able to do again in the future, then among the conditions of repentance is the resolve to abandon that act in the future; otherwise there is persistence (إصرار), with which there is no repentance. If the act is one that he is not able to do, such as one who repents from fornication and is then rendered impotent as a result, or the like, then this does not require the condition of resolving to abandon it. Repentance is obligatory upon the believers by the consensus of the Community (ijma'), and the consensus is the indicator by which His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you﴾ [an-Nur: 31], is understood as obligatory. Repentance from one sin is valid while persisting in another of a different kind, contrary to the Mu'tazila in their saying: "One who persists in a sin is not a penitent." Repentance is also valid even if the penitent later breaks it by returning to the sin, for the first repentance was an act of obedience that has ended and is valid, and he then needs, after committing the sin, a fresh and new repentance. The faith of the disbeliever is not itself his repentance; rather his repentance is his regret over his past disbelief.

His saying, exalted is He, "with Allah" (عَلى اللهِ), contains an elided noun (حذف مضاف), its estimate being: "upon the bounty of Allah and His mercy toward His servants." This is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "O Mu'adh, do you know what the right of Allah upon the servants is?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "That they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him." Then he was silent for a little while, then said: "O Mu'adh, do you know what the right of the servants upon Allah is?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "That He admits them to Paradise." So all of this means only: what is their right by the bounty and mercy of Allah. The creed is that nothing is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, by reason ('aql). Yet His informing, exalted is He, about things He made obligatory upon Himself necessitates the obligation of those things by revelation (sam'). Among these is the eternal punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire, and among these is the acceptance of the faith of the disbeliever. As for repentance, it is not obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, to accept it by reason. As for revelation, its apparent meaning is the acceptance of the penitent's repentance. Abu al-Ma'ali and others said: "These apparent texts only give a probable opinion (غَلَبَةَ ظَنٍّ), not a certainty, regarding Allah's acceptance of repentance."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu al-Ma'ali and others have been opposed in this matter. If we suppose a man who has repented a sincere repentance (توبة نصوحا) complete in its conditions, then the saying of Abu al-Ma'ali is: it is predominantly probable (يَغْلِبُ عَلى الظَنِّ) that his repentance is accepted. Others said: it is certain regarding Allah, exalted is He, that his repentance is accepted, as He informed about Himself, mighty and majestic is He.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

My father, may Allah's mercy be upon him, inclined to this latter view and preferred it, and I say the same. Allah, exalted is He, is more merciful to His servants than that the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He is the One who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [ash-Shura: 25], and His saying, ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving toward one who repents and believes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82], be violated concerning this obligated penitent. The "evil" (السوء) in this verse encompasses both disbelief and sins.

His saying, exalted is He, "in ignorance" (بِجَهالَةٍ), means: with foolishness and lack of deliberation that led to disobedience. The meaning is not that the ignorance is that the act is a disobedience, because one who deliberately commits sins would then be excluded from repentance, and this is invalid by consensus. It is with this explanation of ignorance that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke. Abu al-'Aliya reported this from them. Qatada said: "The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ agreed that every act of disobedience is in ignorance, whether intentional or from lack of knowledge." This was also said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi. It is narrated from Mujahid and al-Dahhak that both said: "Ignorance here means deliberate intent." 'Ikrima said: "All worldly affairs are ignorance."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means by this the particular ignorance that takes one out of obedience to Allah. This meaning, in my view, is consistent with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The life of this world is only play and amusement﴾ [Muhammad: 36]. Some have interpreted the saying of 'Ikrima as meaning: those who do evil in the world.

(p-498) The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion. And do not restrain them that you may take part of what you have given them, unless they commit a clear immorality. And live with them in kindness. For if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes therein much good.﴾

The interpreters (al-muta'awwilun) differed concerning the meaning of His, the Exalted, words: ﴿it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: In the Jahiliyyah, when a man died, his heirs had more right to his wife than her own family: if one of them wished, he would marry her himself; if they wished, they would marry her to someone else; and if they wished, they would prevent her from remarrying. The verse was revealed concerning this. Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf said: When Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat died, his son wanted to marry his wife, and this was permitted for them in the Jahiliyyah, so the verse was revealed concerning this. Al-Naqqash mentioned that the name of Abu Qays's son was Mihsan.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This practice was binding among the Ansar, while among Quraysh it was permitted by mutual consent. Do you not see that Abu 'Amr ibn Umayyah married the wife of his father after his death, and she bore to Abu 'Amr Musafir and Abu Mu'ayt, and she had from Umayyah Abu al-'Is and others; so the sons of Umayyah were the brothers of Musafir and Abu Mu'ayt and their paternal uncles. Saying the same as this statement I have related from Ibn 'Abbas were: 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan al-Basri and Abu Mijlaz. 'Ikrimah said: It was revealed concerning Kubaysha bint Ma'n al-Ansariyyah, whose husband Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat died leaving her. Mujahid said: The eldest son had more right to his father's wife if she was not his mother. al-Suddi said: The heir of the deceased, if he was quicker and threw his garment over the wife of the deceased, then he had more right to her; but if she outran him and went to her family, she had more right to herself.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The reports on this are many, according to the Jahiliyyah customs, and there is no benefit in mentioning all of them, since Allah has removed them by His words: ﴿it is not lawful for you﴾. The meaning of the verse according to this view is: it is not lawful for you to treat women as property, to be inherited from dead men as property is inherited. The ones addressed by the speech are the guardians of the dead. Some interpreters said: The meaning of the verse is: it is not lawful for you to prevent the women for whom you are guardians from marrying, detaining them without marriage until they die, so that their wealth is inherited.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this view, what is inherited is her wealth, not her. Something similar has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others. The ones addressed are the guardians of women and their husbands, when they detain them together with bad treatment, hoping to inherit from them.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "karhan" (كَرْهًا) with a fatha on the kaf wherever it occurs: in al-Nisa', in Surat al-Tawbah and in al-Ahqaf. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read all of these with a damma on the kaf. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read it in al-Nisa' and al-Tawbah with a fatha, and in al-Ahqaf in both places with a damma. Al-karh and al-kurh are two dialectal forms, like al-du'f and al-du'f, and al-faqr and al-fuqr, as Abu 'Ali said. Al-Farra' said: with a damma on the kaf it means hardship, and with a fatha it means compulsion by another; Ibn Qutaybah said the same.

The interpreters differed concerning the meaning of His words: ﴿And do not restrain them﴾... the verse. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: It also refers to those guardians who used to inherit women, because they would marry them if they were beautiful, and would keep them until they died if they were ugly. al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said something similar.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In His words "ataytumuhunna" there is some ambiguity, namely: what men had given them before. It is like His words: ﴿kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54] and other such cases. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it refers to spouses: a man keeps a woman and treats her badly until she ransoms herself from him; that is not lawful for him. Qatadah said the same. Ibn al-Baylamani said: the first part of the verse concerns the matter of the Jahiliyyah, and the second, regarding restraint (al-'adl), concerns the people of Islam who detain a wife harmfully in order to get a ransom. Ibn Mas'ud said: the meaning of the verse is: do not inherit women as the Jahiliyyah did, and do not restrain them in Islam. al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said something similar. al-Suddi said: this verse is addressed to the guardians, like the prohibition of restraint mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

(p-500) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is unsettled, unless the restraint comes from a guardian who is an heir, for then he is hoping for her death; but if he is not an heir, then for what reason would he do it? Ibn Zayd said: This restraint prohibited in this verse is from the practices of the Jahiliyyah among Quraysh in Makkah: when a husband and wife were incompatible, he would divorce her on condition that she not remarry without his permission, and he would have witnesses to that. Then when she was proposed to, if she gave him something and bribed him, well and good; otherwise he would restrain her. Concerning this the verse was revealed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What I say is: 'adl in the language means detaining with severity and harm, and preventing from marriage in that manner. From this come the expressions: the hen was obstructed (a'dalat al-dajajah) and became stuck ('adalat) when laying an egg was difficult for her; and from it: the illness became obstinate (a'dala al-da') when it persisted and did not heal; and from it: a chronic disease (da' 'udal). The usage of the jurists has settled on 'adl meaning the guardians' detaining of women from marriage, but in the language it is more general than this, as I have mentioned, occurring from a guardian and from a husband. The strongest of the previously mentioned views is that the intended ones are husbands, and the evidence for this is His words: ﴿unless they commit an immorality﴾. If they commit an immorality, it is not permissible for the guardian to detain her until he takes her wealth, by consensus of the Ummah; rather that is for the husband, as we will explain later, if Allah wills.

Likewise His words: ﴿And live with them in kindness﴾ to the end of the verse show clearly the strengthening of what I have mentioned; and although this may be the case, it is possible that it is a separate command from the first, specifically for husbands. As for restraint, it is prohibited for everyone who can be imagined as a restrainer in a case; and when it is established against a guardian that he is restraining, the judge looks into the matter of the woman and marries her off without regard to him, except for the father regarding his daughters: if there is a problem in his case, it is not to be contradicted, one opinion only. If his restraint is proven, there are two opinions in the school of Malik: one is that he is like the other guardians, and the judge marries off whom he wishes of his daughters at her request; the other is that he is not to be interfered with.

The words "wa-la ta'dulluhunna" may be read as a jussive, in which case the waw is a conjunction beginning a separate, cut-off sentence from the first; or "ta'dulluhunna" may be in the subjunctive (nasb) as a conjunction with "tarithu", in which case the waw joins one verb to another verb.

(p-501) Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa-la an ta'dulluhunna" (وَلا أنْ تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ). This reading strengthens the possibility of the subjunctive, and that restraint is among what is not lawful by the text itself. On the reading of the jussive, it is a prohibition open to the seeking of indicators as to whether it is forbidden or disliked; the subjunctive possibility is stronger.

People differed concerning the meaning of "fahishah" (immorality) here. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: it is adultery; and if a virgin commits adultery, she is flogged a hundred times and exiled for a year, and she returns to her husband what she took from him. Abu Qilabah said: if a man's wife commits adultery, there is no harm in his harming her and making things hard for her until she ransoms herself from him. al-Suddi said: if they do that, take their dowries. 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: this ruling was in force and then abrogated by the hudud (prescribed punishments); but this is a weak view. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the immorality in this verse is hatred and nushuz (disobedience); al-Dahhak and others said the same, and they said: so if she is disobedient, it is lawful for him to take her property.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the position of Malik, except that I do not know of any explicit text for him on the meaning of "fahishah" in this verse. Others said: "fahishah" is verbal abuse and bad treatment in word and deed, and this has the meaning of nushuz. Some scholars permit taking property from a disobedient wife by way of khul', except that they hold that he should not exceed what he gave her, relying on His words: ﴿that you may take part of what you have given them﴾. Malik and his companions and a group of scholars said: the husband may take from the disobedient wife all that she possesses.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Adultery is harder on the husband than disobedience and harm, and each of these is an immorality which makes taking property lawful. Ibn Mas'ud read: "illa an yafhushna, wa-'ashiruhunna" (إلّا أنْ يَفْحُشْنَ، وعاشِرُوهُنَّ).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an excessive deviation from the Imam's codex (mushaf al-Imam). Abu 'Amr likewise mentioned this from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, but there is room for reflection on this. Ibn Kathir and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read "mubayyinah" and "ayatun mubayyinat" with a fatha on the ya in both; Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "mubayyinah" and "mubayyinat" with a kasrah on the ya in both; Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "mubayyinah" with a kasrah and "mubayyinat" with a fatha. Ibn 'Abbas read: "bi-fahishah mubinah" (بِفاحِشَةٍ مُبِينَةٍ) with a kasrah on the ba' and a sukun on the ya', from abana al-shay' (it became clear). All these readings are eloquent dialects: it is said bayyana al-shay' and abana, when a thing became apparent, and bana al-shay' and bayyantuhu.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And live with them in kindness﴾ are a command to everyone, since everyone has companionship (ishrah), whether a husband or a guardian; but the one primarily engaged in this command is the husband. Ishrah is companionship, close mixing and association; from it is the verse of Tarafah:

"Though her dwelling be far away once, I remain upon the covenant of a beloved who is intimate."

He made "al-habib" (the beloved) a collective noun, like al-khalit and al-fariq. It is said: 'ashara-hu mu'ashirah, ta'ashara al-qawm and i'tasharu. I think the word comes from a'shar al-jazur (the shares of a slaughtered camel), because it is sharing, mixing and fine companionship; so Allah, exalted is He, commanded men to good companionship with women. To this refers the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Enjoy her, though there is a crookedness in her." Then Allah, exalted is He, trained His servants with His words: ﴿For if you dislike them﴾ to the end of the verse. al-Suddi said: the abundant good in a woman is the child; Ibn 'Abbas said something similar.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among the eloquence of the Qur'an is the generality contained in the word "shay'" (thing), because this consideration applies to everything a person dislikes which it is good to bear patiently; so patience is good, since its outcome is good, when it is sought for the sake of Allah's countenance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 20–21:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿But if you desire to replace one wife with another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take back anything from it. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾ ﴿And how could you take it when you have gone in to one another and they have taken from you a solid covenant?﴾

When the ruling on separation whose cause is the wife had passed in the preceding verse, and that the husband may take back property from her, he then mentioned, immediately after that, the separation whose cause is the husband, and the prohibition of taking back her property along with it. So what is in this verse is that which is specific to the husband's own desire.

The scholars differed: if the spouses both want separation, and there is from both of them nushuz (disobedience) and bad conduct, then Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the husband may take from her if she was the cause of the separation, and his own causing of it is not taken into account. (p-503) A group of scholars said: it is not permissible for him to take property except where she alone is in nushuz and he is wronging her in that. Some people said: this verse implies the permissibility of excess in mahr (bridal gift), because Allah, exalted is He, gave the example of a qintar, and He gives examples only with what is permissible.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab delivered a sermon and said: "Beware, do not make the mahr of your women excessive, for a man may exaggerate until that becomes enmity in his heart toward the woman; he says, 'I have toiled for you the sweat of a waterskin or the drops of a waterskin.'" It is related that a woman spoke to him from behind the people and said: "How is this, when Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿and you had given one of them a qintar﴾?" He said: 'Umar lowered his head, then said: "Every person is more knowledgeable in fiqh than you, O 'Umar." It is also related that he said: "A woman was right and a man was wrong," and Allah is the One sought for help; and he left off objecting.

Others said: the verse does not indicate the permissibility of excess in mahr, because the example came in the manner of hyperbole, as if He said: "and you had given this great amount which no one gives." This is like his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, even if it is as small as the nest of a sandgrouse for its eggs, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise." It is known that there is no mosque the size of a nest. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said to Ibn Abi Hadrad, who had come seeking his help regarding his mahr, and he asked him about the mahr, and he said: "two hundred," so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry and said: "It is as if you were cutting gold and silver from the side of a volcanic plain or a mountain..." — the hadith. Some people deduced from this the prohibition of excess in mahr.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This does not necessarily follow, because this one made himself need help and asking, and that is disliked by consensus; the excess that is disputed is only with wealth and ample means. Ibn Muhaysin read the alif of "ihdahunna" with a connected wasl, which is a dialect where it is dropped for lightness. From this is the saying of the poet:

﴿ ................... and you hear from beneath the dust-cloud her azmil ﴾

(p-504) And the saying of another:

﴿ If I do not fight, then dress me in a veil ﴾

The discussion of the amount of the qintar has already preceded in surah [Al 'Imran]. Abu as-Sammal read "minhu shay'an" with a fatha on the ya' and tanwin, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far. Al-buhtan is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), and its meaning: bewildered, confused, because of its enormity and the ugliness of the report and the deed in it.

Then Allah, exalted is He, admonished His servants, reminding them of the affection between the spouses, which necessitates guarding the wife's property, since the compensation for what she was given has been taken from her. "Kayfa" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state. And "afda" means: he came into contact with and went to the utmost extent of contact. From this is the saying of the poet:

﴿ Yes, and by the disorder that reached every troop, its course appeared from the outside after the inside ﴾

And in the proverb: "The people are a chaos of confusion (fawda fada)", meaning: they are mixed, each one engaging in the affair of another. And you say: "the state reached such-and-such," meaning: it became that. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, as-Suddi and others said: the idifa' (going in) in this verse is intercourse. Ibn 'Abbas said: "But Allah is Generous and uses euphemism."

People differed about what is meant by the solid covenant. Al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Qatada, ad-Dahhak, as-Suddi and others said: it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿either retain with kindness or release with goodness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: the solid covenant is the marriage contract, and the man's saying "you have married" and "you have acquired marriage" (p-505) and the like, these are what make intimacy lawful. "Ikrima and ar-Rabi' said: the solid covenant is explained by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Be good to women, for they are with you as captives; you took them under the trust of Allah, and made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah." Some said: the solid covenant is the child.

Among the anomalous opinions regarding this verse: Bakr ibn 'Abdullah al-Muzani said: it is not permissible to take anything, little or much, from a woman who seeks khul' (separation by compensation), even if she is the one wanting divorce. And among them: Ibn Zayd said this verse is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He, in [Surat al-Baqarah]: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] ... the verse.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no abrogating or abrogated element in any of these verses, and they all are built upon one another.
