Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 22–23 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an indecency and hatred, and an evil way.﴾ ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, your sisters' daughters, your mothers who have nursed you, your milk-sisters, your wives' mothers.﴾

This verse is addressed to the believers among the Arabs at the time of its revelation, and the meaning of the verse and the prohibition that follows it is established for all believers. The occasion of the verse was that among the Arabs there were tribes that had become accustomed to a man inheriting (i.e., marrying) his father's wife, as we have mentioned concerning the matter of Abu 'Amr ibn Umayya ibn 'Abd Shams, and from that is the report of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat, and from that is Safwan ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf, who married after his father Fakhita bint al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Asad, and she had been his father's wife, he having been killed and leaving her; and from that is Manzur ibn Zabban, who succeeded to Mulayka bint Kharija, and she had been with his father Zabban ibn Sayyar; and to many such cases. There was also among the Arabs one who married his daughter, namely Hajib ibn Zurara, (p-506) who became a Magian and did this deed; al-Nadr ibn Shumayl mentioned this in the Book of Blemishes (Kitab al-Mathalib). So Allah forbade the believers from what their fathers were upon of these practices. Ibn 'Abbas said: The people of the Jahiliyya would forbid what is forbidden, except the wife of the father and combining two sisters, so this verse was revealed concerning that.

The commentators differed over the implications of the wording of the verse. One group said: His saying "what married" is meant as "women," i.e., do not marry the women whom your fathers married; and His saying "except what has already passed" means: but what has already passed, leave it alone. Some of them said: the meaning is: but what has already passed, it is pardoned for you, for whoever had engaged in it; as if He, may He be exalted, said: "And do not do, except (what) has already passed," so "ma" on this view refers to those who have intellect, in that these women are a category among the categories of those who have intellect, and "ma" is used for categories and attributes of those who have intellect. Another group said: His saying "what married" is meant as "the act of the fathers," i.e., do not marry as your fathers married through their corrupt contracts; and His saying "except what has already passed" means: except what preceded among you and occurred from those corrupt contracts, it is permissible for you to remain in it in Islam, if it is of a kind that can be undertaken from the side of kinship, and the Sharia would permit it had its marriage been initiated in Islam according to its sunna. It was also said: the meaning of "except what has already passed" is: it is pardoned for you.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Ma" on this view is verbal-noun (masdariyya). In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "except what has already passed, except whoever repents."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu 'Amr al-Dani likewise related it.

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of the verse is the prohibition against a man having intercourse with a woman whom the fathers had intercourse with, except what has already passed of the fathers in the Jahiliyya of fornication, not in the manner of marriage; so for you it is permissible to marry them in Islam, because that fornication was an indecency. Ibn Zayd said: thus the verse added the hatred (maqt).

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in interpreting this verse: Every woman whom your father or your son married, whether he consummated it or not, is forbidden to you. The "kana" in this verse implies both past and future (p-507). Al-Mubarrid said: it is superfluous (za'ida), but that is an error, refuted by the presence of the predicate in the accusative.

Maqt means hatred and contempt because of a vile act one commits; so Allah, exalted, called this marriage "maqt" because it is an object of hatred that befalls its doer. Abu 'Ubayda and others said: the Arabs used to call the child born from the husband of the mother "al-maqti."

His saying "and an evil way" means: how evil is the path and the course for one who follows it, since its end is toward the punishment of Allah.

His, exalted, saying: "Forbidden to you..." — the verse is a ruling by which Allah forbade seven through lineage, and six through nursing and affinity; and the established sunna added a seventh, which is combining a woman with her paternal aunt (or maternal aunt), and consensus has upheld it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: seven are forbidden through lineage and seven through affinity, and he recited this verse; 'Amr ibn Salim, mawla of the Ansar, said the same, and made the seventh His saying: "And married women from among women" [al-Nisa: 24]. The prohibition of mothers is general in every circumstance, not specified in any respect, and the scholars call it "al-mubham," meaning there is no gate in it and no path to it, due to the closure and strength of the prohibition. Likewise the prohibition of daughters and sisters: the mother is every woman who bore a person, however far up; the daughter is every one he bore, however far down; as for a full sister, or a sister by the father alone, or by the mother alone, she is the one who shares with him a loin or a womb. The paternal aunt is the father's sister, and the maternal aunt is the mother's sister; in these two too there is generality and indeterminacy. Likewise the father's paternal aunt and maternal aunt, the mother's paternal aunt and maternal aunt, and the paternal aunt's paternal aunt. As for the maternal aunt of the paternal aunt, it requires examination: if the paternal aunt is a sister of a father and mother or a sister of a mother, then the maternal aunt of the paternal aunt is not lawful, because she is the sister of the grandmother; but if the paternal aunt is only a sister of the father, then her maternal aunt is a stranger from among the sons of her brother, lawful to men, and may be combined with women. Likewise the paternal aunt of the maternal aunt requires examination: if the maternal aunt is a sister of the mother by the father, her paternal aunt is forbidden, because she is the sister of a grandfather; but if the maternal aunt is only a sister of the mother by the mother, then her paternal aunt is a stranger from among the sons of her sister. Likewise, concerning the daughters of a brother and the daughters of a sister, there is generality and indeterminacy, whether the siblings are full, or by the father, or by the mother.

Abu Haywa read: "min al-ridaa'a" with a kasra on the ra'. Nursing prohibits what lineage prohibits: the nursing mother is a mother, and whatever children of hers came before or after are brothers and sisters; the stallion of the milk is a father, and whatever children of his came before or after are brothers. Ibn Mas'ud read: "allay" with a kasra on the ya'; Ibn Hurmuz read: "wa-ummahatukum allati" in the singular, as if because of the indeterminacy it may be used with the one and the plural.

(p-508) People differed over the interpretation of His, exalted, saying: "and mothers of your wives." The majority of the scholars said: it is of complete generality, whether or not one has consummated with them; so by contracting marriage with the daughter, the mother is forbidden. This is the view of the entire body of the Companions and the Successors and the jurists of the cities. It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he was asked about a man who married a woman and divorced her before consummation: may he marry her mother? He said: Yes, she is in the position of the stepdaughter.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means that His saying: "of your women with whom you have consummated" is a condition for this and for the stepdaughter. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is also related from him as the majority's view. It is related from Zayd ibn Thabit that he used to say: if she dies while he is with her and he takes her inheritance, it is disliked for him to marry her mother; and if he divorces her before consummation, then if he wishes he may do so. Mujahid said: consummation is intended in both cases, and the saying of the majority of people opposes this view. It is related from Zayd ibn Thabit concerning this that he said: "mothers of your women" is unspecified, and the condition applies only to the stepdaughters. Ibn Jurayj said: I said to 'Ata': Did Ibn 'Abbas read: "and mothers of your women with whom you have consummated"? He said: "Lā tatarra'" (do not...). Hajjaj said: I said to Ibn Jurayj: What is "tatarra'"? He said: It is as if he said "lā, lā" (no, no). What refutes this view from the standpoint of grammar is that when two genitives differ, their adjectives are not the same; the meaning is: when they differ regarding the governing element, and this verse has differing governing elements.

**

His, exalted, saying: ﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your women with whom you have consummated; but if you have not consummated with them, there is no blame upon you; and the wives of your sons who are from your loins; and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed. Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Al-Rabiba: the daughter of a man's wife from another husband; she was named so because he raises her in his lap, so she is his marbuba (one brought up). Rabiba is fa'ila in the sense of maf'ula. His, exalted, saying: "who are in your guardianship" mentions the more frequent case, since that is the usual situation of the stepdaughter, and she is forbidden even if she is not in the guardianship, since she is in the legal status of one who is in the guardianship. Except for what is related from 'Ali, that he said: she is lawful if she is not in the guardianship and he has consummated with the mother, if she is far from him. It is said: hajr, with a kasra or fatha on the ha', is the front of a person's garment and what is before him of it while wearing it; then the word was used for keeping and covering, because the wearer protects a child or similar with that part of the garment.

(p-509) The scholars differed over the meaning of His saying: "with whom you have consummated." Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus and Ibn Dinar said: "entering" in this context means sexual intercourse; so if a man divorces after the wedding night (bina') and before intercourse (wat'), her daughter is lawful to him. The majority of scholars, among them Malik ibn Anas, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and others, said: undressing, kissing, lying together and all kinds of sensual enjoyment forbid the daughter just as intercourse does. "Ḥalā'il" is the plural of "ḥalīla," which is the wife, because she is lawful (tahillu) with the man wherever he is lawful; so it is fa'ila in the sense of fa'ila. Al-Zajjaj and a group went to the view that it derives from the word "ḥalāl" (lawful), so it is ḥalīla in the sense of muḥallala. His saying: "who are from your loins" is a specification to exclude every person whom the Arabs used to adopt who was not from the loin; this was among them a common matter with a strong ruling.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: It is related, and Allah knows best, that it was revealed concerning Muhammad, upon him be peace, when he married the wife of Zayd ibn Harītha; the polytheists said: he has married his son's wife, so the verse was revealed.

The wife of a son by nursing is forbidden even if he is not from the loin, by consensus, based on his, ﷺ, saying: "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing." And His, exalted, saying: "and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed" is a term that covers combining by marriage and by right of possession (milk al-yamin). The community agreed on prohibiting combining the two by marriage. As for by right of possession, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: One verse permitted them, and one verse forbade them; as for me, personally, I do not consider combining them good. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas, mentioned by Ibn al-Mundhir, and he mentioned that Ishaq ibn Rahawayh forbade combining them by intercourse, and that the majority of the scholars disliked it, and he placed Malik among those who disliked it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no disagreement about the permissibility of combining the two in ownership, and likewise a mother and her daughter. It follows from Ishaq's view that one who combines them by intercourse should be stoned, and dislike is inferred from Malik's view: that if he has intercourse with one and then wishes to have intercourse with the other, he refrains from both until he makes one of them unlawful to him, and he does not impose a legal penalty on him.

The scholars differed, after the position of prohibiting combining them by intercourse, if he was having intercourse with one and then (p-510) wished to have intercourse with the other: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: it is not permissible for him to have intercourse with the second until he makes the private part of the other unlawful to himself by removing her from his ownership, through sale, manumission, or by giving her in marriage. Ibn al-Mundhir said: there is also a second view, from Qatada, that if he was having intercourse with one and wished to have intercourse with the other, he intends to make the first unlawful to himself and not approach her, then he refrains from her until the first, now unlawful, is cleansed (istibra'), and then he approaches the second.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Malik's position, may God have mercy on him: if a man has two sisters as slave-concubines (in his ownership), he may have intercourse with whichever of them he wishes, and refraining from the other is left to his trustworthiness. If he wants to have intercourse with the other, then he is obliged to make the private part of the first forbidden to himself by an act he performs, such as removing her from his ownership, marrying her off, freeing her for a fixed term, or assigning her to long-term service. If he has been having intercourse with one of them and then pounces on the other without making the first forbidden, both are withheld from him, and it is not permissible for him to approach either of them until he makes the other forbidden. This is not left to his trustworthiness, because he is suspected regarding the one he has already had intercourse with, whereas he was not suspected before, since he had only had intercourse with the one.

If a man has a slave-concubine whom he has intercourse with, and then he marries her sister, then there are three opinions within the school on this. In the third book of the Mudawwana, it is stated that both are withheld from him when the marriage contract is concluded, until he makes one of them forbidden, along with his disapproval of this marriage, since it is a contract in a situation where intercourse is not permitted, and that is disliked except during menstruation, because it is a common and frequent matter. On this same point there is another opinion: the marriage is not valid. Ashhab said in the Book of Istibra' (the waiting period): concluding the marriage with the free woman makes forbidden the private part of the slave-concubine. The Prophet (ﷺ) is authentically reported to have "forbidden that a woman be combined with her paternal aunt, or with her maternal aunt," and the community (ummah) has agreed upon this. Some scholars have held that this hadith abrogates (naskh) the generality of the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. This hadith is mutawatir (widely transmitted). Likewise his saying, peace be upon him: "What is forbidden by nursing is forbidden by lineage," and it has also been said that this too is abrogating.

As for God's words, the Exalted: ﴿except what has already passed﴾, it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but what has already passed of that and occurred, Islam has removed it, for God forgives it, and Islam wipes it away.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 22–23 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an indecency and hatred, and an evil way.﴾ ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, your sisters' daughters, your mothers who have nursed you, your milk-sisters, your wives' mothers.﴾

This verse is addressed to the believers among the Arabs at the time of its revelation, and the meaning of the verse and the prohibition that follows it is established for all believers. The occasion of the verse was that among the Arabs there were tribes that had become accustomed to a man inheriting (i.e., marrying) his father's wife, as we have mentioned concerning the matter of Abu 'Amr ibn Umayya ibn 'Abd Shams, and from that is the report of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat, and from that is Safwan ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf, who married after his father Fakhita bint al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Asad, and she had been his father's wife, he having been killed and leaving her; and from that is Manzur ibn Zabban, who succeeded to Mulayka bint Kharija, and she had been with his father Zabban ibn Sayyar; and to many such cases. There was also among the Arabs one who married his daughter, namely Hajib ibn Zurara, (p-506) who became a Magian and did this deed; al-Nadr ibn Shumayl mentioned this in the Book of Blemishes (Kitab al-Mathalib). So Allah forbade the believers from what their fathers were upon of these practices. Ibn 'Abbas said: The people of the Jahiliyya would forbid what is forbidden, except the wife of the father and combining two sisters, so this verse was revealed concerning that.

The commentators differed over the implications of the wording of the verse. One group said: His saying "what married" is meant as "women," i.e., do not marry the women whom your fathers married; and His saying "except what has already passed" means: but what has already passed, leave it alone. Some of them said: the meaning is: but what has already passed, it is pardoned for you, for whoever had engaged in it; as if He, may He be exalted, said: "And do not do, except (what) has already passed," so "ma" on this view refers to those who have intellect, in that these women are a category among the categories of those who have intellect, and "ma" is used for categories and attributes of those who have intellect. Another group said: His saying "what married" is meant as "the act of the fathers," i.e., do not marry as your fathers married through their corrupt contracts; and His saying "except what has already passed" means: except what preceded among you and occurred from those corrupt contracts, it is permissible for you to remain in it in Islam, if it is of a kind that can be undertaken from the side of kinship, and the Sharia would permit it had its marriage been initiated in Islam according to its sunna. It was also said: the meaning of "except what has already passed" is: it is pardoned for you.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Ma" on this view is verbal-noun (masdariyya). In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "except what has already passed, except whoever repents."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu 'Amr al-Dani likewise related it.

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of the verse is the prohibition against a man having intercourse with a woman whom the fathers had intercourse with, except what has already passed of the fathers in the Jahiliyya of fornication, not in the manner of marriage; so for you it is permissible to marry them in Islam, because that fornication was an indecency. Ibn Zayd said: thus the verse added the hatred (maqt).

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in interpreting this verse: Every woman whom your father or your son married, whether he consummated it or not, is forbidden to you. The "kana" in this verse implies both past and future (p-507). Al-Mubarrid said: it is superfluous (za'ida), but that is an error, refuted by the presence of the predicate in the accusative.

Maqt means hatred and contempt because of a vile act one commits; so Allah, exalted, called this marriage "maqt" because it is an object of hatred that befalls its doer. Abu 'Ubayda and others said: the Arabs used to call the child born from the husband of the mother "al-maqti."

His saying "and an evil way" means: how evil is the path and the course for one who follows it, since its end is toward the punishment of Allah.

His, exalted, saying: "Forbidden to you..." — the verse is a ruling by which Allah forbade seven through lineage, and six through nursing and affinity; and the established sunna added a seventh, which is combining a woman with her paternal aunt (or maternal aunt), and consensus has upheld it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: seven are forbidden through lineage and seven through affinity, and he recited this verse; 'Amr ibn Salim, mawla of the Ansar, said the same, and made the seventh His saying: "And married women from among women" [al-Nisa: 24]. The prohibition of mothers is general in every circumstance, not specified in any respect, and the scholars call it "al-mubham," meaning there is no gate in it and no path to it, due to the closure and strength of the prohibition. Likewise the prohibition of daughters and sisters: the mother is every woman who bore a person, however far up; the daughter is every one he bore, however far down; as for a full sister, or a sister by the father alone, or by the mother alone, she is the one who shares with him a loin or a womb. The paternal aunt is the father's sister, and the maternal aunt is the mother's sister; in these two too there is generality and indeterminacy. Likewise the father's paternal aunt and maternal aunt, the mother's paternal aunt and maternal aunt, and the paternal aunt's paternal aunt. As for the maternal aunt of the paternal aunt, it requires examination: if the paternal aunt is a sister of a father and mother or a sister of a mother, then the maternal aunt of the paternal aunt is not lawful, because she is the sister of the grandmother; but if the paternal aunt is only a sister of the father, then her maternal aunt is a stranger from among the sons of her brother, lawful to men, and may be combined with women. Likewise the paternal aunt of the maternal aunt requires examination: if the maternal aunt is a sister of the mother by the father, her paternal aunt is forbidden, because she is the sister of a grandfather; but if the maternal aunt is only a sister of the mother by the mother, then her paternal aunt is a stranger from among the sons of her sister. Likewise, concerning the daughters of a brother and the daughters of a sister, there is generality and indeterminacy, whether the siblings are full, or by the father, or by the mother.

Abu Haywa read: "min al-ridaa'a" with a kasra on the ra'. Nursing prohibits what lineage prohibits: the nursing mother is a mother, and whatever children of hers came before or after are brothers and sisters; the stallion of the milk is a father, and whatever children of his came before or after are brothers. Ibn Mas'ud read: "allay" with a kasra on the ya'; Ibn Hurmuz read: "wa-ummahatukum allati" in the singular, as if because of the indeterminacy it may be used with the one and the plural.

(p-508) People differed over the interpretation of His, exalted, saying: "and mothers of your wives." The majority of the scholars said: it is of complete generality, whether or not one has consummated with them; so by contracting marriage with the daughter, the mother is forbidden. This is the view of the entire body of the Companions and the Successors and the jurists of the cities. It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he was asked about a man who married a woman and divorced her before consummation: may he marry her mother? He said: Yes, she is in the position of the stepdaughter.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means that His saying: "of your women with whom you have consummated" is a condition for this and for the stepdaughter. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is also related from him as the majority's view. It is related from Zayd ibn Thabit that he used to say: if she dies while he is with her and he takes her inheritance, it is disliked for him to marry her mother; and if he divorces her before consummation, then if he wishes he may do so. Mujahid said: consummation is intended in both cases, and the saying of the majority of people opposes this view. It is related from Zayd ibn Thabit concerning this that he said: "mothers of your women" is unspecified, and the condition applies only to the stepdaughters. Ibn Jurayj said: I said to 'Ata': Did Ibn 'Abbas read: "and mothers of your women with whom you have consummated"? He said: "Lā tatarra'" (do not...). Hajjaj said: I said to Ibn Jurayj: What is "tatarra'"? He said: It is as if he said "lā, lā" (no, no). What refutes this view from the standpoint of grammar is that when two genitives differ, their adjectives are not the same; the meaning is: when they differ regarding the governing element, and this verse has differing governing elements.

**

His, exalted, saying: ﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your women with whom you have consummated; but if you have not consummated with them, there is no blame upon you; and the wives of your sons who are from your loins; and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed. Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Al-Rabiba: the daughter of a man's wife from another husband; she was named so because he raises her in his lap, so she is his marbuba (one brought up). Rabiba is fa'ila in the sense of maf'ula. His, exalted, saying: "who are in your guardianship" mentions the more frequent case, since that is the usual situation of the stepdaughter, and she is forbidden even if she is not in the guardianship, since she is in the legal status of one who is in the guardianship. Except for what is related from 'Ali, that he said: she is lawful if she is not in the guardianship and he has consummated with the mother, if she is far from him. It is said: hajr, with a kasra or fatha on the ha', is the front of a person's garment and what is before him of it while wearing it; then the word was used for keeping and covering, because the wearer protects a child or similar with that part of the garment.

(p-509) The scholars differed over the meaning of His saying: "with whom you have consummated." Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus and Ibn Dinar said: "entering" in this context means sexual intercourse; so if a man divorces after the wedding night (bina') and before intercourse (wat'), her daughter is lawful to him. The majority of scholars, among them Malik ibn Anas, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and others, said: undressing, kissing, lying together and all kinds of sensual enjoyment forbid the daughter just as intercourse does. "Ḥalā'il" is the plural of "ḥalīla," which is the wife, because she is lawful (tahillu) with the man wherever he is lawful; so it is fa'ila in the sense of fa'ila. Al-Zajjaj and a group went to the view that it derives from the word "ḥalāl" (lawful), so it is ḥalīla in the sense of muḥallala. His saying: "who are from your loins" is a specification to exclude every person whom the Arabs used to adopt who was not from the loin; this was among them a common matter with a strong ruling.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: It is related, and Allah knows best, that it was revealed concerning Muhammad, upon him be peace, when he married the wife of Zayd ibn Harītha; the polytheists said: he has married his son's wife, so the verse was revealed.

The wife of a son by nursing is forbidden even if he is not from the loin, by consensus, based on his, ﷺ, saying: "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing." And His, exalted, saying: "and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed" is a term that covers combining by marriage and by right of possession (milk al-yamin). The community agreed on prohibiting combining the two by marriage. As for by right of possession, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: One verse permitted them, and one verse forbade them; as for me, personally, I do not consider combining them good. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas, mentioned by Ibn al-Mundhir, and he mentioned that Ishaq ibn Rahawayh forbade combining them by intercourse, and that the majority of the scholars disliked it, and he placed Malik among those who disliked it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no disagreement about the permissibility of combining the two in ownership, and likewise a mother and her daughter. It follows from Ishaq's view that one who combines them by intercourse should be stoned, and dislike is inferred from Malik's view: that if he has intercourse with one and then wishes to have intercourse with the other, he refrains from both until he makes one of them unlawful to him, and he does not impose a legal penalty on him.

The scholars differed, after the position of prohibiting combining them by intercourse, if he was having intercourse with one and then (p-510) wished to have intercourse with the other: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: it is not permissible for him to have intercourse with the second until he makes the private part of the other unlawful to himself by removing her from his ownership, through sale, manumission, or by giving her in marriage. Ibn al-Mundhir said: there is also a second view, from Qatada, that if he was having intercourse with one and wished to have intercourse with the other, he intends to make the first unlawful to himself and not approach her, then he refrains from her until the first, now unlawful, is cleansed (istibra'), and then he approaches the second.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Malik's position, may God have mercy on him: if a man has two sisters as slave-concubines (in his ownership), he may have intercourse with whichever of them he wishes, and refraining from the other is left to his trustworthiness. If he wants to have intercourse with the other, then he is obliged to make the private part of the first forbidden to himself by an act he performs, such as removing her from his ownership, marrying her off, freeing her for a fixed term, or assigning her to long-term service. If he has been having intercourse with one of them and then pounces on the other without making the first forbidden, both are withheld from him, and it is not permissible for him to approach either of them until he makes the other forbidden. This is not left to his trustworthiness, because he is suspected regarding the one he has already had intercourse with, whereas he was not suspected before, since he had only had intercourse with the one.

If a man has a slave-concubine whom he has intercourse with, and then he marries her sister, then there are three opinions within the school on this. In the third book of the Mudawwana, it is stated that both are withheld from him when the marriage contract is concluded, until he makes one of them forbidden, along with his disapproval of this marriage, since it is a contract in a situation where intercourse is not permitted, and that is disliked except during menstruation, because it is a common and frequent matter. On this same point there is another opinion: the marriage is not valid. Ashhab said in the Book of Istibra' (the waiting period): concluding the marriage with the free woman makes forbidden the private part of the slave-concubine. The Prophet (ﷺ) is authentically reported to have "forbidden that a woman be combined with her paternal aunt, or with her maternal aunt," and the community (ummah) has agreed upon this. Some scholars have held that this hadith abrogates (naskh) the generality of the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. This hadith is mutawatir (widely transmitted). Likewise his saying, peace be upon him: "What is forbidden by nursing is forbidden by lineage," and it has also been said that this too is abrogating.

As for God's words, the Exalted: ﴿except what has already passed﴾, it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but what has already passed of that and occurred, Islam has removed it, for God forgives it, and Islam wipes it away.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 24:

(p-511) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And [forbidden to you are] the married women, except those whom your right hands possess — the decree of Allah upon you. And lawful for you are [all others] beyond that, provided you seek [them] with your wealth, [seeking] chastity, not unlawful intercourse. So for whatever you have enjoyed of them, give them their compensation as an obligation. And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree to beyond the obligation. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

"Al-muhsanat" is conjoined with the prohibited women mentioned before it. Al-tahassun (chastity, protection) is restraint (al-tamanru'), as one says: "hasuna al-makan" (the place became fortified) when it became inaccessible, and from it comes al-hisn (fortress). "Hasunat al-mar'a" means the woman guarded herself by some means of guarding, and "ahsanat nafsaha" (she protected herself) and "ahsanaha ghayruha" (another protected her). The Arabs use ihsan (chastity, protection) in four senses, and the term in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, follows these meanings. It is used for marriage, since possession of a wife is a protection and safeguard. They use ihsan for freedom, because the female slaves in the Jahiliyya were customarily prone to fornication, whereas the free woman was otherwise; do you not see the saying of Hind bint 'Utba to the Prophet, peace be upon him, when she pledged allegiance to him: "Does a free woman commit fornication?" Thus freedom is a protection and safeguard. They use ihsan in Islam, because it is protective, and from it is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Faith is a restraint against treachery."

From it is the saying of the Hudhali poet:

؎ "It is not like the former state of the abode, O Umm Malik, but the chains have encircled the necks."

From it is the saying of the poet:

؎ "She said: 'Come, let us talk,' and I said: 'No, Allah and Islam forbid it of you.'"

(p-512) From it is the saying of Suhaym:

؎ "... ... ... Grey hair and Islam have sufficed a man as a restrainer."

From it is the saying of Abu Hayya:

؎ "She shot me, and the veil of Allah was between me and her."

For one of the opinions regarding "the veil" is that it refers to Islam.

They use ihsan in the sense of chastity (al-'iffa), because when a person is bound by it and it appears in a person and he acquires it as a character trait, it is a protection and safeguard.

Wherever the term occurs in the Qur'an, you will not find it departing from these meanings, but some of these meanings may be stronger in it than others, according to context, and the explanation of that will come in its places, God willing.

As for His saying in this verse, "wal-muhsanat," Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Qilaba, Ibn Zayd, Makhul, al-Zuhri and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: they are the married women, meaning they are forbidden except what the right hand possesses through captivity from the land of war, for that is lawful to the one whose share it falls to, even if she has a husband.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the verse was revealed concerning the occasion when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent an army to (p-513) Awtas; they met an enemy and took captives, who had husbands among the polytheists, so the Muslims felt sinful about having intercourse with them, and the verse was revealed granting dispensation.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, and Ibn 'Abbas also said: the meaning of "al-muhsanat" is the married women, so they are forbidden, except that a man buys a female slave who has a husband; then her sale is her divorce, her gift is her divorce, her giving in charity is her divorce, her manumission is her divorce, her inheritance is her divorce, and the husband's divorcing her is her divorce. Ibn Mas'ud said: if a female slave is sold while she has a husband, the buyer has more right to her womb. The position of Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars is that the transfer of ownership of a female slave is not a divorce, and she has no divorce except the divorce (of her husband).

Others said: "al-muhsanat" in this verse means the chaste women, that is, all women are forbidden, and the name of ihsan is applied to them since the laws in themselves require this.

"Illa ma malakat aymanukum" — they said: its meaning is: by marriage or purchase; all of that falls under the ownership of the right hand. This view was held by Abu al-'Aliya, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, Tawus, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and 'Ata', and 'Ubayda narrated it from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

(p-514) Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-muhsanat" are the chaste women among the Muslims and among the People of the Book.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

By this interpretation the meaning of the verse returns to the prohibition of fornication.

al-Tabari transmitted from 'Urwa that he said, in interpreting His saying, Exalted is He, "wal-muhsanat": they are the free women, and "illa ma malakat aymanukum" means: by marriage. This is on the basis of a connected exception (istithna' muttasil); but if slave women are intended, the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati').

It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: there were women who would come to us as emigrants, then their husbands would emigrate, so we were prevented from them by His saying, Exalted is He, "wal-muhsanat"... the verse.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an opinion that returns to what has been mentioned among the opinions.

al-Tabari transmitted that a man said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: Did you not see Ibn 'Abbas when he was asked about this verse, "wal-muhsanat min al-nisa'," and he said nothing about it? Sa'id said: Ibn 'Abbas did not know it. He also transmitted from Mujahid that he said: If I knew someone who could explain this verse to me, I would ride camels' livers to reach him. [The verse ends:] "...wal-muhsanat" to "...Hakiman."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I do not know how this opinion was attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, nor how Mujahid arrived at this view.

It is narrated from Ibn Shihab that he was asked about this verse, "wal-muhsanat min al-nisa'," and he said: It is related that in this verse He forbade married women and chaste women, both free and enslaved. He permitted none of that except by marriage or purchase and ownership. This is a good opinion, which generalizes the word ihsan and the phrase "milk al-yamin." On this interpretation, in my view, the position of Malik in the Muwatta' is explained, for he said:

(p-515) "They are the married women," and this goes back to the fact that Allah forbade fornication, so he interpreted ihsan as marriage, and then returned to it as chastity.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamza recited "wal-muhsanat" with a fatha on the sad in the whole Qur'an, and al-Kisa'i recited it so in this place alone. The rest of what is in the Qur'an, "al-muhsinat" with a kasra on the sad, and "muhsinatin" likewise, they recited. It is narrated from 'Alqama that he recited all that is in the Qur'an with a kasra on the sad. The fatha on the sad means: others protected them, by marriage, Islam, chastity or freedom. The kasra on the sad means: they protected themselves by these aspects or some of them.

Yazid ibn Qutayb recited "wal-muhsunat" with a damma on the sad, and this is by making the damma follow the damma.

The majority of people recited "kitab Allah," and that is in the accusative as an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid).

Abu Haywa and Muhammad ibn al-Samayfa' al-Yamani recited "kataba Allahu 'alaykum" as a past verb with Allah the Exalted as its subject.

'Ubayda al-Salmani and others said: His saying, "kitab Allah 'alaykum," is an indication of what is established in the Qur'an in His saying, "mathna wa thula<u>th</u> wa rubaa'" (two, three and four). This is far-fetched. The more apparent view is that His saying "kitab Allah 'alaykum" (p-516) is in fact an indication of the prohibition that separates people from what the Arabs used to do. The commentators differed in the phrasing of His saying, Exalted is He: "wa uhilla lakum ma waraa'a dhalikum." As-Suddi said: the meaning is: "and lawful for you is what is below the five" — that you seek with your wealth in the manner of marriage. 'Ubayda al-Salmani said similarly. 'Ata' and others said: the meaning is: "and lawful for you is what is beyond those who are forbidden of the rest of the relatives; they are lawful for you to marry." Qatada said: "and lawful for you is what is beyond that" refers to slave women.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The wording of the verse encompasses all these opinions.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "wa ahilla lakum" with a fatha on the alif and the ha, and this suits His saying "kitab Allah," since the meaning is: Allah prescribed that as a book. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "wa uhilla" with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the ha, and this suits His saying: "hurrimat 'alaykum" (An-Nisa': 23).

"Al-waraa'" in this verse means what is considered after the prohibited women have been considered. Thus they are "beyond those" in this respect. "An tabtaghu bi-amwalikum" is an expression that combines marriage and purchase; "an" is in the accusative position, and according to Hamza's reading it is in the nominative position, and the accusative is possible by dropping the preposition ba'.

"Muhsinin" means chaste, that is, you protect yourselves thereby; "ghayra musafihin" means not fornicators. Al-sifah is fornication, and it is derived from "safh al-ma'" (pouring out and flowing of water), and this name became attached to fornication. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when he heard the drum at a wedding: "This is marriage, not fornication, nor secret marriage."

The commentators differed about the meaning of His saying: "fa-ma istamta'tum bihi minhunna fa-atuhunna ujurahunna fariḍah." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others said: the meaning is: when you have enjoyed a wife, and intercourse has occurred even once, then it is obligatory to give the compensation, which is the entire dower; and the word "fa-ma" indicates that even slight intercourse makes the giving of compensation obligatory.

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi and others that the verse concerns the marriage of enjoyment (mut'a). Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited: "fa-ma istamta'tum bihi minhunna ila ajalin musamman fa-atuhunna ujurahunna." Ibn 'Abbas said to Abu Nadra: "Thus did Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, send it down."

al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba narrated that 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Had 'Umar not forbidden temporary marriage, none but a wretch would have committed fornication."

Temporary marriage was permitted at the beginning of Islam, then the Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade it. Ibn al-Musayyab said: it was abrogated by the verse of inheritance, since there is no inheritance in temporary marriage. It was also said: by the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: "O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them for their waiting period" (At-Talaq: 1). 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: it was abrogated by His saying: "And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives" (Al-Mu'minun: 5–6). There is no marriage with a fixed term, nor with the lifting of divorce, the waiting period and inheritance. Its form was that a man marries a woman with two witnesses (p-518) and the permission of the guardian for a fixed term, on the condition that there is no inheritance between them. He gives her what they agreed upon; when the term has expired, he has no further claim over her, and she must observe a period to cleanse her womb, because the child is undoubtedly attributed to him; if she does not conceive, she is free for another.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In al-Nahhas's book there is a gross error in wording here, which gives the impression that the child is not attributed in temporary marriage. al-Mahdawi transmitted from Ibn al-Musayyab that temporary marriage was without a guardian or witnesses, but in what he related there is weakness. "Fariḍah" is put in the accusative as an infinitive in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

The commentators differed about the meaning of His saying: "wa la junaha 'alaykum" and the rest of the verse. Those who held that the preceding verse is a command to give women their dowers when consummated said: this refers to what is agreed upon by way of reduction or postponement after the obligation has been settled; that which is done by mutual consent is permissible and valid. Those who held that the preceding verse concerns temporary marriage said: this refers to the permissibility and validity of what they agree upon in terms of an increase in the term of the temporary marriage or an increase in the compensation.

The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿And whoever among you cannot afford (ṭawlan) to marry free believing women, let him marry from what your right hands possess of your believing young women. And Allah knows best your faith; you are of one another.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Malik ibn Anas in al-Mudawwana said: ṭawl here means wealth and means (al-sa'a fi al-mal). Rabi'a and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: ṭawl here means endurance and self-restraint (al-jalad wa al-sabr) for one who loves a slave-woman and is so attached to her that he cannot marry anyone else. For him it is permissible to marry a slave-woman if he cannot control his desire for her, even if he has the means to marry a free woman. Then, on this interpretation, His saying ﴿for him who fears falling into sin (al-'anat)﴾ is an explanation of the description of lacking endurance. On the other interpretation, marrying a slave-woman is conditional on two things: lack of means, and fear of sin; it is not valid unless both are present. This is the explicit doctrine of Malik in al-Mudawwana, in the transmission of Ibn Nafi', Ibn al-Qasim, Ibn Wahb, and Ibn Ziyad: that a free man may in no circumstance marry a slave-woman unless he lacks the means to pay the bridal gift of a free woman and fears sin in that case.

Malik said in the Kitab Muhammad: if he finds the bridal gift but cannot afford maintenance, it is not lawful for him to marry a slave-woman.

Ashhab said: that is permissible, since the maintenance of a slave-woman is the responsibility of her people if he does not take her into his household.

Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: it is not lawful for a free man to marry a slave-woman, and if he does, it is not upheld unless both conditions are met, as God the Exalted said. Ashhab also said this, and said: Ibn al-Qasim used to mention that he heard Malik say: marriage to a slave-woman is lawful in the Book of God, mighty and majestic.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is in al-Mudawwana.

Sahnun said in another work: this is in His saying ﴿And marry the single among you and the righteous of your slaves and maidservants﴾ [al-Nur: 32], and Ibn Muzayn said the same.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse does not necessarily imply that a slave-woman is permitted to a free man without the two conditions. Malik said in al-Mudawwana: a free woman is not a "ṭawl" that prevents marrying a slave-woman if he does not find the means for another and fears sin. In the Kitab Muhammad he said something implying that a free wife counts as ṭawl. The shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi said: this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Something similar is narrated from Ibn Habib, and Abu Hanifa said it. The implication is that whoever has a free wife may not marry a slave-woman, even if he lacks means and fears sin, because he is seeking desire while having a woman. al-Tabari said this too and argued for it. "Ṭawlan" may grammatically be an object of "istita'a," and "an yankiha" is in the position of a substitute (badal) for "ṭawlan," or in the accusative position with the implied "li-an yankiha." This needs consideration.

It is also valid for "ṭawlan" to be an accusative of the verbal noun (maṣdar), with "istita'a" as its governing verb, since they are close in meaning; and "an yankiha" would then be an object of "istita'a" or of the maṣdar. You say: ṭāla al-rajul ṭawlan, with the letter ṭa' vowelled with a fatha, when he is generous, finds means and his standing is widened. Ṭūlan, with a ḍamma on the ṭa', is the opposite of shortness.

"Al-muḥṣanat" here means free women; the division between them and the slave-women indicates this. One group said its meaning is "chaste," but this is weak, because slave-women fall under it. The readings of "al-muḥṣanat" have already been mentioned. "Al-mu'minat" is a descriptive adjective. As for those who say that a man who finds means only for a Christian free woman, not a believing one, must refrain from marrying slave-women: the description is then not a required condition, but was mentioned because it is the purpose of marriage, since the slave-woman is a believer. This is the Maliki position, stated by Ibn al-Majishun in al-Wadiha. Whoever says that a man who finds means only for a Christian woman may marry a slave-woman if he wishes holds that the description of believers in the verse is a required condition for permitting marriage to slave-women. The question is disputed, as we have mentioned.

"Ma" in His saying ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾ may be a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle, its implied sense being "from the ownership of your right hands," or it may be intended as the category of what is owned, in which case it refers to that.

"Fatāt" although in the language it applies to any young woman, its customary use is for slave-women; likewise "fatan." The addressed pronouns in "you" are general: among you are those who marry, among you are the owners, since a man marries the young woman of his own household. This extension in language is common.

"Al-mu'minat" here is a required descriptive condition according to Malik and the majority of his companions, since they say: marriage to a non-Muslim slave-woman is not permitted in any way. A group of scholars, including the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), said: marriage to a Christian slave-woman is permitted, and "al-mu'minat" is meant as a mode of preference. They argued by analogy to free women: since "al-mu'minat" in the case of free women does not prohibit marrying free Christian women, so too in the case of slave-women it does not prohibit marrying Christian slave-women. Ashhab said in al-Mudawwana: it is permitted for a Muslim slave to marry a Christian slave-woman.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Thus the prohibition in his view is that the husband should be superior in both freedom and religion together.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And Allah knows best your faith﴾ means: God knows the hidden matters, and you know their outward aspects. So if a young woman outwardly has faith, her marriage is valid, and the knowledge of her inner state belongs to God. This is only so that one who is perplexed about the faith of some slave-women, such as one recently taken captive, or a mute woman, or the like, should not be troubled. The wording also alerts that the faith of a slave-woman may sometimes be better than that of some free women; that is, do not be impressed by the meaning of freedom.

His saying "you are of one another": a group said it is a nominative construction (mubtada' and khabar), and the purpose of this statement is that you, people, are equal, the sons of free women and the sons of slave-women; the most honoured of you before God is the most pious. This is a preparation for the souls of the Arabs, who used to despise the child of a slave-woman. When the Law came, they were informed that this disdain has no meaning. al-Tabari said: it is in the nominative by a verb whose implied sense is: "let him marry from what your right hands possess of one another." On this, there is an inversion of order, and this is a weak opinion.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people, and give them their bridal gifts fairly, as chaste women, not fornicators nor those who take secret lovers. And when they are married (uḥṣinna), if they commit a lewd act, then upon them is half the punishment for free women. That is for him among you who fears sin, but that you endure is better for you; and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

His saying "with the permission of their people" means with the guardianship of their masters who own them. His saying "and give them their bridal gifts" means their dowries; this was said by Ibn Zayd and others. "Fairly" means according to the Law and the Sunna. This implies that they have more right to their dowries than their masters. This is the doctrine of Malik. He said in the Kitab al-Rahun: it is not for the master to take his slave-woman's dowry and leave her without provision. Sahnun said in al-Mudawwana: how is this, when he does not give her a dwelling with him? Some jurists said: what is in al-Mudawwana means that it applies on condition of providing a dwelling. On this understanding, Sahnun's statement is not a contradiction.

"Muḥṣanat" and what follows it are circumstantial (ḥāl). The apparent meaning is "chaste," since other aspects of ihsan are far-fetched, except "Muslim," which is close. The governing verb of the circumstantial is "fankiḥūhunna." It is also possible that "fankiḥūhunna bi-idhni ahlihinna" is a complete sentence, and then a new sentence begins: "wa-ātawhunna ujūrahunna muzawwajāt ghayr musāfiḥāt," so the governing verb is "wa-ātawhunna," and the meaning of ihsan is marriage.

"Musāfiḥāt" among fornicators refers to those who are openly common, who are a marketplace for fornication. "Muttakhidhāt akhdān" are those who conceal themselves, who keep one lover after another and commit fornication secretly. These were two kinds of fornication in the pre-Islamic period, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Amir al-Sha'bi, al-Dahhak, and others. Moreover, this is a rational division which does not establish actual existence, except that the adulteress either does not repel the hand of any touching her, or she restricts herself to one man.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When they are muhṣanna﴾, the verse ... Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read "uḥṣinna" with the verb in the passive. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the verb in the active, and there is a difference reported from 'Asim. The sense of the first reading is marriage; the second is Islam or something else that is their own action. Each meaning enters the other. The commentators disagreed about what ihsan means here. The majority said it is Islam: if a Muslim slave-woman commits adultery, she receives half the punishment of a free woman, and her Islam is the ihsan mentioned in the verse. One group said her ihsan in the verse is marriage to a free man; so if a Muslim slave-woman who has not married commits adultery, there is no punishment for her. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and Qatada. Another group said ihsan in the verse is marriage, but the punishment is obligatory on a Muslim slave-woman by the Sunna, namely the authentic hadith in Muslim and al-Bukhari that it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, if a slave-woman commits adultery and is not muhsana?" and he prescribed the punishment for her.

al-Zuhri said: the married one is punished by the Qur'an, and the Muslim who is not married is punished by the hadith.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This hadith and the question from the Companions imply that they understood from the Qur'an that the meaning of "uḥṣinna" is "married," and the Prophet's ﷺ answer confirms this meaning. As for one who wishes to weaken the view that it means Islam, on the grounds that the description of their faith has already been stated and established, this is not necessary, because it is permissible in speech to break off and add. If they are in this state of faith already mentioned, then if they commit a lewd act, the punishment applies, and that is sound.

The lewd act (fāḥisha) here is adultery, by the indication of the obligation of the prescribed punishment. "Muḥṣanāt" in this verse means free women, since that is the condition for the full punishment, and stoning does not halve, so it was not intended in the verse by consensus. Then there was disagreement: Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said that the slave-woman receives fifty lashes only, nothing more. al-Tabari and a group of the Successors said that she receives fifty lashes and half the year of exile, which is six months' banishment. The reference of "that" is to marrying slave-women.

Linguistically, "al-'anat" means hardship. One group said the intended meaning here is adultery; this was said by Mujahid. Ibn 'Abbas said: the one who marries a slave-woman refrains from adultery only slightly. He said: al-'anat is adultery. 'Atiyya al-Hufi and al-Dahhak also said this. Another group said it means sin, and another said it means the prescribed punishment.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse admits all of that, and everything that causes hardship, in this world and the next.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿but that you endure is better for you﴾ means abstaining from marrying slave-women. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. This is an encouragement to abstain, and its reason is what marrying slave-women leads to: enslaving the child and their servitude. This clause is a nominal sentence whose implied form is: "and your patience is better for you." "And Allah is Forgiving" means: to whoever did so and married.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 26–28:

(p-525) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways (sunan) of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness. And Allah is Knowing, Wise.﴾ ﴿And Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness, while those who follow their desires desire that you deviate into a tremendous deviation.﴾ ﴿Allah desires to lighten (the burden) for you, and man was created weak.﴾

The grammarians differed concerning the lam in His saying "li-yubayyina" (in order that He may make clear). The position of Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the implied construction is li-an yubayyina (that He may make clear), with the object being understood, its implied form being: Allah desires this. If it is the lam of genitive (lam al-jarr) or the lam of purpose (lam kay), then in both cases an implied "an" must be assumed, because they only enter upon nouns. Al-Farra' and the Kufans said: the lam itself functions in the same way as "an", but this view is weak. A parallel to this lam is the saying of the poet:

"I desire li-ansa dhikraha (to forget her remembrance)..."

Some grammarians said: "My desire is li-ansa (to forget)."

"Wa-yahdiyakum" (and guide you) means: guide you (yurshidukum); it cannot be directed to anything other than this, by the indication of "the ways" (al-sunan). And "al-sunan" means: the paths, the aspects of affairs and their directions.

(p-526) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It appears from the force of this statement that our law regarding legislated matters is like the law of those before us, but this is not so. Rather, this guidance is in one of two respects: either in that we were addressed in every narrative with prohibitions and commands, just as they were addressed in their narratives, and what was legislated for us was legislated for them, so we were guided to their ways in that, even if our rulings and their rulings differ; the second matter is that our being guided to their ways lies in our obeying and hearing as they heard and obeyed, so the similarity occurs from this aspect.

"Those before us" are the believers in every law. The repentance of Allah toward His servant is his return with him from sins to acts of obedience, and His enabling him to do so. The word "Knowing" (ʿAlim) is fitting here in accordance with what preceded of the ways of the laws and the place of the benefits; and "Wise" (Hakim) means: One who places things in their proper places in accordance with wisdom and perfection.

The repetition of Allah's desire to turn to His servants in forgiveness is a reinforcement of the first statement, and the purpose of this verse is nothing but to inform about the desire of those who follow their desires. The desire of Allah was placed first as a preliminary, showing the corruption of the desire of those who follow their desires. The exegetes differed regarding "those who follow their desires." Mujahid said: they are the fornicators. Al-Suddi said: they are the Jews and Christians. A group said: they are specifically the Jews, because they wanted the Muslims to follow them in marrying the sisters from the father's side. Ibn Zayd said: it is general concerning these people and every follower of a desire, and al-Tabari preferred this view.

Al-Jumhur read "mayla" (a tremendous deviation) with a sukun on the ya'; al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "mayala" with a fatha on the ya'.

As for His saying, "Allah desires to lighten (the burden) for you": the apparent purpose of this verse is that it concerns Allah's lightening, by leave of marrying female slaves, the abandonment of marriage to slave women through permitting that; and that His information about man's weakness is specifically in the matter of women, i.e., since We knew your weakness in restraining yourselves from women, We lightened for you by permitting slave women. Likewise said Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and Tawus. Tawus said: a person is never weaker in anything than in the matter of women.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Then, after this purpose, the verse comes out in the mode of bounty, because it encompasses everything that Allah the Exalted lightened for His servants, and made the religion easy; and the information about man's weakness becomes general, according to what he is in himself: weak, whose desire inclines him in most cases. "Al-insan" (man) is in the nominative as the unnamed subject (ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu), and "da'ifan" (weak) is a circumstantial accusative (hal).

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read "wa-khalqu al-insan" (and the creation of man) with the verb in the active form, and "da'ifan" is also a circumstantial accusative on this reading. It is also valid that "khuliqa" carries the sense of "ju'ila" (was made), which gives it the capacity to take two objects, so that His saying "da'ifan" is the second object.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 29–30:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever to you Merciful.﴾ ﴿And whoever does that in aggression and injustice – We will drive him into a Fire, and that is ever for Allah an easy matter.﴾

This is an exception, not from the first clause. The meaning is: "But if it is trade, then consume it."

The people of Medina, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "tijaratun" (تِجارَةٌ) with a nominative ending, taking "an" (أنْ) as a complete (تَمام) verb-form, meaning "it occurred" (وقَعَ). A group, namely the Kufans – Hamza, 'Asim (p-528) and al-Kisa'i – read "tijaratan" (تِجارَةً) with an accusative ending, taking "kana" (كانَ) as a defective (نُقْصان) verb, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd.

Both are strong opinions, except that the completeness of "kana" is preferred by some, because it is a relative clause (صِلَة) of "an", so it is lowered from its rank when it is free of a relative clause and other things. This is a preference that is not strong, but it is good, and "an" is in the position of an accusative. Whoever reads "tijaratan" with the accusative makes the subject of "kana" an implied pronoun, its estimate being: "the wealth is wealth of trade," so the modified noun is omitted and the modifier is put in its place; or the estimate is: "except that trade be trade." Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

"...... when there is a day of many stars, most dreadful"

That is: "when the day is a day." The exception is disconnected (مُنْقَطِع) in every estimate, and in the reading with the nominative. Consuming wealth through trade is permissible by the consensus of the Community, and the majority hold that deception (غَبْن) in trade is permissible. An example of this: a man sells a ruby for a dirham while it is worth a hundred; this is permissible. It is supported by the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A town dweller should not sell for a desert dweller," because he only intended by it that the desert dweller should sell by his own effort, and that the town dweller should not prevent the town dweller from God's provision through his deception. A group said: deception that exceeds a third is rejected, and only what is close and customary in trade is permitted; but what is excessive and gross is not. This was said by Ibn Wahb from among the companions of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him.

"Mutual consent" (عن تَراضٍ) means: "by consent," except that it came in the form of mufa'alah, since trade is from two parties. The people of knowledge differed about mutual consent. A group said: its completion and its certainty is by the separation of the bodies after the contract of sale, or by one of them saying to his companion: "Choose," and he says: "I have chosen," and that is also after the contract, so it becomes binding at that time. This is the saying of al-Shafi'i and a group of the Companions, and their proof is the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not separated, except a sale of option," which is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar and Abu Barza, and their opinion – and they are the two narrators – is that it is the separation of bodies.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Separation does not occur in reality except with bodies, because it is one of the attributes of substances.

Malik and Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on them both, said: the completion of mutual consent is that the sale is concluded by tongues, so the contract becomes binding by that and the option is cancelled. And they both said, regarding the hadith mentioned above, that it is separation by speech. Some of them argued with His saying: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [an-Nisa': 130], so this is separation by speech, because it is by divorce.

Whoever argued for al-Shafi'i said: rather, it is separation of bodies, by the evidence of the dual pronoun. Divorce has no share for the woman in it, and her share is only in the separation of the body, which is the fruit of divorce. Al-Shafi'i said: if the meaning of his saying "they separate" were by speech, which is the contract, the benefit in his saying "The two parties to a sale have the option" would be void, because there is no doubt that every owner of merchandise has the choice as long as he has not contracted, so the information comes to nothing of benefit.

Whoever argued for Malik said: the intent in the hadith is only to inform about the obligation of the contract's establishment, so his saying "The two parties have the option" came as a preparation for that, and although the preparation is known, it prepares the soul to feel the establishment and binding of the contract.

Al-Shafi'i relied on his saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "Let a man not bid over his brother's bid, and let a man not sell over his brother's sale," so he made them two ranks, because the state of the two parties to a sale after the contract and before separation requires that a spoiler spoil it by adding to the merchandise, so its owner chooses to dissolve the first deal; so the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that spoiling. Do you not see that he, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "Let a man not propose over his brother's proposal," so it is in the rank of "Let him not bid," and he did not say: "Let him not marry over his brother's marriage," because there is no rank after the marriage contract that requires choice, by consensus of the Community.

Whoever argues for Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: his saying, upon him be prayer and peace, "Let him not bid" and "Let him not sell" are all one rank before the contract, and he said "Let him not sell" as a figurative usage for "Let him not bid," since its end is to sale; so they are all together in the status of his saying "Let him not propose," and the contract is binding in both of them.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying in the hadith, "except a sale of option," means according to the Malikis: the two bargainers have the option as long as they have not contracted; when they contract, the option is cancelled, except in a sale of option that was contracted from the start with an option for a certain period, for then the option does not lapse in it.

Its meaning according to the Shafi'is: the two parties to a sale, after their contract, are given the choice as long as they remain in their session, except a sale in which one of them says to his companion: "Choose," and he chooses; for the option is then cut off between them even if they have not separated. If a sale of option is supposed, the meaning is: "except a sale of option," for the option then remains after separation of bodies.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾. Al-Hasan read "wa la tuqattilu" (وَلا تُقَتِّلُوا) with intensive form, so the commentators agreed that the aim of this verse is the prohibition of some people killing others. Then its wording includes that a man kills himself with intent to kill, or that he exposes himself to a hazard by which he may die. All of this is covered by the prohibition. 'Amr ibn al-'As argued with this verse when he refrained from bathing in cold water out of fear for his own life, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved his argument.

(p-531) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does that in aggression and injustice﴾. The commentators differed about what "that" (ذَلِكَ) refers to. 'Ata' said: "that" refers to killing, because it is the nearest mentioned thing. A group said: "that" refers to consuming wealth unjustly and killing the self, because the prohibition of both came in a connected sequence, and then the threat came in accordance with the prohibition. A group said: "that" refers to everything He forbade from the beginning of the surah up to His saying: ﴿And whoever does that﴾. Al-Tabari said: "that" refers to what He forbade in the last threat, which is His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾ [an-Nisa': 19], because every prohibition from the beginning of the surah was joined with a threat except from His saying ﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾ [an-Nisa': 19], for it and the prohibitions after it have no threat with them except His saying: ﴿And whoever does that in aggression and injustice﴾.

Aggression (عُدْوان) is transgressing the limit. "Nusliihi" (نُصْلِيهِ) means: We touch him with its heat, as a roasted sheep is exposed to the fire, i.e., We burn him with it.

Al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i read "nasliihi" (نَصْلِيهِ) with a fatha on the nun. The reading of the majority is with a damma on the nun, from the transitive form of "salia" (صَلِيَ) with hamza. The reading of these two is according to the dialect of one who says "sallaytuhu naran" (صَلَّيْتُهُ نارًا) meaning "asliituhu" (أصْلَيْتُهُ). Al-Zajjaj related that it was also read "nusallihi" (نُصَلِّيهِ) with a fatha on the sad and a shadda on the lam with a kasra, and that is easy for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because His proof is conclusive and His judgment has no repeller.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 29–30:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever to you Merciful.﴾ ﴿And whoever does that in aggression and injustice – We will drive him into a Fire, and that is ever for Allah an easy matter.﴾

This is an exception, not from the first clause. The meaning is: "But if it is trade, then consume it."

The people of Medina, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "tijaratun" (تِجارَةٌ) with a nominative ending, taking "an" (أنْ) as a complete (تَمام) verb-form, meaning "it occurred" (وقَعَ). A group, namely the Kufans – Hamza, 'Asim (p-528) and al-Kisa'i – read "tijaratan" (تِجارَةً) with an accusative ending, taking "kana" (كانَ) as a defective (نُقْصان) verb, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd.

Both are strong opinions, except that the completeness of "kana" is preferred by some, because it is a relative clause (صِلَة) of "an", so it is lowered from its rank when it is free of a relative clause and other things. This is a preference that is not strong, but it is good, and "an" is in the position of an accusative. Whoever reads "tijaratan" with the accusative makes the subject of "kana" an implied pronoun, its estimate being: "the wealth is wealth of trade," so the modified noun is omitted and the modifier is put in its place; or the estimate is: "except that trade be trade." Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

"...... when there is a day of many stars, most dreadful"

That is: "when the day is a day." The exception is disconnected (مُنْقَطِع) in every estimate, and in the reading with the nominative. Consuming wealth through trade is permissible by the consensus of the Community, and the majority hold that deception (غَبْن) in trade is permissible. An example of this: a man sells a ruby for a dirham while it is worth a hundred; this is permissible. It is supported by the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A town dweller should not sell for a desert dweller," because he only intended by it that the desert dweller should sell by his own effort, and that the town dweller should not prevent the town dweller from God's provision through his deception. A group said: deception that exceeds a third is rejected, and only what is close and customary in trade is permitted; but what is excessive and gross is not.
