(p-٥٣٢) "Tajtanibū" means: you leave aside, you keep away from. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Jubayr read "in tajtanibū kabīra" (in the singular). Al-Mufaddal, from 'Asim, read "yukaffir" and "wa-yudkhilkum" with the third-person marker (ya-). The rest read them with the first-person nūn. Both readings are good. Ibn 'Abbas read "'ankum min sayyi'atikum," with the added "min." The Seven Readers, except Nafi', read "mudkhalan" with a ḍamma on the mīm. Nafi' read "madkhalan" with a fatḥa. Abu Bakr also transmitted this from 'Asim here and in al-Hajj. There is no disagreement that in Surat Banī Isrā'īl, "mudkhal" and "mukhraja ṣidq" are both read with a ḍamma on the mīm.

Abu 'Ali said: "madkhalan" with a fatḥa may be a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its governing verb is an implied verb indicated by the apparent verb, the sense being: "and He admits you, so you enter an entrance." It may also be a place-noun (ism makān), and then the apparent verb governs it directly. Likewise "mudkhalan" with a ḍamma may bear both meanings. When the apparent verb does not govern it, its second object is omitted, the sense being: "and He admits you to Paradise (al-Janna)."

The scholars differed concerning "al-kabā'ir" (the major sins). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "They are seven: associating partners with Allah (al-shirk), killing a soul, slandering chaste women (qadhf al-muḥṣanāt), consuming the property of orphans, consuming usury (ribā), fleeing on the day of battle, and becoming a bedouin after emigration (al-ta'arrub ba'da al-hijra)." 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "The major sins are seven, and for each of them there is a verse in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

The Qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He mentioned, as 'Ali did, and he took the verse concerning becoming a bedouin to be His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them...﴾ [Muḥammad: 25], to the end of the verse. In al-Bukhari, in the Book of Ḥudūd, in the chapter on "throwing accusations at chaste women," it occurs: "Avoid the seven destroyers: associating partners with Allah, sorcery, killing a soul, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan, turning away on the day of battle, and slandering chaste, unwary, believing women." 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: "They are nine: associating partners with Allah, killing, fleeing, slander, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan, violating sanctity in the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Ḥarām), one who seeks sorcery, and a parent's weeping because of disobedience (al-'uqūq)." 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: it refers to everything forbidden from the beginning of Surat al-Nisā' up to thirty verses into it, and these are: ﴿If you avoid...﴾. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud also said: "They are four as well: associating partners with Allah, despair of the mercy of Allah (al-qunūṭ min raḥmat Allāh), despair of the comfort of Allah (al-yaʾs min rawḥ Allāh), and feeling secure from the plan of Allah (al-amn min makr Allāh)." It is also related from Ibn Mas'ud: "They are three: despair (al-qunūṭ), hopelessness (al-yaʾs), and feeling secure (al-amn), the ones mentioned earlier." Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "The major sins are everything for which a threat of fire, or punishment, or curse is stated, or what resembles that." A group of the usulīyūn (scholars of legal theory) said: in this context, they are the kinds of shirk with which deeds are of no benefit. A man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Inform me about the seven major sins." He said: "They are closer to seventy." Ibn 'Abbas also said: "Everything Allah has forbidden is a major sin (kabīr)." Here enter adultery (zinā), drinking wine (shurb al-khamr), false testimony (zūr), backbiting (ghība), and other things that have been stated explicitly in hadiths, where the intention was not to restrict the major sins to them, but rather some of them were mentioned as examples. On this view stand the imams of kalām: al-Qāḍī, Abu al-Ma'ālī, and others. They said: "The term 'minor' (ṣaghīra) is used only in relation to what is greater than it, while in itself every act of disobedience is major (kabīra) in terms of the one who disobeys, all being alike."

This verse is supported by the hadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Book of Wudu' in Muslim, "from 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'No Muslim man attends a prescribed prayer, and performs its ablution, its humility, and its bowing well, except that it is an expiation for what came before it of sins, so long as he does not commit a major sin, and that is for all time.'"

(p-٥٣٤) The scholars differed on this issue. A group of jurists and people of hadith hold that when a man avoids the major sins and fulfils the obligations, his minor sins are expiated, such as looking and the like, definitively, based on the apparent meaning of this verse and the apparent meaning of the hadith. As for the usulīyūn, they said: it is not necessary, with certainty, that minor sins be expiated by avoiding major sins. Rather, that is to be understood as a strong presumption and a firm hope, while the will of Allah remains. What indicates this is that if we were to hold definitively, for one who avoids major sins and fulfils the obligations, that his minor sins are expiated definitively, then he would be in the position of the permissible act about which one is certain there is no accountability, and that would undermine the bonds of the Sharia. The meaning of "major sins" according to the usulīyūn in this verse is the categories of disbelief (ajnās al-kufr). The verse that qualifies the ruling, to which all these unqualified statements are to be referred, is His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisā': 48]. "Karīman" (noble) implies the nobility of excellence and the absence of defects, just as you say: "a noble garment" (thawb karīm) and "of noble lineage" (karīm al-maḥtid). This is a verse of hope. It is related from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Five verses in Surat al-Nisā' are dearer to me than all of this world: His saying: ﴿If you avoid...﴾, to the end of the verse; His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisā': 48], to the end of the verse; His saying: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ [al-Nisā': 110]; His saying also: ﴿He multiplies it﴾ [al-Nisā': 40]; and His saying: ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾ [al-Nisā': 152], to the end of the verse."

(p. 535) Allah the Exalted says:

﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you excel others. For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of all things.﴾

The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is that the women said: "Would that we were equal to the men in inheritance, and that we shared with them in the military campaigns." It is narrated that Umm Salamah said this or something similar. The men said: "Would that we had in the Hereafter a greater portion than the women, as we have over them in this world." So this noble verse was revealed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because in such wishing there is a passing of judgment upon the Divine Law, and an opening to objection against the ruling of Allah. Therefore this is a prohibition of every wish that contradicts a legal ruling (hukm shar'i). Included in the prohibition is that a man wishes for another's condition, whether in religion or in worldly affairs, on condition that what the other has be removed, for this is envy (hasad) itself. Some scholars disliked that a person wish for the condition of a man that occupies his thoughts, even if he does not wish for the man's condition to end. This applies to the blessings of this world. As for righteous deeds, that is praiseworthy (al-hasan). As for when a person wishes something from Allah without linking his wish to anything we have mentioned, that is permissible. This is found in the Hadith of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in his saying: "I would love to be killed in the way of Allah, then brought to life, then killed," and in other places, and in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾

As for the Exalted's words: ﴿For men there is a share [an-nasib] ...﴾ [al-Nisa': 7] the verse. Qatadah said: "This refers to inheritance, because the Arabs did not give women inheritance."

(p. 536) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak opinion, and the word "iktisab" (earning/acquisition) refutes it clearly. However, it fits with the women's statement, "Would that we had equality with men in inheritance." So it is as if it were said, because of them: "Do not wish for this; for each has his share." Another group said: its meaning is: of reward and good deeds. So it is as if it were said to people: "Do not wish, concerning a matter, for the opposite of what Allah has judged, out of a preference you see for yourselves, for Allah has made for every person a share of reward and bounty according to what he earns in what has been prescribed for him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This statement is the clearest, most evident and most comprehensive. Another group said: its meaning is: do not wish for the opposite of what Allah has set as His distribution of excellence, for He, the Exalted, has made for each person acquisitions specific to him, and these are his share. He has assigned jihad, spending, the striving for livelihood, and bearing burdens such as judgeship, governance, and hisba (enjoining good and overseeing public conduct), and other such things, to men. And He has assigned bearing and the hardship of pregnancy, good conduct toward the husband, guarding the husband's absence, and service of the household, to women.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is like the statement before it, except that it differs by dividing the tasks. In linking the share to acquisition there is an exhortation to work and an alert to the earning of good.

The majority of the Seven Readers read "wa-s'alu" (واسْألُوا) with a hamza and sukun on the sin. Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read "wa-salu" (وَسَلُوا), dropping the hamza's vowel onto the sin. This applies wherever the word occurs, except in His saying ﴿wa-s'aluu ma anfaqtum﴾ (and ask for what you have spent) [al-Mumtahanah: 10], where they all agreed on the hamza. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Layth ibn Abi Salim said: this refers to acts of worship, religion, and righteous deeds, not to the bounties of this world. The majority said: it is general, and this is what the wording requires. And the phrase "wa-s'aluu" requires a second object (maf'ul thani). So it is, according to some grammarians, "min fadlihi" (of His bounty), the estimate being: "ask Allah for His bounty." But Sibawayh does not permit this, because it involves omitting "min" in an obligatory position, and according to him the object is implied, its estimate being: "ask Allah for Paradise, or much, or a portion of His bounty."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the most correct view. In my opinion it is also good to estimate the object as "your hopes" (amanikum), since what precedes supports this estimate.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of all things﴾: its meaning is that Allah's knowledge has necessitated accuracy, perfection and firm decree, so do not oppose it with wishing or anything else. This verse implies that Allah knows things, and the creed requires that He knows the non-existent possibilities whose occurrence is permitted, even if they are not "things." The verse does not contradict that; rather, it points to some of His known matters and refrains from others.

[p. 538]

**Allah the Exalted said:**

﴿For every one We have made heirs to what is left by parents and close relatives, and to those with whom your oaths have bound you. So give them their share. Indeed, Allah is ever a witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Men are the protectors and maintainers of women, because Allah has given some of them more than others, and because they spend from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient and guard in secret what Allah has commanded them to guard. As for those women from whom you fear disobedience (nushuz), admonish them, abandon them in their beds, and strike them. But if they obey you, do not seek a way against them. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Great.﴾

"Kull" (every) is only used in a construct state, whether the word it is attached to is stated or understood. It functions like "qabla" and "ba'da" (before and after). For this reason some grammarians permitted "marartu bi-kullin" ("I passed by each one") on the pattern of "qabla" and "ba'da." **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 35:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿If you fear a breach between the two, then send an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family. If they both desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between them. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Acquainted.﴾

This verse divides women into categories by way of rational division, since she is either obedient or *nashiz* (defiant, disobedient). *Nushuz* (defiance) is either of two kinds: a woman who returns to obedience, or a woman who requires the two arbiters.

The interpreters (*al-mutaʾawwilun*, those who interpret the text) also differed regarding the meaning of "fear" here, according to what has preceded. The two arbiters (*al-hakamān*) are sent only when the fear is intense. *Shiqaq* (breach, discord) is the verbal noun of *shaqqa yushaqqu*. The word *al-bayn* (between) is treated as a noun, and its adverbial sense is removed, since it means: their state, their companionship, and their association. This is from the brevity (*ijaz*) in which the apparent text indicates what is implied.

They differed over who is the one addressed by the sending. It was said: the ruler (*al-hakim*). So when the affair of the spouses becomes intractable for the ruler, the proofs conflict before him, the doubts multiply, and the path of enforcement becomes unclear to one of them, he sends two arbiters from among the family to take up the matter directly. The text specifies "family" because they are the most likely to know the inner state of the affair, and the most likely to be concerned out of kinship. It was also said: the one addressed is the two spouses, and the sending of the two arbiters is to be attributed to them. This is the position of Malik, while the first view belongs to Rabi'a and others.

People differed about the extent of what the two arbiters may examine. Al-Tabari said: a group said: the two arbiters may examine only what the spouses have delegated to them and explicitly authorized them to decide. He presented this view as a chapter heading, then included a report from Ali other than this. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others said: the two arbiters examine reconciliation, and matters of giving and taking, except for separation, since that is not in their hands. Another group said: the two arbiters examine everything, they may compel the wrongdoer, and they enforce what they judge, whether continuation or separation. This is the position of Malik and the majority of scholars, and it is the view of Ali ibn Abi Talib in *al-Mudawwana* and other works. Al-Zajjaj interpreted it otherwise, holding that the two arbiters were authorized only regarding separation, and that separation belongs to the ruler. This was an error on the part of Abu Ishaq.

The interpreters differed over who is meant by His saying: "If they both desire reconciliation." Mujahid and others said: the intended ones are the two arbiters, meaning: if they give sincere advice and intend good, blessing is placed upon their mediation. Another group said: the intended ones are the spouses. The first view is more apparent. Likewise, the pronoun in "between them" admits both readings, and the more apparent is that it refers to the spouses.

The attribute "Knowing, Acquainted" fits with what was mentioned of the desire for reconciliation.

"The waw" is used to conjoin one sentence of speech to another sentence distinct from it. Worship (ʿibadah, servitude/devotion) is humbling oneself through obedience; from it comes "a paved road" (ṭarīq muʿabbad) and "a camel made docile" (baʿīr muʿabbad) when they are trained. "Iḥsānan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its governing verb is an implied verb whose estimate is: "And show kindness to the two parents, with kindness." What al-Ṭabarī mentioned, that it is in the accusative by way of incitement (al-ighrāʾ), is an error. Fulfilling the obligatory rights of the two parents, which are incumbent upon you towards them—honouring them, protecting them, and spending on them if they are in need—is obligatory. All the rest of the forms of righteousness, gentleness, good speech, and taking care of their comfort are a recommended act strongly encouraged in regard to them. This is the righteousness in which the mother is given precedence over the father, in accordance with the saying of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) to the man who said to him: "Who is most deserving of my righteous companionship?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your father. Then the nearest, then the nearest." In another narration: "Then the one nearest to you, the nearest to you."

"Dhū al-qurbā" means the blood relative on the side of the father and the mother, and this is from the command to maintain and preserve the ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim). "Al-yatāmā" is the plural of yatīm, who is one who has lost his father before reaching maturity. Although the usage of the Arabs has the term "yutm" from the mother's side, it is metaphorical and figurative. "Al-masākīn" are those among the Muslims who are in straitened circumstances, who are entitled to zakat, and who openly ask (for help).

There is disagreement regarding the meaning of "wal-jārī dhī al-qurbā" and the meaning of "al-junub." Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and others said: The neighbour who is dhū al-qurbā is the neighbour who is a blood relative, and the neighbour al-junub is the foreign neighbour with whom you have no kinship. Nawf al-Shāmī said: The neighbour who is dhū al-qurbā is the Muslim neighbour, and the neighbour al-junub is the Jewish or Christian neighbour; so the kinship, according to him, is the kinship of Islam, and the foreignness is that of disbelief. A group said: The neighbour who is dhū al-qurbā is the neighbour near in dwelling to you, and the neighbour al-junub is the neighbour far in dwelling from you, and it seems this view is drawn from a hadith. ʿĀʾishah said: "O Messenger of God, I have two neighbours; to which of them should I send a gift?" He said: "To the one whose door is nearer to you."

People differed about the limit of neighbourhood. Al-Awzāʿī said: Forty houses from every direction are neighbourhood. A group said: Whoever hears the call to prayer (iqāmat al-ṣalāh) is the neighbour of that mosque, and the same measure applies to houses. A group said: Whoever lives with a man in a quarter or a city is his neighbour. Neighbourhood has degrees, some closer than others; the least of them is the spouse, as al-Aʿshā said:

"O neighbour of mine, separate..."

Beyond this degree of neighbourhood is the "khulut" (close associates), and from it is the verse of the poet:

"Ask the neighbour of Jarm whether you did against her war that separates the close associates."

Al-Ṭabarī related from Maymūn ibn Mihrān that "the neighbour dhā al-qurbā" is intended to mean the neighbour of the relative, and this is an error in the language, because according to his interpretation it combines the definite article and the annexation (iḍāfah), whereas the proper construction would be: "wa-jāri dhī al-qurbā."

Abū Ḥaywah and Ibn Abī ʿAbalah read "wal-jāra dhā al-qurbā" with the accusative on "al-jār." Makkī related from Ibn Wahb that he said, concerning the neighbour al-junub, citing some of the Companions, that it is the man's wife. al-Mufaḍḍal related from ʿĀṣim that he read "wal-jāri al-janbi," with a fatḥah on the jīm and sukūn on the nūn.

"Al-junub" in this verse means: the distant. And "al-janābah" means distance. From it is the verse of the poet, who is al-Aʿshā:

"I came to Ḥuraith as a visitor from afar, and Ḥuraith was stingy with my gift..."

And from it is the verse of another, who is ʿAlqamah ibn ʿAbadah:

"So do not deprive me of a gift from afar, for I am a stranger among the tents."

It derives from "ijtināb," which is to leave a thing aside. A Bedouin was asked about the neighbour al-junub and said: He is the one who comes and settles wherever your eye falls upon him. Abū ʿAlī said: "junub" is an adjective like "a camel of ujud" and "a gait of sujuḥ." The "junub" of ritual purity is derived from "al-janb" (side).

Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, Qatādah, Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "wal-ṣāḥibi bil-janb" is the companion on the journey. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn Abī Laylā and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī said: "al-ṣāḥib bil-janb" is the wife. Ibn Zayd said: It is the man who visits you and frequents you so that you may benefit him. al-Ṭabarī related with a chain: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was with a man of his Companions, and they were on two mounts. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered a thicket and cut two sticks, one of which was crooked, and he came out and gave his companion the straight one and kept the crooked one himself. The man said to him: 'O Messenger of God, you were more deserving of this.' He said to him: 'O so-and-so, every companion who accompanies another is responsible for his companionship, even for an hour of a day.'"

The commentators said: "Ibn al-sabīl" is the traveller on the road, and he was called "the son of the road" because of his constant attachment to it, just as it is said "son of water" for a bird that constantly stays by the water. From this is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "The son of adultery will not enter Paradise," meaning: the one who is constantly attached to it, who deserves to be ascribed to it through persistence in it. al-Ṭabarī mentioned that Mujāhid explained it as the one who passes by you on his journey, and that Qatādah and others explained it as the guest.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is one view.

"Mā malakat aymānukum" means the enslaved bondsmen. The ownership is attributed to the right hand, since the right hand is customarily the organ of seizing, dominance and possession; these meanings are attributed to it, though they are not in fact from it, by way of metaphor. Slaves are enjoined in more than one hadith, the mention of which would be lengthy, and their wide currency makes it unnecessary to recount them.

The meaning of "yuḥibbu" in this verse: the signs of His blessings do not appear upon him in the Hereafter, nor the signs of His praise in this world. This is the love which is an attribute of act, and it removes it from those whose attribute is arrogance and boasting. It is said: "khāla al-rajul yakhūlu khawlan" when a man becomes proud and conceited with himself. al-Ṭabarī recited:

"If you were our chief, you have led us; and if you were for arrogance, then go and be arrogant."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The negation of love from one who has this attribute is a kind of warning. He specified these two attributes here, since their consequence is self-admiration and vanity, and that is what drives one to neglect the categories of people towards whom Allah's command of kindness has preceded. For each category there is a type of kindness specific to it, and nothing hinders kindness towards them except self-admiration or miserliness; therefore Allah negated His love from the self-admiring and the miserly, according to one of the two interpretations we will mention shortly after this. Abū Rajāʾ al-Harawī said: You will not find someone with bad manners except that you will find him arrogant and boastful, and you will not find an undutiful son except that you will find him tyrannical and wretched. Boasting (fakhr) is the enumeration of virtues with arrogance over others because of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 37–39:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Those who are niggardly and enjoin niggardliness upon people, and conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people, and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. And whoever has Satan as a companion—evil is he as a companion.﴾ ﴿And what would it have been upon them had they believed in Allah and the Last Day and spent from what Allah has provided them? And Allah is ever Knowing of them.﴾

A group said: "Alladhina" is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for "man" in His saying: ﴿whoever is self-deluding and boastful﴾ [an-Nisa': 36]. Its meaning, according to this, is: they are niggardly with their wealth, "and enjoin upon people"—meaning their brethren and those whose obedience to them is expected—niggardliness with wealth, so that it is not spent in any of the ways of kindness toward those mentioned. ﴿And conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾, meaning: of provision and wealth. It follows, according to this, that love of Allah is denied to the niggardly, and the verse is then about believers. The meaning is: Be generous, O believers, toward those mentioned, for Allah does not love whoever possesses the traits that prevent generosity toward them from among the believers. As for the disbelievers, He has prepared for them ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾. Thus He distinguished the threat to the believers from the threat to the disbelievers, by making the first the absence of love and the second a humiliating punishment.

Another group said: "Alladhina" is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is omitted; its estimate, after His saying "of His bounty," is: "will be punished" or "will be recompensed" or the like. Al-Zajjaj said: the predicate is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong an atom's weight, and if it is a good deed He doubles it﴾ [an-Nisa': 40]. In this there is some strain, and the verse on all of this is about disbelievers.

It has been narrated that it was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews in Medina, for they were niggardly in announcing the description of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and in what knowledge they had of that, and they enjoined people to niggardliness in two ways: by telling their followers and common people, "Deny the affair of Muhammad and withhold it," and by telling the Ansar, "Why do you spend your wealth on these emigrants so that you become poor?" A similar report is transmitted from Mujahid, Hadrami, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn 'Abbas.

The reality of bukhl (niggardliness) is withholding what is in one's hand, and shuh (avarice) is the niggardliness accompanied by desire for what is in people's hands. Concealing the bounty is, according to this, concealing knowledge, and the threat of a humiliating punishment for them.

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and al-Hasan read "bi-l-bukul" with a damma on the ba' and the kha'. The majority read with a damma on the ba' and sukun on the kha'. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read here and in [al-Hadid] "bi-l-bakhal" with a fatha on the ba' and the kha'. Ibn al-Zubayr, Qatada, and a group read with a fatha on the ba' and sukun on the kha'. All of these are dialectal variants.

"A'tadna" means: We made ready, prepared, and presented. "Al-'Atid" means the present, ready. "Al-muhin" is that which is accompanied by disgrace and abasement, and it is more severe and harsher upon the one punished.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who spend﴾ the verse. Al-Tabari said: "Alladhina" is in the genitive position as a conjunction (atf) upon "al-kafirin." It may also be in the nominative position as a conjunction upon "alladhina yabkhalun," on the interpretation of one who regards it as disconnected and regards the predicate as omitted. He said it was revealed concerning the Jews. Mujahid said this verse was revealed concerning the Jews; al-Tabari said: This is weak, because it negated from this description belief in Allah and the Last Day, and the Jews are not like that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Mujahid's saying is sound on the basis of exaggeration and obligation, since their belief in the Last Day is as no belief, in that it does not benefit them.

The majority said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and this is the correct view. Their spending is what they gave as zakat, and what they spent on journeys with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), out of showing off and warding off harm from themselves, not out of belief in Allah nor love for His religion. "Ri'a'" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yunfiqun," and the governing element is "yunfiqun." His saying "and do not believe" is within the relative clause, because a circumstantial clause is not separated if it is of what is within the relative clause. Al-Mahdawi related that the circumstantial clause may be from "alladhina," and according to this "and do not believe" is disconnected and not part of the relative clause. The first is more correct, and what al-Mahdawi related is weak. It is possible that "and do not believe" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: not believing, so that the waw is the waw of circumstance.

"Qarin" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il, from "muqarana" (accompaniment), which is constant attachment and companionship. Here it is accompaniment with close association and affection. Every person is accompanied by Satan, but the one who agrees with him disobeys him. From this it is said of camels and cattle that are yoked together, "two companions" (qarinan), and the rope with which they are tied is called "qaran." The poet said:

Like one who puts his head in, no one has brought it near, between the two yoked animals, until the rope has bound it tight.

The meaning: Whoever has Satan as a companion and constant associate, he is close to obeying him, and his end will be evil. "Qarinan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and the agent of "saa'a" is implied; its estimate is: "the companion was evil as a companion," after the pattern of "bi'sa." Al-Tabari linked this verse with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Evil is it as a substitute for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and that is rejected, because "badalan" is a circumstantial clause, and there is scrutiny in this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what would it have been upon them﴾: "ma" is in the nominative as subject, "dha" is a relative supplement, and "'alayhim" is the predicate of the subject; the estimate is: "And what thing is upon them?" It is also possible that "ma" is a noun on its own and "dha" means "alladhi," a subject and predicate, and the answer to "law" is in His saying "madha," which is a preposed answer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems that this speech implies that belief is connected with their capacity and is from their action. And one does not say to anyone, "What is upon you if you did such-and-such," except regarding what is within his capacity. This is a doubt raised by the Mu'tazila, and the resolution of it is that what is required is their striving, their effort, and their turning toward belief; as for the creation, it is Allah alone who originates it. In this speech there is a lament over what is upon them, and a gracious invitation that calls for caution and compassion.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing of them﴾: a statement that contains a warning and alerts to the evil of their collusion, meaning: concealment does not benefit them with Allah's knowledge of them.

"A'tadna" means: We made ready, prepared, and presented. "Al-'Atid" means the present, ready. "Al-muhin" is that which is accompanied by disgrace and abasement, and it is more severe and harsher upon the one punished.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who spend﴾ the verse. Al-Tabari said: "Alladhina" is in the genitive position as a conjunction (atf) upon "al-kafirin." It may also be in the nominative position as a conjunction upon "alladhina yabkhalun," on the interpretation of one who regards it as disconnected and regards the predicate as omitted. He said it was revealed concerning the Jews. Mujahid said this verse was revealed concerning the Jews; al-Tabari said: This is weak, because it negated from this description belief in Allah and the Last Day, and the Jews are not like that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Mujahid's saying is sound on the basis of exaggeration and obligation, since their belief in the Last Day is as no belief, in that it does not benefit them.

The majority said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and this is the correct view. Their spending is what they gave as zakat, and what they spent on journeys with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), out of showing off and warding off harm from themselves, not out of belief in Allah nor love for His religion. "Ri'a'" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yunfiqun," and the governing element is "yunfiqun." His saying "and do not believe" is within the relative clause, because a circumstantial clause is not separated if it is of what is within the relative clause. Al-Mahdawi related that the circumstantial clause may be from "alladhina," and according to this "and do not believe" is disconnected and not part of the relative clause. The first is more correct, and what al-Mahdawi related is weak. It is possible that "and do not believe" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: not believing, so that the waw is the waw of circumstance.

"Qarin" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il, from "muqarana" (accompaniment), which is constant attachment and companionship. Here it is accompaniment with close association and affection. Every person is accompanied by Satan, but the one who agrees with him disobeys him. From this it is said of camels and cattle that are yoked together, "two companions" (qarinan), and the rope with which they are tied is called "qaran." The poet said:

Like one who puts his head in, no one has brought it near, between the two yoked animals, until the rope has bound it tight.

The meaning: Whoever has Satan as a companion and constant associate, he is close to obeying him, and his end will be evil. "Qarinan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and the agent of "saa'a" is implied; its estimate is: "the companion was evil as a companion," after the pattern of "bi'sa." Al-Tabari linked this verse with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Evil is it as a substitute for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and that is rejected, because "badalan" is a circumstantial clause, and there is scrutiny in this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what would it have been upon them﴾: "ma" is in the nominative as subject, "dha" is a relative supplement, and "'alayhim" is the predicate of the subject; the estimate is: "And what thing is upon them?" It is also possible that "ma" is a noun on its own and "dha" means "alladhi," a subject and predicate, and the answer to "law" is in His saying "madha," which is a preposed answer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems that this speech implies that belief is connected with their capacity and is from their action. And one does not say to anyone, "What is upon you if you did such-and-such," except regarding what is within his capacity. This is a doubt raised by the Mu'tazila, and the resolution of it is that what is required is their striving, their effort, and their turning toward belief; as for the creation, it is Allah alone who originates it. In this speech there is a lament over what is upon them, and a gracious invitation that calls for caution and compassion.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing of them﴾: a statement that contains a warning and alerts to the evil of their collusion, meaning: concealment does not benefit them with Allah's knowledge of them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verse 40:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (anyone) by the weight of an atom (dharrah), and if it is a good deed He doubles it and gives from Himself a great reward.﴾

(p-554) "Mithqal" is on the pattern *mif'al*, from *thiql* (weight). The *dharrah* is the small red ant, and it is at its smallest when a year has passed over it, because it shrinks and moves the way a snake does. The Arabs say: *af'a jariyah* (a running snake), meaning the most vigorous kind. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Of the chaste-eyed women, if a yearling of the *dharr* crawled upon the saddle-cloth of one of them, it would leave a mark."

*Al-mahwal* is the one that has completed a year. Hassan said:

"If the yearling of the young of the *dharr* were to crawl over her, the wounds would leave her scarred."

Yazid ibn Harun described the *dharrah* as a red worm, but this description is incorrect. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the *dharrah* is the head of an ant. Ibn 'Abbas also read: "Indeed, Allah does not wrong the weight of an ant (namlah)." Here *mithqal* is the second object of *yazlimu* (wrongs), and the first object is implied, the sense being: "Indeed, Allah does not wrong anyone by (the amount of) the weight of..." *Yazlimu* is not transitive except to one object, but here it is treated as taking two objects, by understanding it in the sense of verbs that take two objects, as if he had said: "Indeed, Allah does not diminish, or defraud, or usurp." It is also permissible for *mithqal* to be in the accusative as an explanatory qualifier of the amount of wrong that is negated. In that case it is a description of an implied verbal noun, the sense being: "Indeed, Allah does not wrong with a wrong (of the amount) of the weight of an atom," just as you say: "Indeed, the commander does not wrong, neither little nor much," meaning he does not commit a wrong that is little or much. On this reading, *yazlimu* takes one object only. Qatadah said, relating it from himself and transmitting it from some scholars: "That my good deeds exceed my bad deeds by the weight of an atom is dearer to me than the whole world."

The *nun* of *takun* is dropped because of frequency of use, and because it resembles the long vowel letters in lightness.

(p-555) The majority of the Seven read *hasanatan* with the accusative, as the predicate of a defective *kana* (was), whose subject is an implied pronoun, the sense being: "And if the weight of the atom is a good deed." Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read *hasanatun* with the nominative, as a complete *kana* (existed), the sense being: "And if a good deed occurs or exists." *Yudha'ifha* is the answer of the conditional. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *yudha'if'ha* with a doubled 'ayn and no alif. Abu 'Ali said: "The meaning of both is one, and they are two dialects." Al-Hasan read *yud'ifha* with a sukun on the *dad* and a light 'ayn. The *mudha'afah* (multiplying) of a thing in Arab speech is adding its like to it. When you say *dhaʻʻaftu* (I multiplied), you have used the intensive form, and when the verbal form without intensification implies folding twice, the intensive form implies more than twice, up to whatever number you intend. When you say *dhaʻafttu* (with the alif), it is not an intensive form, but a verb whose form signifies folding twice or more. These are the principles of this topic according to the school of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna mentioned in *Kitab al-Majaz* that *ḍa'afa* implies many repetitions, while *ḍa''afa* implies two. Al-Tabari said the same and took it from him. What shows the closeness of the matter in meaning is what has been read in His saying: ﴿So He multiplies it for him many times over﴾ (2:245), where it is read *yudha'ifahu* and *yud'ifahu*; and what has been read in His saying, may He be exalted: "The punishment will be doubled for her, double" (33:30), where it is read *yudha''af lahā al-'adhābu di'fayn*.

Some of the interpreters said: This verse was specific to the Emigrants (muhajirun), because Allah informed in His Book that a good deed for every believer is multiplied tenfold, and He informed in this verse that it is multiplied many, very many times, according to what Abu Hurayrah narrated, that it is multiplied two million times, while others narrated that it is multiplied one million times. It is not sound for two reports to contradict each other, so this is specific to the foremost Emigrants, according to what 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar narrated: when the verse ﴿Whoever brings a good deed, for him is ten times its like﴾ (6:160) was revealed concerning people in general, a man said: "What then of the Emigrants?" He said: "(They have) what is greater than this: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong...﴾" (4:40). So they were singled out with this, just as the expenditure in the way of Allah was singled out for multiplication seven hundred times, and there is no contradiction in the reports.

Others said: Rather, He promised this to all believers. Traditions have been related on this, and they are: "Allah, mighty and majestic, will gather the first and the last in one level place, then He will call out: 'This is so-and-so, son of so-and-so; whoever has a right with him, let him stand.' He said: 'A man will wish that he had a claim against his father or his son that day. Everyone who has a right will come and take from his good deeds until retribution is completed, and nothing will remain for him but the weight of an atom. Then Allah, exalted, will say: Multiply it for My servant, and take him to Paradise.'" This combines the meanings of what has been related that we have not mentioned.

The verse encompasses believers and disbelievers. As for the believers, they will be rewarded in the Hereafter for the weights of atoms and more. As for the disbelievers, whatever good they do, its reward is given to them in the blessings of this world, and they will come on the Day of Resurrection with no good deed for them.

*Ladunhu* means "from Him." Sibawayh said: it is used for the beginning of the end point (ibtida' al-ghayah), so it corresponds to one of the uses of *min* (from), and for that reason they fit together, and *min* is attached to it.

The great reward is Paradise, as said by Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Zayd. When Allah bestows His favor by His bounty, He brings His servant to the ultimate goal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 41–42:

[p. 557]

His statement, may He be exalted:

﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were levelled over them, and they will not conceal from God any statement.﴾

The verse before it announced the establishment of the rulings on the Day of Resurrection. So it was fitting, after that, to draw attention to the state in which this will be brought about, and in which the witnesses will be brought forward against the nations. The meaning of the verse is that God brings the prophets as witnesses against their nations, testifying to their truthfulness and their denial. The meaning of "nation" (ummah) in this verse differs from the usual meaning when nations are attributed to prophets. The common usage is that by "the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ)" one means all who believed in him, and likewise for every prophet. Here, however, it means all to whom a prophet was sent, both those who believed among them and those who disbelieved. Likewise the commentators said that the indication by "these people" refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and others among the disbelievers. The disbelievers of Quraysh were specifically mentioned because the weight of the threat falls more heavily upon them than upon others.

"Fa-kayfa" (how, then) is in a position of accusative, a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam) governed by a verb whose implied form at the end of the verse is: "you see their state," or "they will be," or something similar. Makki said in al-Hidayah: "We brought" (ji'na) is the governing element of "fa-kayfa," and that is an error.

It is narrated that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would, when he recited this verse, have his eyes overflow with tears." Likewise his eyes (ﷺ) shed tears when 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recited it to him, in the well-known hadith. As for what al-Tabari mentioned about the testimony of the nation of Muhammad to the conveying of the messengers, and what was related in the sense of that from the stories which Makki mentioned, such as the questioning of the Preserved Tablet, then Israfil, then Jibril, then the prophets, these are not its verse. Its verse is: ﴿So that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

[p. 558]

"Yawma-idhin" is an adverbial of time (zarf). It is permissible that the accusative of "yawma" in this place be on the basis of it being an adverb of time, as it is indeclinable (mu'rab) together with the nouns that are not fully declinable (ghayr mutamakkinah). It is also permissible that its accusative be on the basis of it being built (mabni) on the accusative together with the nouns that are not fully declinable. The wishing (wadd) is indeed on that Day.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "tassawwa" with the assimilation of the second ta' of "tatasawwa." Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "tasawwa" with a light sin and a doubled waw, by dropping the second ta' mentioned. Both have one meaning. It has been disputed: one group said the earth will split open, they will enter into it, and then the earth itself will be levelled over them and with them. Another group said the meaning is: "if the earth were levelled along with them," in that they would become dust like their forefathers. So the wording came in such a way that the earth is the one being levelled together with them, while the meaning is only that they become level with the earth. Thus there is an inversion (qalb) in the wording, which proceeds in the manner of the usage recorded by Sibawayh: "I put the cap on my head," "I put my mouth into the stone," and what goes in the same direction. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "tusawwa" with the verb built for the passive, whose subject is not named. So God does that according to the two meanings mentioned above. Abu 'Ali said: the inclination (imalah) of the fatha towards the kasra, and of the alif towards the ya', in "tusawwa" is good.

One group said: the meaning of the verse is that the disbelievers, because of the terror they see and the severity of the fears, wish that the earth would be levelled over them so that this fear would not reach them. Then the speech proceeds afresh, informing that they will not conceal from God any statement, since their limbs will speak all of that, when some of them say: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and God says: "You have lied," then He makes their limbs speak, so they conceal no statement. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and he said concerning it: when God gathers the first and the last, some of the disbelievers suppose that denial will save them, so they say: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and God says: "You have lied," then He makes their limbs speak, so they conceal no statement. In this way Ibn 'Abbas opened the matter for a questioner for whom it had been unclear.

Another group, like the first view, except that they said: the speech was only resumed with His statement, ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾, in order to inform that concealment will not benefit them even if they conceal, because God knows all their secrets and their conversations. So the meaning of that is: "That formidable station is not a station in which concealment benefits."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The difference between these two views is that the first implies that concealment does not benefit in any way, whereas the other implies that concealment does not benefit whether it occurs or not, as you say: "This is a gathering in which no falsehood is spoken," while you mean: "nothing is benefited from it, nor is it listened to."

Another group said: the whole speech is connected, and its meaning is: ﴿those who disbelieved will wish that the earth were levelled over them﴾, and they will wish that they had not concealed from God any statement, and their wishing for that is only regret over their lying when they said: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. Another group said: these are different stations and different occasions. And another group said: the meaning of the verse is: those who disbelieved wish that the earth were levelled over them, and that they had not concealed from God any statement. This too is in the manner of regret for the lie, as you say: "I wished that I had resolved on such-and-such," and it is not such-and-such in the manner of ransom, meaning: they would ransom their concealment by the earth being levelled over them.

"The Messenger" in this verse is for the genus (lil-jins), honoured by mention. It is singular in form but indicates the plural. Abu al-Sammal and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read "wa-'asawi al-rasul," with a kasra on the waw of "'asaw."
