Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 43 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted:
﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying, nor [while you are] in a state of janabah, except those passing through [a place of prayer], until you have washed. And if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have contacted women, and you do not find water, then go to clean earth and wipe over your faces and your hands. Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾

The occasion for the prohibition of approaching prayer while intoxicated: a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ drank wine at the house of one of them before it was prohibited, among them Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. Then the time of prayer came, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib led them forward and recited: ﴿"Say, O you disbelievers"﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1], and he garbled it by saying: "I worship what you worship, and you worship what I worship." So the verse was revealed. It is also narrated that the one leading the prayer was 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf.

The majority of the exegetes hold that what is meant is intoxication from wine, except al-Dahhak, who said: what is meant is only the intoxication of sleep.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is weak.

The address is to all the righteous of the Ummah. As for the intoxicated person, when he has lost discernment due to his intoxication, he is not addressed at that time; rather, he is addressed when he sobers, to perform what is obligatory upon him, and to make up for the rulings that were neglected during the time of his intoxication, the obligations that were established upon him before the intoxication. There is no imposition of what cannot be borne in this, contrary to what some people have held.

The group [of readers] who read "sukara" (intoxicated) as the plural of "sakran" (intoxicated), and a group who read "sukra" with a fatha on the sin, on the pattern of fa'la, and al-A'mash read "sukra" with a damma on the sin and a sukun on the kaf, on the pattern of fu'la, and al-Nakha'i read "sakra" with a fatha on the sin. Abu al-Fath said: it is a broken plural of "sakran" into "sakra," as they said "rawba niyaman," and as in their saying "halki" and "maydi" as the plurals of "halik" and "ma'id." It is possible that it is an adjective for a single feminine noun, as if the meaning is: "and you are a group who are intoxicated." As for "sukra" with a damma on the sin, it is an adjective for a singular feminine, like "hublа." Intoxication (sukr) is the blocking of understanding, and from it: "sakartu al-ma'" when you block its path.

A group said: "al-salah" here is the known worship, according to the occasion of the revelation of the verse. Another group said: "al-salah" here is meant to be both the place of prayer and the prayer together, because at that time they would not come to the mosque except for prayer, and they would not pray except gathered together, so the two were mutually connected.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The need for this disagreement arises in accordance with what comes concerning "passing through [a place]."

It appears from His saying "until you know" that the intoxicated person does not know what he says. For this reason 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, and others said that the divorce of an intoxicated person does not bind him. Thus the rulings of speech are dropped from him on this basis, and on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to the one who confessed to fornication: "Are you intoxicated?" Its meaning: if he had been intoxicated, his confession would not have been binding.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
There is a difference between the divorce of the intoxicated person and his confession of fornication. The divorce, the confession regarding property, slander, and what resembles these are connected to the rights of others among the children of Adam, so the intoxicated person is suspected if he claims he did not know, and the ruling of one who knows is applied to him. The confession of fornication is only a right of Allah, the Exalted; so if he claims after sobering that he was not aware of the religious obligation in it... As for the rulings on crimes, they are all binding upon the intoxicated person.

His saying "while you are intoxicated" is a nominal sentence (mubtada' and khabar), a clause in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal). It is reported from Ibn Furak that he said: the meaning of the verse is a prohibition against intoxication, that is, let there not be intoxication among you so that one approaches prayer, since a person is constantly called to prayer; and the apparent matter is that it is not so. It has been narrated that after this verse the Companions would drink and reduce [their drinking] after dawn and after the 'atama, and no prayer would come upon them except that they were sober.

His saying "nor [while in] janabah" is a conjunction (atf) upon the position of this accusative clause. Janabah is being not in a state of purity due to emission of semen or passing the circumcised part [past the other's circumcised part]; this is the saying of the majority of the Ummah. It was narrated from some Companions: there is no ritual washing except for one who has emitted semen. Janabah comes either from "al-bu'd" (distance), as if one has moved away from purity, or from "al-janb" (side), as if one has lain down and touched another with one's side. A group read "junuban" with the nun sukun.

"Illa 'abiri sabil" is from al-'ubur, that is, passing and crossing; from it: the "'ubr" of a ship is the river; and from it: a camel that is "'ubr al-sayr" and "al-falah" and "al-muhajara," meaning you cross them with swift travel. The poet said, and it was a woman:

A swift, long-necked she-camel, with thin hands, fleet of the midday heats, like a dyed palm-stalk.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hakam, and others said: "'abir al-sabil" is the traveler, so it is not permissible for anyone to approach prayer while in janabah except after washing, except the traveler, who performs tayammum. Ibn 'Abbas also, and Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ikrima, al-Nakha'i, and others said: "'abir al-sabil" is one who passes through the mosque, and this is what is intended in the verse. This requires what was mentioned earlier, that the view that "salah" means the mosque and the place of prayer... Some narrated that the occasion of the verse was that some of the Ansar had doors of their houses opening into the mosque, so when one of them was struck by janabah he was compelled to pass through the mosque, and so the verse was revealed concerning that. Then the words ﴿And if you are ill﴾ to the end of the verse were revealed because the Companions lacked water during the expedition of al-Muraysi', when she [A'isha] stayed behind searching for the necklace. Thus said the majority. al-Nakha'i said: "It was revealed concerning people who suffered wounds and then became janub, so they mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse was revealed." al-Naqqash mentioned that this was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. The sick person intended in this verse is the one who is resident, and the one for whom tayammum is valid is one who fears death from the coldness of water or from the illness that it would aggravate. Such a person performs tayammum by consensus, except what was narrated from 'Ata', that he purifies himself even if he dies. One who fears the occurrence of an illness upon an illness, or the increase of an illness, or fears slow recovery—these perform tayammum by consensus within the school, as far as I have memorized. The causes for which a sick person does not find water are either the absence of someone to bring it, or fear of what has been mentioned. Dawud said: everyone upon whom the name of "sick" applies is permitted tayammum; this is the view of Khalaf, and it is, according to the scholars of the Ummah, the one with a skin disease, the one with a wound, and the illnesses in which water is harmful.

The traveler in this verse is the one absent from home, whether the journey is one in which shortening the prayer is permitted or not. This is the position of Malik and the majority of jurists. al-Shafi'i said in Kitab al-Ashraf: some said: one performs tayammum only on a journey in which shortening is permitted, and this is weak.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Likewise a group said: one does not perform tayammum on a journey of disobedience, and this too is weak.

The causes for which the traveler does not find water are either its total absence, or fear of losing the companion through seeking it, or fear for the baggage through seeking it, or fear of predators or harm.

It is disputed concerning the time of performing tayammum. al-Shafi'i said: at the beginning of the time; Abu Hanifa and others said: at the end of the time. Malik distinguished between one who has despaired [of finding water], one who knows and hopes to find it within the time, and one who is entirely ignorant of his situation. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: the traveler is not obligated to seek water except what is before him and around him. Some said: he goes out to seek it up to two gholwas or so. In Malik's school he walks in search of it three miles. al-Shafi'i said: he walks in search of it as long as he does not fear losing a companion or losing the time.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is a good statement.

The root of "al-ghait" is what is low of the land, and the Arabs would intend that type of place for relieving themselves, until its use became common for relieving oneself and became its custom. Qatada and al-Zuhri read "min al-ghayt" with a silent ya without an alif. Ibn Jinni said: it is elided from fay'al, its middle letter being a waw. This word comprehensively includes in meaning all the nullifiers of minor purity. People differed in enumerating them, and the soundest of what is believed in this is that the types of nullifiers are three: what exits from the two passages habitually, what removes the intellect, and touching. This is according to the school of Malik. According to the school of Abu Hanifa: what exits from the body of the impurities, without regard to the exit or anything else, and touching is not counted among them. According to the school of al-Shafi'i: what exits from the two passages, without regard to habituality. The consensus on nullifiers is nine: four from the penis, namely urine, semen, wadi, and madhi; one from the female genital, namely menstrual blood; and two from the rear, namely wind and feces. Loss of intellect, such as madness, fainting, and deep sleep, these nullify minor purity by consensus; and other than these, such as touching, and a worm emerging from the rear, and what resembles them, are disputed.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "lamastum." In the language it is a word that may be used for touching which is intercourse, and for touching which is the feeling of the hand, kissing, and the like, since all of that is touching. The people of knowledge differed about its application here. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, says: the word here, in its fullest generality, implies both meanings; so one who has touched by intercourse performs tayammum, and one who has touched by the hand performs tayammum, because touching nullified his ablution. A group said: here it is specified for the touch of the hand, and the janub has no mention except with water, and there is no path for him to tayammum; rather, the janub washes or abandons prayer until he finds water. This view was narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and others. Abu Hanifa said: here it is specified for the touch that is intercourse, so the janub performs tayammum; and the one who touches by hand, no mention of it has occurred, so it is not a minor impurity, nor does it nullify ablution. So if a man kisses his wife for pleasure, his ablution is not nullified. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that touching nullifies if it is for pleasure, and does not nullify if not intended for pleasure, nor if it is with a daughter or a mother. al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, generalizes the word "women," so if a man touches his mother or his daughter in any manner, his ablution is nullified.

Lack of water applies to the sick and the traveler as we have mentioned, and applies to the resident healthy person through expensiveness that affects all kinds [of goods]. This is disputed. al-Hasan said: a man buys water with all his wealth and remains destitute; this is a weak view, "because the religion of Allah is ease," as the Prophet ﷺ said, and He desires ease for us and has not placed hardship upon us in the religion. A group said: he buys what does not exceed the value by a third or more; a group said: he buys the value of a dirham for two or three dirhams and the like. All of this is in Malik's school, may Allah have mercy on him. Ashhab was asked: is a waterskin bought for ten dirhams? He said: I do not think that is required of people.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The measure of this question depends on the wealth and need of the buyer. In my view, the proper course is that he buys as long as its high price does not harm him. Lack of water also applies to the healthy resident through being imprisoned or bound, and this is the case about which it is said that he did not find water or dust, as al-Bukhari titled a chapter. There are four opinions on it: Malik and Ibn Nafi' said: he does not pray and does not repeat. Ibn al-Qasim said: he prays and repeats. Ashhab said: he prays and does not repeat. Asbagh said: he does not pray and makes it up. If the resident fears that the time will pass if he takes water, Malik has two statements in the Mudawwana: that he performs tayammum and does not repeat, and that he repeats. In al-Wadiha and elsewhere it is narrated from him that he takes water and washes even if the sun rises. According to the view that he performs tayammum and does not repeat, if some of the time remains equal to the amount needed for performing ablution and praying one rak'a, it is said: he repeats; and it is said: he does not repeat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 43 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of His words "fa-tayammamu" (then seek) is: aim for (iqsidu). From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"He aimed for the spring that is near Darij, whose shade-covered pools, its waters overflowing, are shaded by the trees."

From this is also the saying of A'sha Banu Tha'laba:

"I aimed for Qays, though between me and him lie many lands, through a desert of vast wastes with rough ground."

Then this word became established in the Shari'ah for the well-known act of worship (tayammum, dry ablution: ablution with clean earth in place of water when water is unavailable).

Al-sa'id in the language means the surface of the earth, as stated by al-Khalil and others. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"As if, in the forenoon, it were throwing the surface of the earth with it, a beetle with a snout on the bones of its head."

The jurists differed on this because the verse restricts it with the word "clean" (tayyib). One group said: one performs tayammum on the surface of the earth, whether it is dust, sand, stones, a mineral, or saline ground, and they took "clean" to mean "pure." This is the position of Malik. Another group said: "clean" means "lawful (halal)," but this is weak in this context. Al-Shafi'i and a group said: "clean" means "producing plants," as He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿As for the good land, its plants come forth﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. On this view, "al-sa'id" means dust (turab), and this group does not permit tayammum with anything other than that. The area of consensus (ijma') is that a man may perform tayammum on pure, plant-producing dust that is not transported or usurped. The area of consensus on prohibition is that a man may not perform tayammum on pure gold, silver, ruby, emerald, foods such as bread and meat and the like, or on impurities. Opinions differ on other things, such as minerals: some permitted it, which is the position of Malik, and some prohibited it, which is the position of al-Shafi'i. Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi indicated that the disagreement exists within the school (madhhab) as well. As for salt, in the school it was permitted both as mined salt and as solid salt, and prohibited both; mined salt was permitted and solid salt was prohibited. In the Mudawwana, its permissibility regarding ice is stated, while Malik in other works prohibited it. Al-Naqqash reported from Ibn 'Aliyya and Ibn Kaysan that they permitted tayammum with musk and saffron.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"This is outright error from several angles."

As for dust that is transported in a tray or otherwise, the majority of the school holds it permissible to perform tayammum with it, though within the school there is a prohibition, and outside the school the prohibition is more common. As for what has been fired, such as baked brick and plaster, the school has two opinions: permissibility and prohibition. As for tayammum on a wall, the disagreement is the same. As for tayammum on plants and wood, there is disagreement within Malik's school. The majority prohibit tayammum on wood. In Mukhtasar al-Waqar it is stated that it is permitted. Al-Tabari reported a disagreement regarding the word "al-sa'id": that it is smooth ground, that it is level ground, that al-sa'id is dust, and that it is the surface of the earth.

(p. 568)The order in the Qur'an is the face before the hands, and this is the view of the majority. In a version of the hadith of 'Ammar in al-Bukhari, the hands are mentioned first, and some scholars held this, analogizing it to reversing the order of wudu'. In tayammum, the face must be wiped within its known limits as in wudu'. The majority hold that wiping the entire face in tayammum is obligatory, that one should go over it thoroughly as one does with water, and that one should not intend to leave out any part of it. Some permitted not going over every part, such as the folds in boots and the spaces between the fingers. This is, within the school, the view of Muhammad ibn Maslama. Malik's position in the Mudawwana is that tayammum is with two strikes (of the hands on the earth). Ibn al-Jahm said tayammum is one strike. Malik said in the Kitab Muhammad that if one performs tayammum with one strike, it suffices. Others within the school said: one repeats it within the time (of prayer). Ibn Nafi' said: one repeats it forever. Malik said in the Mudawwana: one begins with the fingers of the left hand over the fingers of the right hand, then passes in this manner up to the elbow, then turns the left palm over the inner forearm of the right arm until it reaches the wrist, then does the same with the right hand over the left. The apparent meaning of these words is that one needs no separate wiping of the palm with the other, because in passing over the forearm each hand is both wiping and being wiped. Ibn Habib said: one then passes over both palms. This, along with the apparent reading of the Mudawwana, is a point of disagreement. Al-Lakhmi said: in the words of the Mudawwana, he means: then one wipes his palm with the other. So, under Abu al-Hasan's interpretation, Ibn Habib's statement is an explanation. Another group said: one begins with the left hand as in the Mudawwana. When one reaches the wrist on the inner forearm, one moves on to the palm, then likewise with the right hand over the left. The rationale for this view is that one should not leave any part of a limb once one has begun with it, and then need to return to it after doing something else. Another group said: one applies the dust as one applies water, in the form of passing over, without a fixed sequence. Malik said in the Mudawwana: one wipes his hands up to the elbows. If one wipes up to the wrists, one repeats within the time (of prayer). Ibn Nafi' said: one repeats forever. Others said, within the school: one wipes up to the wrists. This is the view of Makhul and a group of scholars. Outside the school, one wipes only the palms. This is supported by a hadith from 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and it is the view of al-Sha'bi. Ibn Shihab said: one wipes up to the armpits. Al-Tabari reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said to 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, when the verse of tayammum was revealed: "You are blessed indeed; a concession was revealed concerning you. We struck once for our faces, and once for our hands up to the shoulders and armpits." In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from al-A'mash: "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wiped up to the midpoints of his forearms." No one among the scholars, as far as I have known, has held this hadith.

As for what al-Dawudi related, that the two wrists are obligatory, the elbows are sunnah, and the armpits are a virtue, this is a statement that no analogy or evidence supports. Some generalized the word "hand" and so made obligatory (wiping) up to the shoulder. Some analogized to wudu' and made the elbows obligatory. The majority of the Ummah took the general sense. Some kept to the hadith regarding the two wrists. Some also analogized to amputation, since it is a legal ruling and a purification, as this is a purification. Others kept to the hadith of 'Ammar regarding the two palms. Within the school, there is a disagreement about moving the ring and about passing the fingers through each other (takhlil al-asabi'), on two views: it is obligatory, and it is not obligatory.

[p-570]

The seeing in His saying "Have you not seen" is seeing with the heart, which is knowledge of a thing. Some said its meaning is: "Have you not known?" Others said: "Have you not been informed?" All of these are close in meaning. Seeing with the heart is connected with a preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) and without one. What is meant by "those" (alladhīna) is the Jews. This was said by Qatada and others. Then the wording also includes the Christians along with them. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Rifa'a ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut, the Jew.

"Were given" (ūtū) means were given. Naṣīb (portion) means share. Kitāb (the Book) means the Torah and the Gospel. The recipient is called a "portion" with respect to each individual separately, because knowledge of the Book is not confined to one person in any respect.

"They buy" (yashtarūna) is an expression for their preferring disbelief and abandoning faith. It is as if it were a giving and taking. This is the view of a group. Another group said: it means those who used to give their wealth to the rabbis in order to uphold their law. On this interpretation, this is buying in its literal sense.

﴿And they wish that you should go astray from the way﴾: its meaning is that you should disbelieve. Al-Nakha'i recited "and you wish" (tarīdūna) with the letter tā' dotted from above in "tarīdūna."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse and what follows require rebuke of the believers for leaning toward a group of the rabbis of the Jews, whether in asking about religion, in alliance, or in something similar. This is clear in its wording. Among that is: ﴿and they wish that you should go astray﴾, i.e., that you abandon the right course by turning to them, and consider them not to be enemies. "And Allah knows best about them."

His saying: ﴿And Allah knows best your enemies﴾ is a statement containing within it a warning against them. The "bi-" in His saying "and sufficient is Allah" is in a place of raising (rafʿ), by way of supposing an added preposition (khāfiḍ). The benefit of its addition is to make clear the meaning of the command within the form of a statement, i.e., "be content with Allah." So the bāʾ indicates the intended meaning of that. "Walīyan" is of the pattern fa'īl, and "naṣīran" is likewise, from wilāya (guardianship) and naṣr (support).

[p-571]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among those who are Jews﴾. Some of the interpreters said: "min" refers back to the first "alladhīna," so on this view it is connected to "tarā" (see). A group said: it is connected to "naṣīran," and the meaning is: He will support you against those who are Jews. On these two interpretations, one does not stop at "naṣīran." A group said: it is for the beginning of the speech, and within it there is an implied element, its estimated form being "yuḥarrifūna" (they distort). This is the view of Abu 'Ali, and its parallel is the poet's saying:

They were of the camels of Abu Uqaysh, rattling behind their two legs with a waterskin.

Al-Farra' and others said: its estimated form is "man" (those who). A similar example is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

So they remained, while among them one whose tear is flowing ahead of him, and another who wipes the tear of his eye with his hand.

On this interpretation, one stops at "naṣīran." But Sibawayh's view is more correct, because omitting the relative pronoun is heavy, whereas omitting the described noun is easier.

"Hādū" is derived from hāda, meaning he repented, or from Yahūdh ibn Ya'qub, and the arabization changed it. Or it is from tahawwud, which is walking slowly and gently in speech. Al-Khalil mentioned all of these, and their explanation and clarification has already passed in [Surat al-Baqara].

[p-572]

The distortion of words (taḥrīf al-kalim) is in two ways: either by changing the wording, and they did that in a few cases; or by changing the interpretation, and they did that in most cases. Al-Tabari took this view. All of this is in the Torah according to the view of the majority. Another group said: it refers to the words of the Qur'an. Makki said: the speech of the Prophet Muhammad, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him. On this view, distortion occurs only in the interpretation. Al-Nakha'i recited "yuḥarrifūna al-kalām" with an alif.

Whoever made "min" connected to "naṣīran" makes "yuḥarrifūna" in the place of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). Whoever made it disconnected (munqaṭiʿa) makes "yuḥarrifūna" a ṣifa (descriptive clause).

His saying, exalted is He, about them, "We heard and we disobeyed," is an expression for their extreme arrogance in their disbelief and their transgression in it.

"Musmaʿin" is only conjugated from "asmaʿa." As for "ghayra musmaʿin," two meanings can be drawn from it. One: not commanded and not humbled, as if He said: "not that you hear while commanded to that." The other: in the form of supplication, meaning: may you not hear. Just as you say: "Go, may you not be correct," and the like. So when the Jews addressed the Prophet with "ghayra musmaʿin," they intended inwardly a supplication against him, while outwardly they showed that they intended his honor. Ibn 'Abbas and others said something similar. Likewise "rā'inā": they meant by it in their souls the meaning of foolishness (ruʿūna), while Makki reported the meaning of tending livestock. They showed by it the meaning of consideration (murāʿāh). This is the meaning of "twisting the tongue." Al-Zajjaj said: they meant: make your name a pasture for our speech.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this there is a rudeness that is not to be addressed to a prophet. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud the reading is "rāʿūnā." As for whoever said "ghayra musmaʿin" means "not accepted from you," this does not agree with the morphology (taṣrīf). Al-Tabari transmitted it from al-Hasan and Mujahid. "Layyan": its origin is lawyan; the waw was changed to yā' and assimilated. "Wa ṭaʿnan fī al-dīn" means belittling it and showing contempt for it.

[p-573]

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This twisting of the tongue, with the tongue contrary to what is in the heart, is still present today among the Children of Israel. In our age examples of it can be observed, but it is not fitting to mention them in this book.

"And if they had": the verse means: if they had believed, heard and obeyed. The commentators differed about His saying "wa-nẓurnā." Mujahid, Ikrima and others said its meaning is "wait for us," in the sense of: make us understand and be patient with us until we understand you and retain your words. This is like what al-Hutay'a said:

And I have awaited you, the pausing of one who returns from a journey, for five days, my wiping and my ... have been prolonged with it.

Another group said: "unẓur" means: look at us. It is as if it were a request for attentiveness and attention. From this is the saying of Ibn al-Ruqayyat:

Manifest in beauty and loveliness, they look, as gazelles look upon the arak trees.

"And more upright" (wa-aqwam) means more just and more correct. "La'na" is expulsion, so its meaning is: He removed them far from guidance. "Qalīlan" is an adjective, either of faith, or of a band or a people, and the meaning differs. Whoever expressed the paucity as an expression of faith said: either it is an expression of its absence, as Sibawayh related from their saying: "a land which produces hardly anything of such-and-such," where it produces none of it at all. Or He reduced faith because the things they believed in were few, so that this did not benefit them. This is because they believed in monotheism and disbelieved in Muhammad and in all the commands and prohibitions of his law.

[p-574]

Whoever expressed the paucity as a small group said: "Only a few of them believe, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, Ka'b al-Ahbar and others." If you take the speech as "a small group" (nafaran qalīlan), then it is in the accusative in the place of a ḥāl.

One: not commanded and not humbled, as if He said: "not that you hear while commanded to that." The other: in the form of supplication, meaning: may you not hear. Just as you say: "Go, may you not be correct," and the like. Ibn 'Abbas and others said something similar. Likewise "rā'inā": they meant by it in their souls the meaning of foolishness (ruʿūna), while Makki reported the meaning of tending livestock. In this there is a rudeness that is not to be addressed to a prophet. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud the reading is "rāʿūnā." [p-573]

This twisting of the tongue, with the tongue contrary to what is in the heart, is still present today among the Children of Israel. In our age examples of it can be observed, but it is not fitting to mention them in this book.

"And if they had": the verse means: if they had believed, heard and obeyed. The commentators differed about His saying "wa-nẓurnā." Mujahid, Ikrima and others said its meaning is "wait for us," in the sense of: make us understand and be patient with us until we understand you and retain your words. This is like what al-Hutay'a said:

And I have awaited you, the pausing of one who returns from a journey, for five days, my wiping and my ... have been prolonged with it.

Another group said: "unẓur" means: look at us. It is as if it were a request for attentiveness and attention. From this is the saying of Ibn al-Ruqayyat:

Manifest in beauty and loveliness, they look, as gazelles look upon the arak trees.

"And more upright" (wa-aqwam) means more just and more correct. "La'na" is expulsion, so its meaning is: He removed them far from guidance. Or He reduced faith because the things they believed in were few, so that this did not benefit them. This is because they believed in monotheism and disbelieved in Muhammad and in all the commands and prohibitions of his law.

[p-574]

Whoever expressed the paucity as a small group said: "Only a few of them believe, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, Ka'b al-Ahbar and others." If you take the speech as "a small group" (nafaran qalīlan), then it is in the accusative in the place of a ḥāl.

[p-570]

The seeing in His saying "Have you not seen" is seeing with the heart, which is knowledge of a thing. Some said its meaning is: "Have you not known?" Others said: "Have you not been informed?" All of these are close in meaning. Seeing with the heart is connected with a preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) and without one. What is meant by "those" (alladhīna) is the Jews. This was said by Qatada and others. Then the wording also includes the Christians along with them. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Rifa'a ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut, the Jew.

"Were given" (ūtū) means were given. Naṣīb (portion) means share. Kitāb (the Book) means the Torah and the Gospel. The recipient is called a "portion" with respect to each individual separately, because knowledge of the Book is not confined to one person in any respect.

"They buy" (yashtarūna) is an expression for their preferring disbelief and abandoning faith. It is as if it were a giving and taking. This is the view of a group. Another group said: it means those who used to give their wealth to the rabbis in order to uphold their law. On this interpretation, this is buying in its literal sense.

﴿And they wish that you should go astray from the way﴾: its meaning is that you should disbelieve. Al-Nakha'i recited "and you wish" (tarīdūna) with the letter tā' dotted from above in "tarīdūna."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse and what follows require rebuke of the believers for leaning toward a group of the rabbis of the Jews, whether in asking about religion, in alliance, or in something similar. This is clear in its wording. Among that is: ﴿and they wish that you should go astray﴾, i.e., that you abandon the right course by turning to them, and consider them not to be enemies. "And Allah knows best about them."

His saying: ﴿And Allah knows best your enemies﴾ is a statement containing within it a warning against them. The "bi-" in His saying "and sufficient is Allah" is in a place of raising (rafʿ), by way of supposing an added preposition (khāfiḍ). The benefit of its addition is to make clear the meaning of the command within the form of a statement, i.e., "be content with Allah." So the bāʾ indicates the intended meaning of that. "Walīyan" is of the pattern fa'īl, and "naṣīran" is likewise, from wilāya (guardianship) and naṣr (support).

[p-571]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among those who are Jews﴾. Some of the interpreters said: "min" refers back to the first "alladhīna," so on this view it is connected to "tarā" (see). A group said: it is connected to "naṣīran," and the meaning is: He will support you against those who are Jews. On these two interpretations, one does not stop at "naṣīran." A group said: it is for the beginning of the speech, and within it there is an implied element, its estimated form being "yuḥarrifūna" (they distort). This is the view of Abu 'Ali, and its parallel is the poet's saying:

They were of the camels of Abu Uqaysh, rattling behind their two legs with a waterskin.

Al-Farra' and others said: its estimated form is "man" (those who). A similar example is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

So they remained, while among them one whose tear is flowing ahead of him, and another who wipes the tear of his eye with his hand.

On this interpretation, one stops at "naṣīran." But Sibawayh's view is more correct, because omitting the relative pronoun is heavy, whereas omitting the described noun is easier.

"Hādū" is derived from hāda, meaning he repented, or from Yahūdh ibn Ya'qub, and the arabization changed it. Or it is from tahawwud, which is walking slowly and gently in speech. Al-Khalil mentioned all of these, and their explanation and clarification has already passed in [Surat al-Baqara].

[p-572]

Al-Tabari took this view. All of this is in the Torah according to the view of the majority. Another group said: it refers to the words of the Qur'an. Makki said: the speech of the Prophet Muhammad, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him. On this view, distortion occurs only in the interpretation. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 47–48:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what you already have, before We obliterate faces and turn them back upon their backs, or curse them as We cursed the companions of the Sabbath; and the command of Allah is always carried out﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills. And whoever associates partners with Allah has indeed fabricated a tremendous sin﴾

This is an address to the Jews and the Christians. "What you already have" means: of law and religion, not what they possessed of altered and changed [scripture].

Al-taamis (obliterating) is the effaced, whose markers have been altered, as Dhu al-Rummah said:

"From every sweating, fragrant-necked [camel] when her reins are wet, a track whose markers are obliterated and unknown."

From this it was said of a blind man whose eyes are sealed: "a blind man, obliterated." A group said: the obliteration of faces here means that the traces of the senses in them are erased and the form is removed from them, so that it returns like the other limbs, empty of sense organs. Then "turning back upon their backs" in this place is meant figuratively, i.e., its emptiness of the senses is like the back, because it is full of them. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' al-'Awfi said: the obliteration of faces is that the two eyes alone are removed from them and returned to the nape, so that this is a turning back upon the rear, and one walks backwards. At-Tabari related from a group that the obliteration of faces is that their markings change and they become places for hair; this is the turning back upon the rear, and at-Tabari rejected this view. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The first Islam of Ka'b was that he passed by a man at night who was reciting this verse: (p-575) "O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what you already have," so he placed his palms upon his face and returned backwards to his house, and embraced Islam on the spot, and said: "By Allah, I feared that I would not reach my house before my face was obliterated." Mujahid, al-Hasan, as-Suddi and ad-Dahhak said: that is a figure of speech, and what is meant is the faces of guidance and right direction; their obliteration is the decree of misguidance, turning away from it, and directing to disbelief, and this is the turning back upon the rear. Ibn Zayd said: the faces are their homelands and dwellings in their lands to which they went out; their obliteration is their expulsion from them, and the turning back upon the rear is their return to Syria from where they first came.

"The companions of the Sabbath" are the people of Aylah who transgressed on the Sabbath by hunting, as has been mentioned before, and their curse was that they were transformed into swine and apes, as said by Qatadah, al-Hasan and as-Suddi.

"The command of Allah" in this place is the singular noun denoting the category of affairs, not the singular of commands; it is an expression for created things, such as the punishment and the curse here, or whatever each context requires that is specific to it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾, the verse. This is the question of promise and threat (al-wa'd wa al-wa'id), and the summary of the discussion on it is that it is said: people are of four categories. A disbeliever who died in his disbelief: this one is eternal in the Fire by consensus. A believer who is virtuous, who never sinned and died in that state: this one is certainly in Paradise by consensus, according to the report from Allah exalted. A penitent who died in his repentance: according to the People of the Sunnah and the majority of the jurists of the community, he is joined to the virtuous believer, except that the rule of the theologians is that he is subject to the Will. A sinner who died before his repentance: this is the point of disagreement. The Murji'ah said: he is in Paradise by his faith, and his misdeeds do not harm him, and they based this view on making all verses of threat specific to disbelievers, and verses of promise general to believers, pious and disobedient alike. The Mu'tazilah said: if he is one who committed a major sin, then he is in the Fire without doubt. The Kharijites said:

if he is one who committed a major or minor sin, then he is in the Fire eternally, and has no faith, because they consider every sin a major sin; and they based this view on making all verses of promise specific to the believer who is virtuous and never disobeyed, and the penitent believer, and making the verses of threat general to the disobedient, whether disbelievers or believers. The People of the Sunnah and truth said: the verses of promise are apparently general in their wording, and the verses of threat are apparently general in their wording, and it is not valid to implement all of them in their apparent sense because they contradict one another, such as His saying, exalted: ﴿None will enter it but the most wretched﴾ [al-Layl: 15] ﴿who denied and turned away﴾ [al-Layl: 16], and His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then for him is the Fire of Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 23]. This verse is the decisive one that clarifies what conflicts among verses, so we must say: the verses of promise are general in wording but the intended meaning is particular to the virtuous believer, to the penitent, and to those whom Allah knew in His knowledge He would pardon among the disobedient without punishment; and the verses of threat are general in wording but the intended meaning is particular to the disbelievers, and to those whom Allah knew in His knowledge He would punish among the disobedient. We conclude by our saying: "this verse" is the explicit text on the point of dispute, namely His saying, exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾. It has removed doubt and refuted both groups, the Murji'ah and the Mu'tazilah. That is because His saying, exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ is a decisive separation on which there is consensus, and His saying: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that﴾ is a decisive separation against the Mu'tazilah, a refutation of their view from which there is no escape; and had we stopped at this point of the statement, the view of the Murji'ah would have been valid, so His saying "for whomever He wills" came as a refutation of them, establishing that the forgiveness of what is less than association is only for some people and not others, contrary to what they claimed about it being forgiven for every believer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Mu'tazilah sought to turn this verse back to their doctrine by saying: "for whomever He wills" refers to the penitent. But what they intended is invalid, because the benefit of the division in the verse would be nullified, since the penitent from association is forgiven.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Murji'ah sought to turn the verse back to their doctrine by saying: "for whomever He wills" means: He wills that he believe, not that He forgive him; so the will is linked to faith on the part of the one who believes, not to Allah's forgiveness for the one whom He forgives. This is refuted by the fact that the verse, on this interpretation, requires that His saying "and He forgives what is less than that" be general over disbeliever and believer; so when the believers are specified by His saying "for whomever He wills," it follows that the disbelievers are not forgiven what is less than that, and they are requited for it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, although it has been said, is a view that was not intended by the verse according to any interpretation of the scholars, and this approach is refuted by the length of the division, because association is also forgiven for whomever Allah wills to believe.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among the verses of threat that the Mu'tazilah cited as evidence is His saying, exalted: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment﴾ [an-Nisa': 93]. The verse is excluded from their reading for several reasons. Among them: the most correct interpretation of His saying, exalted, "intentionally" is what Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant "considering it lawful"; and whoever considers lawful what Allah has forbidden has indeed disbelieved. What supports Ibn 'Abbas's view is that we find that when Allah, exalted, mentions retaliation (qisas) regarding killing, He does not mention the threat, and when He mentions the threat of the Fire, He does not mention retaliation; so it becomes clear that retaliation is for the believing killer who is disobedient, and the threat is for the one who considers it lawful, who is in the position of a disbeliever. Another reason, from a different angle: "abiding" (khulud), when not joined to the word "forever" (abadan), may be taken to mean a long duration, since this is known in Arabic usage. Do you not see that they greet kings with "may Allah make your kingdom eternal" (khallada Allahu mulkaka)? Among this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Will anyone enjoy life except a fortunate, long-lived one, free of worries, who does not spend the night in fetters?"

'Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: "When the verse ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾ [az-Zumar: 53] was revealed, some of the Companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'And what of association, O Messenger of Allah?' Then it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾." When He made it decisive that He does not forgive association, He mentioned the ugliness of its position and its rank among sins. Al-Fiyah (slander/fabrication) is the most ugly degree of lying, and it is the inventing of falsehood for the sake of partisanship.

Among them: the most correct interpretation of His saying, exalted, "intentionally" is what Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant "considering it lawful"; and whoever considers lawful what Allah has forbidden has indeed disbelieved. What supports Ibn 'Abbas's view is that we find that when Allah, exalted, mentions retaliation (qisas) regarding killing, He does not mention the threat, and when He mentions the threat of the Fire, He does not mention retaliation; so it becomes clear that retaliation is for the believing killer who is disobedient, and the threat is for the one who considers it lawful, who is in the position of a disbeliever. Another reason, from a different angle: "abiding" (khulud), when not joined to the word "forever" (abadan), may be taken to mean a long duration, since this is known in Arabic usage. Do you not see that they greet kings with "may Allah make your kingdom eternal" (khallada Allahu mulkaka)? Among this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Will anyone enjoy life except a fortunate, long-lived one, free of worries, who does not spend the night in fetters?"

'Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: "When the verse ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾ [az-Zumar: 53] was revealed, some of the Companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'And what of association, O Messenger of Allah?' Then it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾." When He made it decisive that He does not forgive association, He mentioned the ugliness of its position and its rank among sins. Al-Fiyah (slander/fabrication) is the most ugly degree of lying, and it is the inventing of falsehood for the sake of partisanship.

[p. 578]

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged the least bit.﴾ ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah; and that is sufficient as a manifest sin.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in al-jibt and al-taghut, and they say of those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who believe, in the way."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed. And whomever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper.﴾

This wording is general in its outward form, and none of the exegetes disagreed that the intended people are the Jews. They differed over the matter by which they "claimed purity for themselves." Qatadah and al-Hasan said: it is their saying, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved" [al-Ma'idah: 18], and their saying, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews" [al-Baqarah: 111]. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it is their saying, "We have no sins. What we did by day was forgiven by night, and what we did by night was forgiven by day, and we are like children in being free of sins." Mujahid, Abu Malik and Ikrimah said: it is their putting forward their small children to lead them in prayer, because those children have no sins.

The author [Ibn 'Atiyya] said: This is far from the purpose of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is their saying, "Our children who have died will intercede for us and purify us." 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: it is some of them praising others and commending them and purifying them.

The al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse entails censure of one who purifies himself with his own tongue, and it informs us that the one who is truly pure and purified is the one whose deeds are good and whom Allah, mighty and majestic, has purified. The pronoun in "yuzakkūn" [they claim purity] refers either to those mentioned who purified themselves, or to those whom Allah purifies. Apart from these two categories, it is known from other evidence that Allah, the Exalted, does not wrong them.

A group read "wa-lā tuẓlamūn" [and you will not be wronged] with the letter tāʾ, as direct address.

Al-fatīl (the thread, a small twisted fibre) is what is twisted; it is a form fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl (twisted). Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid and others said: al-fatīl is the thread that is in the split of a date-stone. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Malik and al-Suddi said: it is what comes out from between your two fingers or your two palms when you twist them. All of this comes back to a metaphor for the smallness and triviality of a thing, meaning that Allah does not wrong even that, and nothing is smaller than it, so how much less would He wrong what is greater than it. Its accusative (naṣb) is as the second object of "yuẓlamūn" [they will be wronged].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Look how they invent lies⦆ [the verse], shows that their claiming purity for themselves was by falsehood and lying, and it strengthens the view that the claim of purity was by their saying, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved" [al-Ma'idah: 18], since invention is more likely in this statement.

"Kayfa" [how] may be in the accusative position governed by "yaftarūn" [they invent], and it may be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being "yaftarūn."

"Wa-kafā bihi ithman mubīnan" [and that is sufficient as a manifest sin] is a statement whose implied meaning is wonder and astonishment at the matter. For this reason the particle bāʾ (bi-) entered, to indicate the sense of amazement, and to indicate that this lie should be considered by itself a sin, and no further punishment should be sought for them beyond it, since it is destructive and ruinous. "Ithman" [as a sin] is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyīz).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who⦆ [the verse]. Its outward meaning encompasses the Jews and the Christians, but the exegetes agreed that what is meant is a group of the Jews, and the narratives make this clear. They differed concerning "bi-l-jibt wa-l-ṭāghūt" [in al-jibt and al-ṭāghūt]. Ikrimah and others said: they are, in this context, two idols that belonged to the Quraysh. This is because Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and a group with him came to Makkah inciting [the people] to fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Quraysh said to them: "You are the People of the Book, and Muhammad is a man of a Book, and we do not trust you to be with him, unless you prostrate to these two idols that belong to us." So they did, and this verse was revealed concerning that. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-jibt here is Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and al-ṭāghūt is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. According to this view, the intended people in the verse are those among the Children of Israel who were with them, because they believed in them and followed them. Ibn 'Abbas also said: al-jibt means the idols, and al-ṭāghūt means the people who translate for the idols, who lead people astray by teaching them to worship the idols. It was related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: al-jibt is magic, and al-ṭāghūt is the Devil. Mujahid and al-Sha'bi also said this. Zayd ibn Aslam said: al-jibt is the sorcerer, and al-ṭāghūt is the Devil. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Rafi' said: al-jibt is the sorcerer, and al-ṭāghūt is the soothsayer. Qatadah said: al-jibt is the Devil, and al-ṭāghūt is the soothsayer. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: al-jibt is the Devil, and al-ṭāghūt is the Devil. Ibn Sirin said: al-jibt is the soothsayer, and al-ṭāghūt is the sorcerer. Mujahid, in the book of al-Tabari, said: al-jibt is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and al-ṭāghūt is the Devil, who was in the form of a human being.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The totality of these views entails that "al-jibt wa-l-ṭāghūt" is everything that is worshipped and obeyed besides Allah. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve⦆ [the verse]. Its occasion was: "When Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf arrived in Makkah, the Quraysh said to him: 'You are our chief and the chief of your people. Al-Suddi related that Abu Sufyan addressed Ka'b with this statement. "Ahdā" [better guided]: its measure is afʿal, and it is for comparison (tafḍīl). "Alladhīna āmanū" [those who believe] are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. "Sabīlan" [in the way] is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyīz).

A sect said: rather, what is meant in the verse from the Children of Israel is Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and he is the one intended from the beginning of the verses, and the one indicated by His saying "ulā'ika" [those] are what is meant from the Children of Israel. "Ahdā" [better guided]: its measure is afʿal, and it is for comparison (tafḍīl). "Alladhīna āmanū" [those who believe] are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. "Sabīlan" [in the way] is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyīz).

A sect said: rather, what is meant in the verse from the Children of Israel is Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and he is the one intended from the beginning of the verses, and the one indicated by His saying "ulā'ika" [those] are what is meant from the Children of Israel. As for one who says they were a group, that is correct both in wording and in meaning. And as for one who says it was Ka'b or Huyayy, and expresses him with the plural form, that is because he was a leader whose statement was accompanied by the statement of a group.

"La'anahum" [He cursed them] means: He removed them far from His good and detested them. Whomever Allah does this to and forsakes, there is no helper for him among the created beings. Even if a group supports him, their support is like no support, since they cannot avail him anything.

[p. 578]

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged the least bit.﴾ ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah; and that is sufficient as a manifest sin.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in al-jibt and al-taghut, and they say of those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who believe, in the way."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed. And whomever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper.﴾

This wording is general in its outward form, and none of the exegetes disagreed that the intended people are the Jews. They differed over the matter by which they "claimed purity for themselves." Qatadah and al-Hasan said: it is their saying, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved" [al-Ma'idah: 18], and their saying, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews" [al-Baqarah: 111]. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it is their saying, "We have no sins. What we did by day was forgiven by night, and what we did by night was forgiven by day, and we are like children in being free of sins." Mujahid, Abu Malik and Ikrimah said: it is their putting forward their small children to lead them in prayer, because those children have no sins.

The author [Ibn 'Atiyya] said: This is far from the purpose of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is their saying, "Our children who have died will intercede for us and purify us." 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: it is some of them praising others and commending them and purifying them.

The al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse entails censure of one who purifies himself with his own tongue, and it informs us that the one who is truly pure and purified is the one whose deeds are good and whom Allah, mighty and majestic, has purified. The pronoun in "yuzakkūn" [they claim purity] refers either to those mentioned who purified themselves, or to those whom Allah purifies. Apart from these two categories, it is known from other evidence that Allah, the Exalted, does not wrong them.

A group read "wa-lā tuẓlamūn" [and you will not be wronged] with the letter tāʾ, as direct address.

Al-fatīl (the thread, a small twisted fibre) is what is twisted; it is a form fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl (twisted). Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid and others said: al-fatīl is the thread that is in the split of a date-stone. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Malik and al-Suddi said: it is what comes out from between your two fingers or your two palms when you twist them. All of this comes back to a metaphor for the smallness and triviality of a thing, meaning that Allah does not wrong even that, and nothing is smaller than it, so how much less would He wrong what is greater than it. Its accusative (naṣb) is as the second object of "yuẓlamūn" [they will be wronged].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Look how they invent lies⦆ [the verse], shows that their claiming purity for themselves was by falsehood and lying, and it strengthens the view that the claim of purity was by their saying, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved" [al-Ma'idah: 18], since invention is more likely in this statement.

"Kayfa" [how] may be in the accusative position governed by "yaftarūn" [they invent], and it may be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being "yaftarūn."

"Wa-kafā bihi ithman mubīnan" [and that is sufficient as a manifest sin] is a statement whose implied meaning is wonder and astonishment at the matter. For this reason the particle bāʾ (bi-) entered, to indicate the sense of amazement, and to indicate that this lie should be considered by itself a sin, and no further punishment should be sought for them beyond it, since it is destructive and ruinous. "Ithman" [as a sin] is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyīz).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who⦆ [the verse]. Its outward meaning encompasses the Jews and the Christians, but the exegetes agreed that what is meant is a group of the Jews, and the narratives make this clear. They differed concerning "bi-l-jibt wa-l-ṭāghūt" [in al-jibt and al-ṭāghūt]. Ikrimah and others said: they are, in this context, two idols that belonged to the Quraysh. This is because Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and a group with him came to Makkah inciting [the people] to fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Quraysh said to them: "You are the People of the Book, and Muhammad is a man of a Book, and we do not trust you to be with him, unless you prostrate to these two idols that belong to us." So they did, and this verse was revealed concerning that. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-jibt here is Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and al-ṭāghūt is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. According to this view, the intended people in the verse are those among the Children of Israel who were with them, because they believed in them and followed them. Ibn 'Abbas also said: al-jibt means the idols, and al-ṭāghūt means the people who translate for the idols, who lead people astray by teaching them to worship the idols. It was related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: al-jibt is magic, and al-ṭāghūt is the Devil. Mujahid and al-Sha'bi also said this. Zayd ibn Aslam said: al-jibt is the sorcerer, and al-ṭāghūt is the Devil. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Rafi' said: al-jibt is the sorcerer, and al-ṭāghūt is the soothsayer. Qatadah said: al-jibt is the Devil, and al-ṭāghūt is the soothsayer. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: al-jibt is the Devil, and al-ṭāghūt is the Devil. Ibn Sirin said: al-jibt is the soothsayer, and al-ṭāghūt is the sorcerer. Mujahid, in the book of al-Tabari, said: al-jibt is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and al-ṭāghūt is the Devil, who was in the form of a human being.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The totality of these views entails that "al-jibt wa-l-ṭāghūt" is everything that is worshipped and obeyed besides Allah. Likewise Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "al-ṭāghūt is everything that is worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted." Some people mentioned that al-jibt is from the language of Abyssinia (al-Habashah). Qutrub said: al-jibt is originally al-jibs, which is what is heavy and has no good in it. As for al-ṭāghūt, it is one who transgresses (ṭaghā); its origin is ṭaghūwt, its measure is faʿlūt, and its tāʾ is an added letter. It was transposed and then restored, so it became falʿūt, its origin being ṭawaghūt. The wāw moved and the letter before it was vowelled with fatḥah, so it changed into an alif.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve⦆ [the verse]. Its occasion was: "When Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf arrived in Makkah, the Quraysh said to him: 'You are our chief and the chief of your people. And this cut-off one [i.e., the Prophet] from among his people has severed the ties of kinship. So who is more rightly guided, we or he?'" Ka'b said: "You are more rightly guided than him and more upright in religion." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Suddi related that Abu Sufyan addressed Ka'b with this statement. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 53–55:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Or do they have a share of the kingdom? Then they would not give people even a speck (naqir).﴾ ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? We had already given the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.﴾ ﴿Among them were those who believed in it, and among them were those who turned away from it. Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire.﴾

The usage of *am* (or) is that it is coordinated after a preceding interrogative, as in your saying: "Did Zayd stand up or 'Amr?" When it occurs without a preceding interrogative, the view of Sibawayh is that it implies the sense of *idrab* (turning away from the first statement and breaking off from it), and it also implies the sense of interrogation. It therefore means *bal* (rather) together with the interrogative alif, as in the Arabs' saying: "Is it camels, or sheep?" The implied meaning according to Sibawayh is: "Is it camels? Rather, is it sheep?" Likewise in this place, its implied meaning is: "Rather, do they have a share of the kingdom?" It has been reported from some grammarians that *am* may be used interrogatively at the beginning without a preceding interrogative. Ibn Qutayba related this in *al-Mushkil*, but it is not well known among the Arabs. Some exegetes said that *am* means *bal*, without mentioning the obligatory alif. On this view they were obliged to hold that the kingdom was attained by those mentioned in the verse, and they accepted this and interpreted accordingly. Their meaning is: "Rather, they are kings of the world, people of arrogance (utuww)(p-582) and luxury, who seek nothing else. Therefore they are stingy with it, eager that no one else should have any prominence."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning according to the more preponderant view, which is the view of Sibawayh and the expert grammarians, is that it is an interrogative in the sense of denial, i.e., "Do they have a kingdom? Then, if they did have it, they would be stingy."

Ibn Mas'ud read: *fa-idhan la yu'tu* (without the nun), applying the governing function (i'mal) of *idhan*. The Mushaf (the written codex) reads it with its cancellation (ilgha'), and both readings are permissible, even though *idhan* is placed at the beginning because the fa' (then) has come before it.

*Naqir*: the best-known meaning of it is that it is the small mark on the back of a date pit (nawa) from which the date palm sprouts. This is the view of the majority. A group said it is the small point on the inside of the pit. It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: it is the pressing of a person's finger (naqr al-insan bi-usbu'ihi). All of these meanings share the idea that it is a metaphor for the utmost of insignificance and smallness, according to the figurative usage (majaz) and borrowing (isti'arah) of the Arabs. *Idhan* in this verse is cancelled (mulgha) because the conjunctive fa' has come before it, though it is permissible to make it operative. Cancellation is more eloquent, and that is the dialect of the Qur'an. Its nature is that when *idhan* comes first it is operative in one way only; when a fa' or waw precedes it, it may be made operative, but cancellation is more eloquent. *Idhan* is written both with a nun and with an alif. The nun is the original form, like *'an* and *min*, and writing it with an alif is permitted because pausing on it is sound, so it resembles the nun of tanwin. Pausing on *'an* and *min* is not sound.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they envy the people...﴾ the verse. This *am* is in its proper function, because the interrogative in our reading ("Rather, do they have...") has come before it.

The interpreters differed about who is meant by "the people" (al-nas) in this place. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: it is the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the bounty is only prophethood. The meaning is: why do they single him out for envy, and not envy the family of Abraham for all that We gave them of this and other things, including the kingdom? Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi also said: it is the Prophet ﷺ, and the bounty is only what was permitted to him of women. The occasion of revelation according to them is that the Jews said to the disbelieving Arabs: "Look at this one who claims that he was sent with humility, and that he does not fill his belly with food; his only concern is women," and similar things. So the verse was revealed. The meaning is: why do they single him out for envy and not envy the family of Abraham, peace be upon him? That is, Solomon and David, peace be upon them both,(p-583) in that they were given prophethood and the Book, and, in addition to that, they were given a great kingdom in the matter of women. This is what is reported: Solomon had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and David had a hundred wives, and similar reports are transmitted about this. So in this view, the kingdom is the permission of women, as if that was the primary intended point of mention. Qatada said: "the people" in this place are the Arabs, whom the children of Israel envied because the Prophet, peace be upon him, was from them. The bounty according to this interpretation is Muhammad, peace be upon him. The meaning is: why do they envy the Arabs for this Prophet ﷺ, when the family of Abraham ﷺ, who are their forefathers, were given prophets and scriptures such as the Torah and the Psalms, and wisdom, which is understanding in religion and what is guidance that the Book does not explicitly state. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "We are the people," meaning the Quraysh.

"A great kingdom": that is, Solomon. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: the great kingdom in the verse is prophethood. Hammam ibn al-Harith and Abu Maslama said: it is the support (ta'yid) by the angels.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The more correct view is that it is the kingdom of Solomon, or the matter of women in the earlier interpretation.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among them were those who believed in it...﴾ the verse. The interpreters differed about what the pronoun in "in it" (bihi) refers to. The majority said it refers to the Qur'an mentioned in His saying: ﴿Believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces﴾ [al-Nisa': 47]. Allah then informed that among them were those who believed as they were commanded, and for this reason the threat of obliteration was lifted and did not occur. Some turned away, and the threat against them was confirmed in the Hereafter by His saying: ﴿and Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire.﴾ A group said: the pronoun refers to Abraham, peace be upon him, and Makki related stories about this that are not authentic. Another group said: it refers to the bounty that Allah gave the Prophet, peace be upon him, or to the Arabs according to what was mentioned earlier.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

A group read *suddda 'anhu* ("he was turned away from it") with a dammah on the *sad*, building the verb in the passive. *Sa'ir* means blazing and flaming. *Sa'ir* is the intensity of the fire's kindling. This is therefore a metaphor for the intensity of punishment and retribution.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: it is the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the bounty is only prophethood. The meaning is: why do they single him out for envy, and not envy the family of Abraham for all that We gave them of this and other things, including the kingdom? Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi also said: it is the Prophet ﷺ, and the bounty is only what was permitted to him of women. The occasion of revelation according to them is that the Jews said to the disbelieving Arabs: "Look at this one who claims that he was sent with humility, and that he does not fill his belly with food; his only concern is women," and similar things. So the verse was revealed. The meaning is: why do they single him out for envy and not envy the family of Abraham, peace be upon him? That is, Solomon and David, peace be upon them both,(p-583) in that they were given prophethood and the Book, and, in addition to that, they were given a great kingdom in the matter of women. This is what is reported: Solomon had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and David had a hundred wives, and similar reports are transmitted about this. So in this view, the kingdom is the permission of women, as if that was the primary intended point of mention. Qatada said: "the people" in this place are the Arabs, whom the children of Israel envied because the Prophet, peace be upon him, was from them. The bounty according to this interpretation is Muhammad, peace be upon him. The meaning is: why do they envy the Arabs for this Prophet ﷺ, when the family of Abraham ﷺ, who are their forefathers, were given prophets and scriptures such as the Torah and the Psalms, and wisdom, which is understanding in religion and what is guidance that the Book does not explicitly state. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "We are the people," meaning the Quraysh.

"A great kingdom": that is, Solomon. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: the great kingdom in the verse is prophethood. Hammam ibn al-Harith and Abu Maslama said: it is the support (ta'yid) by the angels.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The more correct view is that it is the kingdom of Solomon, or the matter of women in the earlier interpretation.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among them were those who believed in it...﴾ the verse. The interpreters differed about what the pronoun in "in it" (bihi) refers to. The majority said it refers to the Qur'an mentioned in His saying: ﴿Believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces﴾ [al-Nisa': 47]. Allah then informed that among them were those who believed as they were commanded, and for this reason the threat of obliteration was lifted and did not occur. Some turned away, and the threat against them was confirmed in the Hereafter by His saying: ﴿and Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire.﴾ A group said: the pronoun refers to Abraham, peace be upon him, and Makki related stories about this that are not authentic. Another group said: it refers to the bounty that Allah gave the Prophet, peace be upon him, or to the Arabs according to what was mentioned earlier.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

A group read *suddda 'anhu* ("he was turned away from it") with a dammah on the *sad*, building the verb in the passive. *Sa'ir* means blazing and flaming. *Sa'ir* is the intensity of the fire's kindling. This is therefore a metaphor for the intensity of punishment and retribution.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 56–57:

(p-584) His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our verses – We will drive them into a Fire. Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. For them therein are purified spouses, and We will admit them to a shade, deep and extending.﴾

Earlier in the verses there was a description of the rebellious ones among the Children of Israel, and a mention of their deeds and sins. Then came the explicit threat addressed to them, in a clear and general wording that includes them and others who commit the same disbelief as they did. The well-known reading is "nuslīhim" (We will drive them) with a damma on the nūn, from aslaytu (to cause to enter), meaning: you brought near to the fire and cast into it, which is the same meaning as ṣallaytu (with a shadda on the lām). Ḥumayd read "naṣlīhim" from ṣalaytu, meaning ṣallaytu, and its meaning is shawaytu (to roast). From it is the ḥadīth: "A roasted sheep (shāh maṣliyyah) was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," i.e., roasted (mashwiyyah). Likewise the conjugation of the verb occurs with the ʿayn and otherwise. Salām and Yaʿqūb read "nuṣlīhum" with a damma on the hā'.

The interpreters differed regarding the meaning of the replacement of the skins. One group said: other skins are substituted for them, since it is their souls that are punished, and the skins do not feel pain in themselves; so they are replaced so that they may taste the renewal of punishment. Another group said: the replacement of the skins is the restoration of that very same skin which was in the world, which the fire consumes and which Allah returns continually for the renewal of the punishment. He called it a replacement only because its attributes change and then it is restored, as you say: "Replace this ring of mine with a ring," and it is the same silver itself, so the substitution occurred only in the change of its qualities. Ibn ʿUmar said: whenever their skins are burned, they are replaced with white skins like parchments. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan said: they are replaced seventy thousand times in a day. Another group said: the "skins" in this place are garments of tar (sarābīl al-qaṭrān); He called them skins because they cling (to the body) so that they become like skins, and they are replaced continually. May Allah protect us from His punishment by His mercy. This is related by al-Ṭabarī.

After these preliminaries, it is fitting that the attributes of might and perfect wisdom follow, because no one who opposes Allah can overcome Him except that Allah overcomes him, and He does nothing except with wisdom and correctness. There is no god but He, blessed and exalted.

When Allah mentioned the threat to the disbelievers, He followed it with the promise to the believers of Paradise for their faith and righteous deeds. Ibn Wathhāb read "sa-yudkhiluhum" with a yā', and likewise "yudkhiluhum" after that. The meaning of "min taḥtihā" has already been discussed in [Surat al-Baqara]. The meaning of "muṭahharah" is: purified from the doubts and filth that are familiar in this world. As for "ẓalīlan," its meaning according to some is: it protects from heat and cold. It is possible that it means it is a shade that does not change or move, as the shade of this world does; so he emphasized it with the word "ẓalīlan" for that reason. It is also possible to describe it as "ẓalīl" because of its extent. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, in Paradise there is a tree under whose shade a rider on a swift, well-trained horse would travel a hundred years without crossing it."
