Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 58–59:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Indeed, excellent is that which Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those of authority among you. And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should be believers in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and most suitable in outcome.﴾

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him), Zayd ibn Aslam, Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, and Ibn Zayd said: This address is specifically to the rulers of the Muslims.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his commanders, and then it extends to those after them. Ibn Jurayj (p-586) and others said: That is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, concerning the matter of the key of the Kaʿba, when he took it from ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥa ibn Abī Ṭalḥa al-ʿAbdarī, and from his cousin Shayba ibn ʿUthmān ibn Abī Ṭalḥa. Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib requested it so that the custodianship (al-sidāna) might be combined with the provision of water (al-siqāya) for him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the Kaʿba and broke what was in it of idols, and took out the Station of Ibrahim, and Jibril descended upon him with this verse. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out reciting this verse, and I had not heard it from him before. He called ʿUthmān and Shayba and said to them: "Take it, as a perpetual and lasting possession, which none will take from you except a wrongdoer." Makkī related that Shayba wished not to hand over the key, then he handed it over and said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Take it with the trust of Allah."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The narrators differed in some wordings of this report, by addition and omission, but its meaning is the same. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The verse concerns the rulers, that they should admonish women regarding disobedience (nushūz) and the like, and return them to their husbands. The more apparent view regarding the verse is that it is general to all people. Although its occasion is what we have mentioned, it encompasses the rulers in matters entrusted to them, such as the division of wealth, the restitution of wrongs, the justice of rulings and other things, and it encompasses them and those below them among people in the safekeeping of deposits, in exercising caution in testimony, and other matters, such as a man judging in some incident and the like. Prayer, zakat, fasting and all acts of worship are trusts (amānāt) of Allah, the Exalted. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Allah has not permitted the wealthy or the poor to withhold the trust. (p-587) As for "niʿimmā": its origin is niʿma mā. The first was made sukūn and assimilated into the second, and the ʿayn was vocalized with kasra due to the meeting of two sakins, and it was specifically given kasra in accordance with the nūn. The "mā" appended to "niʿma" is only there to prepare the verb to be joined to it, as it is in "rubbamā" and "mimmā" in His saying: "And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was of that which moves his lips" and like the words of the poet:

And indeed we strike the ram with a blow upon its head, which casts the tongue out of the mouth.

And the like of it. In this it has the status of "rubbamā", though it differs from it in meaning, because "rubbamā" means diminution, while "mimmā" means intensification. Although "mā" here is a preparatory particle, it has the meaning of "alladhī" (that which), and it prepares only when it is a noun; but the intent is only the meaning that follows it, which lies in the verb.

After these preliminaries, attributing hearing and sight is fitting, because in the observable world they are what produce the result of what the one commanded does in that which he was commanded.

As for His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah﴾: when He addressed the rulers in the preceding verse, He addressed the subjects in this one, commanding obedience to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, which is: carrying out His commands and prohibitions, and obedience to His Messenger, and obedience to the leaders according to the view of the majority: Abū Hurayra, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Zayd and others. Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, Mujāhid and a group said: "Ulū al-amr" are the people of the Qur'an and knowledge. Accordingly, the word "amr" under this interpretation refers to the Qur'an and the Sharia, meaning: those who hold this matter and this affair. Al-Ṭabarī related from Mujāhid that he said: the reference here by "ulū al-amr" is to the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) specifically. It is related from ʿIkrima that it refers specifically to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both). In this restriction there is remoteness. Some who said "they are the leaders" related that it was revealed concerning the commanders of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the occasion was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a expedition (p-588) in which was ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, and its commander was Khālid ibn al-Walīd. They headed for a people from the Arabs, but a warner came to them and they fled under cover of night. A man from them came to Khālid's camp and entered upon ʿAmmār, and said: "O Abū al-Yaqẓān, my people have fled, and I have embraced Islam. If my Islam benefits me, I will remain; otherwise I will flee." ʿAmmār said to him: "It benefits you, so stay." When they rose in the morning, Khālid raided and found none but the man mentioned, so he seized him and took his property. ʿAmmār came and said: "Release the man, for he has embraced Islam, and he is under my protection." Khālid said: "And do you grant protection?" They quarreled and took the matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who upheld ʿAmmār's protection and forbade him from granting protection a second time over a commander. They argued before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Khālid said: "O Messenger of Allah, will you leave this slave, the cut-eared one, to revile me?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Khālid, do not revile ʿAmmār, for whoever reviles ʿAmmār, Allah reviles him; whoever hates ʿAmmār, Allah hates him; and whoever curses ʿAmmār, Allah curses him." ʿAmmār became angry, stood up and left. Khālid followed him until he apologized to him, and they reconciled. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down His saying: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those of authority among you.﴾

Obedience to the Messenger means following his Sunna, as said by ʿAṭāʾ and others. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of the verse is: and obey the Messenger.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

He means also his Sunna after his death.

"Fa-in tanāzaʿtum": the meaning is: if you dispute among yourselves, or you and your rulers. The meaning of dispute (tanāzuʿ) is that each one seizes the proof of the other and nullifies it.

(p-589) Referring to Allah is looking into His Mighty Book, and referring to the Messenger is asking him during his lifetime, and looking into his Sunna after his death, peace and blessings be upon him. This is the saying of Mujāhid, al-Aʿmash, Qatāda and al-Suddī, and it is the correct view. Some said its meaning is: say, "Allah and His Messenger know best," and this is the referring.

In His saying: ﴿if you should be believers in Allah and the Last Day﴾ there is some warning, because it contains the recompense of the wrongdoer who transgresses. He addressed them with "if you should be believers", though they had already believed, in the manner of affirmation, so that the obligation would be reinforced.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 60–61:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, yet they desire to take their disputes to the false judge (al-ṭāghūt), though they were commanded to reject it? And Satan wishes to lead them far astray.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what God has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion.﴾

The Arabs say: "Zaʿama fulān kadhā" (so-and-so claimed such-and-such), in a matter where verification is weak and the grounds for refutation are strong. The furthest degree of *zaʿm* (claim), when it is strong, is that it is merely supposed. It is said *zaʿm* with a fatḥa on the *zāy*, which is the verbal noun (maṣdar), and *zuʿm* with a ḍamma, which is the noun (ism). Likewise, the claim of the hypocrites that they are believers is of the kind in which the grounds for refutation are strong because of their evil deeds, until the report from God, may He be exalted, about them corrects it. These two opinions are far from the correct sense of the wording of the verse. *Yuḍillahum* means "destroys them." *Ḍalālan* came in a form other than the verbal noun; its implied form is "fa-yaḍillūna ḍalālan" (so they go astray with straying). *Baʿīdan* (far) is an expression for the magnitude of the straying and its firmness, to the point that return from it becomes remote and guidance with it becomes unlikely.

The majority read *taʿālaw* with a fatḥa on the *lām*. Al-Ḥasan, as transmitted from him by Qatāda, read *taʿālū* with a ḍamma. Its explanation is that the final radical of the verb *taʿālaytā* was dropped for lightness, and the *lām*, which is the middle radical of the verb, was given a ḍamma, because of the plural *wāw* that follows it, as in your saying *taqaddamū* and *taʾakhkharū*. It is a word derived from height (ʿulūw). When it was used to call a person and summon him in person, it was taken from height out of courtesy in speech, as you say *irtafiʿ ilā al-ḥaqq* (rise up to the truth) and similar expressions.

If it is seeing with the heart, then *yaṣuddūna* is in the accusative as the second object.

The reason is that the pattern *fuʿūl* is only a verbal noun for intransitive verbs, like *jalasa juluusan* and *qaʿada quʿūdan*, whereas *ṣadda* is a verb that is transitive directly once, as in His saying: ﴿So He turned them away from the way﴾ [al-Naml: 24], and transitive with a preposition once, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They turn away from you with aversion﴾ and elsewhere. Therefore its verbal noun is *ṣadd*, and *ṣudūdan* is a noun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 62–64:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So how will it be when a misfortune strikes them because of what their hands have sent forth, and then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and conciliation"?﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves.﴾ ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah. And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had come to you and asked forgiveness of Allah, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾

A group said: this refers to the hypocrites who sought judgment (from the idolatrous tyrant), as mentioned previously. So the meaning is: how will it be with them when Allah punishes them for these sins with a vengeance from Him? Then they swore, "We intended by seeking judgment from the tyrant only conciliation and bringing about a settlement, not the bitterness of a ruling or the pursuit of the full truth." Another group said: this refers to the hypocrites who demanded the blood of the man whom 'Umar had killed. So the meaning is: how will it be with them when a misfortune strikes them in the killing of their relative and the like of it, of the vengeances of Allah, exalted is He? Then they swore that they had intended by demanding his blood nothing but good and right. This is the view inclined to by al-Zajjaj. The position of "kayfa" is in the accusative, governed by a verb whose implied sense is: "How do you see them?" and the like. It is also permissible for its position to be in the nominative, with the implied sense: "How is their conduct?"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾ is a refutation of the hypocrites mentioned earlier and a warning to them, meaning: He will repay them for what He knows.

"So turn away from them" means: from punishing them, from preoccupying oneself with them, and from accepting their false oaths mentioned in His saying "they swear." It is not the turning away that means severance and abandonment, for His saying "and admonish them" prevents that. "Admonish them" means: by warning them of the punishment of Allah and other exhortations.

The "far-reaching word" has been differed about. It was said: it is rebuke, deterrence, and restraint through eloquent speech. It was also said: it is a threat of killing if they persist in the state of hypocrisy, related from al-Hasan, and this is the most effective thing that can reach their souls.

Eloquence (balagha) is derived from attaining the intended aim through speech. It is related from Mujahid that His saying "in themselves" is connected to "misfortune," and that it is postponed in meaning to the front; but this is weak.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah﴾ is an alert to the greatness of the messengers, meaning: you, O Muhammad, are among them; your obedience is obligatory, and responding to the call to you is required. "To be obeyed" is in the subjunctive after the particle "li" (in order that). "By the permission of Allah" means: by the command of Allah. The expression "permission" is apt, since by the very fact of being sent, obedience to him is obligatory even if no explicit command to that effect is stated. It is also permissible for the preposition in "by the permission" to be connected to "We sent," meaning: We did not send any messenger, by the command of Allah, that is, with His law and worship, except to be obeyed; but the more apparent is that it is connected to "to be obeyed," meaning: We did not send any messenger except that he be obeyed by the command of Allah, by obeying him.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On both connections, the statement is general in wording and specific in meaning, because we are certain that Allah, blessed and exalted, has willed of some of His creation that they not obey. For this reason, one group interpreted the "permission" as knowledge, and another group interpreted it as guidance for some people rather than others. This is a good interpretation, because when Allah knows of someone that he will believe, and enables him to do so, it is as if He has granted him permission for it. The true meaning of permission is enablement together with knowledge of the measure of what has been enabled.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves﴾ to the end of the verse, means: by disobedience and hypocrisy, and by diminishing their share of faith. "And asked forgiveness of Allah" means: they sought His forgiveness and repented to Him. "Accepting of repentance" (tawwab) means: one who turns back toward His servants.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 65–68:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not truly believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided, and submit with full submission.﴾ ﴿And had We prescribed for them, "Kill yourselves" or "Leave your homes," they would not have done it, except a few of them. And had they done what they were admonished to do, it would have been better for them and firmer in strengthening (them).﴾ ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾ ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾

Al-Tabari said: His saying "fa-la" (but no) is a rejection of what preceded it. Its meaning: the matter is not as they claim, that they believe in what has been revealed to you. Then he resumed the oath with His saying: ﴿by your Lord, they will not believe﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Others said: he placed "la" (no) before the oath only to give emphasis to the negation and to show its strength. Then he repeated it after the oath to stress the negation further. It would have been valid to drop the second "la" and the emphasis would still remain largely with the first; and it would have been valid to drop the first and the meaning of negation would remain, though the sense of emphasis would be lost.

"Shajara" (to dispute / to become intermingled) means: to be mixed and entangled in their affairs. It is from "shajar" (trees), resembling the interlacing of branches; and likewise the "shajir" (one whose affection is mingled with that of his companion). Abu al-Sammal read "shajra" with a sukun on the jim.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I think he sought to avoid a succession of vowels, but this is not a strong reading, given the lightness of the fatha.

"Yuhakkimuka" is in the subjunctive after "hatta" (until), because here it is a pure limit (ghaya mujarrada). "Yajidu" is conjoined to it. "Haraj" means narrowness, constraint and hardship. Mujahid said: "haraj" means doubt. His saying "taslim" is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar) indicating the confirmation of submission; for the Arabs only follow the verb with its verbal noun when they intend that the act truly occurred, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa with speech﴾ [al-Nisa: 164]. His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets, the steadfast in truth (al-siddiqin), the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.﴾ ﴿That is the bounty from Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Knower.﴾

When Allah mentioned the matter which, if they had done it, would have brought them favour, He afterwards mentioned the reward of the one who does it. This verse is an explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha: 6] ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7]. (p-598) A group said: this verse was revealed when 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn 'Abd Rabbih al-Ansari, the one who was shown the adhan (call to prayer), said: "O Messenger of Allah, when you die and we die, you will be in 'Illiyyin, so we will not see you nor will we gather with you," and he mentioned his grief over that, so this verse was revealed." Makki related from this 'Abd Allah that when the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, died, he said: "O Allah, make me blind so that I see nothing after him," and he became blind. He also mentioned that a group of the Ansar said this or something similar. al-Tabari related it from Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and al-Suddi.

The meaning of "they are with them" is that they are in one abode and one state of bliss, and each one in it has been granted contentment with his own condition, and it does not occur to him to believe that he is lesser, although we know from the Shari'a that the ranks of the people of Paradise differ according to their deeds and according to the extent of Allah's favour upon whom He wills.

Al-siddiq (the one who is truthful in word and deed): it is on the pattern fi'il from truthfulness (al-sidq), and it was said: from charity (al-sadaqa). It is related from the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "The siddiqun are those who affirm (the truth)."

Al-shuhada' (the martyrs): those killed in the way of Allah. They are the ones specially distinguished by the excellence of this kind of death, and they are the ones whose ruling the Shari'a distinguishes regarding the omission of ritual washing and the funeral prayer, because they are too noble to be interceded for. They were so named because Allah bore witness for them to Paradise; it was also said: because they bore witness to Allah with the truth in their death, seeking His pleasure. However, the word al-shuhada' in this verse includes all types of martyrs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 69–70:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets, the steadfast in truth (al-siddiqin), the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.﴾ ﴿That is the bounty from Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Knower.﴾

When Allah mentioned the matter which, if they had done it, would have brought them favour, He afterwards mentioned the reward of the one who does it. This verse is an explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha: 6] ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7]. (p-598) A group said: this verse was revealed when 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn 'Abd Rabbih al-Ansari, the one who was shown the adhan (call to prayer), said: "O Messenger of Allah, when you die and we die, you will be in 'Illiyyin, so we will not see you nor will we gather with you," and he mentioned his grief over that, so this verse was revealed." Makki related from this 'Abd Allah that when the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, died, he said: "O Allah, make me blind so that I see nothing after him," and he became blind. He also mentioned that a group of the Ansar said this or something similar. al-Tabari related it from Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and al-Suddi.

The meaning of "they are with them" is that they are in one abode and one state of bliss, and each one in it has been granted contentment with his own condition, and it does not occur to him to believe that he is lesser, although we know from the Shari'a that the ranks of the people of Paradise differ according to their deeds and according to the extent of Allah's favour upon whom He wills.

Al-siddiq (the one who is truthful in word and deed): it is on the pattern fi'il from truthfulness (al-sidq), and it was said: from charity (al-sadaqa). It is related from the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "The siddiqun are those who affirm (the truth)."

Al-shuhada' (the martyrs): those killed in the way of Allah. They are the ones specially distinguished by the excellence of this kind of death, and they are the ones whose ruling the Shari'a distinguishes regarding the omission of ritual washing and the funeral prayer, because they are too noble to be interceded for. They were so named because Allah bore witness for them to Paradise; it was also said: because they bore witness to Allah with the truth in their death, seeking His pleasure. However, the word al-shuhada' in this verse includes all types of martyrs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 71–73:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution and go forth in details or go forth all together.﴾ ﴿And indeed, among you is he who will surely lag behind. So if a misfortune strikes you, he says, "Certainly Allah has bestowed favor upon me in that I was not a witness with them."﴾ ﴿But if bounty comes to you from Allah, he will surely say, as if there had never been between you and him any affection, "Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have attained a great attainment."﴾

This is an address to the sincere believers of the community of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and a command to them to wage jihad against the disbelievers, to go out in the way of Allah, and to protect the Shari'ah.

"Take your precaution" (khudhu hidhrakum) means: be resolute and prepare with all kinds of preparation, so taking up weapons and other things falls within it. "Go forth" (infiru) means: go out diligent and determined. It is said: nafara al-rajulu yanfiru (with a kasra on the fa') nafiran, and nafarat al-dabbatu tanfuru (with a damma on the fa') nufuran. "Details" (thubat) means: separate groups, so it is a metaphor for the expeditionary units (al-saraya).

"All together" (jami'an) means: the dense army with the Prophet ﷺ, so said Ibn 'Abbas and others. As for thubah: it is reported that it is more than ten men. Its form is fu'alah with a fatha on the 'ayn; its original root is thubwah, and it was said thubayah. Its lam was dropped after it was vowelled and turned into an alif, a non-analogical deletion, and for this reason it is pluralized as thibun, with the waw and nun as a substitute for the deleted letter. The first letter was given a kasra in the plural to indicate that it has left its usual pattern, because its pattern is always to be pluralized with the ta', so one says thubat. Its diminutive is thubayyah, originally thubaywah. As for thubat al-hawd (the middle of the basin, where the water gathers), the deleted letter is the 'ayn, and its original form is thuwabah, its diminutive thuwabyah, and it derives from thaba yathubu. Likewise Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said regarding the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

؎ When she made it clear with the days, it withdrew in thubat over it, its humiliation and its sorrow.

He said it is a singular noun, not a plural, used in its original form, because the original of thubah is thuwabah; the waw moved and what preceded it was open, so it became an alif, and Abu Dhu'ayb used it in this state.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed among you﴾: "inna" is an affirmative particle, and the address is to the body of the believers, and what is meant by "min" (among) are the hypocrites. He expressed them by "among you" since they are counted among the believers and claim their call. The lam that enters upon "man" (he who) is the lam of emphasis, which entered upon the subject of "inna" because the predicate was placed first as a prepositional phrase, and this is a familiar usage in their speech, like your saying: "Indeed in the house is surely Zayd." The lam that enters upon "la-yubatti'anna" is, according to the majority, the lam of oath, its estimate being: "And indeed among you is he who, by Allah, will surely lag behind." It was said that it is the lam of emphasis. "Yubatti'" means: he causes others to lag, that is, he discourages them and drives them to stay behind from the expeditions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Mujahid read "liyubti'anna" with a light pronunciation of the ta'. "Misfortune" (musibah) means from killing and martyrdom, and it is a misfortune only according to the belief and corrupt view of the hypocrites, or because death in its entirety is a misfortune, as Allah, exalted is He, willed; and indeed martyrdom in reality is a blessing because of its good outcome. "Witness" (shahidan) means: present, so the meaning is that the hypocrite is pleased by his absence when there is hardship, and this indicates that his staying behind is only fear of fighting and cowardice regarding jihad.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if bounty comes to you from Allah﴾, the verse, the meaning is: and if you gain victory and booty, and all of that is from the bounty of Allah, the hypocrite regrets that he did not attend and obtain the spoils, and says: ﴿Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have attained a great attainment,﴾ wishing for something he had pledged to do and then betrayed his pledge, because the believer only wishes such a thing when what prevented him from attending is a clear excuse and a matter over which he had no power. So he grieves afterward over the loss of good. The hypocrite offers the believers affection, pledges to undertake the obligations of Islam, then stays behind out of hypocrisy, doubt and disbelief in Allah and His Messenger, and then, when the unseen is revealed, wishes for the victory of the believers. On this basis, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as if there had never been between you and him any affection﴾ comes as an eloquent turn of speech (iltifat), and a parenthetical interjection between the speaker and the spoken words, with a phrasing that shows increased ugliness of their act. Al-Tabari related from Qatadah and Ibn Juraij that they both interpreted the hypocrite's saying: ﴿Oh, I wish I had been with them﴾ as meaning envy on his part toward the believers in attaining a desired gain.

Al-Hasan read "layaqulunna" with a damma on the lam, according to the meaning of "man" (he who), and the damma on the lam indicates the deleted waw.

The combination of these two verses indicates that the one who went out among the hypocrites was seeking booty, and the one who stayed behind among them was seeking doubt and waiting for misfortunes to befall the believers.

"Ka'anna" incorporates the meaning of comparison, but it is not like the heavy form (inna) in needing a subject and predicate; rather, sentences follow it. Ibn Kathir and 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "takun" with a ta', and others read "yakun" with a ya', and that is good because of the separation between the verb and its subject.

And His saying: "fa-afuza" is put in the accusative by the fa' in answer to the wish. Al-Hasan and Yazid al-Nahwi read "fa-afuzu" with a damma, as an independent resumption, the estimate being: "fa-ana afuzu" (so I attain). Ruh said: he did not make a response for "laita" (oh, I wish). Al-Zajjaj said: His saying, "as if there had never been between you and him any affection," is displaced, and its proper place is: "But if a misfortune strikes you."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And this is weak, because it corrupts the eloquence of the speech.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 74–75:**

His statement, exalted is He:

﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter. And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or is victorious, We will give him a great reward.﴾ ﴿And why should you not fight in the way of Allah and for the oppressed among men, women, and children, who say, "Our Lord, bring us out of this city whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper"?﴾

This is a command from Allah, mighty and majestic, to the believers, whom He described as those who strive in the way of Allah.

"Yashrūna" (يَشْرُونَ) means "they sell" in this place, although it comes in other places with the meaning "they buy" (يَشْتَرُونَ). The meaning here indicates that it means "they sell."

Then Allah described the reward of the one who fights in the way of Allah. He mentioned the two ultimate outcomes of his situation and suffices with these two outcomes over what lies between them. That is because the ultimate outcome of the one who is defeated in combat is that he is killed, and the ultimate outcome of the one who kills and takes spoils is that he is described as being victorious absolutely. "The great reward" is Paradise.

A group said: "Falyuqātil" (فَلْيُقاتِلْ) is read with the imperative lām sukūn (لامِ الأمْرِ). A group read "falyuqātil" (فَلِيُقاتِلْ) with a kasra on the lām. Muhārib ibn Dithār read "fayaqtul aw yaghlib" (فَيَقْتُلْ أو يَغْلِبْ) with both verbs in the active voice (lil-fā'il). The majority read "nu'tīhi" (نُؤْتِيهِ) with the nūn, while al-A'mash and Talha ibn Musarrif read "fasawfa yu'tīhi" (فَسَوْفَ يُؤْتِيهِ) with the yā'.

His statement, exalted is He: "Wa mā lakum" (وَما لَكُمْ). The lām is connected to what is connected to the thing being asked about from the meaning of the verb. Its estimated sense is: "And what thing exists, or is occurring, or the like, for you?" "Lā tuqātilūna" (لا تُقاتِلُونَ) is in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), its estimated sense being: "abandoning" or "neglecting." His statement, "wal-mustaḍ'afīna" (وَالمُسْتَضْعَفِينَ), is conjoined to the name of Allah, exalted is He; that is, "and in the way of the oppressed." It was also said that it is conjoined to "the way" (al-sabīl), that is, "and in [the cause of] the oppressed, for their rescue." By "the oppressed" he means those believers in Makkah who were under the humiliation and harm of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and who were unable to leave, and for whom residing [there] under harm was not pleasant. Concerning these people, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'O Allah, save Salama ibn Hisham and Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a. O Allah, save the oppressed believers.'"

"Wal-wildān" (وَالوِلْدانِ) is by its pattern the plural of "walīd," and it may also be the plural of "walad," like "warl" and "wirlān." So in both cases it refers to children. The "city" (al-qaryah) here is Makkah, by the consensus of the interpreters.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse encompasses the believers, the captives, and the centers of polytheism until the Day of Resurrection. He used the singular "al-ẓālim" (الظالِمِ) because it is the place of the verb's derivation. Do you not see that the verb's estimated sense is: "the one who wronged its people"? Since the oppressed had no recourse except supplication, they supplicated for rescue, and for the aid of Allah, exalted is He, that would follow them, and for the victory of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, that would give them triumph over those oppressors.

[p. 603]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 74–75:**

His statement, exalted is He:

﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter. And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or is victorious, We will give him a great reward.﴾ ﴿And why should you not fight in the way of Allah and for the oppressed among men, women, and children, who say, "Our Lord, bring us out of this city whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper"?﴾

This is a command from Allah, mighty and majestic, to the believers, whom He described as those who strive in the way of Allah.

"Yashrūna" (يَشْرُونَ) means "they sell" in this place, although it comes in other places with the meaning "they buy" (يَشْتَرُونَ). The meaning here indicates that it means "they sell."

Then Allah described the reward of the one who fights in the way of Allah. He mentioned the two ultimate outcomes of his situation and suffices with these two outcomes over what lies between them. That is because the ultimate outcome of the one who is defeated in combat is that he is killed, and the ultimate outcome of the one who kills and takes spoils is that he is described as being victorious absolutely. "The great reward" is Paradise.

A group said: "Falyuqātil" (فَلْيُقاتِلْ) is read with the imperative lām sukūn (لامِ الأمْرِ). A group read "falyuqātil" (فَلِيُقاتِلْ) with a kasra on the lām. Muhārib ibn Dithār read "fayaqtul aw yaghlib" (فَيَقْتُلْ أو يَغْلِبْ) with both verbs in the active voice (lil-fā'il). The majority read "nu'tīhi" (نُؤْتِيهِ) with the nūn, while al-A'mash and Talha ibn Musarrif read "fasawfa yu'tīhi" (فَسَوْفَ يُؤْتِيهِ) with the yā'.

His statement, exalted is He: "Wa mā lakum" (وَما لَكُمْ). The lām is connected to what is connected to the thing being asked about from the meaning of the verb. Its estimated sense is: "And what thing exists, or is occurring, or the like, for you?" "Lā tuqātilūna" (لا تُقاتِلُونَ) is in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), its estimated sense being: "abandoning" or "neglecting." His statement, "wal-mustaḍ'afīna" (وَالمُسْتَضْعَفِينَ), is conjoined to the name of Allah, exalted is He; that is, "and in the way of the oppressed." It was also said that it is conjoined to "the way" (al-sabīl), that is, "and in [the cause of] the oppressed, for their rescue." By "the oppressed" he means those believers in Makkah who were under the humiliation and harm of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and who were unable to leave, and for whom residing [there] under harm was not pleasant. Concerning these people, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'O Allah, save Salama ibn Hisham and Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a. O Allah, save the oppressed believers.'"

"Wal-wildān" (وَالوِلْدانِ) is by its pattern the plural of "walīd," and it may also be the plural of "walad," like "warl" and "wirlān." So in both cases it refers to children. The "city" (al-qaryah) here is Makkah, by the consensus of the interpreters.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse encompasses the believers, the captives, and the centers of polytheism until the Day of Resurrection. He used the singular "al-ẓālim" (الظالِمِ) because it is the place of the verb's derivation. Do you not see that the verb's estimated sense is: "the one who wronged its people"? Since the oppressed had no recourse except supplication, they supplicated for rescue, and for the aid of Allah, exalted is He, that would follow them, and for the victory of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, that would give them triumph over those oppressors.

[p. 603]

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 76–77:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of the Taghut (false deity). So fight against the allies of Satan. Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands, establish prayer, and give zakat"? But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a faction of them fear men as they should fear Allah, or even with greater fear. And they say, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us to a near term."﴾

This verse entails strengthening the hearts of the believers and urging them on. "Taghut" refers to everything that is worshipped and followed besides Allah. The mention of Satan after that indicates that what is meant by Taghut here is Satan. His informing them, exalted is He, of the weakness of Satan's plot is a strengthening of the hearts of the believers and an emboldening of them to confront the weak plot, for resolve and firmness that rest upon the realities of faith break it and crush it. The particle "kāna" (was) is used to indicate the permanence of the attribute.

As for His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were told...﴾, the commentators differed about who is meant by the phrase ﴿those who were told﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: they were 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr al-Kindi, and a group besides them, who had been averse to humiliation in Makkah before the Hijra, and who asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to permit them to fight the polytheists. Allah, exalted is He, commanded them to restrain their hands and not to act. But when they were in Madinah and fighting was prescribed, it was hard for some of them, its occasion was difficult, and they were afflicted with what afflicts human beings of weakness and hesitation in confronting the enemy. So the verse was revealed concerning them.

Others said: many of the Arabs had found it good to enter the religion of Muhammad, peace be upon him, with its obligations that existed before fighting, such as prayer, zakat and the like, and truce and restraint of hands. When fighting was revealed, it was hard for them, and they were distressed by it, so the verse was revealed concerning them. Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas also said: the verse is a report about the Jews, that they did this with their prophet in his time. So the meaning of the report about them is to disparage their act and to forbid the believers from doing the like.

A group said: the verse refers to the hypocrites of Madinah, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his like, because they had settled, reluctantly, into the obligations of Islam together with ease and the absence of fighting. When fighting was revealed, it was hard for them and extremely difficult, since they were deniers of the reward. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What strengthens this view is that the mention of the hypocrites continues through the verses that follow.

The meaning of "restrain your hands" is: refrain from fighting. "Al-fariq" is a group of people, as if it has separated from others. His saying, ﴿they fear men as they should fear Allah﴾, means that they were fearing Allah in respect of death, for they feared death only from Him. So when He prescribed fighting men for them, they saw that they might die at their hands, and so they feared them with respect to death, just as they used to fear Allah. Al-Hasan said: His saying "as they should fear Allah" indicates that it refers to believers, and it is a fear of dread, not a fear of dread-induced terror; and it is possible that the meaning is: they fear men to the degree of the believers' fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a preference, not a certainty.

As for His saying ﴿or even with greater fear﴾, a group said: "aw" here means "wa" (and); another group: it means "bal" (rather); another: it is for choice; another: it retains its original sense of doubt with regard to the addressee; and another: it is for indefiniteness toward the addressee.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I have explained all these views in [Surat al-Baqarah] in His saying: ﴿or harder than stone﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74], because the two places are the same.

Their saying ﴿Why have You prescribed fighting for us?﴾ is a rejection at the start of the commands of Allah, exalted is He, and a lack of submission. "The near term" they mean by it their death upon their beds; so the exegetes have said.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is fitting if the verse concerns the Jews or the hypocrites. But if it concerns a group of the Companions, then they only asked for a delay until the time when Islam became manifest and their number grew.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿قُلْ مَتاعُ الدُنْيا قَلِيلٌ والآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لِمَنِ اتَّقى ولا تُظْلَمُونَ فَتِيلا﴾ [النساء: ٧٧] ﴿أيْنَما تَكُونُوا يُدْرِكْكُمُ المَوْتُ ولَوْ كُنْتُمْ في بُرُوجٍ مُشَيَّدَةٍ وإنْ تُصِبْهم حَسَنَةٌ يَقُولُوا هَذِهِ مِن عِنْدِ اللهِ وإنْ تُصِبْهم سَيِّئَةٌ يَقُولُوا هَذِهِ مِن عِنْدِكَ قُلْ كُلٌّ مِن عِنْدِ اللهِ فَمالِ هَؤُلاءِ القَوْمِ لا يَكادُونَ يَفْقَهُونَ حَدِيثًا﴾

The meaning: Say, O Muhammad, to these people: the enjoyment of worldly life, that is, the pleasure of living in it which you have coveted and feared to lose, is little, because it is perishable and passing away. But the Hereafter, which is everlasting bliss, is better for those who obey Allah and fear Him by complying with His commands in what they love and what they dislike.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "تُظْلَمُونَ" with the taa' (ta), as direct address. Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "يُظْلَمُونَ" with the yaa' (ya), leaving out direct address and mentioning the third person.

Al-fatil (the thread) is the thin line in the split of a date stone. This has been discussed earlier.

﴿أيْنَما تَكُونُوا يُدْرِكْكُمُ المَوْتُ﴾ is a conditional (jaza', the protasis-apodosis structure) with its response (jawab). This is the reading of the majority. Talha ibn Sulayman read "يُدْرِكُكُمُ" with the two kafs vowelled with a damma and the verb in the nominative (raf'). Abu al-Fath said: this is on the assumption that the fa' (the particle of consequence) has been inserted, as if he had said: "fa-yudrikukumu al-mawt" (then death will overtake you). It is a weak reading. This is a report from Allah that contains a belittling of the world, and that there is no escape from annihilation and from transition.

The interpreters differed over His words "فِي بُرُوجٍ". Most of them, and the more correct view, hold that He meant towers and fortresses built on the earth, since these are the furthest that people go in fortifying and protecting themselves, so Allah gave them this as an example. Qatada said: the meaning is in fortified palaces. Ibn Jurayj and the majority said the same. As-Suddi said: they are towers built in the lowest heaven. Makki transmitted this view from Malik, and that he said: "Do you not see His words: ﴿والسَماءِ ذاتِ البُرُوجِ﴾ [al-Buruj: 1]?" An-Naqqash transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "﴿فِي بُرُوجٍ مُشَيَّدَةٍ﴾ means: in palaces of iron."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is not what the wording indicates. Rather, when "burudj" occurs in the Qur'an alongside mention of the sky, it means the mansions (stations) of the moon and others, according to what the Arabs named them and knew them by. Baraja means: it appeared, and from it comes "al-buruj", meaning the elevated and conspicuous structures; and from it comes "tabarruj al-mar'a" (a woman displaying her adornment).

As for "مُشَيَّدَةٍ", az-Zajjaj and others said: its meaning is raised and lofty, because "shada al-rajulu al-binaa'" means when he built it with "al-shid", which is plaster (gypsum); and "ashada" and "shayyada" mean when he raised it and made it high. From this comes "ashada al-rajulu dhikr al-rajul" (he raised the mention of a man) when he elevated him. Another group said: "مُشَيَّدَةٍ" means embellished with plaster, since "shada al-rajulu" means he plastered it with "al-shid", and "shayyada" means he repeated that action, so it is for intensification, just as you say: "I broke the stick once", and "I broke it in many places, many times", and "I tore the garment" and "I tore it repeatedly" when the tearing was in many places. On this basis it is correct to say: "shada al-rajulu al-jidar" (he plastered the wall once), and "shayyada al-rajulu al-jidar" when you want to intensify, because the plastering occurred in many places. From this meaning is the saying of the poet:

He plastered it with marble and covered it with ... (kalsan), so there are nests of birds on its heights.

The "ha'" and "mim" in His words "وَإنْ تُصِبْهُمْ" refer back to those who were told: "Restrain your hands." This indicates that they are the hypocrites, because the believers would not be fit for this statement, and because the Jews were not under the command of the Prophet ﷺ, so that misfortunes would befall them because of him. The meaning of the verse: if a good thing befalls these hypocrites, such as the defeat of an enemy, or spoils of war, or something else, they consider that to be by chance from the work of Allah, not because of the blessing of following you and believing in you. And if an evil befalls them, that is, a defeat, or severe hunger, or other things, they say: "This is because of you, due to your poor management," as Ibn Zayd said. It was also said: "because of your ill omen for us," as az-Zajjaj and others said.

His words: ﴿قُلْ كُلٌّ مِن عِنْدِ اللهِ﴾ are an announcement from Allah, Exalted, that good and evil, and good deed and bad deed, are all His creation and from Him, with no lord other than Him, and no creator or originator besides Him. The meaning: say, O Muhammad, to these people: the matter is not as you claim, from me or from anyone other than me, but all of it is from Allah. Qatada said: blessings and calamities are from Allah. Ibn Zayd said: victory and defeat. Ibn 'Abbas said: the evil deed and the good deed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

All of this is one thing.

Then He rebuked them with a question about the cause of their ignorance and the scarcity of their understanding and their failure to grasp the realities about which they speak. Fiqh (understanding) in the language means comprehension; the Shari'a restricted it to understanding of religion and its matters, and later its use came to dominate for the knowledge of legal rulings. The eloquence in the question about the scarcity of their fiqh is clear, because when you ask about the cause of a matter, your speech has implicitly affirmed that matter in a subtle and eloquent way.

Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i paused on "فَما", and the rest paused on the lam in "فَمالِ", following the written form (of the Mushaf). Some people forbade this entirely, because it is a preposition (harf jarr), so it is part of the word it governs. All of this is according to necessity and a breath running out. As for choosing to pause at what we have mentioned as a starting point, that is not permitted.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى:

﴿ما أصابَكَ مِن حَسَنَةٍ فَمِنَ اللهِ وما أصابَكَ مِن سَيِّئَةٍ فَمِنَ نَفْسِكَ وأرْسَلْناكَ لِلنّاسِ رَسُولا وكَفى بِاللهِ شَهِيدًا﴾ ﴿مَن يُطِعِ الرَسُولَ فَقَدْ أطاعَ اللهَ ومَن تَوَلّى فَما أرْسَلْناكَ عَلَيْهِمْ حَفِيظًا﴾ ﴿وَيَقُولُونَ طاعَةٌ فَإذا بَرَزُوا مِن عِنْدِكَ بَيَّتَ طائِفَةٌ مِنهم غَيْرَ الَّذِي تَقُولُ واللهُ يَكْتُبُ ما يُبَيِّتُونَ فَأعْرِضْ عنهم وتَوَكَّلْ عَلى اللهِ وكَفى بِاللهِ وكِيلا﴾

Some scholars said: "mā" is a conditional particle (*shartiyya*), and "min" entered after it because the condition is not obligatory, so it resembles the negation after which "min" is used. Other scholars said: "mā" means "alladhī" (that which), and "min" is for specifying the kind (*bayān al-jins*), because what befalls a person is many things, good and bad, ease and hardship, and other than that. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and others are included in the meaning. It was also said that the address is to a person in general.

The meaning of this verse, according to Ibn 'Abbās, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, al-Rabī', Ibn Zayd, Abū Ṣāliḥ and others, is a full stop (*qaṭ'*) and the resumption (*istiʾnāf*) of an announcement from God, the Exalted, that the good is from Him and by His bounty, and the bad is from the human being because of his own misdeeds (*ibtidhānihi*), while it is also from God through creation and origination.

In the codex (*muṣḥaf*) of Ibn Mas'ūd: "فَمِن نَفْسِكَ وأنا قَضَيْتُها عَلَيْكَ" ("then it is from yourself, and I decreed it upon you"). Ibn 'Abbās recited it with this reading. Abū 'Amr reported that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ūd it is: "وَأنا كَتَبْتُها" ("and I wrote it"). It is also narrated that Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ūd recited: "وَأنا قَدَّرْتُها عَلَيْكَ" ("and I decreed it upon you").

This interpretation is supported by hadiths from the Prophet ﷺ whose meaning is that whatever misfortune befalls the son of Adam is only the punishment for his sins. Among them: "When the verse ﴿مَن يَعْمَلْ سُوءًا يُجْزَ بِهِ﴾ ("whoever does evil will be recompensed for it") [al-Nisā': 123] was revealed, Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, became distressed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Do you not fall ill? Do you not fall sick? Do you not grieve?'" He ﷺ also said: "Nothing afflicts a man, not a scratch from a twig, nor a stumble of a foot, nor the twitching of a vein, except because of a sin, and what Allah pardons is greater." (p-609) In this is an explanation that all of these are a recompense for what a person does.

Another group said: the meaning of the verse is like the meaning of the previous verse in His words: ﴿وَإنْ تُصِبْهم سَيِّئَةٌ يَقُولُوا هَذِهِ مِن عِنْدِكَ﴾ ("if a misfortune befalls them, they say, 'This is from you'") [al-Nisā': 78], with the omission of "yaqūlūna" (they say). Its estimated reading is: "Why is it that these people hardly understand any statement? They say: 'What befalls you of good is...'" And the full stop in this view comes from His words: "وَأرْسَلْناكَ" ("and We sent you").

Another group said: rather, the full stop in the verse is at its beginning, and the verse includes the announcement that the good is from God and by His bounty, and the rest is estimated as: "And what befalls you of evil is from yourself?" as a form of denial and affirmation (*inkār wa-taqrīr*). According to this view, the interrogative alif (*alif al-istifhām*) is omitted from the speech. Al-Mahdawī reported this view. "رَسُولًا" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), and this state carries the meaning of emphasis in His words: ﴿وَأرْسَلْناكَ لِلنّاسِ رَسُولا﴾ ("and We sent you to mankind as a messenger"). Then He followed it with His words: ﴿وَكَفى بِاللهِ شَهِيدًا﴾ ("and Allah is sufficient as a witness"), a threat to the disbelievers and an intimidation required by the force of the speech, because the meaning is: a witness against the one who denied him. The meaning is that the Messenger only commands and forbids as a clarification and conveyance from Allah, so the commands and prohibitions are only the commands and prohibitions of Allah.

One group said: the occasion of revelation of this verse is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever loves me has loved Allah" (p-610), and the Jews objected to him regarding this statement and said: "This Muḥammad commands the worship of Allah alone, and yet in this statement he claims lordship." So this verse was revealed, confirming the Messenger ﷺ and clarifying the nature of the connection between him and the bounty of Allah, the Exalted.

"تَوَلّى" means "turned away" (*aʿraḍa*). The original usage of "tawallā" is that it takes a preposition, so we say: "tawallā fulānun ʿan al-īmān" (so-and-so turned away from faith) and "tawallā ilā al-īmān" (turned toward faith), because the word includes both turning toward and turning away. **The commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah an-Nisāʾ, verses 82–83:**

His statement, may He be exalted:

﴿Will they not then reflect (yatadabbarūn) upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.﴾ ﴿And when there comes to them a matter concerning security or fear, they spread it around. But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who deduce it (yastanbiṭūnahu) from among them would have known it. And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few.﴾

The meaning: These hypocrites, who criticise you and raise objections without proof regarding the prophethood you hold, do they not return to fairness, look at the place of the proof, and reflect (yatadabbarūn) upon the speech of Allah, the Exalted, so that its proofs become apparent to them and its evidences shine forth?

Tadabbur (reflection, deep contemplation) is looking into the outcomes of matters and the interpretations of things. All of this is required by His statement: ﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ This is a command to consider and to reason. Then He, the Exalted, made known the places of the proof, meaning: if it were the speech of humans, it would contain the deficiencies found in human speech, and contradiction and mutual conflict would appear in it that cannot be reconciled, since such things exist in human speech, whereas the Qur'an is exempt from them, for it is the speech of the One who encompasses everything in knowledge.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

If a doubt arises for anyone and he thinks there is discrepancy in some matter of the Book of Allah, then it is obligatory for him to suspect his own examination and to ask one who is more knowledgeable than him.

Al-Zajjāj (d. 311 AH) held that the meaning of the verse is: they would have found in what We inform you of, of what they plot (yubayyitūn), a discrepancy. That is: when you inform them of it, in accordance with how it occurs, this is evidence that it is from Allah, a hidden matter from the unseen. This is the meaning of his statement, and Ibn Fūrak and al-Mahdawī have also clarified it.

As for His statement, ﴿And when there comes to them a matter concerning security…﴾ (the verse), the majority of the exegetes (mufassirūn) said: the verse concerns the hypocrites as already mentioned, and the verse was revealed concerning the military expeditions (sarāyā, sing. sariyya) and detachments (bu'ūth, sing. ba'th) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The meaning is that the hypocrites used to eagerly seek to hear whatever would distress the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding his expeditions. So when a rumour of security for the Muslims arose, or a victory was achieved for them, they belittled it, reduced its importance, and spread that belittling and disparagement. And when a rumour of fear for the Muslims arose, or a calamity, they magnified it and spread that magnification. "Adhāʿū bihi" (they spread it) means: they disseminated it. It is a verb that takes a preposition (ḥarf jarr), and sometimes takes its object directly; you say: adhaʿtu kadhā (I spread such-and-such) and adhaʿtu bihi (I spread it). From this is the saying of Abū al-Aswad:

*They spread it among the people until it was as if, on a height, a fire had been kindled at the openings*

Another group said: the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and concerning those among the believers whose endurance in faith was weak and whose experience was limited.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Either this applies to the matter of the expeditions, for they used to hear the statements of the hypocrites and repeat them in the company of the one who said them, and spread them in the company of the one who spread them, while being unsure of their accuracy; and this is what indicates their limited experience. Or it applies to all matters that occur, as in what ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "A people came to the mosque saying: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has divorced his wives.' He said: I went in to ʿĀʾishah and said: 'O daughter of Abū Bakr, has your matter reached the point that you harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' She said: 'O son of al-Khaṭṭāb, keep to your own affairs.' He said: I went in to Ḥafṣah and said: 'O Ḥafṣah, you know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not love you, and were it not for me he would have divorced you.' So she began to weep. He said: I went out until I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was in an upper room of his, and his freedman Rabāḥ was sitting at the threshold of the room. I said: 'O Rabāḥ, ask permission for me to see the Messenger of Allah.' He looked at the room, then looked at me and remained silent. I said: 'O Rabāḥ, ask permission for me to see the Messenger of Allah,' perhaps he thinks I came on account of Ḥafṣah. By Allah, if he ordered me to strike her neck, I would have struck it. Then he looked and gestured to me with his hand to enter. I entered, and behold, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was lying on a mat, and it had left a mark on his side, and in his room there was nothing but a handful of barley and a handful of tanning-leaves (qarẓ), and two hides hanging. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you are Allah's chosen one among His creation and His Messenger, and you have nothing of this world except this, while Chosroes and Caesar are among the trees and rivers!' He said: 'Are you here, O ʿUmar? Are you not content that they have the world and we have the Hereafter?' I said: 'Yes.' Then I began speaking to him until his face beamed and he smiled. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, they claimed that you divorced your wives.' He said: 'No.' I said: 'Do you permit me to inform the people?' He said: 'Do so if you wish.' The meaning is: if they had refrained from plunging into it, and had sought out the matters from the Messenger, or from those in authority (ulī al-amr), who are the commanders, as said by al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd. The interpreters differed regarding what the exception "except for a few" (illā qalīlan) refers to. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd said: it is an exception from His statement, "they spread it… except for a few." Al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. Qatādah said: it is an exception from His statement, "those who deduce it… except for a few." Another group said: it is an exception from His statement, ﴿you would have followed Satan, except for a few﴾, according to the continuous flow of speech without any assumed reordering. Then this group differed. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: Allah guided all of them to faith, and among them were those who became so firmly established in it that no thought of doubt ever occurred to them, nor did any suspicion of uncertainty come upon them; that is the few. The rest of those among the Arabs who embraced Islam were not free from passing thoughts, so were it not for the grace of Allah in granting them guidance without any admixture, they would have gone astray and followed Satan.

This is the meaning of al-Ḍaḥḥāk's statement. Others said: His statement "except for a few" is an expression of nonexistence, meaning: you would all have followed Satan. However, al-Ṭabarī mentioned it.

The meaning: These hypocrites, who criticise you and raise objections without proof regarding the prophethood you hold, do they not return to fairness, look at the place of the proof, and reflect (yatadabbarūn) upon the speech of Allah, the Exalted, so that its proofs become apparent to them and its evidences shine forth?

If a doubt arises for anyone and he thinks there is discrepancy in some matter of the Book of Allah, then it is obligatory for him to suspect his own examination and to ask one who is more knowledgeable than him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 84–86:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So fight in the cause of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself. And urge the believers. Perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve, and Allah is stronger in might and stronger in punishment.﴾ ﴿Whoever intercedes for a good intercession will have a share of it, and whoever intercedes for an evil intercession will have a portion of its burden. And ever is Allah, over all things, Keeper.﴾ ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Reckoner.﴾

This is, in the apparent wording, a command addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone. However, we have never found in any report that fighting was obligated upon the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, without the community, for any period. The meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) in wording, while it is an example of what is said to each individual concerning himself, i.e.: "You, O Muhammad, and every one of your community, say to him: ﴿So fight in the cause of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾." For this reason, every believer should feel inclined to strive even if alone. Among this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "By Allah, I will fight them even if I am left alone with my neck," and the saying of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) at the time of the apostasy (ridda): "Even if my right hand opposed me, I would fight it with my left."

Some people confused the connection of the fa' in His saying "fa-qatil" with what is far-fetched. The correct view is that it is a conjunction joining one sentence to another, and it indicates the abandonment of other than what he was commanded. Then he singled out the Prophet (ﷺ) with the command to urge (tahrid), i.e., to urge the believers to carry out the obligatory duty upon them.

As for "'asa" (perhaps) when it comes from Allah, Ikrima and others said that it is binding, because from a human it is an expectation and a hope, so Allah's bounty makes its realization obligatory. In this there is a promise to the believers of their victory over the disbelievers. Then He strengthened their hearts after that by informing them of the severity of Allah's might, that He is more capable over the disbelievers and more severe in punishing them. Tankil (punishment) means seizing them with various kinds of torment and repeating it upon them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever intercedes for a good intercession﴾, the verse. The root of shafa'a (intercession), shufa (pair/ right of pre-emption) and similar words is from shaf', which is the even number in counting, because the intercessor is a second to the sinner's odd one, and the shafi' (intercessor/ pre-emptor) is a second to the buyer's odd one.

The exegetes differed concerning this verse. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is: whoever intercedes, making the odd (single) state of Islam even by aiding the Muslims, or whoever intercedes, making the odd state of disbelief even by aiding disbelief against Islam. What led him to this interpretation is the preceding matter of fighting. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others said: it concerns the intercessions of people among themselves regarding their needs; whoever intercedes so as to benefit, he has a share, and whoever intercedes so as to harm, he has a burden. Al-Hasan and others said: the good intercession is in righteousness and obedience, and the evil one is in sins. All of this is close to one another.

Al-kifl means the share, and it is used for a share of good and of evil. In the Book of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 28].

"Muqit" means capable (qadir). From it is the saying of the poet, who is al-Zubayr ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib:

"And one with rancor, I restrained myself from him, and I was, against his ill will, capable (muqit)."

That is, capable. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid expressed it as "watchful" (hafiz) and "witness" (shahid). 'Abdullah ibn Kathir said it means the one who oversees and maintains affairs. All of these are close in meaning. From it is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "It is sufficient sin for a man to neglect those whom he sustains (yuqit)," according to those who narrate it thus, i.e., those who are under his power and in his grip of dependents and others. Muqatil ibn Hayyan went to the view that it means the one who provides sustenance to every living creature. This would be on the basis that aqat means qat (both: to provide sustenance), and on this basis the Prophet's saying "man yuqit" would come from aqat. Al-Kisa'i related: aqata yuqitu. As for the poet's saying:

"Would that I knew, and I would know when they brought it folded and I was called, is the favour mine or upon me when I am reckoned? Indeed I am, over the reckoning, muqit."

Al-Tabari said concerning it that it is from a meaning other than the one previously mentioned, and that it means: "restrained" (mawquf).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weakened by the fact that the form fa'il would be used in the sense of maf'ul.

His saying, exalted is He: "And when you are greeted," the verse. Tahiyya (greeting) has the form tafi'ila from hayiya, and this is the more common pattern of the verbal noun of fa'ila in defective roots. It is narrated from Malik that this verse concerns the response to one who sneezes and says "yarhamukum Allah" (tashmit al-'atis), but this is weak, because there is no indication in the wording for that. As for responding to the one who blesses the sneezer, it enters by analogy into the meaning of returning a greeting, and this is the course of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, if that is correctly attributed to him, and Allah knows best.

The exegetes differed. One group said: the greeting is that a man says "salamun 'alayka," and the other must say "'alayka as-salam wa rahmatu Allah." If the initiator says "as-salamu 'alayka wa rahmatu Allah," the responder says "'alayka as-salam wa rahmatu Allah wa barakatuhu." If the initiator says "as-salamu 'alayka wa rahmatu Allah wa barakatuhu," then it has ended, and there is no remaining room for the responder to greet with something better; here the response mentioned in the verse occurs. The meaning according to the people of this view is: when you are greeted with a greeting, if the one greeting falls short of the full formula, then greet with better; and if he has completed it, then return it. Another group said: the meaning of the verse is the choice of the responder. When the initiator says "as-salamu 'alayka," the responder may say "wa 'alayka as-salam" only, and this is the return; or he may say "wa 'alayka as-salam wa rahmatu Allah," and this is greeting with something better. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: the verse means: when you are greeted with a greeting, if it comes from a believer, greet with better than it; and if it comes from a disbeliever, return it in the way the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, that it be said to them: "wa 'alaykum." It is related from Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and others: the greeting ends at "wa barakatuhu." The majority of the scholars hold that people of the Book should not be initiated with a greeting; if anyone greets them inadvertently or out of ignorance, it is recommended that they retract his greeting. A group deviated by permitting initiating them, but the first view is more correct, because by it their humiliation is realized. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever greets you from among Allah's creatures, return it to him even if he is a Magian. 'Ata' said: the verse concerns believers specifically, and whoever greets from other than them is told: "'alayka," as in the hadith. Most scholars hold that initiating the greeting is a emphasized sunnah, and returning it is obligatory, because it is one of the rights, as said by al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others.

"Hasiban" means watchful (hafiz), and it is a fa'il form from reckoning (hisab). This attribute is fitting here, since the meaning of the verse concerns a person increasing, decreasing, or fully giving the measure of what he brings.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 87–88**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Allah—there is no god but Him. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ ﴿What is [the matter] with you that you have become two factions concerning the hypocrites? Allah has reverted them [to disbelief] for what they earned. Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾

When the warning and admonition contained in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever over all things a Reckoner﴾ [An-Nisa: 86], had preceded, He followed it by strengthening it: the announcement of the attribute of Lordship (ruboobiyya) and the state of Oneness (wahdaniyya), and the announcement of the gathering (hashr) and the resurrection from the graves for reward and punishment, as an announcement made with an oath. The sworn-by element is estimated as: "By Him" (wa-Huwa), or "by His right" (wa-haqqihi), or "by His greatness" (wa-'azamatihi), [the oath being] "He will surely gather you" (la-yajma'annakum). The word *al-jam'* here means *al-hashr* (gathering), and therefore *ila* (to) is appropriately placed after it, meaning: to Him is the driving and the gathering. As for *al-qiyama* (the Resurrection), its root is *al-qiyam* (standing). Since the standing at the gathering is a movement from the most humiliating and weakest state to the most severe and greatest of terrors, the *ha'* of intensification (ha' al-mubalagha, the intensive ha') was attached to it.

"There is no doubt about it" (la rayba fihi) is a negation, and it together with what follows functions as a *mubtada'* (subject) seeking a predicate (khabar). Its meaning: there is no doubt about it in itself and in the reality of the matter, even if the disbelievers doubt it, that is of no harm.

"And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?" Its outward form is interrogative, but its meaning is the affirmation of a statement, estimated as: no one is more truthful than Allah, the Exalted. This is because the entry of falsehood into human speech is caused either by fear and hope, or by bad disposition, and these are negated with respect to Allah, may His names be sanctified. Truthfulness in its reality is that what flows from the tongue of the speaker agrees with what is in his heart and with the matter he reports concerning its existence. *Hadithan* (in statement) is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification).

His saying: "What is [the matter] with you concerning the hypocrites?" The address is to the believers, and its outward form is interrogative, while its purpose is rebuke. The interpreters differed over: who is meant by "the hypocrites"? Ibn 'Abbas said: They were a people in Makkah who wrote to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) in Madinah that they had believed and had abandoned emigration, and remained among the disbelievers. Then a group of them travelled to al-Sham, and Quraysh gave them merchandise, and said to them: "You do not fear the companions of Muhammad, because you deceive them by displaying faith to them." Their news reached Madinah, and the believers differed about them. One group said: "Let us go out against the enemies of Allah, the hypocrites." Another group said: "Rather, they are believers, and we have no way against them." Then the verse was revealed. Mujahid said: Rather, it was revealed concerning a people who came to Madinah from Makkah, displayed Islam, then said: "We have merchandise in Makkah," and they returned there and concealed disbelief. So the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) differed concerning them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two views are supported by what is at the end of the verse, His saying: ﴿until they emigrate﴾ [An-Nisa: 89]. Zayd ibn Thabit said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites who turned back from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, because the Companions of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, differed concerning them.

Al-Suddi said: Rather, it was revealed concerning a people of hypocrites who were in Madinah, who sought to leave it, out of hypocrisy and disbelief, and said: "We have found it unhealthy" (ijtawaynaha). Ibn Zayd said: It was only revealed concerning the hypocrites who spoke about the story of the slander (hadith al-ifk), because the Companions differed concerning them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The disagreement in this incident was between Usayd ibn Hudayr and Sa'd ibn 'Ubada, as is recorded in [Sahih] al-Bukhari, and each of them had followers among the believers who agreed with his view. Whoever said regarding this verse that it concerns those who were in Madinah is refuted by His saying, "until they emigrate." Yet they [the commentators] explain emigration (muhajara) as abandoning (hajr) what Allah has forbidden, and leaving off dissension and hypocrisy, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The emigrant is one who abandons what Allah has forbidden."

As for *fi'atayn* (two factions), its meaning is two groups (firqatayn), and its accusative is in the state (hal) form, as you say: "What is the matter with you standing?" This is the view of the Basran grammarians. The Kufan grammarians said: its accusative is governed by the verb implied in "What is [the matter] with you" (fa-ma lakum), and the estimate is: "What is [the matter] with you, that you were two factions, or became [two factions]?" According to them this estimated verb governs both indefinite and definite nouns, as you say: "Malik the reviler of Zayd" (malik al-shatima li-Zayd). Al-Zajjaj refuted this view, because a definite noun cannot be a state (hal).

As for *arkasahum* (He has reverted them), its meaning is: He returned them into their disbelief and their misguidance. *Al-rikṣ* means refuse (al-rajī'), and from it is the hadith of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, concerning istinja' (cleansing after relieving oneself): "He took two stones and threw away the dung, and said: 'Indeed it is rikṣ (refuse).'" From it is also the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

*So they were reverted into the scalding fire of the Fire, for indeed they were sinners, and they uttered falsehood and lies.*

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and al-Kisa'i reported that *rakasa* and *arkasa* have one meaning, namely: He returned them. As for those among the interpreters who said: "He destroyed them," or "He misguided them," that is only by way of meaning, because all of that includes their being returned to disbelief.

As for *bima kasabu* (for what they earned), its meaning is: for what they committed of disbelief and hypocrisy. That is, their disbelief is by creation and origination from Allah, and by acquisition (taksib) from them. His saying: "Do you wish" is an interrogative whose meaning is distancing and despair from what they desired. The meaning is: Do you wish, O believers, who hold that those hypocrites are believers, to put on the mark of guidance (tasimu bi-l-huda) someone whom Allah has facilitated for misguidance and has decreed upon him? Then He, may He be exalted, informed that "whoever Allah sends astray," there is no way to reform him, nor to guide him.
