**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, Verse 89:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike. So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the cause of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them any ally or helper.﴾

The pronoun in "wadduu" (they wish) refers to the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). This is a disclosure by Allah of the corruption of their beliefs and a warning to the believers against them. The meaning is: they wish for your disbelief, which is the utmost of calamities for you. This wishing from them may arise from envy (hasad) toward you because of what they see of the believers' prominence in this world. The verse would then run: "together with the wish of many among the People of the Book that they might turn you back into disbelievers after your faith, out of envy from their own selves." It is also possible that the hypocrites' wish arose because they saw the believers in a state of no advantage, so they wished for their return to the worship of idols. The first interpretation is more apparent.

As for His saying, "So do not take," (the verse), this is a prohibition against allying with them until they emigrate, because emigration in the cause of Allah includes faith. "In the cause of Allah" means: in the path of seeking Allah's good pleasure, because the paths to Allah are many, and they are all His acts of obedience. The meaning is: if they turn away from emigration and turn back from faith, then seize them. This is a command to attack them and to confront them openly with fighting.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 90:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Except for those who join a people between whom and you there is a covenant, or who come to you with their breasts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people. Had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you. So if they keep away from you and do not fight you, and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you any way against them.﴾

This ruling was in the early days of Islam, before the authority of obedience among the people had become firmly established. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had made truces with some Arab tribes, such as the clan of Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir al-Aslami, Suraqa ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum, and Khuzayma ibn 'Amir ibn 'Abd Manaf. This verse decided that whoever among the polytheists, with whom there was no covenant between them and the Prophet (ﷺ), joined these people of the covenant, entered into their ranks, and observed the mutual truce, then there is no way (sabil) against him. Ikrima, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said: Then, when Islam became strong and its supporters multiplied, this verse and the one after it were abrogated (nusikhat) by what is in Surat [Bara'a] (al-Tawba).

(p-623) Abu 'Ubayda and others said: "yasilun" (join) in this place means "yantasibun" (are affiliated with), and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

؎ When she is connected, she says to the clan of Bakr ibn Wa'il, and Bakr has cursed her, and the noses are humbled.

He means: when she is affiliated.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is not correct. al-Tabari said: The fighting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against Quraysh, who were the kin of the first to embrace Islam, requires that the kin of one who has a covenant is more deserving of being fought. If it is said that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) did not fight Quraysh except after the abrogation of this verse, it is said: the historical records contradict that, because the abrogating verse for this verse is Surat [Bara'a], which was revealed after the conquest of Makka and the Islam of all of Quraysh.

And His saying, exalted is He, "aw ja'ukum" (or who come to you) is coordinated (ma'tuf) on "yasilun" (join), and it may be on His saying "baynakum wa baynahum mithaq" (between whom and you there is a covenant). The meaning differs between the two conjunctions. This too was a ruling that existed before the affairs of Islam became firmly established: whoever among the polytheists withdrew from fighting and came to the abode of Islam peacefully, unwilling to fight his people alongside the Muslims or to fight the Muslims alongside his people, there is no way against him. This too was abrogated by what is in [Bara'a].

"Hasirat" means: became constricted and distressed, and from it comes "hasar" in speech, which is the constriction of speech upon the speaker.

(p-624) al-Hasan and Qatada read "hasiratun" (constricted), thus said al-Tabari, and al-Mahdawi related this from 'Asim through the narration of Hafs. It is reported from al-Hasan that he read "hasirat" (constricted, plural). In the codex of Ubayy, "aw ja'ukum" is dropped. According to the majority of grammarians, "hasirat" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), with the implied "qad" (indeed): qad hasirat.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This accompanies the past verb when it is in the position of a circumstantial clause. The reason for this is to distinguish between the estimation of a circumstantial clause and a new, independent statement. Such as your saying: "jaa Zayd rakiba al-faras" (Zayd came, he mounted the horse). If you intend by "rakiba al-faras" another statement about Zayd, you do not need to estimate "qad." If you intend it as a circumstantial clause for Zayd, you estimate it with "qad." al-Zajjaj said: "hasirat" is a statement after a statement. al-Mubarrad said: "hasirat" is a supplication against them.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Some commentators said: a supplication is not correct here, because it would require a supplication against them that they not fight their own people, and that is corrupt.

The author said:

al-Mubarrad's view may be understood as follows: the supplication against them that they not fight the Muslims is a declaration of their incapacity, and the supplication against them that they not fight their own people is a belittling of them, meaning: they are weaker and more contemptible, and one can do without them, as you say when you intend this meaning: "May Allah not make so-and-so over me, nor with me either," meaning: I do without him and consider myself sufficient without him.

The lam in His saying "lasallatahum" is the answer to "wa law" (even if/had). The lam in His saying "falaqatalukum" is the lam of correspondence and pairing, because it stands in the position of the first; if the first were not there, you would say: "law sha'a Allahu laqatalukum" (had Allah willed, they would have fought you). The meaning is to make the believers recognize the measure of the blessing and its averting: that is, had Allah willed, He would have strengthened them and emboldened them against you; since Allah has favored you with the truce, accept it and obey within it.

A group read "falaqatalukum" (then they would have killed you). al-Jahdari and al-Hasan read "falaqattalukum" with a doubled ta'. The meaning of "fa-in i'tazalukum" is: they made a truce with you and left you alone regarding killing. "As-salam" here means: peace (sulh), as said by al-Rabi'; and from it is the saying of al-Tirimmah ibn Hakim:

(p-625) That is because Tamim left Salam to the Asad, every fine horse with a fluttering liver.

al-Rabi' said: "as-salam" here is peace (sulh), and so the common reciters recited it. al-Jahdari read "as-salm" with a sukun on the lam, and al-Hasan read "as-silm" with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam. The meaning of the whole of this verse is: take the hypocrites and disbelievers and kill them wherever you find them, except those who enter into the ranks of those between whom and you there is a covenant and who commit themselves to your truce, or who come to you having disliked fighting you and fighting their people. This is by Allah's grace upon you and His defense of you, for had He willed, He would have empowered these, who are in this state of non-hostility, over you, and they would have fought you. "So if they keep away from you" means: if this occurs and they do not fight you, then there is no way for you against them. This, and what is in [Surat al-Mumtahina] in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being righteous to them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves the just﴾ [al-Mumtahina: 8], is abrogated by what is in [Surat Bara'a], as said by Qatada, Ibn Zayd, and others.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 91:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿You will find others who wish to be safe from you and to be safe from their own people. Every time they are returned to temptation (fitnah), they are plunged back into it. So if they do not withdraw from you, nor offer you peace, nor restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. Against these We have given you clear authority.﴾

When God, exalted is He, described earlier the attributes of those who were sincere in refraining from fighting and eager to offer peace, He drew attention to a deceitful, false, and hidden group who wished to remain in their places together with their people. They would say to them, "We are with you and upon your religion," and they would also say to the Muslims, when they came as envoys or were sent to them, "We are with you and upon your religion," out of their duplicity and treachery. It was said that the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan were of this description. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i, who used to carry news between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the disbelievers. It was also said that it was revealed concerning a people who would come from Makkah to the Prophet (ﷺ) for show, displaying Islam, and then return to Quraysh and disbelieve. So God, exalted is He, exposed these people and made known that they were not in the same condition as those mentioned before.

His saying "to temptation" (ila al-fitnah) means "to testing" (al-ikhtibar). It is reported that they would return to their people, and it would be said to one of them, "Is your lord the beetle? Is your lord the stick? Is your lord the scorpion?" and the like, and he would say it (p-626). The meaning of "urkisu" is that they returned in a manner of misguidance, i.e., they were destroyed in their choice by what they had committed of disbelief. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read "rukisu" with a damma on the ra' and without an alif, and Abu al-Fath related it from him with a shadda on the kaf, as a doubling form. The difference concerning "al-salam" is as previously mentioned. This verse is an exhortation to kill these deceivers if they do not turn back from their state to the state of the others who withdraw and offer peace.

Qadi Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq, may God have mercy on him, said:

Reflect on the eloquence of the speech in that its context in the earlier formulation before this one was the context of enjoining withdrawal, enjoining the offering of peace, and negating fighting, since they were sincere in that and held it as their belief; and its context in this later formulation is the context of negating withdrawal and negating the offering of peace, since they were false and deceptive in it. The ruling is the same under both contexts, because those upon whom God has placed no path, were they not to withdraw, their ruling would be the ruling of these upon whom clear authority has been placed. Likewise, these upon whom authority is placed, when they do not withdraw; were they to withdraw, their ruling would be the ruling of those upon whom there is no path. But by this expression they are under the threat of killing if they do not withdraw.

"Thaqiftumuhum" is derived from "al-thiqaf," meaning you overcame them while they were defeated and you had power over them. "Al-sultan" means the proof. 'Ikrimah said: Wherever "sultan" occurs in the Book of God, exalted is He, it means the proof.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 92:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer by mistake - then the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation (diyah) paid to his family, unless they give it as charity. But if he was from a people hostile to you and he was a believer, then [the penalty is] the freeing of a believing slave. And if he was from a people between you and them is a treaty, then compensation paid to his family and the freeing of a believing slave. But whoever does not find [the means], then fasting for two consecutive months - a repentance from Allah. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

The majority of the exegetes said: the meaning of this verse is: it is not within the permission of Allah, nor within His command, that a believer should kill a believer in any way. Then He made an exception which is disjunctive (munqati') and not from the first, in which "illa" (except) carries the meaning of "lakinna" (but), and the sense is: "But mistake may occur." This is like the saying of the poet:

؎ Suqam has become an empty waste with no companion in it, except the beasts and the passing of the wind through the gharaf trees.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Suqam is the name of a valley, and al-gharaf is a tree whose bark is used for tanning. And as Jarir said:

؎ Of the fair ones, she has not travelled far, nor has she trodden on the earth, except the trailing hem of a striped, embroidered cloak.

There is scrutiny regarding this evidence.

Another interpretation of the verse is possible, namely that "kana" be understood as meaning: "was established and found," as if He said: "It was not found, nor established, nor permissible for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake, since it is sometimes overcome in him." In this case the exception is not disjunctive. According to this, the verse includes magnifying the intentional killing and the gravity of its matter, as you say: "It was not for you, O so-and-so, to speak of this except forgetfully," magnifying intention and purpose along with the absolute danger of speaking about it.

Al-Zuhri read "khata'" (with short vowel, without hamza), while al-Hasan and al-A'mash read it with hamza and elongation. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: "This verse was revealed concerning 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a al-Makhzumi when he killed al-Harith ibn Yazid ibn Nabisha. That was because he (al-Harith) used to torment him in Makkah. Then al-Harith embraced Islam and came as a muhajir (emigrant), and 'Ayyash met him at al-Harra, thought he was still upon his disbelief, and killed him. Then he came and informed the Prophet ﷺ, and that grieved him, and the verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Stand up and free [a slave].'"

Ibn Zayd said:

It was revealed concerning a man whom Abu al-Darda' killed. He was tending sheep and was reciting the testimony of faith, but he killed him and drove his sheep to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse was revealed.

It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Hudhayfa al-Yamani when he was killed by mistake on the day of Uhud. It was also said other than this, and Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever kills a believer﴾ etc. In this verse Allah, exalted is He, explains the ruling for a believer who kills a believer by mistake. The reality of mistake (khata') is that one does not intend to kill him, and the forms of mistake are many and uncountable; what unites them is the absence of intention. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Qatada, and others said: the believing slave is one who is adult, has prayed, and has adopted faith; a child does not suffice in this. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: whoever is judged under the rulings of Islam suffices, by the prayer performed over him if he dies and by his burial. Malik said: whoever prays and fasts is more beloved to me. The scholars agreed that a person with a great defect, such as the loss of both hands or both feet, or one who is blind, does not suffice, as far as I have memorised; if the defect is slight, such that livelihood and earning are still possible with it, such as lameness and the like, then there are two opinions regarding it.

"Musallamah" means: paid and delivered. It falls upon the 'aqilah (paternal kin who bear the blood-money) for what exceeds one third of the diyah. "Illa an yassaddaqu" refers to the heirs of the slain. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "yatasaddaqu". Al-Hasan, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and 'Abd al-Warith on the authority of Abu 'Amr read "tassaddaqu" with ta' addressing the present, and Nubayh al-'Anzi read "tasaddaqu" with ta' and a light sad.

The diyah is one hundred camels, upon the owners of camels according to one group; according to others, it is upon all people, except that when people of gold and silver do not have camels, they then switch to gold and silver, giving from them the value of camels at the time of the incident, whatever it may reach. There was disagreement concerning the hundred camels. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are in quarters: thirty hiqqah, thirty jadha'ah, twenty bint makhad, and twenty bint labun. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: they are in fifths: twenty hiqqah, twenty jadha'ah, twenty bint makhad, twenty bint labun, and twenty ibn labun male. Some jurists have an order other than this. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and others held that the diyah from cattle is two hundred cows, from sheep two thousand sheep, and from hullal one hundred hullah. This is reported in a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. A hullah in the speech of the Arabs is two garments of one kind, and in that era it was an item whose value equalled one hundred camels, so the view went along with this. As for gold, it is one thousand dinars, which 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, established, and people followed it. As for silver, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, established it at twelve thousand, and Malik held this; a group says it is ten thousand dirhams.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if he was from a people hostile to you﴾ etc. The meaning according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibrahim, 'Ikrimah, and others is: if this slain person, killed by mistake, was a believing man who had embraced faith and remained among his people, who were disbelievers and hostile to you, then there is no diyah for him, and his expiation is only the freeing of a believing slave. According to them the occasion of its revelation was that the armies of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pass by tribes of disbelievers, and so sometimes someone who had embraced faith but had not emigrated was killed, or one who had emigrated and then returned to his people was killed in the charges of battle, considered to be among the disbelievers; so the verse was revealed. According to those who hold this view, the diyah falls away for two reasons: first, that the heirs of the slain are disbelievers, so it is not valid to pay the diyah to them, to strengthen themselves with it; and second, that the sanctity of this one who embraced faith but did not emigrate is slight, so there is no diyah for him. They argued with the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no guardianship over them at all until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. Another group said: rather, the reason for the falling away of the diyah is that the heirs are disbelievers only; so whether the slain person was killed by mistake among the Muslims or among his own people, having not emigrated, or having emigrated and then returned to his people, his expiation is the freeing of a slave and there is no diyah for him, because it is not valid to pay it to the disbelievers.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The proponent of the first opinion says: if the believer is killed in the land of the Muslims while his people are at war, then the diyah is due to the public treasury (bayt al-mal), and the expiation applies.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if he was from a people between you and them is a treaty﴾ The meaning according to al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ibrahim, and others is: if this slain person, killed by mistake, was a believer from a people who are your covenanted allies, then their covenant requires that they are entitled to the diyah of their companion; so his expiation is the freeing of a slave and the payment of the diyah. Al-Hasan read: "And if he was from a people between you and them is a treaty - and he is a believer -". Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, and Ibrahim also said: the one slain from the people of the covenant by mistake, whether he was a believer or a disbeliever, according to the covenant of his people, has the diyah due for him like the diyah of a Muslim, and the freeing of a slave. On this basis there was disagreement concerning the diyah of a covenanted person (mu'ahad). Abu Hanifa and others said: his diyah is like the diyah of a Muslim, and this was reported from Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Malik and his companions said: his diyah is half the diyah of a Muslim. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: his diyah is one third the diyah of a Muslim.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But whoever does not find﴾ etc. He means, according to the majority: whoever does not find the means of freeing a slave, nor does his wealth allow it for him, then fasting two consecutive months suffices for him, in days without any breaking of the fast between them. Makki reported from al-Sha'bi: fasting the two months suffices in place of the diyah and the freeing for one who does not find either of them. This view is an error, because the diyah is upon the 'aqilah and not upon the killer; al-Tabari reported the view from Masruq. "Tawbah" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and its meaning is: a returning of you to ease and facilitation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 93:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein eternally, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment.﴾

Al-muta'ammid (the intentional killer) in the language of the Arabs is one who intends a thing. The scholars differed concerning the description of the intentional killer. 'Ata' and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and others said: he is one who kills with an iron implement such as a sword, a dagger, the point of a spear, and the like of what is sharpened and prepared for cutting, or with something of which he knows that death results, such as a heavy stone and the like. A group said: the intentional killer is everyone who kills, whether the killing is by iron, by a stone, by a stick, or by other than that. This is the saying of the majority (al-jumhur), and it is the most sound. The opinion of al-Shafi'i and others is that killing by other than sharpened iron is shibh al-'amd (quasi-intentional killing), and they held that it entails an aggravated blood-money (diyah). Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, does not recognize shibh al-'amd and does not hold it in anything; rather, killing for him is only what Allah, exalted is He, mentioned as intentional or erroneous, and nothing else. And killing by poison, according to him, is intentional even if he says: "I only intended its intoxication."

As for His saying, "his recompense is Hell," its implied sense according to the People of the Sunnah is: "his recompense is (Hell) if He recompenses him with that," i.e., he deserves it and is entitled to it because of the magnitude of his sin. Abu Mijlaz, Abu Salih and others stated this explicitly. This is based on the view that forgiveness is subject to the will of Allah for all sinners, killers and others. The Mu'tazila went to the generality of this verse, holding that it is not specified, and that it is to be restricted by the generality of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. They also rejected what is narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, that he said: "The severe (verse) was revealed after the lenient (verse)," meaning: ﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ was revealed after ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. They hold that this threat is certainly executed upon every killer who kills a believer, and they regard it as a generality that stands in its outward sense, specifying the generality in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], as if He had said: "except one who kills intentionally."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The People of Truth say to them: this generality is rejected and does not stand in its outward sense, for two reasons. The first is what you and we agree upon regarding the man who is witnessed against, or who confesses to intentional killing, and the authority or the guardians come and the legal punishment is carried out upon him, and he is executed as retaliation (qawad). This one is not pursued in the Hereafter, and the threat is not executed upon him, by consensus, based on the authentic hadith through the route of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit: "Whoever is punished in this world, that is an expiation for him." This is an annulment of the generality. The second reason is that the wording of this verse is not a wording of generality, but a shared term that occurs frequently for specificity, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], and the rulers of the believers, when they judge unjustly in a matter, are not disbelievers in any respect. And like the saying of the poet:

Whoever does not defend his basin with his sword will be destroyed, and whoever does not wrong people will be wronged.

Its meaning is only specificity, because not everyone who does not wrong is wronged. This is another reason showing that the generality is not established. As for what they cited from the saying of Zayd ibn Thabit, it is not as they stated. Zayd only meant that this verse was revealed after the surah of [al-Furqan], and by "the lenient" he meant His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], the verse. Although al-Mahdawi has related from him that he said: the verse ﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ was revealed after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], by four months. If it is subject to specification, then the correct view is that this verse is specified regarding the disbeliever who kills a believer. As for what is narrated, that it was revealed concerning Miqyas ibn Subabah, when a man of the Ansar killed his brother Hisham ibn Subabah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took the blood-money for him, then after that he sent him with a man of Fihr on some matter, whereupon Miqyas attacked him and killed him, and returned to Makkah apostate, and began reciting:

I killed for his sake a man of Fihr, and I bore his blood-money, the chiefs of the Banu al-Najjar, lords of Fari'.
I have dissolved by it my vengeance, and attained my wrath, and I was the first to return to the idols.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I will not grant him security in a sanctuary or outside it," and he ordered his killing on the day of the Conquest of Makkah while he was clinging to the Ka'bah. Or else it is as related from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "intentionally" means: considering his killing lawful. This also ultimately leads to disbelief. And concerning the believer whom it has preceded in the knowledge of Allah that He will punish him for his disobedience, according to the interpretation we have already mentioned, then his recompense, if He recompenses him, and his saying "abiding therein" when it concerns the believer means remaining for a long duration, in the manner of their supplications for kings with eternity (al-takhlid) and the like. And what supports this is the omission of His saying "abadan" (forever), for eternal permanence (al-ta'bid) is not joined with khulud (abiding) except in mention of the disbelievers.

The scholars differed concerning the acceptance of the repentance of the killer. A group held that his repentance is not accepted, and this was related from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn 'Umar. Ibn 'Abbas used to say: "Shirk and killing are unspecified; whoever dies upon them is abiding forever." He also used to say: "This verse is Madani, and it abrogated the verse in al-Furqan, since al-Furqan is Makki." The majority hold that his repentance is accepted. It was related from some scholars that they would intend severity and warning at times, and so they would say: "The repentance of the killer is not accepted." Among them is Ibn Shihab, who, when someone asked him who appeared to have killed, would say to him: "Your repentance is accepted," and when someone asked him who had not done so, he would say: "There is no repentance for the killer." Among them is Ibn 'Abbas, and it occurred from him in the tafsir of 'Abd ibn Humayd that a man asked him: "Is there repentance for the killer?" He said to him: "There is no repentance for the killer, and his recompense is Hell." When the questioner had gone, his companions said to him: "This is not how we knew you to speak; rather you used to say that the killer has repentance." He said to them: "I saw him angry, and I think he intends to kill." They got up, searched for him, and asked about him, and it turned out to be so. Hibat Allah mentioned in his book "al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh" that this verse is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], and said: "This is the consensus of the people except Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, for they said: it is muhkam (not abrogated)."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What Hibat Allah said is open to scrutiny, because this is a place of generality and specification, not a place of abrogation. He built his statement only upon the disagreement of the people concerning the acceptance of the killer's repentance. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 94:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully, and do not say to one who gives you the greeting of peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life. For with Allah are many spoils. Thus were you before, and Allah conferred His favor upon you. So investigate carefully. Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾

(p-٦٣٥) The Arabs say, "ḍaraba fī al-arḍ" (he traveled in the land) when one journeys for trade, raiding, or other purposes, using "fī" (in). They say "ḍaraba al-arḍ" (he struck the earth) without "fī" when one intends to relieve a human need. From this is the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "Two men should not go out relieving themselves while talking, uncovering their private parts, for indeed Allah detests that."

The occasion of revelation of this verse was that a detachment (sariyya) from the detachments of the Messenger of Allah encountered a man who had a camel and goods, and it was said: spoils. He gave the greeting of peace to the people and said, "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." One of them charged at him and killed him. This grieved the Messenger of Allah, and the verse was revealed concerning it.

The exegetes differed about identifying the killer and the one killed in this incident. The view held by most, which is in the Sira of Ibn Ishaq, in the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, and in others, is that the killer was Muhallim ibn Jaththama and the one killed was 'Amir ibn al-Adbat. The full narration is in the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, in the biographies (al-siyar), and in al-Isti'ab. A group said the killer was Usama ibn Zayd and the one killed was Mirdas ibn Nahik al-Ghatafani. A group said the killer was Abu (p-٦٣٦) Qatada. A group said the killer was Ghalib al-Laythi, and the one killed was Mirdas. A group said the killer was Abu al-Darda'. There is no disagreement that the one whom the earth rejected when he died was Muhallim ibn Jaththama.

The majority of the reciters of the Seven read "fa-tabayyanu" (investigate carefully). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "fa-tathabbatu" with the letter thā' (ث) at both places and in [al-Hujurat]. Some said "tabayyanu" is more eloquent and stronger than "tathabbatu," because one who seeks firmness (mutathabbit) may not reach clarity. Abu 'Ubayd said the two are close in meaning.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is what Abu 'Ubayd said, because a man's "tabayyun" does not require that the matter has become clear to him; rather it requires striving for certainty, just as "tathabbut" requires striving for certainty. So the two are the same.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and Ibn Kathir in some of his transmissions read "al-salam" with a doubled sīn, with fatḥa on it and fatḥa on the lām. Its meaning is submission (al-istislam), i.e., he cast down his hand and submitted to you, and showed his call to you. The rest of the Seven read "al-salam" (the greeting), meaning that the slain man greeted the detachment, because his greeting with the greeting of Islam indicates his obedience and submission. It is also possible that it means withdrawal and abandonment; al-Akhfash said: one says "fulan salam" when he does not mix with anyone. It is related in some transmissions of 'Asim: "al-silm" with a kasra on the sīn, a doubled sīn, and a sukun on the lām, which means peace (al-sulh). The meanings intended by these three readings are close. al-Jahdari read "al-salm" with a fatḥa on the sīn and a sukun on the lām.

"Al-'aradh" is the goods and the camel, or the spoils that belonged to the slain man. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Abu Hamza, and al-Yamani read "lasta mu'manan" with a fatḥa on the mīm, meaning: we do not grant you security for yourself. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿For with Allah are many spoils﴾ is a promise of what Allah will bring in its proper way and from its lawful source without committing a prohibited act; that is, do not rush to ruin.

The interpreters differed concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Thus were you before﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: its meaning is that you used to conceal your Islam from your people, fearing them for yourselves, and then Allah favored you by strengthening your religion and making your law manifest. So now it is likewise: each one of them fears his people and is watchful lest he reach you; so when he arrives it is not proper to kill him until you investigate his matter. Ibn Zayd said: thus were you disbelievers, and then Allah favored you by your becoming Muslims; so do not deny that he might be a disbeliever who then immediately embraces Islam at the moment he meets you, and therefore his matter must be scrutinized. It is also possible that the meaning is that "thus" refers to killing before investigation, i.e., in this condition you were in your pre-Islamic ignorance, not investigating, until Allah brought Islam and bestowed favor upon you. Then, blessed and exalted is He, reinforced the command to investigate, and informed that He is Acquainted with what the servants do. This is a report that carries a warning from Him, exalted is He, because the meaning is: indeed Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do; so guard your souls and avoid the slip that will destroy you.

﴿Those who sit at home among the believers, other than those with a harm, are not equal to those who strive in the way of God with their wealth and their selves. God has preferred those who strive with their wealth and selves over those who sit at home by a degree, and to each God has promised the best reward, and God has preferred those who strive over those who sit at home with a great reward.﴾ ﴿Degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. God is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

In His saying "lā yastawī" (is not equal), there is an ambiguity for the listener, and it is more eloquent than specifying the rank that lies between the one who strives and the one who sits. So the one who reflects walks along with his thought, and keeps imagining the degrees between them.

"Al-qā'idūn" (those who sit) is an expression for those who stay behind, since sitting (al-qu'ūd) is the state of one who does not move toward the matter from which he sits back, in most cases.

Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr and Ḥamza read "ghayru ulī al-ḍarar" with the *rā'* of "ghayr" raised (ghayru). Nāfi', Ibn 'Āmir and al-Kisā'ī read "ghayra" with the accusative (naṣb). With 'Āṣim there is a difference: it is narrated from him both the raising and the accusative. Al-A'mash and Abū Ḥaywa read "ghayri" with the *rā'* in the genitive (kasr). Whoever reads with the raising (ḍamm) makes "ghayru" an attribute (ṣifah) of "al-qā'idīn," according to Sībawayh, just as it is for him an attribute in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"ghayri al-maghḍūbi 'alayhim"﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 7], with "ghayri" in the genitive as an attribute. Similar to it is the verse of Labīd:

*"And when you are repaid a loan, then repay it, for the young man is only repaid by one who is not al-Jamal."*

[Page 638]

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Thus Abū 'Alī mentioned it, but it is also narrated as "laysa al-Jamal" (is not al-Jamal). Whoever reads with the *rā'* in the accusative makes it an exception (istithnā') from "al-qā'idīn." Abū al-Ḥasan (al-Akhfash) said: What strengthens this is that it was revealed after it in the manner of exception and correction (istidrāk).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correction (istidrāk) may also be achieved by singling out those who sit by the attribute. Al-Zajjāj said: It is also permissible in the reading of the raising that it be by way of exception, as if He had said: "Those who sit and those who strive are not equal, except the people of harm, for they are equal to those who strive."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is rejected, because the people of harm are not equal to those who strive, and at most they have been freed from the rebuke and blame that befell those who sat without an excuse. He said: It is permissible in the reading of the accusative of the *rā'* that it be a state (ḥāl). As for the genitive of the *rā'*, it is an attribute of "al-mu'minīn."

It is narrated through more than one chain that: "The verse was revealed, ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers, other than those with a harm, and those who strive﴾, and Ibn Umm Maktūm came when he heard it and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there any concession for me, for I am blind?' Then at that moment it was revealed: ﴿other than those with a harm﴾." Al-Fillaqān ibn 'Āṣim said: We were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when it was revealed to him. When revelation came to him, his eyes would remain open and his hearing and sight would be free for what came to him from Allah. We would recognize that in his face. When he finished, he said to the scribe: "Write: ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers, other than those with a harm, and those who strive﴾," to the end of the verse. He said: Then the blind man stood up and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is our fault?" He said: Then Allah revealed to His Messenger, and we said to the blind man: "It is being revealed to him." He said: He feared that something would be revealed about him, so he remained standing in his place saying: "I repent to the Messenger of Allah," until the Messenger of Allah finished, and he said to the scribe: "Write ﴿other than those with a harm﴾." 

And "ulū al-ḍarar" (those with a harm) are the people of excuses, since harm has afflicted them until it prevented them from striving. This was said by Ibn 'Abbās and others.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with their wealth and their selves﴾ is the ultimate in the perfection of striving. Since the people of the register (ahl al-dīwān), who are possessed of that stipend, spend in hardships, and expeditions and orders terrify them, some scholars said: They are greater in reward than the volunteer, because of the calmness of their hearts and the ease of their minds during the great summer campaigns (al-ṣawā'if) and the like.

Whoever holds that wealth is superior to poverty has argued from this verse that displays the virtue of wealth, and that the connection to it is clear. The people explained the verse as: the completion of the preference in it is by the degree, then by the degrees, is only emphasis, intensification and clarification. Ibn Jurayj said: The preference by a degree is over those who sit from among the people of excuse.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because they are with the believers in their intentions, as the Prophet ﷺ said in the expedition of Tabuk: "There are men in Madīnah whom we did not cross a valley, nor traverse a mountain or a path, except that they were with us; the excuse restrained them." Ibn Jurayj said: The preference by the great reward and the degrees is over those who sit without an excuse. "Al-ḥusnā" (the best): it is Paradise, which the believers were promised. Likewise al-Suddī and others said.

Ibn Muḥayrīz said: The degrees are degrees in Paradise, the distance between two degrees being the gallop of a swift, trained horse for seventy years. al-Ṭabarī said this and preferred it. Ibn Zayd said: The degrees in the verse are the seven mentioned in Sūrat [Barā'ah] (al-Tawbah), which is His saying: ﴿That is because they are not struck by thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 120], and the verses that follow, in which he mentioned the trampling that enrages the disbelievers, the gaining of something from the enemy, the small and great expenditure, and the crossing of valleys and distances.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The degrees of striving, if they were counted, would be more than these; but what gathers them is the sacrifice of self and wealth, and exerting the body and wealth so that the word of Allah is the highest. There is no doubt that according to the ranks and degrees of deeds, the ranks and degrees of Paradise will be. The sayings are all close to one another, and the rest of the verse is a noble promise and comfort.

The accusative of "darajāt" (degrees) is either in apposition (badal) to "ajran" (reward), or by implying a verb so that it is an emphasis for "ajran," as you say: "You are owed a thousand dirhams from me, as a recognized debt," as if you had said: "I acknowledge it as recognized."

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on surah 4, verses 97–100 (part 1 of 2)

His words, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, [the angels] will say, "In what [condition] were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." [The angels] will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿Except for the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children, who are unable to devise a plan and do not find a way.﴾ ﴿For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them, and Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on earth many a refuge and abundance. And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger, and then death overtakes him, his reward has indeed fallen upon Allah, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The people intended by this verse, up to His words "wretched is the destination," are a group from the people of Makkah who had embraced Islam and had shown the Prophet (ﷺ) that they believed in him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated, they remained with their people. Some of them were subjected to trials and yielded to them. Then, when the affair of Badr came, a group of them went out with the disbelievers and were killed at Badr, and the verse was revealed concerning them.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "There were some people from Makkah who had embraced Islam, but they concealed their Islam. The polytheists took them out on the day of Badr, and some of them were struck down. The Muslims said, 'These companions of ours were Muslims, but they were coerced.' So they asked forgiveness for them, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death﴾ [the verse]." He said: "Then a letter was written to the Muslims who remained in Makkah with this verse, [stating] that they had no excuse. So they went out, but the polytheists overtook them and subjected them to trial, and then this other verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿And among the people is one who says, 'We believe in Allah,' but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people as like the punishment of Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10] [the verse]. So the Muslims wrote to them with this, and they went out, having despaired of every good. Then this was revealed concerning them: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried and then struggled and were patient — indeed your Lord, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. So they wrote to them with this, that Allah had made for you a way out. So they went out, and the polytheists overtook them and fought them, until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed."

'Ikrimah said: "This verse was revealed concerning five men who were killed at Badr: Qays ibn al-Fakih ibn al-Mughirah, al-Harith ibn Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu al-'As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, and 'Ali ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf."

Al-Naqqash said: "[It was revealed] concerning others besides them who had embraced Islam, then went out to Badr. When they saw the small number of the Muslims, they said, 'These people's religion has deceived them.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Al-'Abbas was among those who went out with the disbelievers, but he was saved and taken captive. He was one of those who fed [the army] at the Nafir of Badr. Al-Suddi said: "When al-'Abbas, 'Aqil, and Nufayl were taken captive, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to al-'Abbas, 'Ransom yourself and your nephew.' Al-'Abbas said to him, 'O Messenger of Allah, did we not pray towards your qiblah and bear witness to your testimony of faith?' He said, 'O 'Abbas, you disputed and so you were defeated,' and then he recited to him this verse: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate therein?﴾" Al-Suddi said: "On the day this verse was revealed, whoever embraced Islam but did not emigrate was a disbeliever until he emigrated, except for one who is unable to devise a plan and does not find a way."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

There is room for scrutiny in what al-Suddi said. What accords with the principles [of the law] is that whoever died among those [people], after having accepted the trial and apostatised, is a disbeliever, and his refuge is Hell eternally. This is the apparent meaning of the situation of that group. Even if we suppose that among them there was one who died as a believer but had been coerced into leaving, or who died in Makkah, then he is merely a sinner for abandoning emigration, and his refuge is Hell as a [punishment for] disobedience, not eternally. However, since it cannot be determined that any one of them died in faith, it was not appropriate to mention them among the Companions, nor to take into account what had been known of them before. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that holds that the grave sinner is in an intermediate position) have no proof in this matter for their takfir (declaring someone a disbeliever) of people because of sins.

As for al-'Abbas, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned that he embraced Islam before Badr, and for this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of Badr: "Whoever meets al-'Abbas, let him not kill him, for he was brought out only under compulsion."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is also mentioned that he embraced Islam only while a captive, when the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned to him the matter of the money he had left with Umm al-Fadl. It is mentioned that he embraced Islam in the year of Khaybar, and that he used to write to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with news of the polytheists, and that he wished to emigrate. "So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to him, 'Stay in Makkah, for your remaining there is more beneficial to us.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

However, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dealt with him, when he was taken captive, according to the outward appearance of his affair.

His words, exalted is He: "tawaffahum" (they take them in death) may be a past-tense verb without a feminine marker, since the feminine form of the word "al-mala'ikah" (the angels) is not real [grammatical gender]. It may also be a future-tense verb in the sense of "tatawaffahum" (they will take them), with one of the two ta's elided, and the expression would then contain an indication of what would come to pass in the future after the revelation of the verse. Ibrahim read "tuwaffahum" with a dammah on the ta'. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: "It is as though they are handed over to the angels and reckoned against them." "Tawaffahum" with a fatha on the ta' means: they take their souls. Ibn Furak related from al-Hasan that the meaning is: they gather them to the Fire.

"Zalimi anfusihim" (wronging themselves) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: wronging themselves by abandoning emigration. Al-Zajjaj said: "The nun was dropped from 'zalimin' for lightness, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿bāligha al-Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]." The angels' words "fima kuntum" (in what [condition] were you) are a rebuke and reproach. These people's words "kunna mustad'afina fi al-ard" (we were oppressed in the land) are an invalid excuse, since they were able to devise plans and find the way. Then the angels held them to account for their sin by saying: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious﴾. "Al-ard" (the earth) in the words of these [angels] refers specifically to the land of Makkah, and "ard Allah" (the earth of Allah) refers to the earth in general. The intended meaning is: "so that you could emigrate therein to a place of safety."

This statement [of the angels] came only after the angels had taken the souls of these people, and it indicates that they died as Muslims. Otherwise, had they died as disbelievers, nothing of this would have been said to them. The reason they were not mentioned among the Companions was the severity of what they had committed, the fact that none of them could be identified as a believer, and the possibility of their apostasy.

Allah, exalted is He, threatened them that their refuge is Hell. Then He excepted from them those whose weakness was genuine: the weak men, the weak women, and the children, such as 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn Hisham, and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: "I and my mother were among the oppressed: she was among the women and I was among the children." "Al-hilah" (a plan) is a general term for the means of every kind of escape. "Al-sabil" (the way) is, as Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others mentioned, the way to Madinah. The correct view is that it is general to all ways.

Then Allah, exalted is He, gave these people hope of His pardon, and "'asa" (perhaps) from Allah is binding, just as it indicates the gravity of the matter being pardoned. Al-Hasan said: "'Asa' from Allah is binding." Others said: it has the force of a promise, since one does not speak with "'asa" out of doubt or expectation, and this returns to [the meaning of] obligation. Others said: it is according to the perspective of humans, meaning: your assumption regarding one in this condition is to hope for the pardon of Allah, exalted is He.

"Al-muragham" (a refuge) means the place one turns to and the course one takes. So said Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi', and others. From it is the saying of al-Nabighah al-Ja'di:

> Like a mountain whose pillars give refuge, mighty in its refuge and its course.

And the saying of another:

> To a land far from its abode, far in its refuge and its tumult.

Mujahid said: "Al-muragham" means one who removes himself from what is disliked. Ibn Zayd said: "Al-muragham" means the place of emigration. Al-Suddi said: "Al-muragham" means one who seeks livelihood.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

All of this is interpretation according to meaning. As for the specific lexical sense of the word, "al-muraghamah" is a place of contention, namely that each of the two disputants humbles (ya'righam) the nose of the other by overpowering him in his aim. The Quraysh humbled the noses of those imprisoned in Makkah. So if one of them emigrated in the earth of Allah, he would humble the noses of the Quraysh by being in a place of protection from them. These people's words "kunna mustad'afina fi al-ard" (we were oppressed in the land) are an invalid excuse, since they were able to devise plans and find the way. Then the angels held them to account for their sin by saying: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious﴾. "Al-ard" (the earth) in the words of these [angels] refers specifically to the land of Makkah, and "ard Allah" (the earth of Allah) refers to the earth in general. The intended meaning is: "so that you could emigrate therein to a place of safety."

This statement [of the angels] came only after the angels had taken the souls of these people, and it indicates that they died as Muslims. Otherwise, had they died as disbelievers, nothing of this would have been said to them. The reason they were not mentioned among the Companions was the severity of what they had committed, the fact that none of them could be identified as a believer, and the possibility of their apostasy.

Allah, exalted is He, threatened them that their refuge is Hell. Then He excepted from them those whose weakness was genuine: the weak men, the weak women, and the children, such as 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn Hisham, and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: "I and my mother were among the oppressed: she was among the women and I was among the children." "Al-hilah" (a plan) is a general term for the means of every kind of escape. Then Allah, exalted is He, gave these people hope of His pardon, and "'asa" (perhaps) from Allah is binding, just as it indicates the gravity of the matter being pardoned. Al-Hasan said: "'Asa' from Allah is binding." Others said: it has the force of a promise, since one does not speak with "'asa" out of doubt or expectation, and this returns to [the meaning of] obligation. Others said: it is according to the perspective of humans, meaning: your assumption regarding one in this condition is to hope for the pardon of Allah, exalted is He.

> Like a mountain whose pillars give refuge, mighty in its refuge and its course.

And the saying of another:

> To a land far from its abode, far in its refuge and its tumult.

Mujahid said: "Al-muragham" means one who removes himself from what is disliked. Ibn Zayd said: "Al-muragham" means the place of emigration. Al-Suddi said: "Al-muragham" means one who seeks livelihood.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on surah 4, verses 97–100 (part 1 of 2)

His words, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, [the angels] will say, "In what [condition] were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." [The angels] will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿Except for the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children, who are unable to devise a plan and do not find a way.﴾ ﴿For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them, and Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on earth many a refuge and abundance. And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger, and then death overtakes him, his reward has indeed fallen upon Allah, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated, they remained with their people. Some of them were subjected to trials and yielded to them. Then, when the affair of Badr came, a group of them went out with the disbelievers and were killed at Badr, and the verse was revealed concerning them.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "There were some people from Makkah who had embraced Islam, but they concealed their Islam. The polytheists took them out on the day of Badr, and some of them were struck down. The Muslims said, 'These companions of ours were Muslims, but they were coerced.' So they asked forgiveness for them, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death﴾ [the verse]." He said: "Then a letter was written to the Muslims who remained in Makkah with this verse, [stating] that they had no excuse. So they went out, but the polytheists overtook them and subjected them to trial, and then this other verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿And among the people is one who says, 'We believe in Allah,' but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people as like the punishment of Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10] [the verse]. So the Muslims wrote to them with this, and they went out, having despaired of every good. Then this was revealed concerning them: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried and then struggled and were patient — indeed your Lord, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. So they wrote to them with this, that Allah had made for you a way out. So they went out, and the polytheists overtook them and fought them, until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed."

'Ikrimah said: "This verse was revealed concerning five men who were killed at Badr: Qays ibn al-Fakih ibn al-Mughirah, al-Harith ibn Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu al-'As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, and 'Ali ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf."

Al-Naqqash said: "[It was revealed] concerning others besides them who had embraced Islam, then went out to Badr. When they saw the small number of the Muslims, they said, 'These people's religion has deceived them.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Al-'Abbas was among those who went out with the disbelievers, but he was saved and taken captive. He was one of those who fed [the army] at the Nafir of Badr. Al-Suddi said: "When al-'Abbas, 'Aqil, and Nufayl were taken captive, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to al-'Abbas, 'Ransom yourself and your nephew.' The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

There is room for scrutiny in what al-Suddi said. What accords with the principles [of the law] is that whoever died among those [people], after having accepted the trial and apostatised, is a disbeliever, and his refuge is Hell eternally. This is the apparent meaning of the situation of that group. Even if we suppose that among them there was one who died as a believer but had been coerced into leaving, or who died in Makkah, then he is merely a sinner for abandoning emigration, and his refuge is Hell as a [punishment for] disobedience, not eternally. However, since it cannot be determined that any one of them died in faith, it was not appropriate to mention them among the Companions, nor to take into account what had been known of them before.
