(p-5) His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame on you for shortening the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve will harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are ever an open enemy to you.﴾ ﴿And when you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group of them stand with you and let them take their weapons.﴾

"Ḍarabtum" (you traveled): its meaning is "you journeyed." The People of the Apparent (Ahl al-Ẓāhir, the literalist school) hold that shortening (qaṣr) applies to every journey that takes one beyond the settled area (al-ḥāḍira), which is the place from which the Friday prayer is established. This is a weak view. The scholars differed over the distance at which the prayer is shortened. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Ibn Rāhawayh said: "The prayer is shortened over four barīd, which is forty-eight miles." Their proof is reports transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Ḥasan and al-Zuhrī said: "The prayer is shortened over a journey of two days," and they did not mention miles. This view is also transmitted from Mālik. Another view transmitted from Mālik is: "The prayer is shortened over a day and a night." These three opinions are close in meaning. It is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn ʿUmar that the prayer is shortened over a full day's journey. Ibn ʿUmar shortened it at thirty miles. From Mālik, in al-ʿUtbiyya, concerning one who went out to his estate at a distance of forty-five miles, he said: "He shortens." From Ibn al-Qāsim, in al-ʿUtbiyya: "If he shortened it at thirty-six [miles], there is no obligation to repeat it." Yaḥyā ibn ʿUmar said: "He must repeat it forever." Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam said: "He must repeat it within its time." Ibn Masʿūd, Sufyān, al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfa and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: "Whoever travels a distance of three [days] shortens." Abū Ḥanīfa said: "Three days and their nights, at the pace of camels and of walking feet." It is transmitted from Anas ibn Mālik that he shortened at fifteen miles. Al-Awzāʿī said: "The majority of scholars hold shortening over a full day's journey, and we adopt this."

The people differed concerning the type of journey over which the prayer is shortened. There is consensus (ijmāʿ) on jihad, Ḥajj, ʿUmra, and what resembles them, such as maintaining the ties of kinship and saving a life. The people differed regarding other journeys. The majority hold that shortening is permitted on a lawful journey, such as trade and the like. It is transmitted (p-6) from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: "The prayer is not shortened except on Ḥajj or jihad." ʿAṭāʾ said: "The prayer is not shortened except on a journey of obedience and one of the paths of goodness." It is transmitted from ʿAṭāʾ that it is shortened on every lawful journey. The majority of scholars hold that there is no shortening on a journey of disobedience, such as that of a rebel, a highwayman, and whatever is similar to them. It is transmitted from al-Awzāʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa that shortening is permitted in all of these cases.

The majority of scholars hold that the traveler does not shorten until he leaves the houses of the village, and at that point he is "one who strikes the land." This is the view of Mālik in al-Mudawwana, and of Ibn Ḥabīb and the community of the school. Ibn al-Qāsim said in al-Mudawwana: "Mālik did not set for us a limit concerning proximity." It is transmitted from Mālik: "If there is a village whose people gather [for prayer], one does not shorten until he passes it by three miles. The same applies on the return. If its people do not gather, he shortens when he passes its orchards." It is transmitted from al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Rabīʿa that he intended a journey, so he prayed two units (rakʿatayn) with them in his dwelling. Among them were al-Aswad ibn Yazīd and more than one of the companions of Ibn Masʿūd. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ and Sulaymān ibn Mūsā said the same. It is transmitted from Mujāhid that he said: "The traveler does not shorten on his first day until night." This is an anomalous (shādh) view. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed Ẓuhr in Madina with four units, and ʿAṣr at Dhū al-Ḥulayfa with two units, and there was not a third of a day between them.

It appears from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿there is no blame on you for shortening﴾, that shortening is permissible, or optional. Ibn Wahb transmitted from Mālik that the traveler has a choice; this was said by al-Abharī, and the foremost scholars of the school hold it. Mālik said in al-Mabsūṭ: "Shortening is a sunna." This is the majority view of the school, and the answer in al-Mudawwana, requiring repetition within the time for one who completed the prayer during travel, is based on it. Muḥammad ibn Saḥnūn and Ismāʿīl al-Qāḍī said: "Shortening is obligatory (farḍ)." Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān held this view, and something similar is transmitted from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. It is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "Whoever prays four [units] while traveling is like one who prays two units while at home." Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that he said: "The prayer of travel is two units, a complete prayer and not a shortened one, upon the tongue of your Prophet (ﷺ), and whoever fabricates has failed." This is supported by the saying of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "The prayer was prescribed as two units in both the settled state and travel. Then the travel prayer was confirmed, and the settled prayer was increased."

The scholars differed over the meaning of His saying: ﴿that you shorten﴾. A group of scholars held that it means shortening from four [units] to two. It is transmitted from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that he said: "A group of merchants asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'We travel in the land, so how should we pray?' Then Allah sent down: ﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame on you for shortening the prayer﴾. Then the speech ended. After a year, the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to fight, and he prayed Ẓuhr. The polytheists said: 'Muḥammad and his companions were within your reach from behind them; why did you not press upon them?' One of them said: 'Surely they have another [prayer] after it.' So Allah sent down between the two prayers: ﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve will harm you﴾, up to the end of the prayer of fear." (The reference is to ṣalāt al-khawf, the prayer of fear, i.e., the prayer performed under threat of attack.)

Al-Ṭabarī, in narrating this view, mentioned the ḥadīth of Yaʿlā ibn Umayya, who said: "I said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿If you fear﴾, and the people are now secure.' He said: 'I wondered at what you wondered at, so I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "It is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity."'" Al-Ṭabarī said: "All of this is a good view, except that His saying: ﴿And when you are among them﴾ indicates that what follows is severed from what precedes it. From the wording of the verse, nothing follows except that shortening is conditioned upon fear."

In the recitation (qirāʾa) of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, it reads: "that you shorten the prayer, that those who disbelieve will harm you," with the omission of "if you fear." But it is established in the codex of ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him.

Another group held that this verse only permits shortening during travel for one who fears the enemy. So whoever is secure has no shortening. It is transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she used to say concerning travel: "Complete your prayer." They said: "Indeed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to shorten." She said: "He was in a war and he was fearful. Are you fearful?" ʿAṭāʾ said: "Among the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ used to complete the prayer, and ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān completed it. But he (ʿUthmān) gave reasons for that other than these. Likewise, she gave a reason for her completing [the prayer] other than this."

(p-8) Others said: "The shortening permitted in this verse is only the shortening of two units to one unit. The two units during travel are a complete prayer, and shortening it means that it becomes one unit." Al-Suddī said: "If you pray two units during travel, it is complete. Shortening is not lawful except in fear. So this verse permits each group to pray one unit, without adding anything to it, and the imam has two units." It is transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Two units during travel are complete, not shortened. Shortening applies only to the prayer of fear: the imam prays with one group one unit, then they go to the place of the others, and the others come to the place of these, and he prays with them one unit. So the imam has two units, and they have one unit each." Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, and Kaʿb, among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), said similarly. Ḥudhayfa did this at Ṭabaristān, when the commander Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ asked him to. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, transmitted that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in this manner at the Battle of Dhū Qarad, one unit with each group, and they did not make up the prayer. Mujāhid said, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Allah prescribed the prayer upon the tongue of your Prophet: four [units] in the settled state, two during travel, and one in fear." Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh transmitted that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in this manner with his companions on the day he fought Khaṣafa and Banī Thaʿlaba. Abū Hurayra transmitted that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in this manner between Ḍajnān and ʿUsfān.

Others said: this verse permits shortening of the limits, form and manner of the prayer at the time of close combat and the outbreak of war. So one in this condition is permitted to pray by gesturing with his head, and to pray one unit wherever he faces, with one takbīr or two takbīrs, according to what preceded of the scholars' explanations of His saying: ﴿But if you fear, then [pray] on foot or riding﴾ [al-Baqara: 239]. Al-Ṭabarī preferred this view, and said that it is parallel to His saying: ﴿And when you are secure, then establish the prayer﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 103], meaning: with its limits and its complete form.

The majority read: "taqṣurū" (you shorten), with a fatḥa on the tāʾ and a ḍamma on the ṣād. Al-Ḍabbī transmitted from his companions: "taqṣirū," with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, a kasra on the ṣād, and a sukūn on the qāf. Al-Zuhrī read: "tuqaṣṣirū," with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, a fatḥa on the qāf, and a kasra on the ṣād with shadda.

"Yaftinakum" (that they harm you): its meaning is "that they test you by attacking you and occupying your souls with your prayer." A similar usage is the saying of the owner of the garden: "Indeed, a trial (fitna) has befallen me in this my property." The root meaning of fitna is testing through hardships, and all its various uses return to this meaning.

"ʿAduww" (enemy) is a descriptive term applying to the singular and the plural. "Mubīn" is of the form mufʿil, from abāna. The meaning: "They have been violent in their enmity toward you, and they have sought from you every aim."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you are among them﴾, the verse. The majority of the community said: the verse is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it encompasses the leaders after him until the Day of Resurrection. Abū Yūsuf and Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya said: "The verse is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), because the prayer led by the Prophet (ﷺ) has no substitute, whereas for other leaders there is a substitute. So the people pray with two imams, one group after another, and nothing else is needed."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Likewise, the majority of scholars hold that the prayer of fear is prayed in the settled state when fear arises." Some people said: "There is no prayer of fear in the settled state." ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn held this view within the school. Al-Ṭabarī said: "﴿Then you led them﴾ means: its limits and its form, without shortening, according to what was permitted earlier in the state of close combat."

His saying: ﴿So let a group of them stand with you﴾ is a command to divide. That is: the rest of them stand facing the enemy, on guard, anticipating his charge.

(p-10) The most established reports and ḥadīths hold that the concession of the prayer of fear was revealed at the Battle of Dhāt al-Riqāʿ, which is the Battle of Muḥārib and Khaṣafa. In some reports, it was revealed in the area of ʿUsfān and Ḍajnān. The enemy was the cavalry of Quraysh, under the command of Khālid ibn al-Walīd. It has been disputed who is meant here by those commanded to take up their weapons. It was said: "It is the praying group." It was said: "Rather, it is the guarding group."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 101–102 (part 2 of 2):

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The wording of the verse covers all of these forms, but the weapons of those praying are those that are light. The reports differ on the manner in which the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the prayer of fear (ṣalāt al-khawf) with his Companions, and the jurists differed accordingly. Yazid ibn Ruman reported, from Salih ibn Khawwat, from Sahl ibn Abi Hathma: "He prayed the prayer of fear with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Dhat al-Riqa'. A group lined up behind him, and another group stood facing the enemy. He prayed one rak'ah with those who were with him, then he remained standing while they completed (their prayer) alone. Then they departed and lined up facing the enemy. The other group came, and he prayed with them the rak'ah that remained of his prayer. Then he remained seated while they completed (their prayer) for themselves. Then he gave the salam with them."

Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad reported from Salih ibn Khawwat, from Sahl, this same ḥadīth exactly, except that he reported: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the last group one rak'ah, he gave the salam. Then they completed their prayer after his salam." Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted this ḥadīth for the prayer of fear. He initially inclined toward the narration of Yazid ibn Ruman, then he returned to the narration of al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr.

Mujahid and others narrated from Ibn 'Ayyash al-Zurqi, whose name is Zayd ibn al-Samit (there is disagreement about this), that: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the prayer of fear at 'Usfan, while the enemy was in his direction of prayer. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) led us in the Dhuhr prayer. The polytheists said: 'They were in a state where, had we caught them unawares, (we would have struck them).' They said: 'Now a prayer is coming upon them that is dearer to them than their children and their selves.' He said: Then Jibril descended between Dhuhr and 'Asr with these verses, and informed him of their plot. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood and arranged the army behind him in two rows. Then he said takbīr, and they all said takbīr. Then he bowed, and we all bowed. Then he raised (his head), and we all raised (our heads). Then the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated with the row that was next to him, while the others stood guarding them. When they had prostrated and stood up, the others prostrated in their places. Then they advanced to the positions of the front (row), and the front (row) withdrew to the positions of the rear (row). Then he bowed, and they all bowed. Then he raised (his head), and they all raised (their heads). Then the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated, and the row next to him prostrated. When he raised (his head), the others prostrated. Then he gave the salam, and they all gave the salam. Then they departed."

'Abd al-Razzaq ibn Hammam said in his Musannaf: al-Thawri narrated from Hisham something similar to this, except that he said: "The front row retreats backward when they raise their heads from prostration, and the others advance and prostrate in the positions of the first (row)."

'Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from Khallad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Mujahid, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not pray the prayer of fear except twice: once at Dhat al-Riqa' from the land of Bani Sulaym, and once at 'Usfan, while the polytheists were at Dajnan, between them and the qiblah."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The apparent difference in the reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) requires that "he prayed the prayer of fear in other than these two places." Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that during the expedition of Dhu Qurad there was a prayer of fear.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar reported that "the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed one rak'ah with one of the two groups, while the other group faced the enemy. Then they departed and stood in the positions of their companions, facing the enemy. Then those (others) came, and the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed one rak'ah with them, then gave the salam. Then these (first) ones completed one rak'ah, and those (others) one rak'ah, at one time." Ashhab (Malik's school) adopted this form for the prayer of fear, and he followed the principle that no one should complete (a prayer) before the Imam's ruling has ceased, so likewise one should not build upon it. Several (scholars) mentioned this from Ashhab, among them Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Ibn Yunus, and others. Al-Lakhmi related from him that his position is that the Imam prays one rak'ah with a group, then they depart facing the enemy, and the other (group) comes, and he prays one rak'ah with them, then gives the salam, and those who are with him stand and complete (their prayer). When they have finished, they go to face the enemy, and the other (group) completes (its prayer). This is a sunnah reported from Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr preferred the view based on what was reported from Ibn 'Umar. It was also reported that Sahl ibn Abi Hathma had narrated from him something exactly like what was narrated from Ibn 'Umar.

Hudhayfa, when he described the Prophet's prayer (ʿalayhi al-ṣalāt wa-al-salām) in fear, reported: "He prayed one rak'ah with each group, and neither group completed anything beyond one rak'ah." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others mentioned from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed two rak'ahs with each group, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had two rak'ahs with each group, so he had four, and each man had two rak'ahs." It was with this (view) that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to issue rulings. It is an opinion permitted by everyone who permits the difference of intention between the Imam and the follower in prayer.

Ashab al-ra'y (the proponents of opinion) said: When it is the Maghrib prayer, the Imam begins the prayer with a group, while another group is facing the enemy. He prays with those who are with him two rak'ahs, then they move to face the enemy, and the other (group) comes and they join the Imam, and he prays one rak'ah with them, then gives the salam alone. Then they stand facing the enemy, and the group that prayed two rak'ahs with the Imam returns to their first position in the prayer, and they complete one rak'ah and two prostrations individually, and give the salam. Then they come to face the enemy, and the other group departs to the place of prayer, and they complete two rak'ahs with recitation individually, and give the salam. Their prayer is complete.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "This is the extension of the view of the proponents of opinion in all other prayers."

"Marwan ibn al-Hakam asked Abu Hurayra: 'Did you pray the prayer of fear with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' Abu Hurayra said: 'Yes.' Marwan said: 'When?' Abu Hurayra said: 'In the year of the expedition of Najd. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood for the 'Asr prayer, and a group stood with him, and another group stood facing the enemy, with their backs to the qiblah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said takbīr, and they all said takbīr: those who were with him and those facing the enemy. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bowed, and those with him bowed with him, and they prostrated likewise. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood, and the group that had been with him moved to face the enemy, and the group that had been facing the enemy came forward, and they bowed and prostrated, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained standing as he was. Then they stood up, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bowed another rak'ah, and they bowed with him, and he prostrated, and they prostrated with him. Then the group that had been facing the enemy came forward and bowed and prostrated, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting. Then came the salam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the salam, and they all gave the salam.'"

Abu Dawud, in his Musannaf, related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, a description of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer of fear that is close to what was reported from Abu Hurayra, and differs from it in some matters. However, its wording contains confusion (tadā') and contradiction, so I have abridged it.

The total of what we have mentioned regarding the prayer of fear, from the statement of Abu Yusuf and Ibn 'Ulayya onward, is eleven opinions, together with the prayer of fear being specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), and ten descriptions, according to the well-known view that it remains valid for the rulers (umarā').

**

His, the Exalted's, statement:

﴿And when they have prostrated, let them be behind you, and let another group who have not prayed come forward and pray with you, and let them take their precaution and their weapons. Those who disbelieve wish that you would be heedless of your weapons and your belongings, so that they might attack you in a single assault. And there is no blame upon you if you lay down your weapons because of rain, or if you are ill; but take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

The pronoun in "sajadū" (﴿سَجَدُوا﴾) refers to the praying group. The meaning is: "When they have prostrated with you the first rak'ah, then let them depart." This is according to one of the reported forms. It was also said that the meaning is: "When they have prostrated the rak'ah of qaḍā' (completion)," and this is according to the form of Sahl ibn Abi Hathma. The pronoun in His statement "fa-la-yakūnū" (﴿فَلْيَكُونُوا﴾) may refer to those who prostrated, or it may refer to the group that first stood facing the enemy. The speech comes as an admonition in a state of caution and war.

al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "falitaqum" (﴿فَلِتَقُمْ﴾) with a kasra on the lām. The majority read "wa-lta'ti ṭā'ifatun" (﴿وَلْتَأْتِ طَائِفَةٌ﴾) with a tā'. Abu Haywa read "wa-l-ya'ti" (﴿وَلْيَأْتِ﴾) with a yā'.

His, the Exalted's, statement "wadda alladhīna kafarū" (﴿وَدَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾), and the rest of the verse, is a report about the belief of the people and a warning against heedlessness, lest the enemy attain their hope.

"Asliḥa" (أَسْلِحَةٌ) is the plural of "silāḥ" (سِلاحٌ). In His statement "mayla wāḥida" (﴿مَيْلَةً وَاحِدَةً﴾), the form is one of intensification, meaning: "utterly destroying, such that no second (attack) would be needed."

His, the Exalted's, statement "wa-lā junāḥa 'alaykum" (﴿وَلا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾), and the rest of the verse, is a concession. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who was ill, so he set down his weapon, and some people reproached him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It seems they had understood the command to take up weapons as obligatory, so Allah, the Exalted, granted a concession in these two states. Every excuse that arises at that time is analogous to these two."

Then Allah strengthened the hearts of the believers with His statement: ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

(p-5) His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame on you for shortening the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve will harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are ever an open enemy to you.﴾ ﴿And when you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group of them stand with you and let them take their weapons.﴾

"Ḍarabtum" (you traveled): its meaning is "you journeyed." The People of the Apparent (Ahl al-Ẓāhir, the literalist school) hold that shortening (qaṣr) applies to every journey that takes one beyond the settled area (al-ḥāḍira), which is the place from which the Friday prayer is established. This is a weak view. The scholars differed over the distance at which the prayer is shortened. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Ibn Rāhawayh said: "The prayer is shortened over four barīd, which is forty-eight miles." Their proof is reports transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Ḥasan and al-Zuhrī said: "The prayer is shortened over a journey of two days," and they did not mention miles. This view is also transmitted from Mālik. Another view transmitted from Mālik is: "The prayer is shortened over a day and a night." These three opinions are close in meaning. It is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn ʿUmar that the prayer is shortened over a full day's journey. Ibn ʿUmar shortened it at thirty miles. From Mālik, in al-ʿUtbiyya, concerning one who went out to his estate at a distance of forty-five miles, he said: "He shortens." From Ibn al-Qāsim, in al-ʿUtbiyya: "If he shortened it at thirty-six [miles], there is no obligation to repeat it." Yaḥyā ibn ʿUmar said: "He must repeat it forever." Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam said: "He must repeat it within its time." Ibn Masʿūd, Sufyān, al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfa and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: "Whoever travels a distance of three [days] shortens." Abū Ḥanīfa said: "Three days and their nights, at the pace of camels and of walking feet." It is transmitted from Anas ibn Mālik that he shortened at fifteen miles. Al-Awzāʿī said: "The majority of scholars hold shortening over a full day's journey, and we adopt this."

The people differed concerning the type of journey over which the prayer is shortened. There is consensus (ijmāʿ) on jihad, Ḥajj, ʿUmra, and what resembles them, such as maintaining the ties of kinship and saving a life. The people differed regarding other journeys. The majority hold that shortening is permitted on a lawful journey, such as trade and the like. It is transmitted (p-6) from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: "The prayer is not shortened except on Ḥajj or jihad." ʿAṭāʾ said: "The prayer is not shortened except on a journey of obedience and one of the paths of goodness." It is transmitted from ʿAṭāʾ that it is shortened on every lawful journey. The majority of scholars hold that there is no shortening on a journey of disobedience, such as that of a rebel, a highwayman, and whatever is similar to them. It is transmitted from al-Awzāʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa that shortening is permitted in all of these cases.

The majority of scholars hold that the traveler does not shorten until he leaves the houses of the village, and at that point he is "one who strikes the land." This is the view of Mālik in al-Mudawwana, and of Ibn Ḥabīb and the community of the school. Ibn al-Qāsim said in al-Mudawwana: "Mālik did not set for us a limit concerning proximity." It is transmitted from Mālik: "If there is a village whose people gather [for prayer], one does not shorten until he passes it by three miles. The same applies on the return. If its people do not gather, he shortens when he passes its orchards." It is transmitted from al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Rabīʿa that he intended a journey, so he prayed two units (rakʿatayn) with them in his dwelling. Among them were al-Aswad ibn Yazīd and more than one of the companions of Ibn Masʿūd. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ and Sulaymān ibn Mūsā said the same. It is transmitted from Mujāhid that he said: "The traveler does not shorten on his first day until night." This is an anomalous (shādh) view. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed Ẓuhr in Madina with four units, and ʿAṣr at Dhū al-Ḥulayfa with two units, and there was not a third of a day between them.

It appears from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿there is no blame on you for shortening﴾, that shortening is permissible, or optional. Ibn Wahb transmitted from Mālik that the traveler has a choice; this was said by al-Abharī, and the foremost scholars of the school hold it. Mālik said in al-Mabsūṭ: "Shortening is a sunna." This is the majority view of the school, and the answer in al-Mudawwana, requiring repetition within the time for one who completed the prayer during travel, is based on it. Muḥammad ibn Saḥnūn and Ismāʿīl al-Qāḍī said: "Shortening is obligatory (farḍ)." Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān held this view, and something similar is transmitted from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. It is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "Whoever prays four [units] while traveling is like one who prays two units while at home." Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that he said: "The prayer of travel is two units, a complete prayer and not a shortened one, upon the tongue of your Prophet (ﷺ), and whoever fabricates has failed." This is supported by the saying of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "The prayer was prescribed as two units in both the settled state and travel. Then the travel prayer was confirmed, and the settled prayer was increased."

The scholars differed over the meaning of His saying: ﴿that you shorten﴾. A group of scholars held that it means shortening from four [units] to two. It is transmitted from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that he said: "A group of merchants asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'We travel in the land, so how should we pray?' Then Allah sent down: ﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame on you for shortening the prayer﴾. Then the speech ended. After a year, the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to fight, and he prayed Ẓuhr. The polytheists said: 'Muḥammad and his companions were within your reach from behind them; why did you not press upon them?' One of them said: 'Surely they have another [prayer] after it.' So Allah sent down between the two prayers: ﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve will harm you﴾, up to the end of the prayer of fear." (The reference is to ṣalāt al-khawf, the prayer of fear, i.e., the prayer performed under threat of attack.)

Al-Ṭabarī, in narrating this view, mentioned the ḥadīth of Yaʿlā ibn Umayya, who said: "I said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿If you fear﴾, and the people are now secure.' He said: 'I wondered at what you wondered at, so I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "It is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity."'" Al-Ṭabarī said: "All of this is a good view, except that His saying: ﴿And when you are among them﴾ indicates that what follows is severed from what precedes it. From the wording of the verse, nothing follows except that shortening is conditioned upon fear."

In the recitation (qirāʾa) of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, it reads: "that you shorten the prayer, that those who disbelieve will harm you," with the omission of "if you fear." But it is established in the codex of ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him.

Another group held that this verse only permits shortening during travel for one who fears the enemy. So whoever is secure has no shortening. It is transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she used to say concerning travel: "Complete your prayer." They said: "Indeed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to shorten." She said: "He was in a war and he was fearful. Are you fearful?" ʿAṭāʾ said: "Among the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ used to complete the prayer, and ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān completed it. But he (ʿUthmān) gave reasons for that other than these. Likewise, she gave a reason for her completing [the prayer] other than this."

(p-8) Others said: "The shortening permitted in this verse is only the shortening of two units to one unit. The two units during travel are a complete prayer, and shortening it means that it becomes one unit." Al-Suddī said: "If you pray two units during travel, it is complete. Shortening is not lawful except in fear. So this verse permits each group to pray one unit, without adding anything to it, and the imam has two units." It is transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Two units during travel are complete, not shortened. Shortening applies only to the prayer of fear: the imam prays with one group one unit, then they go to the place of the others, and the others come to the place of these, and he prays with them one unit. So the imam has two units, and they have one unit each." Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, and Kaʿb, among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), said similarly. Ḥudhayfa did this at Ṭabaristān, when the commander Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ asked him to. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, transmitted that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in this manner at the Battle of Dhū Qarad, one unit with each group, and they did not make up the prayer. Mujāhid said, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Allah prescribed the prayer upon the tongue of your Prophet: four [units] in the settled state, two during travel, and one in fear." Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh transmitted that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in this manner with his companions on the day he fought Khaṣafa and Banī Thaʿlaba. Abū Hurayra transmitted that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in this manner between Ḍajnān and ʿUsfān.

Others said: this verse permits shortening of the limits, form and manner of the prayer at the time of close combat and the outbreak of war. So one in this condition is permitted to pray by gesturing with his head, and to pray one unit wherever he faces, with one takbīr or two takbīrs, according to what preceded of the scholars' explanations of His saying: ﴿But if you fear, then [pray] on foot or riding﴾ [al-Baqara: 239]. Al-Ṭabarī preferred this view, and said that it is parallel to His saying: ﴿And when you are secure, then establish the prayer﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 103], meaning: with its limits and its complete form.

The majority read: "taqṣurū" (you shorten), with a fatḥa on the tāʾ and a ḍamma on the ṣād. Al-Ḍabbī transmitted from his companions: "taqṣirū," with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, a kasra on the ṣād, and a sukūn on the qāf. Al-Zuhrī read: "tuqaṣṣirū," with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, a fatḥa on the qāf, and a kasra on the ṣād with shadda.

"Yaftinakum" (that they harm you): its meaning is "that they test you by attacking you and occupying your souls with your prayer." A similar usage is the saying of the owner of the garden: "Indeed, a trial (fitna) has befallen me in this my property." The root meaning of fitna is testing through hardships, and all its various uses return to this meaning.

"ʿAduww" (enemy) is a descriptive term applying to the singular and the plural. "Mubīn" is of the form mufʿil, from abāna. The meaning: "They have been violent in their enmity toward you, and they have sought from you every aim."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you are among them﴾, the verse. The majority of the community said: the verse is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it encompasses the leaders after him until the Day of Resurrection. Abū Yūsuf and Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya said: "The verse is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), because the prayer led by the Prophet (ﷺ) has no substitute, whereas for other leaders there is a substitute. So the people pray with two imams, one group after another, and nothing else is needed."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Likewise, the majority of scholars hold that the prayer of fear is prayed in the settled state when fear arises." Some people said: "There is no prayer of fear in the settled state." ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn held this view within the school. Al-Ṭabarī said: "﴿Then you led them﴾ means: its limits and its form, without shortening, according to what was permitted earlier in the state of close combat."

His saying: ﴿So let a group of them stand with you﴾ is a command to divide. That is: the rest of them stand facing the enemy, on guard, anticipating his charge.

(p-10) The most established reports and ḥadīths hold that the concession of the prayer of fear was revealed at the Battle of Dhāt al-Riqāʿ, which is the Battle of Muḥārib and Khaṣafa. In some reports, it was revealed in the area of ʿUsfān and Ḍajnān. The enemy was the cavalry of Quraysh, under the command of Khālid ibn al-Walīd. It has been disputed who is meant here by those commanded to take up their weapons. It was said: "It is the praying group." It was said: "Rather, it is the guarding group."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 101–102 (part 2 of 2):

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The wording of the verse covers all of these forms, but the weapons of those praying are those that are light. The reports differ on the manner in which the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the prayer of fear (ṣalāt al-khawf) with his Companions, and the jurists differed accordingly. Yazid ibn Ruman reported, from Salih ibn Khawwat, from Sahl ibn Abi Hathma: "He prayed the prayer of fear with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Dhat al-Riqa'. A group lined up behind him, and another group stood facing the enemy. He prayed one rak'ah with those who were with him, then he remained standing while they completed (their prayer) alone. Then they departed and lined up facing the enemy. The other group came, and he prayed with them the rak'ah that remained of his prayer. Then he remained seated while they completed (their prayer) for themselves. Then he gave the salam with them."

Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad reported from Salih ibn Khawwat, from Sahl, this same ḥadīth exactly, except that he reported: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the last group one rak'ah, he gave the salam. Then they completed their prayer after his salam." Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted this ḥadīth for the prayer of fear. He initially inclined toward the narration of Yazid ibn Ruman, then he returned to the narration of al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr.

Mujahid and others narrated from Ibn 'Ayyash al-Zurqi, whose name is Zayd ibn al-Samit (there is disagreement about this), that: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the prayer of fear at 'Usfan, while the enemy was in his direction of prayer. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) led us in the Dhuhr prayer. The polytheists said: 'They were in a state where, had we caught them unawares, (we would have struck them).' They said: 'Now a prayer is coming upon them that is dearer to them than their children and their selves.' He said: Then Jibril descended between Dhuhr and 'Asr with these verses, and informed him of their plot. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood and arranged the army behind him in two rows. Then he said takbīr, and they all said takbīr. Then he bowed, and we all bowed. Then he raised (his head), and we all raised (our heads). Then the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated with the row that was next to him, while the others stood guarding them. When they had prostrated and stood up, the others prostrated in their places. Then they advanced to the positions of the front (row), and the front (row) withdrew to the positions of the rear (row). Then he bowed, and they all bowed. Then he raised (his head), and they all raised (their heads). Then the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated, and the row next to him prostrated. When he raised (his head), the others prostrated. Then he gave the salam, and they all gave the salam. Then they departed."

'Abd al-Razzaq ibn Hammam said in his Musannaf: al-Thawri narrated from Hisham something similar to this, except that he said: "The front row retreats backward when they raise their heads from prostration, and the others advance and prostrate in the positions of the first (row)."

'Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from Khallad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Mujahid, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not pray the prayer of fear except twice: once at Dhat al-Riqa' from the land of Bani Sulaym, and once at 'Usfan, while the polytheists were at Dajnan, between them and the qiblah."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The apparent difference in the reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) requires that "he prayed the prayer of fear in other than these two places." Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that during the expedition of Dhu Qurad there was a prayer of fear.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar reported that "the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed one rak'ah with one of the two groups, while the other group faced the enemy. Then they departed and stood in the positions of their companions, facing the enemy. Then those (others) came, and the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed one rak'ah with them, then gave the salam. Then these (first) ones completed one rak'ah, and those (others) one rak'ah, at one time." Ashhab (Malik's school) adopted this form for the prayer of fear, and he followed the principle that no one should complete (a prayer) before the Imam's ruling has ceased, so likewise one should not build upon it. Several (scholars) mentioned this from Ashhab, among them Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Ibn Yunus, and others. Al-Lakhmi related from him that his position is that the Imam prays one rak'ah with a group, then they depart facing the enemy, and the other (group) comes, and he prays one rak'ah with them, then gives the salam, and those who are with him stand and complete (their prayer). When they have finished, they go to face the enemy, and the other (group) completes (its prayer). This is a sunnah reported from Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr preferred the view based on what was reported from Ibn 'Umar. It was also reported that Sahl ibn Abi Hathma had narrated from him something exactly like what was narrated from Ibn 'Umar.

Hudhayfa, when he described the Prophet's prayer (ʿalayhi al-ṣalāt wa-al-salām) in fear, reported: "He prayed one rak'ah with each group, and neither group completed anything beyond one rak'ah." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others mentioned from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed two rak'ahs with each group, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had two rak'ahs with each group, so he had four, and each man had two rak'ahs." It was with this (view) that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to issue rulings. It is an opinion permitted by everyone who permits the difference of intention between the Imam and the follower in prayer.

Ashab al-ra'y (the proponents of opinion) said: When it is the Maghrib prayer, the Imam begins the prayer with a group, while another group is facing the enemy. He prays with those who are with him two rak'ahs, then they move to face the enemy, and the other (group) comes and they join the Imam, and he prays one rak'ah with them, then gives the salam alone. Then they stand facing the enemy, and the group that prayed two rak'ahs with the Imam returns to their first position in the prayer, and they complete one rak'ah and two prostrations individually, and give the salam. Then they come to face the enemy, and the other group departs to the place of prayer, and they complete two rak'ahs with recitation individually, and give the salam. Their prayer is complete.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "This is the extension of the view of the proponents of opinion in all other prayers."

"Marwan ibn al-Hakam asked Abu Hurayra: 'Did you pray the prayer of fear with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' Abu Hurayra said: 'Yes.' Marwan said: 'When?' Abu Hurayra said: 'In the year of the expedition of Najd. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood for the 'Asr prayer, and a group stood with him, and another group stood facing the enemy, with their backs to the qiblah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said takbīr, and they all said takbīr: those who were with him and those facing the enemy. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bowed, and those with him bowed with him, and they prostrated likewise. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood, and the group that had been with him moved to face the enemy, and the group that had been facing the enemy came forward, and they bowed and prostrated, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained standing as he was. Then they stood up, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bowed another rak'ah, and they bowed with him, and he prostrated, and they prostrated with him. Then the group that had been facing the enemy came forward and bowed and prostrated, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting. Then came the salam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the salam, and they all gave the salam.'"

Abu Dawud, in his Musannaf, related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, a description of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer of fear that is close to what was reported from Abu Hurayra, and differs from it in some matters. However, its wording contains confusion (tadā') and contradiction, so I have abridged it.

The total of what we have mentioned regarding the prayer of fear, from the statement of Abu Yusuf and Ibn 'Ulayya onward, is eleven opinions, together with the prayer of fear being specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), and ten descriptions, according to the well-known view that it remains valid for the rulers (umarā').

**

His, the Exalted's, statement:

﴿And when they have prostrated, let them be behind you, and let another group who have not prayed come forward and pray with you, and let them take their precaution and their weapons. Those who disbelieve wish that you would be heedless of your weapons and your belongings, so that they might attack you in a single assault. And there is no blame upon you if you lay down your weapons because of rain, or if you are ill; but take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

The pronoun in "sajadū" (﴿سَجَدُوا﴾) refers to the praying group. The meaning is: "When they have prostrated with you the first rak'ah, then let them depart." This is according to one of the reported forms. It was also said that the meaning is: "When they have prostrated the rak'ah of qaḍā' (completion)," and this is according to the form of Sahl ibn Abi Hathma. The pronoun in His statement "fa-la-yakūnū" (﴿فَلْيَكُونُوا﴾) may refer to those who prostrated, or it may refer to the group that first stood facing the enemy. The speech comes as an admonition in a state of caution and war.

al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "falitaqum" (﴿فَلِتَقُمْ﴾) with a kasra on the lām. The majority read "wa-lta'ti ṭā'ifatun" (﴿وَلْتَأْتِ طَائِفَةٌ﴾) with a tā'. Abu Haywa read "wa-l-ya'ti" (﴿وَلْيَأْتِ﴾) with a yā'.

His, the Exalted's, statement "wadda alladhīna kafarū" (﴿وَدَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾), and the rest of the verse, is a report about the belief of the people and a warning against heedlessness, lest the enemy attain their hope.

"Asliḥa" (أَسْلِحَةٌ) is the plural of "silāḥ" (سِلاحٌ). In His statement "mayla wāḥida" (﴿مَيْلَةً وَاحِدَةً﴾), the form is one of intensification, meaning: "utterly destroying, such that no second (attack) would be needed."

His, the Exalted's, statement "wa-lā junāḥa 'alaykum" (﴿وَلا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾), and the rest of the verse, is a concession. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who was ill, so he set down his weapon, and some people reproached him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It seems they had understood the command to take up weapons as obligatory, so Allah, the Exalted, granted a concession in these two states. Every excuse that arises at that time is analogous to these two."

Then Allah strengthened the hearts of the believers with His statement: ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 103–104:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides. And when you are secure, establish the prayer. Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times.﴾ ﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the enemy. If you are suffering, indeed they are suffering as you are suffering, but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

The majority of scholars (jumhur al-'ulama') held that this remembrance commanded here is only after the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf), in the same manner as they were commanded, at the completion of the rites (manasik), to remember Allah. Thus it is remembrance by the tongue.

Others held that ﴿"qadaytum"﴾ means "fa'altum" (you performed), i.e., when you engage in the prayer, let it be in these postures, according to what necessity requires: illness and other things. Based on this verse, Ibn al-Mawwaz ordered the prayer of the sick, saying: "He prays sitting; if he cannot, then on his right side; if he cannot, then on his left side; if he cannot, then on his back." The position of Malik in al-Mudawwana is that of choice (al-takhyir), for he said: "on his side, or on his back." Ibn Habib related from Ibn al-Qasim that he said: "He begins with the back, then with the side." Ibn Habib said: "This is a mistake (wahm)." Al-Lakhmi said: "It is not a mistake; rather it is more prudent regarding facing the qibla." Sahnun said: "He prays on his right side, as he is placed in his grave; if he cannot, then on his back."

The "tuma'nina" (security/tranquility) in the verse means "the calming of the soul from fear." Some of those who interpreted said the meaning is: "When you return from your journey to home, then establish them complete, four [rak'ahs]."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿decreed at specified times﴾ means: "divided into portions at times; this is the apparent sense of the wording." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: "an obligation that is obligatory (fard mafrud); these are two words with one meaning, repeated for emphasis."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the enemy﴾ shows that the "completion" referred to earlier is only the completion of the prayer of fear. The word ﴿"tahinu"﴾ means: become soft and become weak. "Habl wahin" means a weak rope, and from it: ﴿"wahana al-'azm"﴾ [Maryam: 4]. And ﴿"ibtighda' al-qawm"﴾ means their seeking (talab).

'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj read "an takunu" with a fatha on the alif. Yahya ibn Wthab and Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir read "tha'lamuna" [i.e., "ta'lamuna" variant with "ti'lamuna" pattern] in all three occurrences; it is a dialect (lugha). This is encouragement for the souls of the believers and belittling of the matter of the disbelievers. Of this same meaning is the saying of the poet:

"The people are like you: they have hair on the head that is not spread out [in life] if they are slain."

Then the encouragement is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for﴾. This is a clear proof, by which the souls of the believers should be strengthened. The rest of the verse is clear.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 105–107**

His statement, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between the people by that which Allah has shown you. And do not be an advocate for the treacherous.﴾ ﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who deceive themselves. Indeed, Allah does not like one who is a habitual betrayer and sinful.﴾

In this verse there is an honouring of the Prophet (ﷺ), an entrusting to him (of judgement), and also a correction of him regarding the right course in judging, and a reproof for his acceptance, with haste, of what was brought to him concerning the affair of the Banu Ubayriq.

(p-16) His statement, exalted is He: ﴿by that which Allah has shown you﴾ means: in accordance with the laws of the Shari'a (sharʿ), either by revelation and explicit text, or by reasoning that proceeds along the paths of revelation. Allah, exalted is He, has guaranteed His prophets infallibility (ʿiṣma). His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾ and ﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Its occasion (sabab), by consensus of the commentators (al-mutaʾawwilin), was the affair of the Banu Ubayriq. They were brothers: Bishr, Bashir and Mubashshir. Bashir was a hypocrite (munafiq) who would satirise the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and attribute poetry to others. The Muslims would say: "By Allah, it is nothing but the poetry of the wicked one." So he composed a poem disclaiming it, among which is his saying:

Will every time men compose a poem, it is attributed to others, and they say: "Ibn al-Ubayriq composed it"?

Qatada ibn al-Nu'man said: "The Banu Ubayriq were a people of poverty. My paternal uncle Rifa'a ibn Zayd bought a load of dried Syrian dates (dawmak); he placed it in a storeroom (mashraba) of his, and in the storeroom were two of his coats of mail and two swords. A thief attacked the storeroom during the night; it was breached and the food and weapons were taken. When morning came, my uncle Rifa'a came to me and said: 'O nephew, you know that we were attacked last night; our storeroom was breached, and our food and weapons were taken.' He said: 'We searched the house and asked, and we were told: We saw the Banu Ubayriq light a fire this night, and we think it is only from some of your food.' He said: The Banu Ubayriq had said, while we were asking: 'By Allah, we do not think your companion is anyone but Labid ibn Sahl, a man from among us who has piety and Islam.' Labid heard that, drew his sword, then came to the Banu Ubayriq and said: 'By Allah, this sword will certainly reach you, or you will make this theft clear!' They said: 'Away from us, O man! By Allah, you are not our companion.' We searched the house until we had no doubt that they were its perpetrators. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 108–110:

(p-19) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿They hide themselves from the people, but they cannot hide themselves from Allah, for He is with them when they spend the night in planning speech that He does not approve. And Allah is ever encompassing of what they do.﴾ ﴿Here you are, arguing on their behalf in the life of this world, but who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian?﴾ ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness from Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The pronoun in ﴿"yastakhfoona" (they hide themselves)﴾ refers to the category of those who commit sins while concealing that from people, deceiving them. Included within this generality, and falling under these categories, are: the people of treachery in the incident mentioned; those who partisanly defend them; and those who scheme to deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and confuse him. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the people of this incident specifically, and every person who acts similarly falls under the meaning of this reproach.

The meaning of ﴿"wa huwa ma'ahum" (while He is with them)﴾ is by encompassing, knowledge, and power. "Yubayyitoona" means they plan at night. The expression is applied to every concealment of this kind, since the night is the setting for hiding and concealment. Al-Tabari said: "Some of the Ta'i claimed that tabyit in their language means substitution (tabdil), and he recited for al-Aswad ibn 'Amir ibn Huwayn al-Ta'i:

﴾ And you substituted my speech in the presence of the king; may Allah fight you, you ungrateful servant. ﴿

Abu Zayd said: "Yubayyitoona" means they arrange (yu'allifoon). It is also possible that the word is derived from "al-bayt" (the house), meaning they conceal themselves in their planning behind walls."

As for His saying, ﴿"Ha antum ha'ulaa'" (Here you are)﴾: the modes of its recitation have already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran. The address in this verse is to the people who partisanly defend the doubtful and the sinners, and within this generality fall the people of the incident. It is also possible that the address is to the partisans in this specific incident, and this is the more apparent in my view, given the emphasis by ﴿"ha'ulaa'" (these)﴾, which indicates present persons. The grammatical analysis of such a verse has already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-mujadalah (argument) is defense by speech, and it involves twisting and turning words, since al-jadal means twisting.

(p-20) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"Fa-man yujadilu Allaha 'anhum yawma al-qiyamah" (who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection)﴾: this is a pure threat. That is, Allah knows the reality of the matter, so it cannot be obscured from Him by argument or anything else, as you did with the Prophet (ﷺ), for he is a human who judges according to what he hears.

When this threat became firmly established, and the intellects judged that there is no one who can argue against Allah, nor any guardian who will manage the affairs of the disobedient in His presence, He followed this with a great hope and a broad opening through His saying: ﴿"And whoever does evil"﴾ and the verse. His saying ﴿"or wrongs himself"﴾ is a variation of the doing of evil; both have one meaning, repeated with different wording for emphasis. Seeking forgiveness from Allah, together with genuine resolve in that, is repentance.

His saying ﴿"yajid Allah" (will find Allah)﴾ is a metaphor: since mercy and forgiveness are prepared for those who seek forgiveness and repent, they are like those who find a sought-after thing; it is as if repentance is an arrival at the mercy of Allah and a drawing near to Allah. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said one day in his assembly: "When one of the Children of Israel committed a sin, he would wake up to find the expiation of that sin written at his door. And if urine struck any of his clothes, he would cut it off with scissors." A man from the people said: "Allah has indeed given the Children of Israel good." 'Abdullah said: "What Allah has given you is better than what He gave them: He made water purifying for you, and He said: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ and the verse." This is a verse of promise conditioned by Allah's will, according to what the creed of the People of the Sunnah requires. Allah's grace is hoped for, and He is the One sought for help.

And Allah is ever encompassing of what they do.﴾ ﴿Here you are, arguing on their behalf in the life of this world, but who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian?﴾ ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness from Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The pronoun in ﴿"yastakhfoona" (they hide themselves)﴾ refers to the category of those who commit sins while concealing that from people, deceiving them. Included within this generality, and falling under these categories, are: the people of treachery in the incident mentioned; those who partisanly defend them; and those who scheme to deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and confuse him. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the people of this incident specifically, and every person who acts similarly falls under the meaning of this reproach.

The meaning of ﴿"wa huwa ma'ahum" (while He is with them)﴾ is by encompassing, knowledge, and power. "Yubayyitoona" means they plan at night. The expression is applied to every concealment of this kind, since the night is the setting for hiding and concealment. Al-Tabari said: "Some of the Ta'i claimed that tabyit in their language means substitution (tabdil), and he recited for al-Aswad ibn 'Amir ibn Huwayn al-Ta'i:

﴾ And you substituted my speech in the presence of the king; may Allah fight you, you ungrateful servant. ﴿

Abu Zayd said: "Yubayyitoona" means they arrange (yu'allifoon). It is also possible that the word is derived from "al-bayt" (the house), meaning they conceal themselves in their planning behind walls."

As for His saying, ﴿"Ha antum ha'ulaa'" (Here you are)﴾: the modes of its recitation have already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran. The address in this verse is to the people who partisanly defend the doubtful and the sinners, and within this generality fall the people of the incident. It is also possible that the address is to the partisans in this specific incident, and this is the more apparent in my view, given the emphasis by ﴿"ha'ulaa'" (these)﴾, which indicates present persons. The grammatical analysis of such a verse has already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-mujadalah (argument) is defense by speech, and it involves twisting and turning words, since al-jadal means twisting.

(p-20) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"Fa-man yujadilu Allaha 'anhum yawma al-qiyamah" (who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection)﴾: this is a pure threat. That is, Allah knows the reality of the matter, so it cannot be obscured from Him by argument or anything else, as you did with the Prophet (ﷺ), for he is a human who judges according to what he hears.

When this threat became firmly established, and the intellects judged that there is no one who can argue against Allah, nor any guardian who will manage the affairs of the disobedient in His presence, He followed this with a great hope and a broad opening through His saying: ﴿"And whoever does evil"﴾ and the verse. His saying ﴿"or wrongs himself"﴾ is a variation of the doing of evil; both have one meaning, repeated with different wording for emphasis. Seeking forgiveness from Allah, together with genuine resolve in that, is repentance.

His saying ﴿"yajid Allah" (will find Allah)﴾ is a metaphor: since mercy and forgiveness are prepared for those who seek forgiveness and repent, they are like those who find a sought-after thing; it is as if repentance is an arrival at the mercy of Allah and a drawing near to Allah. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said one day in his assembly: "When one of the Children of Israel committed a sin, he would wake up to find the expiation of that sin written at his door. And if urine struck any of his clothes, he would cut it off with scissors." A man from the people said: "Allah has indeed given the Children of Israel good." 'Abdullah said: "What Allah has given you is better than what He gave them: He made water purifying for you, and He said: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ and the verse." This is a verse of promise conditioned by Allah's will, according to what the creed of the People of the Sunnah requires. Allah's grace is hoped for, and He is the One sought for help.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 111–113:**

(p-21) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And whoever earns an error or a sin and then throws it onto an innocent person has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin.﴾ ﴿And if not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, a faction of them would have resolved to mislead you. But they do not mislead except themselves, and they cannot harm you at all. And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom and taught you what you did not know. And the grace of Allah upon you has been magnificent.﴾

The meaning of kasb (earning) has already been discussed. Ithm (sin) is the judgment that attaches to disobedience (ma'siyah) and the attribution of punishment to a person because of it. His saying, ﴿he earns it only against himself﴾, means: it is only to himself that he brings ruin, and by it he brings upon himself what is hated.

As for His saying, ﴿an error or a sin﴾, some people held that the two are words with one meaning, repeated for the variation of wording. Al-Tabari said: "He only distinguished between khati'ah (error) and ithm (sin) because khati'ah may occur intentionally or unintentionally, whereas ithm occurs only intentionally." The wording of this verse is general, and within that generality fall the people of the mentioned incident who are rebuked for it. The innocent one of the incident has been said to be Labid ibn Sahl; it has been said to be Zayd ibn al-Samin the Jew; and it has been said to be Abu Mulayl al-Ansari. His saying, ﴿has certainly borne﴾, is a metaphor, since sins are a burden and a load, so they are like things carried. And ﴿"buhtanan"﴾ means: a lie against the innocent. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you say about your brother what he dislikes to hear, you have backbitten him; and if you say what is not in him, you have slandered him." So throwing an innocent person with an accusation is slander against him, and the error or sin itself is a manifest sin; the one who throws it commits two disobediences.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, made His Prophet aware of this, and of His protection of him, and that it was by a grace from Allah and His mercy.

His saying, ﴿lahammat﴾, means: it would have made it their concern and occupation, until they carried it out. This indicates that the wording is general beyond the people of the incident; otherwise, the partisans of the Banu Ubayriq had already resolved and it was established. Rather, the meaning is: "And if not for Allah's protection of you, there would have been among the people those who occupy themselves with misleading you and make it the concern of their own selves"; that is, as these people did. But protection nullifies the scheming of all of them, so misguidance remains within their own domain.

(p-22) Then Allah's promise to him was affirmed, that they will not harm him in any way; and He confirmed His blessings upon him: the sending down of the recited Book, and the wisdom, part of which was addressed to him and part of which was made his natural disposition that he possessed, and an innate gift from which he acts and by which he judges among people, not speaking from desire. By these two He taught him what he did not know. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 114–116:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or reconciliation between people. And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward.﴾ ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him, and follows other than the way of the believers, We will leave him in what he has turned to, and cast him into Hell, and evil is it as a destination.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly strayed far astray.﴾

The pronoun in ﴿"their secret talk"﴾ refers to people in general. These verses are of general application, and within their generality fall the people of the occasion (of revelation). This is from the eloquence and conciseness that encompasses the past and the future in a single expression.

Al-najwa (secret talk): it is a verbal noun meaning confidential speech, and it may also be used to refer to a group, as one says, "a people of justice and contentment" (qawm 'adl wa ridan). In this verse the word may be understood as a group, or as the verbal noun itself. If we take it as a group, the exception is continuous (muttasil), as if he said: "There is no good in much of their groups that confide privately, except for those who..." If we take the word as the verbal noun itself, then it is as if he said: "There is no good in much of their private conversations," and the exception is discontinuous (munqati') by the wording, though its continuity may be assumed by deleting a modifier, as if he said: "except the secret talk of those who..." Some exegetes said: "al-najwa is the speech of a group in private, whether it is secret or openly spoken."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"The privacy of a group is a form of secrecy, and the intended meaning is that secret talk is not confined to whispering in the ear and the like."

(p-23) And "al-ma'ruf" (what is right): it is a term that encompasses charity and reconciliation, but these two were singled out for mention out of concern for them, since they have great benefit for the welfare of people. Then Allah, exalted is He, promised a great reward for doing these good deeds with an intention and purpose seeking the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He.

"Ibtigha'" (seeking) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read "fa-sawfa nu'tihi" with the nun; Abu 'Amr and Hamza read "yu'tihi" with the ya'; both readings are good.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾ — the verse is a general expression, though it was revealed concerning Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, because he apostatized and went off to Mecca. The censure against him is included within this general expression that applies to whoever has these attributes until the Day of Resurrection. His saying: ﴿"We will leave him in what he has turned to"﴾ is a threat that he will be left with his corrupt choice in turning to the false deity (taghut). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yuwallihi" and "yusnihi" with the ya' in both.

Then Allah, exalted is He, affirmed that He does not forgive that He be associated with; the explanation of this verse and what is connected to it of creed has already passed. The remoteness in the description of straying necessitates the remoteness of returning to the clear path, and its difficulty, though it remains not impossible.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 117–118:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿They invoke, apart from Him, none but females; and they invoke none but a rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿Allah has cursed him, and he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion."﴾

The pronoun in ﴿"yad'ūna" (they invoke)﴾ refers to the disbelievers mentioned earlier, in His saying: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾ [an-Nisa': 115]. The ﴿"in"﴾ is negating, with the meaning of (mā). The ﴿"yad'ūna"﴾ is a concise and comprehensive expression meaning "they worship" and "they take gods." Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi recited ﴿"in tad'ūna"﴾ with a tā'. Abu Malik, as-Suddi, and others said: "This is because the Arabs used to name their idols with feminine names, such as al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat, and Na'ilah."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "This is refuted by the fact that they were also named with many masculine names."

ad-Dahhak and others said: "The intended meaning is what the Arabs believed regarding the femininity of the angels and their worship of them, so this was said to them as a means of establishing the proof against their corrupt saying."

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatadah said: "The intended meaning is wood and stones, which are feminine and do not reason; so He speaks of them as one speaks of feminine things, and His saying ﴿"illa ināthan" (none but females)﴾ comes as an expression for inanimate objects."

It was also said: "This is only because the Arabs used to call an idol 'a female,' so they would say: 'the female of the children of so-and-so.'"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "This, despite its differences, implies their being reproached with femininity, and that femininity is a deficiency and baseness in comparison with masculinity."

It was also said: "The meaning of ﴿"ināthan"﴾ is ﴿"awthānan" (idols)﴾." In the Mushaf of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, it reads: ﴿"in yad'ūna min dūnihi illā awthānan"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, as narrated from him by Abu Salih, recited: ﴿"illā anathan"﴾, meaning ﴿"wathanan"﴾, so he replaced the hamzah with a waw. It is a plural of a plural, according to what some people have related: as if he made ﴿"wathan"﴾ into ﴿"withān"﴾ on the pattern of ﴿"jamal"﴾ and ﴿"jimāl"﴾, then made ﴿"withān"﴾ into ﴿"wuthun"﴾ on the pattern of ﴿"rihān"﴾ and ﴿"ruhun"﴾, and like ﴿"mithāl"﴾ and ﴿"muthul"﴾.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "This is an error, because ﴿"fi'āl"﴾ in the plural of ﴿"fa'al"﴾ is for multiplicity, and a plural that expresses multiplicity is not pluralized again; only the plurals of paucity are pluralized. The correct view is that you say: ﴿"wuthun"﴾ is the plural of ﴿"wathan"﴾ directly, without an intermediary, like ﴿"usud"﴾ and ﴿"asad"﴾."

Abu 'Amr said: "Ibn 'Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Muslim ibn Jundub, and 'Ata' also recited it thus." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited ﴿"illā wathanan"﴾ with a fatha on the waw and the tha', as a singular noun of genus. Ibn 'Abbas also recited ﴿"wuthunan"﴾ with a damma on the waw and the tha'. A group recited ﴿"illā wathnan"﴾, and a group recited ﴿"illā athnan"﴾ with a sukun on the tha'. [The Prophet (ﷺ) recited ﴿"illā unuthan"﴾, with the nun placed before the tha'.] It is the plural of ﴿"anīth"﴾, like ﴿"ghadir"﴾ and ﴿"ghudur"﴾ and the like. Al-Tabari related that it is the plural of ﴿"inath"﴾, like ﴿"thimar"﴾ and ﴿"thumur"﴾. Abu 'Amr ad-Dani related this recitation from the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "It was also recited by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Haywah, and al-Hasan."

There is disagreement about who is meant by "the devil." One group said: "It is the devil attached to every idol, so it is singular in wording but plural in meaning, since the singular denotes the genus." The majority said: "The intended one is Iblis."
