**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 119–122**

His saying (Exalted is He):

﴿And I will surely mislead them, and I will surely arouse in them false hopes, and I will surely command them so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will surely command them so they will alter the creation of Allah." And whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss.﴾ ﴿He promises them and arouses in them false hopes, but Satan promises them nothing except delusion.﴾ ﴿Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will find no escape from it.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds—We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾

His saying: ﴿"And I will surely mislead them"﴾ means: I will turn them away from the path of guidance. ﴿"And I will surely arouse in them false hopes"﴾ means: I will surely beautify (falsehood) for them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is not restricted to one type of false hope, because each person is aroused by false hopes according to his own disposition and the circumstances of his state. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed, Satan says to one who rides (an animal) and does not mention Allah: 'Sing!' If he does not do well (at singing), he says to him: 'Wish!'" All the particles of oath (lam) in this verse are for emphasis of an oath.

*Al-batk* (بتك) means cutting. The verb is intensified (*kaththara*) because the cutting is frequent, in various manners. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, referred by it to the *baḥīra* (a she-camel whose ear was slit), the *sā'iba* (a freed animal), and the like, of which they used to establish a ruling by reason of their gods, and by other than that. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' read ﴿*wa-la-āmurannahum*﴾ without an *alif*. Ubayy read: ﴿*wa-undillu-hum wa-umanniyihim wa-āmuruhum*﴾.

The meaning of "altering the creation of Allah" has been disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibrahim, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, and others said: it means they alter the religion of Allah. They argued for this with His saying: ﴿The nature of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no alteration of the creation of Allah﴾ (Rum 30:30), meaning the religion of Allah. Alteration (*tabdīl*) falls in the place of change (*taghyīr*), although change is more general than it. A group said: "The alteration of Allah's creation is that Allah, exalted is He, created the sun, the day, the stones, and other created things so that they would be taken as lessons and benefited from, and the disbelievers altered them by making them deities worshipped." Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Anas, 'Ikrima, and Abu Salih: "Among the alteration of Allah's creation is castration. The verse refers to the castration of animals and what resembles it; these are, according to them, prohibited things." A group permitted the castration of animals when the benefit is intended, whether for fattening or other purpose. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz restricted it to horses. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan said: it refers to tattooing and what is similar to it of adornment for beauty. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, cursed the women who tattoo and those who are tattooed, those who pluck (facial hair), those who file the teeth for beauty, those who change the creation of Allah." From this is also his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "May Allah curse the woman who joins hair (with false hair) and the one who asks for it to be joined."

The foundation for interpreting this verse is that every harmful alteration is included in the verse, and every beneficial alteration is permissible.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the rebellion of Satan and what he threatened of spreading his deception, He, blessed and exalted is He, warned His servants against him by stipulating for whoever takes him as a protector the reward of loss. The conception of loss is only that this one who takes him has taken Satan's share, so it is as if he was given Allah's share in it and left it for his sake.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"He promises them and arouses in them false hopes"﴾ means He promises them with his falsehoods: of wealth, of standing, that there is no resurrection and no punishment, and the like; for each person, what suits his state. He arouses in them likewise. Then Allah, exalted is He, began the report about the reality of that with His saying: ﴿"but Satan promises them nothing except delusion."﴾

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about the destiny of those who take Satan as a protector, and threatened them that their refuge is Hell, and they cannot repel it by any trick, nor turn away from it, nor deviate, nor evade. *Al-maḥīṣ* (محيص) is a noun of place from *ḥāṣa* (حاص), when one swerves and flees. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I did not know whether, from the death, there was a refuge (ḥayṣa), / while the lifespan remains and the term is long."

From this is the hadith: "They fled in flight like the flight of wild donkeys toward the gates." And *jāḍa* (جاض), with the letter *jīm* and the dotted *ḍād*, means to swerve in fright; but the language of the Qur'an is with the *ḥā'* and the undotted *ṣād*.

When Allah, exalted is He, informed about the disbelievers who take Satan as a protector, and made known the deception of Satan's promise to them, and made known the outcome of their matter, that it is toward Hell, all of that required warning. He, mighty and majestic, followed that with encouragement by mentioning the state of the believers, and made known the outcome of their matter, (p-28) that it is toward everlasting bliss, and made known the truth of His promise to them. Then He confirmed that with questioning in His saying: ﴿"And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?"﴾ *Al-qīl* (القيل) and *al-qawl* (القول) are one and the same, and its accusative is as a specification (*tamyīz*).

A group read ﴿*sa-nudkhiluhum*﴾ with the *nūn*, and a group read ﴿*sa-yudkhiluhum*﴾ with the *yā'*. ﴿"The promise of Allah"﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and ﴿"truly"﴾ (*ḥaqqan*) is also a verbal noun, emphasizing what precedes it.

Alteration (*tabdīl*) falls in the place of change (*taghyīr*), although change is more general than it. A group said: "The alteration of Allah's creation is that Allah, exalted is He, created the sun, the day, the stones, and other created things so that they would be taken as lessons and benefited from, and the disbelievers altered them by making them deities worshipped." Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Anas, 'Ikrima, and Abu Salih: "Among the alteration of Allah's creation is castration. The verse refers to the castration of animals and what resembles it; these are, according to them, prohibited things." A group permitted the castration of animals when the benefit is intended, whether for fattening or other purpose. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz restricted it to horses. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan said: it refers to tattooing and what is similar to it of adornment for beauty. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, cursed the women who tattoo and those who are tattooed, those who pluck (facial hair), those who file the teeth for beauty, those who change the creation of Allah." From this is also his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "May Allah curse the woman who joins hair (with false hair) and the one who asks for it to be joined."

The foundation for interpreting this verse is that every harmful alteration is included in the verse, and every beneficial alteration is permissible.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the rebellion of Satan and what he threatened of spreading his deception, He, blessed and exalted is He, warned His servants against him by stipulating for whoever takes him as a protector the reward of loss. The conception of loss is only that this one who takes him has taken Satan's share, so it is as if he was given Allah's share in it and left it for his sake.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"He promises them and arouses in them false hopes"﴾ means He promises them with his falsehoods: of wealth, of standing, that there is no resurrection and no punishment, and the like; for each person, what suits his state. He arouses in them likewise. Then Allah, exalted is He, began the report about the reality of that with His saying: ﴿"but Satan promises them nothing except delusion."﴾

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about the destiny of those who take Satan as a protector, and threatened them that their refuge is Hell, and they cannot repel it by any trick, nor turn away from it, nor deviate, nor evade. *Al-maḥīṣ* (محيص) is a noun of place from *ḥāṣa* (حاص), when one swerves and flees. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I did not know whether, from the death, there was a refuge (ḥayṣa), / while the lifespan remains and the term is long."

From this is the hadith: "They fled in flight like the flight of wild donkeys toward the gates." And *jāḍa* (جاض), with the letter *jīm* and the dotted *ḍād*, means to swerve in fright; but the language of the Qur'an is with the *ḥā'* and the undotted *ṣād*.

When Allah, exalted is He, informed about the disbelievers who take Satan as a protector, and made known the deception of Satan's promise to them, and made known the outcome of their matter, that it is toward Hell, all of that required warning. He, mighty and majestic, followed that with encouragement by mentioning the state of the believers, and made known the outcome of their matter, (p-28) that it is toward everlasting bliss, and made known the truth of His promise to them. Then He confirmed that with questioning in His saying: ﴿"And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?"﴾ *Al-qīl* (القيل) and *al-qawl* (القول) are one and the same, and its accusative is as a specification (*tamyīz*).

A group read ﴿*sa-nudkhiluhum*﴾ with the *nūn*, and a group read ﴿*sa-yudkhiluhum*﴾ with the *yā'*. ﴿"The promise of Allah"﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and ﴿"truly"﴾ (*ḥaqqan*) is also a verbal noun, emphasizing what precedes it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 123–125:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book. Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will not find for himself, besides Allah, any protector or helper.﴾ ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged the least bit.﴾ ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah, while he is a doer of good, and follows the creed of Ibrahim, a hanif? And Allah took Ibrahim as a close friend.﴾

The subject of ﴿"laysa"﴾ is a pronoun (implied). "Al-amani" is the plural of "umniyya," whose pattern is "uf'uwla," and it means what a person desires and makes his soul hope for. It is pluralized as "fa'alil," so two yas come together, and therefore one of them is assimilated into the other and it comes with a shadda. This is the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Shayba ibn Nassah, al-Hakam and al-A'raj read ﴿"laysa bi-amaniyyikum"﴾ with a sukun on the ya, and likewise in the second occurrence. Al-Farra' said: "This is a plural on the pattern 'fa'alil,' as one says 'qaraqir' and 'qaraqir,' and so on."

People differed regarding: to whom is this verse addressed? Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih, Masruq, Qatada, al-Suddi and others said: "The address is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ)." Some said: "The reason for the verse is that the believers disputed with a group of the People of the Book. The People of the Book said: 'Our religion is older than your religion and superior; and our prophet came before your prophet; so we are better than you.' The believers said: 'Our Book abrogates the (other) books, and our prophet is the Seal of the Prophets'; or something similar to this exchange. So the verse was revealed." Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "Rather, the address is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because they said: 'We will not be resurrected, nor will we be punished; there is only our worldly life, in which we have pleasure, and then there is no punishment.' The Jews said: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 18]; and similar sayings, such as their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqara: 111], and others." So Allah responded to both groups: ﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book.﴾ Then He began the true report with His saying: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it.﴾ This wording came general in every evil, so both mentioned groups fall under its generality.

The interpreters differed over the generalization of this report's wording. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "This verse is about the disbeliever." He recited ﴿And do We recompense except the ungrateful?﴾ [Saba': 17] and said: "The verse means the disbelievers by it, and does not mean the people of prayer." He also said: "By Allah, Allah does not recompense anyone with good or evil except that He punishes him; but He forgives the sins of the believers." Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾: "Allah promised the believers that He would expiate their bad deeds from them, and He did not promise those, meaning the polytheists." Al-Dahhak said: "﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ means by it the Jews, the Christians, the Magians and the disbelievers of the Arabs."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "This is a specification of the wording of the verse. These scholars held that the disbeliever is recompensed for every evil he does, and that Allah has promised the believer the expiation of his bad deeds." Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: His saying, ﴿Whoever does evil﴾, its meaning is: "whoever is a polytheist (mushrik)"; and "evil" here is shirk. This is a specification of the generality of the wording from another direction, because those (the first group) specified the word "man" (whoever), and these two specified the word "evil" (su'). The majority of people said: The wording of the verse is general; the disbeliever and the believer are both recompensed for the evil they do. As for the recompense of the disbeliever, it is the Fire, because his disbelief destroyed him; and as for the believer, it is the afflictions of this world. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ was revealed, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how severe this verse is!' He said: 'O Abu Bakr, do you not grieve? Do you not fall ill? Do afflictions not befall you? That is its recompense.'" 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "When this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr said: 'The back-breaking calamity has come!' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'It is only the calamities of the world.'" 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, gave a similar interpretation. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, when al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad asked him about the meaning of the verse, and he seemed to fear it, said to him: "I did not think you were more knowledgeable than what I see. No scratch or anything else afflicts a man except because of a sin; and what Allah pardons is more."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The creed on this is that the disbeliever is recompensed, and the believer is generally recompensed in this world. So whoever has evil remaining for him until the Hereafter, he is under the Will (of Allah): Allah forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.

The majority read ﴿"wa-la yajid"﴾ with a jazm, as a conjunction with ﴿"yujza"﴾. Ibn Bakkar related from Ibn 'Amir: ﴿"wa-la yajidu"﴾ with a raf', as an independent clause (qat'). His saying ﴿"min dun Allah"﴾ is an expression that requires the absence of what is mentioned after it of the descent (of help); some commentators explain it as "ghayr" (other than), but this explanation is not consistent.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾: ﴿"min"﴾ is used for partition (tab'id), since perfect righteous deeds are beyond human capacity; so in this there is kindness to the servants. But this part includes the obligatory acts and what is possible of the recommended acts. Then He restricted the matter to faith, since no deed benefits without it. Al-Tabari related from some people that "min" is superfluous (za'ida); and he considered this weak, as it is weak. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿"yadkhulun al-jannata"﴾ with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the kha, and likewise wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. The same was related from 'Asim. Abu 'Amr read in this verse, and in [Maryam], [al-Mala'ika] and [al-Mu'min]: ﴿"yudkhalun"﴾ with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the kha; and he read with a fatha on the ya in: ﴿"sayadkhulun jahannama dakhirin"﴾. The naqir is the spot on the back of the date-pit from which it sprouts; and it is related from 'Asim that the naqir is what you scratch with your finger. All of this is an example of the small and trivial.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Here the refutation of the people of wishful thinking is complete, and the report of the reality of the matter is complete.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, gave a report in agreement that there is no better religion than one who submits his face to Allah; that is, he purifies his aim and his direction, and does good in his deeds, and follows the hanifiyya, which is the creed of Ibrahim, the leader of the world and the exemplar of the people of religions. Then, when Allah mentioned Ibrahim as the one whose following is obligatory, He honored him by mentioning the friendship (khulla). Ibrahim, may peace be upon him, was named by Allah "khalil" (close friend), since his sincerity, his worship and his striving were to the utmost degree to which a loving one who strives to the extreme proceeds; and Allah's gentleness toward him, His mercy and His support for him were in accordance with that.

Some people went to the view that Ibrahim was named khalil from "al-khalla," with a fatha on the kha; that is, because he brought down his need and his poverty before Allah, may He be exalted. Some said: he was named khalil because he—as related in a hadith—came from the presence of a friend he had in Egypt, who had denied him the grain for which he had set out. When he approached his home, he filled his two sacks with sand so that his children would be comforted by it. When he entered his house, he slept out of exhaustion and worry. His wife got up and opened the sack, and found the finest flour; so she kneaded some of it. When he woke up he said: "What is this?" She said: "From the flour you brought from your Egyptian friend." He said: "Rather, it is from my friend Allah, may He be exalted." So he was named by this "khalil."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this there is weakness; this story does not require that he be named by this as a dominant name. Rather, it is something Allah honored him with, just as He honored Muhammad (ﷺ). It is authenticated in the Sahih of Muslim and others that Allah took him as a khalil.

The majority read ﴿"wa-la yajid"﴾ with a jazm, as a conjunction with ﴿"yujza"﴾. Ibn Bakkar related from Ibn 'Amir: ﴿"wa-la yajidu"﴾ with a raf', as an independent clause (qat'). His saying ﴿"min dun Allah"﴾ is an expression that requires the absence of what is mentioned after it of the descent (of help); some commentators explain it as "ghayr" (other than), but this explanation is not consistent.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾: ﴿"min"﴾ is used for partition (tab'id), since perfect righteous deeds are beyond human capacity; so in this there is kindness to the servants. But this part includes the obligatory acts and what is possible of the recommended acts. Then He restricted the matter to faith, since no deed benefits without it. Al-Tabari related from some people that "min" is superfluous (za'ida); and he considered this weak, as it is weak. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿"yadkhulun al-jannata"﴾ with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the kha, and likewise wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. The same was related from 'Asim. Abu 'Amr read in this verse, and in [Maryam], [al-Mala'ika] and [al-Mu'min]: ﴿"yudkhalun"﴾ with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the kha; and he read with a fatha on the ya in: ﴿"sayadkhulun jahannama dakhirin"﴾. The naqir is the spot on the back of the date-pit from which it sprouts; and it is related from 'Asim that the naqir is what you scratch with your finger. All of this is an example of the small and trivial.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Here the refutation of the people of wishful thinking is complete, and the report of the reality of the matter is complete.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, gave a report in agreement that there is no better religion than one who submits his face to Allah; that is, he purifies his aim and his direction, and does good in his deeds, and follows the hanifiyya, which is the creed of Ibrahim, the leader of the world and the exemplar of the people of religions. Then, when Allah mentioned Ibrahim as the one whose following is obligatory, He honored him by mentioning the friendship (khulla). Ibrahim, may peace be upon him, was named by Allah "khalil" (close friend), since his sincerity, his worship and his striving were to the utmost degree to which a loving one who strives to the extreme proceeds; and Allah's gentleness toward him, His mercy and His support for him were in accordance with that.

Some people went to the view that Ibrahim was named khalil from "al-khalla," with a fatha on the kha; that is, because he brought down his need and his poverty before Allah, may He be exalted. Some said: he was named khalil because he—as related in a hadith—came from the presence of a friend he had in Egypt, who had denied him the grain for which he had set out. When he approached his home, he filled his two sacks with sand so that his children would be comforted by it. When he entered his house, he slept out of exhaustion and worry. His wife got up and opened the sack, and found the finest flour; so she kneaded some of it. When he woke up he said: "What is this?" She said: "From the flour you brought from your Egyptian friend." He said: "Rather, it is from my friend Allah, may He be exalted." So he was named by this "khalil."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this there is weakness; this story does not require that he be named by this as a dominant name. Rather, it is something Allah honored him with, just as He honored Muhammad (ﷺ). It is authenticated in the Sahih of Muslim and others that Allah took him as a khalil.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 126–127:

(p-32) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever, of all things, encompassing.﴾ ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say, "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, and whom you desire to marry, and concerning the oppressed among the children, and that you should maintain justice for the orphans. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it."﴾

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the vastness of His dominion and His encompassing of everything immediately after mentioning the religion and the clarification of its path, as an encouragement to obey Allah and to devote oneself to Him.

As for His saying, ﴿"They ask you"⁠﴾: it was revealed because a group of the Companions asked about the matter of women and their rulings concerning inheritance and other things. So Allah commanded His Prophet to say to them: ﴿Allah gives you a ruling concerning them﴾, meaning: He will explain to you the ruling on what you have asked about. His saying, ﴿"And what is recited to you"⁠﴾, the "mā" may be in the genitive position, coordinated with the pronoun in His saying ﴿"concerning them"⁠﴾, meaning: and He gives you a ruling concerning what is recited to you. This was said by Muhammad ibn Abi Musa, who said: Allah gave them rulings concerning what they asked about and what they did not ask about. This interpretation is weakened by the coordination with a genitive pronoun without repeating the genitive particle. It is also possible that the "mā" is in the nominative position, coordinated with the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, meaning: and what is recited to you in the Book gives you a ruling. "The Book" means the Qur'an, and the reference by "this" is to the verses preceding concerning the matter of women, namely His saying, at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [an-Nisa': 3], etc. 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "This verse was revealed first; then some people asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after it about the matter of women, and so there was revealed: (p-33) ﴿They ask you concerning women. Say, Allah gives you a ruling concerning them and what is recited to you.⁠﴾"

His saying, ﴿concerning the orphan women to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them⁠﴾: its meaning is a prohibition of what the Arabs used to do, namely taking in a beautiful, wealthy orphan girl without giving her the dower she deserves; and preventing an ugly, poor girl from marriage forever, and likewise an ugly wealthy girl, until she dies, so that the guardian who prevented her inherits from her; and similar things by which the guardian intends his own benefit, not the benefit of the orphan. What Allah prescribed for them is giving them the full dower they deserve and joining them with their equals.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Madani read: "fi yayama an-nisa'" with two yas. Abu al-Fath said: The explanation of this reading is that he intended "ayama," so the hamza was changed to ya, as they changed it in their saying "Bahilat ibn Ya'sur," whereas it is "Ibn A'sur," since he is only called by his saying:

"O my son, your father's color has changed, by the turning of nights and the alternation of ages."

And as the ya was changed to hamza in their saying "qata'a Allahu adahu," meaning "yadahu." And "ayama" is the plural of "ayyim," whose origin is "ayayim"; the lam was moved to the place of the 'ayn, so it became "ayama," then the kasra was replaced by a fatha, and the ya by an alif.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It seems that what prompted this is the heaviness of the damma on the ya."

Abu al-Fath said: If someone were to say that "ayyim" was broken into "aymā" on the pattern of "sakrā" and "qatlā," since widowhood is an affliction that enters unwillingly, and then "aymā" was broken into "ayama," it would be a good explanation.

His saying, ﴿and whom you desire to marry⁠﴾: if the girl is wealthy and beautiful, the desire is to marry her; and if it is the opposite, the aversion is from marrying her. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, used to make people follow the best course in this matter. When he asked a guardian about his ward and it was said, "She is wealthy and beautiful," he would say to him, "Seek for her one better than you and more beneficial to her." And when it was said to him, "She is ugly and poor," he would say to him, "You are more entitled to her, and to covering her faults, than anyone else."

His saying, ﴿and the oppressed among the children⁠﴾: it is coordinated with ﴿the orphan women⁠﴾. What was recited concerning the oppressed among the children is His saying: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children⁠﴾ [an-Nisa': 11], because the Arabs did not give inheritance to a girl or to a small boy; the eldest would take the wealth alone, and they used to say: "Only one who protects the territory, repels the spoils, and fights for the sanctuary inherits the wealth." So Allah prescribed for each one his right.

His saying, ﴿and that you should maintain justice for the orphans⁠﴾: this is also coordinated with what preceded. What was recited concerning this meaning is His saying: ﴿And do not devour their property along with your own property⁠﴾ [an-Nisa': 2], and other things mentioned concerning the property of the orphan. "Al-qist" means justice. The rest of the verse is a promise of a beautiful reward for doing good, and it is clear.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 128–129:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿If a woman fears ill-treatment or aversion from her husband, there is no blame upon them both if they make a settlement between themselves, and settlement is best. And souls are present with stinginess. And if you do good and are mindful [of Allah], then indeed Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you should strive. So do not incline completely [away from one], leaving her as if suspended. And if you amend and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This verse is a ruling from Allah, exalted is He, concerning the woman who is advanced in years, or disfigured, or something similar which makes her husband averse to her, so that the husband goes towards divorcing her, or towards preferring a young woman over her, or something similar, by which he intends the betterment of himself. He does not harm her with a harm that obliges him to her, but rather he offers her separation, or patience with being given less favour. She wishes to remain married. This is the case in which Allah, exalted is He, permitted the settlement between them and lifted the blame in it, since blame attaches to every settlement that arises from a harm the husband commits, until it is remedied. Allah, exalted is He, permitted settlement in the presence of fear and the appearance of signs of nushuz (ill-treatment, from the root meaning "to rise up," i.e., the husband's or wife's rebellion against the good conduct of marriage) or i'rad (aversion); and this is permissible even if it has occurred. "Nushuz" means raising oneself above the rank of good companionship, and "i'rad" is lighter than nushuz.

All kinds of settlement are permissible in this situation: that the husband gives on condition that she be patient; or that she gives on condition that the husband not prefer another; or on condition that he prefers [another] and holds on to the marital bond; or that the settlement occurs on the basis of patience with being given less favour. All of this is permissible.

The exegetes differed concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas and a group with him said: it was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and Sawda bint Zam'a. al-Tabari related with a chain of narration from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Sawda feared that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would divorce her, so she said: 'Do not divorce me, and keep me among your wives, and do not divide [your time] for me.' So he did that, and the verse was revealed: ﴿If a woman fears ill-treatment or aversion from her husband﴾ — the verse." In the compilations [of hadith] it is [narrated] "that when Sawda grew old she gave her day to 'A'isha." This is similar to the first [report].

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Ubayda al-Salmani, and others said: the verse was revealed on account of Rafi' ibn Khadij and Khawla bint Muhammad ibn Maslama. The reason was that he (Rafi') became aged, so he married a young woman over her, and he preferred the young woman. She did not endure this, so he divorced her with one talaq. Then they reconciled, and he returned to preferring the young woman, and she did not endure it, so he divorced her a second time. When a short time remained of the 'idda (waiting period), he said to her: "If you wish, I will take you back and you will be patient with being given less favour; and if you wish, I will leave you until your term runs out." She said: "Rather, take me back, and I will be patient." So he took her back, and he preferred the young woman, and she did not endure it. So he said: "Indeed you are only one [wife]; so either you accept what you see of being given less favour, or I will divorce you." So she accepted. This is the settlement which Allah revealed concerning: "If a woman fears…"

Mujahid said: the verse was revealed on account of Abu al-Sanabil ibn Ba'kak and his wife.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read "yusalihā" as "yaṣṣālaḥā," with a fatha on the ya', a shadda on the sad, and an alif after it; its original form is "yatasālaḥā." Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim read "yuslihā," with a damma on the ya' and a sukun on the sad, without an alif. Ubayda al-Salmani read "yusālihā," with a damma on the ya', from the form of mufa'ala. al-Jahdari and 'Uthman al-Batti read "yaṣṣalihā," with a fatha on the ya' and a shadda on the sad; its original form is "yaṣṭalihā." Abu al-Fath [Ibn Jinni] said: he changed the ta' into a sad, then assimilated into it the sad which is the first radical, so it became "yaṣṣalihā." al-A'mash read "in iṣṣālahā," and it is likewise in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud.

As for His saying: ﴿"ṣulḥan"﴾ — the word ṣulḥ is not a verbal noun (maṣdar) of any of these verbs that were read. Rather, it is possibly a noun (ism), like "al-'aṭā'" (the gift) alongside "a'ṭaytu" (I gave), and "al-karāma" (the honour) alongside "akramtu" (I honoured). So whoever reads "yuṣlihā" — its transitivity to ṣulḥ is like its transitivity to nouns, as you say: "I repaired a garment." And whoever reads "yaṣṣālaḥā," from tafā'ala — it is known that tafā'ala is not transitive; its justification is that tafā'ala has come transitively, as in the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"And from a smooth, sleek-coated (mare), whose beauty was adorned by the flutter of the wind and its breeze, with the embroidered [pattern]…"

It is also permissible that ṣulḥ be a verbal noun whose extra letters have been dropped, as he said:

"…and if I perish, that was my lot (qadri)."

i.e., my decree (taqdīrī).

The qadi Abu Muhammad — may Allah have mercy on him — said: this is the statement of Abu 'Ali [al-Fārisī], on the basis that "qadr" is a verbal noun following "qadartu al-amr," in the sense of "qaddartu" with the shadda.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and settlement is best﴾ — this is a general, unrestricted expression, which implies that true settlement, in which souls find rest and by which disagreement is removed, is best absolutely. Included under this generality is that the settlement of the spouses — according to what we have mentioned — is better than separation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And souls are present with stinginess﴾ — this is an excuse on behalf of His servants; that is, it is necessary for a human being, by the decree of his creation and disposition, to be tight-fisted about his will, so that he moves his companion to some of what he dislikes. The exegetes specified this term here: Ibn Jubayr said: it is the stinginess of the woman with regard to maintenance from her husband and with regard to his dividing her days for her. Ibn Zayd said: stinginess here comes from him and from her.

The qadi Abu Muhammad — may Allah have mercy on him — said: this is the best [view], for what predominates in a woman is stinginess regarding her share from her husband, and what predominates in a husband is stinginess regarding his share of the young woman.

And shuḥḥ (stinginess) is holding tightly to beliefs, wills, aspirations, wealth, and the like. Whatever of it is excessive contains some blame, and this is what He, exalted is He, referred to in: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. And what reaches the domain of withholding legal rights, or those required by manliness, is bukhl (miserliness), which is a vice; yet it may be found in a believer. And from it is the hadith: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, can a believer be miserly? He said: 'Yes.'" As for shuḥḥ, it is found in everyone; but it does not become excessive except in religion. What indicates that shuḥḥ is in everyone is His saying: ﴿and souls are present with stinginess﴾ and His saying: ﴿the stinginess of his soul﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]; so He has affirmed that every soul has shuḥḥ. And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "[The best charity is] that you give charity while you are healthy and stingy." This was not intended for one specific person; and it is not fitting to say here: "that you give charity while you are healthy and miserly."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you do good﴾ — this is an encouragement to goodness in making companionship good, bearing with the wife's character, and being patient with what is disliked in her condition. The encouragement to goodness is established, since the husband may be stingy and so not do good.

﴿"And are mindful [of Allah]"﴾ — its meaning: be mindful of Allah in His command concerning women, since they are 'awan (captives, prisoners) with husbands, as the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it by his saying: "Treat women well, for they are 'awan with you."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives﴾ — the verse. Its meaning: complete justice, absolutely, equal in actions, words, love, intercourse, and other things. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to divide [his time] among his wives, then he would say: 'O Allah, this is my action in what I control; so do not hold me accountable for what You control and I do not control,'" meaning his inclination of the heart. And 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say: "O Allah, my heart — I do not control it; as for everything else, I hope that I am just." It is also related that this verse was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and his inclination of the heart towards 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her. So Allah, exalted is He, described the human condition: that by the decree of creation they do not control the inclination of their hearts towards some wives over others, nor their eagerness towards them, nor their cheerfulness with them. Then He forbade inclining "kulla al-mayl" (completely), which is to do an act of preference that one intends, while one is able not to do it. This is "kulla al-mayl," even if it is in a trivial matter. It is as if the statement means: "Do not incline in the kind that is complete inclination, which is what is intended by a word or an action."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so you would leave her as if suspended﴾ — that is, she is neither a widow nor a married woman. This is a simile with something suspended from something, for it does not settle on the ground, nor is it carried by that from which it is suspended. This is consistent with their proverb: "Be content with the vehicle by suspension" (irḍ min al-markab bi-al-ta'liq); and in the usage of the grammarians regarding the suspension of a verb (ta'liq al-fi'l). From it is the hadith of Umm Zar': the woman's saying: "My husband is al-'Ashanaq: if I speak, I am divorced; and if I am silent, I am left suspended (u'allaq)."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "fa-tadharūhā ka-al-masjūna" (so you leave her like one imprisoned). 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-tadharūhā ka-annahā mu'allaqa" (so you leave her as if she were suspended).

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you amend and fear Allah﴾ — that is: and if you commit yourselves to what justice requires of you in what you control; ﴿then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ — concerning what you do not control, overlooking it. al-Tabari said: the meaning of the verse is: Forgiving of what has passed from you of complete inclination before the revelation of the verse.

The qadi Abu Muhammad — may Allah have mercy on him — said:

According to this, it is a forgiveness specific to particular people who fell into the forbidden during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ).

In the previous [verse] came: ﴿"And if you do good"﴾, and in this one: ﴿"And if you amend"﴾, because the first concerns what is recommended (mandub), while this one concerns what is obligatory (lazim). This is because the man has, in that case, the option of not doing good, and of being stingy and reconciling by what satisfies him. But in this case he has no option to amend; rather, justice in what he controls is binding upon him.

All of this is permissible.

The exegetes differed concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas and a group with him said: it was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and Sawda bint Zam'a. al-Tabari related with a chain of narration from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Sawda feared that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would divorce her, so she said: 'Do not divorce me, and keep me among your wives, and do not divide [your time] for me.' So he did that, and the verse was revealed: ﴿If a woman fears ill-treatment or aversion from her husband﴾ — the verse." In the compilations [of hadith] it is [narrated] "that when Sawda grew old she gave her day to 'A'isha." This is similar to the first [report].

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Ubayda al-Salmani, and others said: the verse was revealed on account of Rafi' ibn Khadij and Khawla bint Muhammad ibn Maslama. The reason was that he (Rafi') became aged, so he married a young woman over her, and he preferred the young woman. She did not endure this, so he divorced her with one talaq. Then they reconciled, and he returned to preferring the young woman, and she did not endure it, so he divorced her a second time. When a short time remained of the 'idda (waiting period), he said to her: "If you wish, I will take you back and you will be patient with being given less favour; and if you wish, I will leave you until your term runs out." She said: "Rather, take me back, and I will be patient." So he took her back, and he preferred the young woman, and she did not endure it. So he said: "Indeed you are only one [wife]; so either you accept what you see of being given less favour, or I will divorce you." So she accepted. This is the settlement which Allah revealed concerning: "If a woman fears…"

Mujahid said: the verse was revealed on account of Abu al-Sanabil ibn Ba'kak and his wife.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read "yusalihā" as "yaṣṣālaḥā," with a fatha on the ya', a shadda on the sad, and an alif after it; its original form is "yatasālaḥā." Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim read "yuslihā," with a damma on the ya' and a sukun on the sad, without an alif. Ubayda al-Salmani read "yusālihā," with a damma on the ya', from the form of mufa'ala. al-Jahdari and 'Uthman al-Batti read "yaṣṣalihā," with a fatha on the ya' and a shadda on the sad; its original form is "yaṣṭalihā." Abu al-Fath [Ibn Jinni] said: he changed the ta' into a sad, then assimilated into it the sad which is the first radical, so it became "yaṣṣalihā." al-A'mash read "in iṣṣālahā," and it is likewise in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud.

As for His saying: ﴿"ṣulḥan"﴾ — the word ṣulḥ is not a verbal noun (maṣdar) of any of these verbs that were read. Rather, it is possibly a noun (ism), like "al-'aṭā'" (the gift) alongside "a'ṭaytu" (I gave), and "al-karāma" (the honour) alongside "akramtu" (I honoured). So whoever reads "yuṣlihā" — its transitivity to ṣulḥ is like its transitivity to nouns, as you say: "I repaired a garment." And whoever reads "yaṣṣālaḥā," from tafā'ala — it is known that tafā'ala is not transitive; its justification is that tafā'ala has come transitively, as in the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"And from a smooth, sleek-coated (mare), whose beauty was adorned by the flutter of the wind and its breeze, with the embroidered [pattern]…"

It is also permissible that ṣulḥ be a verbal noun whose extra letters have been dropped, as he said:

"…and if I perish, that was my lot (qadri)."

i.e., my decree (taqdīrī).

The qadi Abu Muhammad — may Allah have mercy on him — said: this is the statement of Abu 'Ali [al-Fārisī], on the basis that "qadr" is a verbal noun following "qadartu al-amr," in the sense of "qaddartu" with the shadda.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and settlement is best﴾ — this is a general, unrestricted expression, which implies that true settlement, in which souls find rest and by which disagreement is removed, is best absolutely. Included under this generality is that the settlement of the spouses — according to what we have mentioned — is better than separation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And souls are present with stinginess﴾ — this is an excuse on behalf of His servants; that is, it is necessary for a human being, by the decree of his creation and disposition, to be tight-fisted about his will, so that he moves his companion to some of what he dislikes. The exegetes specified this term here: Ibn Jubayr said: it is the stinginess of the woman with regard to maintenance from her husband and with regard to his dividing her days for her. Ibn Zayd said: stinginess here comes from him and from her.

The qadi Abu Muhammad — may Allah have mercy on him — said: this is the best [view], for what predominates in a woman is stinginess regarding her share from her husband, and what predominates in a husband is stinginess regarding his share of the young woman.

And shuḥḥ (stinginess) is holding tightly to beliefs, wills, aspirations, wealth, and the like. Whatever of it is excessive contains some blame, and this is what He, exalted is He, referred to in: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. And what reaches the domain of withholding legal rights, or those required by manliness, is bukhl (miserliness), which is a vice; yet it may be found in a believer. And from it is the hadith: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, can a believer be miserly? He said: 'Yes.'" As for shuḥḥ, it is found in everyone; but it does not become excessive except in religion. What indicates that shuḥḥ is in everyone is His saying: ﴿and souls are present with stinginess﴾ and His saying: ﴿the stinginess of his soul﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]; so He has affirmed that every soul has shuḥḥ. And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "[The best charity is] that you give charity while you are healthy and stingy." This was not intended for one specific person; and it is not fitting to say here: "that you give charity while you are healthy and miserly."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you do good﴾ — this is an encouragement to goodness in making companionship good, bearing with the wife's character, and being patient with what is disliked in her condition. The encouragement to goodness is established, since the husband may be stingy and so not do good.

﴿"And are mindful [of Allah]"﴾ — its meaning: be mindful of Allah in His command concerning women, since they are 'awan (captives, prisoners) with husbands, as the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it by his saying: "Treat women well, for they are 'awan with you."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives﴾ — the verse. Its meaning: complete justice, absolutely, equal in actions, words, love, intercourse, and other things. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to divide [his time] among his wives, then he would say: 'O Allah, this is my action in what I control; so do not hold me accountable for what You control and I do not control,'" meaning his inclination of the heart. And 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say: "O Allah, my heart — I do not control it; as for everything else, I hope that I am just." It is also related that this verse was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and his inclination of the heart towards 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her. So Allah, exalted is He, described the human condition: that by the decree of creation they do not control the inclination of their hearts towards some wives over others, nor their eagerness towards them, nor their cheerfulness with them. Then He forbade inclining "kulla al-mayl" (completely), which is to do an act of preference that one intends, while one is able not to do it. This is "kulla al-mayl," even if it is in a trivial matter. It is as if the statement means: "Do not incline in the kind that is complete inclination, which is what is intended by a word or an action."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so you would leave her as if suspended﴾ — that is, she is neither a widow nor a married woman. This is a simile with something suspended from something, for it does not settle on the ground, nor is it carried by that from which it is suspended. This is consistent with their proverb: "Be content with the vehicle by suspension" (irḍ min al-markab bi-al-ta'liq); and in the usage of the grammarians regarding the suspension of a verb (ta'liq al-fi'l). From it is the hadith of Umm Zar': the woman's saying: "My husband is al-'Ashanaq: if I speak, I am divorced; and if I am silent, I am left suspended (u'allaq)."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "fa-tadharūhā ka-al-masjūna" (so you leave her like one imprisoned). 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-tadharūhā ka-annahā mu'allaqa" (so you leave her as if she were suspended).

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you amend and fear Allah﴾ — that is: and if you commit yourselves to what justice requires of you in what you control; ﴿then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ — concerning what you do not control, overlooking it. al-Tabari said: the meaning of the verse is: Forgiving of what has passed from you of complete inclination before the revelation of the verse.

The qadi Abu Muhammad — may Allah have mercy on him — said:

According to this, it is a forgiveness specific to particular people who fell into the forbidden during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ).

In the previous [verse] came: ﴿"And if you do good"﴾, and in this one: ﴿"And if you amend"﴾, because the first concerns what is recommended (mandub), while this one concerns what is obligatory (lazim). This is because the man has, in that case, the option of not doing good, and of being stingy and reconciling by what satisfies him. But in this case he has no option to amend; rather, justice in what he controls is binding upon him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 130–133:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance. And Allah is ever All-Encompassing, Wise.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you, and [you as well], to fear Allah. And if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth; and Allah is ever Free of need, Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others [in your place]. And Allah is ever capable of that.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "yatafarraqa" (they separate) refers to the two spouses mentioned earlier, meaning: if each of them is niggardly and they do not reconcile, but they separate by divorce, then Allah the Exalted will enrich each of them from the other by His bounty and the subtleties of His handiwork, in wealth, in companionship, in ampleness, in the availability of what is desired, and in the ability to attain it. Some of the Maliki jurists held that separation in this verse means separation by speech, since divorce is speech, and they used this as evidence for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The two parties to a sale have the option [to cancel] as long as they have not separated." This is because the Maliki school's position on the hadith is that separation is by speech, not by the body.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: There is no proof in this verse, because its report concerns their separation in bodies, and the lapse of time with the removal of the marital bond; and enrichment occurs only in a later state. Moreover, if the separation in the verse were divorce, there would be no share for the woman in it that would necessitate the appearance of her pronoun in the verb. This is a brief outline of the objection to the question.

"Al-Wasi'" (the All-Encompassing) means: the one who possesses the treasuries of everything.

As for His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, it is an alert to the place of hope for these two who separate. Then came after it His saying: ﴿And if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, as a reminder of His independence from the servants, and as an introduction to the report that He is "Free of need, Praiseworthy." Then came after that His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾, as an introduction to the warning. These are the aspects of the repetition of this single report three times in close succession.

As for His saying: ﴿And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, it is a term general to everyone who was given a Scripture, for Allah's commandment to His servants to fear Him has not ceased since He brought them into existence. "Al-Wakil" (the Disposer of affairs) is the one who oversees affairs and carries out in them what He sees fit.

As for His saying: ﴿O people﴾, it addresses those present among the Arabs and is a summons to the listeners, to bring their minds to attention. As for His saying "others" (bi-akharin), it means: of your kind. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck the shoulder of Salman al-Farisi with his hand and said: "They are the people of this man." The wording of the verse may allow that it is a warning to all of the children of Adam, and that "the others" are of a kind other than theirs, as it has been reported that there were angels on the earth worshipping Allah before the children of Adam. The power of Allah the Exalted over what has been mentioned is affirmed by the intellects through its self-evidence. Al-Tabari said: this warning and rebuke are directed at the people who interceded on behalf of Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq and argued on his behalf in the matter of his betrayal regarding the armour and the flour.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a distant interpretation; the beauty of the wording appears only through its generality and its extension over the world as a whole, or over the present world.

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world — with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more worthy of both. So do not follow [your own] desire, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾

That is: whoever has no aim except the reward of this world, and does not believe that there is anything other than it, then he is not as he thinks. Rather, with Allah is the reward of both abodes. Whoever intends the Hereafter, Allah gives him from the reward of this world and gives him his intention. Whoever intends only this world, He gives him from this world what has been decreed for him, and he will have punishment in the Hereafter. (p-42) Allah, may He be exalted, is Hearing of statements and Seeing of deeds and intentions.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, addressed the believers: ﴿Be persistently standing firm﴾, to the end of the verse. This is the form of intensification (ṣīghat mubālagha), meaning: let the act of standing firm for "bil-qisṭ" (in justice), which is ʿadl (equity), be repeated constantly from you. His saying "shuhadāʾ" (witnesses) is in the accusative as a predicate after a predicate (khabar baʿda khabar). The circumstantial (ḥāl) reading of it is weak in meaning, because it would restrict standing firm for justice to the sense of testimony alone. His saying "lillāh" (for Allah) means: for the sake of Allah's essence, for His countenance, and for His good pleasure. His saying ﴿even if against yourselves﴾ is connected to "witnesses." This is the apparent reading on which people have interpreted, and that this testimony mentioned is in matters of rights (ḥuqūq).

It is possible that His saying "witnesses for Allah" means: witnesses to His oneness (waḥdāniyya), and that His saying ﴿even if against yourselves﴾ is connected to ﴿persistently standing firm in justice﴾. The first interpretation is clearer.

A person's testimony against himself is his acknowledgment of the facts, and his speaking the truth in every matter, and his standing firm in justice regarding them likewise. Then He mentioned the parents, because of the obligation of kindness to them and the greatness of their status. Then He followed with the relatives, since they are the place of affection and partisanship; so a stranger among people is more fitting to have justice established against him and to be witnessed against. This verse includes only testimony against relatives, so there is no sense in deriving from it testimony in their favor, as some commentators did. There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge regarding the soundness of the rulings of this verse.

For Allah, may He be exalted, is more worthy of both categories and of both states. (p-43) Al-Suddī mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ: a rich man and a poor man came to him in dispute, and he inclined toward the poor man, knowing that the rich man was more likely to wrong the poor man. The judge Abū Muḥammad said, may Allah have mercy on him: This matter is linked to what the Prophet ﷺ said: "I judge for him according to what I hear." This is how the report from Ashhab and others has it. Al-Ṭabarī mentioned that this verse was connected to the incident of Ṭuʿma ibn Ubayriq and the stance of those who stood up for him without justice.

It is also possible that its meaning is "out of love that you be just" (maḥabbat an taʿdilū), in which case ʿadl means qisṭ (justice). That is: whoever has no aim except the reward of this world, and does not believe that there is anything other than it, then he is not as he thinks. Rather, with Allah is the reward of both abodes. Whoever intends the Hereafter, Allah gives him from the reward of this world and gives him his intention. Whoever intends only this world, He gives him from this world what has been decreed for him, and he will have punishment in the Hereafter. The Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah 4, verses 136–137:

**[The Qur'anic text]**

﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before. And whoever disbelieves in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers and the Last Day has certainly strayed far astray.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believed and then disbelieved, then believed and then disbelieved, and then increased in disbelief - Allah will not forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path.﴾

People differed concerning those addressed by His words, ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah﴾. One group said: the address is to those among the People of the Two Books who believed in Moses and Jesus. That is: "O you who have believed in a prophet from among the prophets, believe in Muḥammad (ﷺ)." Al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. It was also said: the address is to the believers, meaning: "Let your faith be thus, in its perfection and completeness, in Allah, in Muḥammad (ﷺ), in the Qur'an and in all the revealed books." This command implies steadfastness and permanence. It was also said: the address is to the hypocrites, meaning: "O you who have displayed faith with your tongues, let your faith be genuine in this form."

Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir recited (in the qirāʾāt, the canonical recitations) "nuzzila" with a damma on the nūn and a kasra on the doubled zāy, in the passive form (ʿalā mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu, the verb whose subject is not named). Likewise they recited "wal-kitābi alladhī ukhzila min qablu" with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the zāy, also in the passive. The rest of the readers recited "nazzala" and "anzala" with a fatḥa on the nūn and the zāy, and with a fatḥa on the hamza in "anzala", attributing both verbs to Allah, the Exalted. It is also narrated from ʿĀṣim that his recitation was like that of Abū ʿAmr. The Book mentioned first is the Qur'an, and the Book mentioned second is a generic noun (ism jins) for everything of the Book that has been sent down.

His words, ﴿And whoever disbelieves in Allah﴾ to the end of the verse, are a threat and a statement, containing a warning to the believers against the state of disbelief.

The commentators differed about the intended meaning of His words, ﴿Indeed, those who believed and then disbelieved, then believed and then disbelieved﴾. A group, among them Qatādah and Abū al-ʿĀliyah, said: the verse refers to the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in Moses and the Torah, then disbelieved; the Christians believed in Jesus and the Gospel, then disbelieved; then they increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muḥammad (ﷺ). Al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: the verse refers to a group of the People of the Book who said: ﴿Believe in what has been sent down to those who believed at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:72). Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: the verse refers to the hypocrites, for among them is one who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, vacillating in this, so this verse was revealed concerning the one who increased in disbelief by persisting in his hypocrisy until he died.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the preferred view. The saying of al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan is good and probable. The saying of Qatādah and Abū al-ʿĀliyah, which al-Ṭabarī preferred, is a weak view, rejected by the wording of the verse. That is because the verse is only about a group in which each individual possesses this attribute of vacillating between disbelief and faith, and then increases in disbelief through dying upon it. As for the Jews and the Christians, in each of them there is only one faith and one disbelief in sequence; faith and disbelief are only imagined among them by compiling groups that did not follow one another in one time. This is not the aim of the verse. Rather, this attribute is found in an individual among the hypocrites, because one man among them believes, then disbelieves, then dies upon disbelief. Consider His words, ﴿Allah will not forgive them﴾. This is an expression that implies that these people were decreed against from the outset of their affair, and for this reason they vacillated. This expression is not like saying "Allah will not forgive them"; rather it is stronger, and it points to the leading-on (istidrāj) of one whose state is this and to his destruction. It is an expression that requires its hearer to take heed and return before the decree is enforced upon him, and not to be among these people. Anyone who disbelieves in one disbelief and dies upon it, Allah, the Exalted, has said that He will not forgive him; but He did not say "Allah will not forgive him." So reflect on the difference between the two expressions, for it is among the subtle wonders of eloquence found in the Book of Allah. It is as if His words "Allah will not [be the one who forgives]" indicate a ruling that has been established against them in this world while they are still alive.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 138–140:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Give the hypocrites the news that there is a painful punishment for them.﴾ ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honour (al-'izza) with them? Indeed, honour belongs entirely to God.﴾ ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of God being disbelieved in and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a different discourse. Indeed, you would then be like them. Indeed, God will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell, all of them.﴾

In this verse there is evidence that the one before it refers to the hypocrites, as has been preferred just above. Good news (bishara) is mentioned here with an explicit qualifier, so its use for what is disliked is fine. When it comes without a qualifier, its usage is for what is loved.

Then Exalted God specified, from among the attributes of the hypocrites, the most harmful one to the believers: their allying with the disbelievers and their casting off of the believers. He drew attention to the corruption of this, so that whoever might fall into some kind of it among the believers, through heedlessness, ignorance or leniency, would abandon it.

Then Exalted God rebuked them regarding their purpose in this: is it the seeking of honour and the gaining of strength through them? That is, the matter is not so. Rather, all honour belongs to God; He gives it to whom He wills. He has promised it to the believers and made the final outcome for the God-fearing. The word "al-'izza" (honour, might) originally means hardness and strength. From it comes "al-ard al-izaz," meaning the hard ground; from it comes "'azzani," meaning he overpowered me by his strength; and "isti'azza al-maradu," meaning the illness became strong, along with other derivations of the term.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you﴾ is addressed to everyone who has shown faith, whether a true believer or a hypocrite, because whoever shows faith is obliged to comply with the commands of the Book of God, Exalted is He. The reference of this verse is to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different discourse﴾ [al-An'am: 68], and to similar verses.

The majority of people recited "nuzzila 'alaykum" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the doubled zay. Al-Tabari said: some of the Kufans recited "nazzala," with a fatha on the nun and a doubled zay, meaning "God revealed." Abu Haywa and Humayd recited "nazala," with a fatha on the nun and a light zay. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited "unzila," with an alif, in the passive form. The word "al-Kitab" in this place means the Qur'an.

In this verse there is strong evidence for the obligation of avoiding the people of innovation (ahl al-bida') and the people of sins, and of not sitting with them. It is narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that he seized a group who were drinking wine. It was said to him about one of those present, "He is fasting." So he imposed discipline upon him, and he recited this verse: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them.﴾

(p-48) This likeness is not in all attributes, but it is a binding conclusion, made similar to a judgement based on the apparent inference from association. This meaning is like the saying of the poet:

"Do not ask about the man, but ask about his companion, for every companion is guided by the one he keeps company with."

Then Exalted God threatened the hypocrites and the disbelievers with being gathered together in Hell. Thereby the prohibition is emphasised, and so is the warning against sitting with them and mixing with them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 138–140:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Give the hypocrites the news that there is a painful punishment for them.﴾ ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honour (al-'izza) with them? Indeed, honour belongs entirely to God.﴾ ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of God being disbelieved in and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a different discourse. Indeed, you would then be like them. Indeed, God will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell, all of them.﴾

In this verse there is evidence that the one before it refers to the hypocrites, as has been preferred just above. Good news (bishara) is mentioned here with an explicit qualifier, so its use for what is disliked is fine. When it comes without a qualifier, its usage is for what is loved.

Then Exalted God specified, from among the attributes of the hypocrites, the most harmful one to the believers: their allying with the disbelievers and their casting off of the believers. He drew attention to the corruption of this, so that whoever might fall into some kind of it among the believers, through heedlessness, ignorance or leniency, would abandon it.

Then Exalted God rebuked them regarding their purpose in this: is it the seeking of honour and the gaining of strength through them? That is, the matter is not so. Rather, all honour belongs to God; He gives it to whom He wills. He has promised it to the believers and made the final outcome for the God-fearing. The word "al-'izza" (honour, might) originally means hardness and strength. From it comes "al-ard al-izaz," meaning the hard ground; from it comes "'azzani," meaning he overpowered me by his strength; and "isti'azza al-maradu," meaning the illness became strong, along with other derivations of the term.

The reference of this verse is to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different discourse﴾ [al-An'am: 68], and to similar verses.

The majority of people recited "nuzzila 'alaykum" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the doubled zay. Al-Tabari said: some of the Kufans recited "nazzala," with a fatha on the nun and a doubled zay, meaning "God revealed." Abu Haywa and Humayd recited "nazala," with a fatha on the nun and a light zay. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited "unzila," with an alif, in the passive form. The word "al-Kitab" in this place means the Qur'an.

In this verse there is strong evidence for the obligation of avoiding the people of innovation (ahl al-bida') and the people of sins, and of not sitting with them. It is narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that he seized a group who were drinking wine. It was said to him about one of those present, "He is fasting." So he imposed discipline upon him, and he recited this verse: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them.﴾

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 141–143:**

His words, may He be exalted:

﴿Those who wait and watch over you: if Allah gives you a victory, they say, "Were we not with you?" But if the disbelievers have a share, they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?" Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will never give the disbelievers any way over the believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He is the One who deceives them. When they stand up to pray, they stand lazily, showing off to people and remembering Allah only a little.﴾ ﴿Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those. And whomever Allah leads astray, you will never find a way for him.﴾

"Alladhina" (those who) is a description of the hypocrites. "Yatarabbasuna" means "they await the turn of the circumstances against you. If the believers win a victory, they claim a share in it on the basis of the faith they display; and if the disbelievers gain an advantage over the believers, they claim a share in it on the basis of their inner allegiance to the disbelievers. This is the condition of the hypocrites."

"Nastahwidh" means: (we overpower your affair, we surround you, and we protect your affair). From this is the saying of al-'Ajjaj describing a bull and cows:

> He drives them, and he has a herding-stick.

That is, he overpowers them in their affair, and he overpowers the bulls over them. It is also narrated as "yahuzuhunna" with a zay. From the same root is the saying of Labid describing a donkey and she-asses:

> When they gather, and he takes hold of both their sides, and brings them down upon the crooked, long paths.

"Ahwadha janibayha" means he subdued them and prevailed over them. Allah's words, "The devil has gained mastery over them" (58:19), mean he prevailed over them. This verb is anomalous in that its waw was not changed (to a ya'), but was used in its original form.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "wa-mana'nakum min al-mu'minin" (and We protected you from the believers). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-nam'ana-kum" with a fatha on the 'ayn, as a morphological variant (sarf).

Then He consoled and reassured the believers with what He promised them in His words, "Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection" — that is, between you and them — and He will do justice to you against all of them. And with His words, "Allah will never give the disbelievers any way over the believers." Yusay' al-Hadrami said: I was with 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, when a man said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, what do you make of Allah's words, 'Allah will never give the disbelievers any way over the believers'? How is that, when they fight us and sometimes prevail over us?" 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Its meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection the judgment will be made." And all the people of ta'wil (interpretation, tafsir) said the same.

"Al-sabil" means the proof and the dominance.

The deception of the hypocrites is directed at the friends of Allah, the Exalted, since they think them not to be friends. So in the speech there is an elision of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), and the imputation of a sin required by their actions, even though their intentions did not require it, because none of mankind intends to deceive Allah, the Exalted.

His words, "and He is their Deceiver" — that is, the One who inflicts deception upon them. This is an expression for a punishment which He named by the name of the sin. Their punishment in this world is their humiliation, fear, and grief of heart; and in the Hereafter, the punishment of Hell. Al-Suddi, Ibn Juraij, al-Hasan, and other exegetes said: this deception is that Allah, on the Day of Resurrection, gives this community a light for every believing person or hypocrite. The hypocrites rejoice and think they have been saved. But when they reach the Path (al-sirat), the light of every hypocrite is extinguished, and the believers rise up with their light. This is the saying of the hypocrites, "Wait for us, so we may borrow from your light" (57:13). That is the deception that befalls the hypocrites. Maslama ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nahwi read "wa-huwa khadi'hum" with a sukun on the 'ayn, as a lightening (takhfif).

Then He mentioned their laziness in standing up for prayer. That is the condition of everyone who does an action while hating it and not believing it to be correct, out of dissimulation (taqiyya) or ingratiation (musana'a). Ibn Hurmuz al-A'raj read "kusala" with a fatha on the kaf. The majority of people read "yura'una" with a hamza, damma, and shadda between the ra' and the waw, without an alif. It is the causative (ta'diya) of "ra'a" with doubling, and it is stronger in meaning than "yurd'una," because its meaning is: "they make people see them, and they display themselves to them in prayer, while they conceal hypocrisy." His mention of their scarcity of remembrance has two possible meanings. Al-Hasan said: it was little because it was for other than Allah. This is one view. The second is that it is little in comparison with their immersion in falsehood, their saying of lies, and their disbelief.

"Mudhabdhabin" means: vacillating, not standing firm in any condition. "Al-tadhabdhub" is wavering from embarrassment, fear, or hastening in walking and the like. From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

> You see every king before her wavering.

From it is also the saying of another:

> A phantom of Umm al-Salsabil, and between her and it a distance of a month's journey for the wavering courier.

(with the second dhal in kasra). Abu al-Fath said: that is, "the agitated, the restless, the one who does not stand firm nor move deliberately." So these hypocrites are torn between the disbelievers and the believers, "belonging neither to these nor to those," just as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of the hypocrite is the likeness of a sheep wandering between two flocks." So the reference by "that" is to the two states of disbelief and faith, and He pointed to it, even though it was not previously mentioned, because the sense of the speech clearly implies it, as in: "until it was hidden behind the veil" (38:32), and "everyone upon it passes away" (55:26).

The majority of people read "mudhabdhabin" with a fatha on both dhals. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Amr ibn Fa'id read "mudhabdhibin" with a kasra on the second dhal. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "mutadhabdhibin" with a ta' and a kasra on the second dhal. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "madhabdhabin" with a fatha on the mim and both dhals; this reading is rejected.

His words, "you will never find a way for him" — its meaning is a way of guidance and direction.
