Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrat an-Nisāʾ, verses 144–147:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do you wish to give Allah against yourselves a clear proof?﴾ ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire, and you will not find for them a helper.﴾ ﴿Except for those who repent, correct themselves, hold fast to Allah, and make their religion sincerely for Allah. Those will be with the believers, and Allah will give the believers a great reward.﴾ ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe? And Allah is ever Appreciative and Knowing.﴾

His address, may He be exalted, by the apparent meaning, includes the hypocrites who display faith; so in the wording there is gentleness toward them. They are the intended ones in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you wish to give Allah against yourselves a clear proof?﴾, because the rebuke is only directed at those who have engaged in some action leading to this state; whereas the sincere believers have never engaged in anything of that kind at all. This line of reasoning is strengthened by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿instead of the believers﴾; that is, the knowing, sincere believers are removed from this alliance. This cannot be said to the sincere believers; rather, the meaning is: O you who have shown faith and taken on its obligations.

"Al-sulṭān" (authority/proof) means the argument. It is a word that may be feminine or masculine, and the masculine is more common; it is the usage of the Qur'an wherever it occurs. When "al-sulṭān" is used as a name for the one holding authority, it is by elision of a modifier, and the implied meaning is "the holder of authority," that is, the one holding the proof over people, since he is their manager and the one who looks after their benefits.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, informed about the hypocrites that they are in the lowest level (al-dark al-asfal) of the Fire of Hell. The levels (adrāk) are layers, one above another, seven in number, each level upon another. The highest of them is Hell (jahannam), and the name of the highest level is sometimes applied to all of them. The hypocrites, who display faith and conceal disbelief, are in the lowest level of the Fire, because they are the worst of dangers among the disbelievers and the most capable of harming the Muslims.

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and Abū ʿAmr read "fī al-darak" with an open rāʾ; Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, al-Aʿmash, and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read "fī al-dark" with a sukūn on the rāʾ; and there is a difference of reading transmitted from ʿĀṣim, where both the fatḥah and the sukūn are reported. Both are dialectal forms. Abū ʿAlī said: like "al-shamʿ" and "al-shamaʿ," and the like.

It is narrated from Abū Hurayrah, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, and others that they said: "The hypocrites are in the lowest level of the Fire, in coffins of Fire, sealed upon them." "Al-naṣīr" is an intensive form (binā' mubālagha) from "al-naṣr" (help).

Then He, may He be exalted, excepted the repentant among the hypocrites. Among the conditions of the repentant is that he corrects his speech and his action, holds fast to Allah, that is, makes Him his protection and refuge, and makes his religion sincerely for Allah, may He be exalted; otherwise he is not truly repentant. Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān said, in the presence of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd: "By Allah, a people who were hypocrites will certainly enter Paradise." Then ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said to him: "And what is your knowledge of that?" Ḥudhayfah became angry and withdrew. When they dispersed, ʿAlqamah passed by him, and he called him and said: "Indeed, your companion knows what you said," then he recited: ﴿Except those who repent and correct themselves and hold fast﴾, the verse. **Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah 4, verses 152–153**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Those who believe in God and His messengers and do not make any distinction between any of them, to them He will give their rewards, and God is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven. But they had asked Moses for something greater than that, when they said, "Show us God openly." So the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf after clear proofs had come to them, but We pardoned that, and We gave Moses clear authority.﴾

When God, may He be exalted, mentioned that those who make distinctions between the messengers are truly disbelievers, He followed it by mentioning those who believe in God and all His messengers, namely those who believe in Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), so that He would state explicitly the promise to these people, just as He had stated explicitly the threat to those others, and thus make clear the difference between the two states.

Some of the Seven (the canonical readers, al-Sabʿa) read *sawfa yu'tīhim* with the *yāʾ*, meaning God will give them. The majority read *sawfa nu'tīhim* with the *nūn*, among them Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr.

The exegetes (al-mutaʾawwilūn) differed concerning the manner in which the People of the Book asked Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him) to bring down to them a book from heaven. Al-Suddī said: The Jews said, "O Muḥammad, if you are truthful, then bring a book from heaven just as Moses brought a book." Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said: "Moses brought tablets on which was the Torah, so you bring tablets on which is your book." Qatāda said: "Rather, they asked him to bring a book specific to the Jews, in which he would command them to believe in Muḥammad." Ibn Jurayj said: The Jews said, "O Muḥammad, we will not follow you in what you call us to until you bring us a book from God addressed to so-and-so and to so-and-so, that you are the messenger of God."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Ibn Jurayj's account implies that their request was similar to the request of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Umayya al-Makhzūmī al-Qurashī.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿They had asked Moses for something greater than that﴾, by way of consolation to Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him) and presenting an example. In the discourse there is an omitted element indicated by what is mentioned. Its implied sense is: "So do not be concerned, O Muḥammad, about their question and their excess, for this is their habit; they had asked Moses for something greater than that."

The majority of readers read *akbara* with a single dot under the *bāʾ*. Al-Ḥasan read *akthara* with the *thāʾ* (three dots). The majority of the exegetes hold that *jahratan* (openly) is the object (maʿmūl) of *arinā* (show us), meaning: until we see Him openly, that is, face to face, a vision that is unveiled and clear. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he held that *jahratan* is the object of *qālū* (they said), meaning: they said it openly, from among themselves, explicitly: "Show us God."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the adherents of the prophetic tradition) hold the belief that these people did not ask for something impossible by reason; rather it is impossible by the revealed law (sharʿ), since God, may He be exalted, informed through the tongues of His prophets that He is not seen in this worldly life, while seeing Him in the Hereafter is established from the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) by a report that is widely transmitted (mutawātir, reported by so many chains that its transmission cannot be doubted). Seeing Him is rationally possible, without limitation, without modality, and without spatial location, just as He is known, not like the known things; likewise He is seen, not like the seen things. This is the argument and position of the People of the Sunna.

My father, may God have mercy on him, related to me from Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Naḥwī that he used to say, when teaching this question: "The example of knowledge of God is the shaving of the beards of the Muʿtazila (the rationalist school) in their denial of the vision." The phrase that said, "Show us God openly," is the one that went with Moses to the appointed time of intimate speech (al-munājāh), and its story has already been mentioned in Sūrat al-Baqara.

The majority of readers read ﴿so the thunderbolt seized them﴾ (*fa-akhadhathumu al-ṣāʿiqa*). Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī read *al-ṣaʿqa*. The meaning is close, since all of that expresses a severe striking of sound which afflicts a person with its intensity, causing him to be stunned, with the senses becoming still. Their wrongdoing (*ẓulmuhum*) is their obstinacy and their asking for what they had no right to ask.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then they took the calf﴾ is a sequence in the narration, not in the actual order of events. The implied sense is: "Then there had occurred among them that they took the calf." That taking of the calf happened at the time of the command to go to the appointed meeting, so those who were struck were not among those who took the calf. Rather, those who took it had been given clear proofs concerning the crossing of the sea, the staff, the drowning of Pharaoh, and other things.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But We pardoned that﴾ means: by what He tested them with, namely the killing of one another (as a sign of repentance). Then the pardon fell upon the rest of them. *Al-sulṭān* means the proof.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah an-Nisa', verses 154–156:**

His statement (Exalted is He):

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 157–159:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa, the son of Maryam, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear to them [so]. Indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt concerning it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him for certain.﴾ ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself. And ever is Allah Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾ ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them.﴾

This verse and the one before it, Allah, may He be exalted, enumerates in them the sayings and deeds of the Children of Israel across different times and the succession of generations. From this there results a rebuke of their successors who were contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), and a demonstration of the proof that they deserved the curse, and that humiliation and poverty were struck upon them. So this group who said, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah," were not the same as those who broke the covenant at Mount Sinai, nor those who took the calf [for worship]. The saying of the Children of Israel extends only up to His saying, "'Isa, the son of Maryam," and His saying, may He be exalted, [p-61] "the messenger of Allah" is only a report from Allah, may He be exalted, about an attribute of 'Isa, namely prophethood, by way of exposing the sin of these people who acknowledged the killing, and the sin fell upon them, although they did not kill 'Isa. For they crucified that person thinking he was 'Isa, and [thinking] that 'Isa was a liar and not a messenger. But the sin fell upon them because they believed that their killing had fallen upon 'Isa, so it was as if they had killed him. And since they had killed him, their belief that he was not a messenger does not remove the sin from them, just as the Quraysh, in their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), are not helped by their belief that he was a liar. Rather, Allah repaid them according to the reality of the matter in itself.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, informed that the Children of Israel did not kill 'Isa, nor did they crucify him; "but it was made to appear to them." The narrators differed greatly concerning this story and its manner. I shall summarize its main points, since nothing in all of it can be definitively affirmed as authentic, because nothing about it was established from the Prophet (ﷺ), and we have no basis for preferring any part of it except the words of the Book of Allah. What we do not doubt is that 'Isa (peace be upon him) used to travel through the land and call to Allah, and the Children of Israel were seeking him, and their king at that time would offer rewards for him. 'Isa (peace be upon him) had been joined by the disciples (al-Hawariyyun), who would travel with him wherever he went. When at some point the matter of 'Isa (peace be upon him) became known, it was related that one of the disciples was bribed against him, accepted the bribe, and pointed out his location. So he was surrounded. Then that disciple regretted it and strangled himself. It was also related that a man from the Jews was given a reward, and he kept searching until he pointed out his location. When 'Isa (peace be upon him) and his companions sensed the pursuers closing in on them, they entered a house in full view of the Children of Israel. It was related that they counted them as thirteen, and it was related as eighteen. They were besieged at night. It was related that 'Isa (peace be upon him) dispersed the disciples away from himself that night and sent them to the various regions, and he remained with one man. Then 'Isa was raised, and his likeness was cast upon the man, so that man was crucified. It was also related that the likeness was cast upon the Jew who had pointed him out, so he was crucified. And it was related that when 'Isa (peace be upon him) was surrounded, he said to his companions: "Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed and delivers these [others], and he will be my companion in Paradise?" Sarjis said: "I will." The likeness of 'Isa was cast upon him. And it is also narrated that the likeness of 'Isa (peace be upon him) was cast upon all of them together. Then when the Children of Israel brought them out, one from the count was missing, so they took one of those upon whom the likeness had been cast, according to these narrations I have mentioned, and that person was crucified. It was also related that the king and those in authority were not unaware of the matter of the raising of 'Isa (peace be upon him), when [p-62] they saw that the number was short and the affair was confused. So that person was crucified, and the people were kept away from his cross for days until he had changed, and no attribute of his remained identifiable. At that point the people approached him, and the disciples went out into the regions speaking that 'Isa had been crucified. This also indicates that he had dispersed them while he was in the house, or that the likeness was cast upon all of them. It was also related that this entire story did not involve the casting of the likeness of the person of 'Isa upon anyone. Rather, the meaning is: "but it was made to appear to them," that is, the king, "al-Mumakhriq" (the deceiver), made them imagine [it], so that his rule would endure. This is because when one of the group was missing and 'Isa was lost, he targeted one of them, seized and crucified him, and separated the people from him, saying: "This is 'Isa, who has been crucified," and his affair was thus settled.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who differ over it﴾ means the disagreement of those who sought to seize him, for when they lost one from the number, and news of the raising of 'Isa spread, they became confused and differed. And according to the report of the one who narrated that a likeness was cast, there remain in that likeness likely points of disagreement. But they all agreed on the crucifixion of one person, on the basis of no reliable transmission and no certainty as to which one he was.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The certainty on which the transmission of the whole community agrees, drawn from their senses, is that a person was crucified. As for whether he was 'Isa or not, that is not a matter of sensory knowledge, and therefore the transmission of all the Jews and Christians did not benefit in this matter. And Allah negated that they had any knowledge concerning his affair, according to what he really was.

Then He made an exception of "the following of assumption," and this is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), since assumption and knowledge are included under one genus: both are beliefs of the soul. And the one who assumes may say, in a figurative manner: "My knowledge in this matter is such-and-such," meaning his assumption.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they did not kill him for certain﴾: The commentators differed concerning the referent of the pronoun in "killed him." One group said it refers to assumption, as you say, "I killed this matter by knowledge," so the meaning is: their assumption was not valid in their view, and they did not verify it with certainty. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, and a group. And a people said the pronoun refers to 'Isa (peace be upon him); He informed that they did not kill him with certainty, so that a consensus [of the transmitters] would be valid for them, and the transmission of the whole community would be established. The implication of the speech is that they did not truly kill him at all, neither with certainty nor with doubt. But because that claim had occurred, his killing became doubtful in their view. And a people from among the people of the language said: the statement is complete at "and they did not kill him," and "for certain" is an emphatic infinitive (masdar) confirming the negation in "and they did not kill him." The meaning is: He informs you with certainty, or He relates to you with certainty, or be certain of this with certainty.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾ means: to His heaven and His honor. 'Isa (peace be upon him) is alive in the second heaven, according to what is contained in the hadith of the Night Journey concerning the two maternal cousins, 'Isa and Yahya. Al-Bukhari mentioned it in the hadith of the Mi'raj, and others mentioned it too. He remains there until Allah sends him down to kill the Dajjal (the Antichrist), and to fill the earth with justice, and he will live in it for forty years, then he will die as human beings die.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾: The commentators differed concerning the meaning of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Malik, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, and others said: the pronoun in "his death" refers to 'Isa, and the meaning is: no one of the People of the Scripture will remain when 'Isa descends to the earth but that he will believe in 'Isa, just as all human beings believe, and all religions will return to being one. Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas also [in another report], and others said: the pronoun in "in him" refers to 'Isa, and in "his death" refers to the People of the Scripture implied in His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture﴾. The implied sense is: "And there is none of [p-64] the People of the Scripture, any one of them," They said: a Jew does not die until he believes in 'Isa, the Spirit of Allah, and knows that he is a prophet; but at the moment of facing death, this belief will not benefit him, just as the belief of Pharaoh did not benefit him at the moment of facing death. This view was also held by 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan as well. 'Ikrima also said: the pronoun in "in him" refers to Muhammad (peace be upon him), and in "before his death" refers to the People of the Scripture. He said: No Jew or Christian leaves this world until he believes in Muhammad, even if he drowns or a wall falls upon him; he will believe at that time. In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it reads: "before their death," and in this reading there is a strengthening for the pronoun referring to the People of the Scripture. Al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan recited: "And indeed, of the People of the Scripture," with the "in" (inna) doubled, and the concealed pronoun in "yakun" refers to 'Isa (peace be upon him) according to most of the sayings, and to Muhammad (peace be upon him) according to the saying of 'Ikrima.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 160–162:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Because of a wrong done by those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things that had been lawful for them, and because of their hindering many from the way of Allah﴾ ﴿and their taking usury, though they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming people's wealth unjustly. We have prepared for those of them who disbelieve a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿But those firmly rooted in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and those who establish prayer and give zakat, and those who believe in Allah and the Last Day. Those, We will give them a great reward.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: "fa-bi-zulmin" (because of a wrong). It is joined (ʿuṭifa) to His saying "fa-bi-mā naqḍihim" (because of their breaking of their covenant). It is as if He said: "Because of their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their punishment obligatory. Because of a wrong from them, We made the foods unlawful for them." God made this worldly punishment a counterpart to the wrongdoing of the Children of Israel in their obstinacy, and the rest of their blameworthy characteristics. The "good things" (ṭayyibāt) here are the fats, some of the slaughtered animals, birds, fish, and other things. Ibn ʿAbbas recited: "ṭayyibātin (kānat) uḥillat lahum."

As for His saying: ﴿"and their hindering many from the way of Allah"﴾, it may mean: their hindering [others] in their own persons; and it may mean: their hindering others. Al-Ṭabarī went to this view and said: it is their denial of the command of Muḥammad (ﷺ), for by that they hindered a great number of people from the way of Allah.

And "wa-akhdhihimu al-ribā" (and their taking usury): it is a dirham for two dirhams up to a term, and similar things that are corrupting. They had been forbidden from it, yet they legislated it for themselves and persisted in it. Among this is the rental of money (kirāʾ al-ʿayn) and the like.

"Wa-akli amwāli al-nās bil-bāṭil" (and consuming people's wealth unjustly) is bribery.

Then Allah, exalted is He, excepted from the Children of Israel those firmly rooted in the knowledge of the Torah, who had verified the matter of Muḥammad (ﷺ) and his signs. They are ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Mukhayriq, and those who went the same way as the two of them.

"Wa-al-mu'minūna" (and the believers) is joined to "al-rāsikhūna" (those firmly rooted). "What was revealed to Muḥammad (ﷺ)" is the Qur'an, and "what was revealed before him" is the Torah and the Gospel.

People differed concerning the meaning of His saying "wa-al-muqīmīna" (and those who establish), and how its i'rāb (grammatical case-ending, syntactic analysis) departs from the i'rāb of what precedes and follows it. Abān ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān and ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "That is an error of the scribe of the codex (muṣḥaf)." It is reported that it was in the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "wa-al-muqīmūna," and it is also reported that it was in it: "wa-al-muqīmīna," as it is in the codex of ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him).

Al-Farrāʾ said: In the codex of Ibn Masʿūd it is "wa-al-muqīmūna." Likewise ʿIṣma reported from al-Aʿmash; likewise Saʿīd ibn Jubayr recited; likewise ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recited; and al-Jahdarī, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, and Mālik ibn Dīnār; likewise Yūnus and Hārūn reported from Abū ʿAmr. Others said: That is not an error of the scribe, nor an error in the codex; rather this is from the cutting off of adjectives (qaṭʿ al-nuʿūt) when they become numerous, into the accusative with "aʿnī" (I mean), and into the nominative after that with "hum" (they). Some grammarians of Kufa and Basra went to this meaning. It is transmitted from Sībawayh that it is a cutting off for praise, and the predicate of "lākin" (but) is "yu'minūna" (they believe), because praise does not occur except after the completion of the first clause. This is like the saying of Khirniq bint Haffān:

Let not my people be far away, those who are
the poison of the enemies and the plague of the stingy,
(p-٦٦) Those who alight at every battlefield,
and who are the good ones at the knots of the waist-wrapper.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The verse and the line of poetry have been distinguished by the conjunction in the verse, for according to some, the supposing of a verb is prevented there. In this there is room for consideration.

Some people said: His saying "wa-al-muqīmīna" is not joined to His saying "wa-al-mu'minūna," but is joined to "mā" in His saying ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾. The meaning is: they believe in those who establish prayer, and they are the angels. Others said: Rather, it refers to the prophets who came before. They said: Then He returned with His saying "wa-al-mu'tūna," so it is joined to His saying "wa-al-mu'minūna." Some people said: "wa-al-muqīmīna" is joined to "mā unzila" and what is meant by them is the believers in Muḥammad, i.e., those firmly rooted believe in them and in what they are upon; and His saying "wa-al-mu'tūna" means: and they are the givers of zakat. Some people said: "wa-al-muqīmīna" is joined to the pronoun in "minhum." Others said: Rather, it is joined to the kāf in His saying "min qablika," and it means the prophets. One group recited "sa-nu'tīhim" with the nūn, and one group recited "sa-yu'tīhim" with the yā'.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 4, verses 160–162:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Because of a wrong done by those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things that had been lawful for them, and because of their hindering many from the way of Allah﴾ ﴿and their taking usury, though they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming people's wealth unjustly. We have prepared for those of them who disbelieve a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿But those firmly rooted in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and those who establish prayer and give zakat, and those who believe in Allah and the Last Day. Those, We will give them a great reward.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: "fa-bi-zulmin" (because of a wrong). It is joined (ʿuṭifa) to His saying "fa-bi-mā naqḍihim" (because of their breaking of their covenant). It is as if He said: "Because of their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their punishment obligatory. Because of a wrong from them, We made the foods unlawful for them." God made this worldly punishment a counterpart to the wrongdoing of the Children of Israel in their obstinacy, and the rest of their blameworthy characteristics. The "good things" (ṭayyibāt) here are the fats, some of the slaughtered animals, birds, fish, and other things. Ibn ʿAbbas recited: "ṭayyibātin (kānat) uḥillat lahum."

As for His saying: ﴿"and their hindering many from the way of Allah"﴾, it may mean: their hindering [others] in their own persons; and it may mean: their hindering others. Al-Ṭabarī went to this view and said: it is their denial of the command of Muḥammad (ﷺ), for by that they hindered a great number of people from the way of Allah.

And "wa-akhdhihimu al-ribā" (and their taking usury): it is a dirham for two dirhams up to a term, and similar things that are corrupting. They had been forbidden from it, yet they legislated it for themselves and persisted in it. Among this is the rental of money (kirāʾ al-ʿayn) and the like.

"Wa-akli amwāli al-nās bil-bāṭil" (and consuming people's wealth unjustly) is bribery.

Then Allah, exalted is He, excepted from the Children of Israel those firmly rooted in the knowledge of the Torah, who had verified the matter of Muḥammad (ﷺ) and his signs. They are ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Mukhayriq, and those who went the same way as the two of them.

"Wa-al-mu'minūna" (and the believers) is joined to "al-rāsikhūna" (those firmly rooted). "What was revealed to Muḥammad (ﷺ)" is the Qur'an, and "what was revealed before him" is the Torah and the Gospel.

People differed concerning the meaning of His saying "wa-al-muqīmīna" (and those who establish), and how its i'rāb (grammatical case-ending, syntactic analysis) departs from the i'rāb of what precedes and follows it. Abān ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān and ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "That is an error of the scribe of the codex (muṣḥaf)." It is reported that it was in the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "wa-al-muqīmūna," and it is also reported that it was in it: "wa-al-muqīmīna," as it is in the codex of ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him).

Al-Farrāʾ said: In the codex of Ibn Masʿūd it is "wa-al-muqīmūna." Likewise ʿIṣma reported from al-Aʿmash; likewise Saʿīd ibn Jubayr recited; likewise ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recited; and al-Jahdarī, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, and Mālik ibn Dīnār; likewise Yūnus and Hārūn reported from Abū ʿAmr. Others said: That is not an error of the scribe, nor an error in the codex; rather this is from the cutting off of adjectives (qaṭʿ al-nuʿūt) when they become numerous, into the accusative with "aʿnī" (I mean), and into the nominative after that with "hum" (they). Some grammarians of Kufa and Basra went to this meaning. It is transmitted from Sībawayh that it is a cutting off for praise, and the predicate of "lākin" (but) is "yu'minūna" (they believe), because praise does not occur except after the completion of the first clause. This is like the saying of Khirniq bint Haffān:

Let not my people be far away, those who are
the poison of the enemies and the plague of the stingy,
(p-٦٦) Those who alight at every battlefield,
and who are the good ones at the knots of the waist-wrapper.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The verse and the line of poetry have been distinguished by the conjunction in the verse, for according to some, the supposing of a verb is prevented there. In this there is room for consideration.

Some people said: His saying "wa-al-muqīmīna" is not joined to His saying "wa-al-mu'minūna," but is joined to "mā" in His saying ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾. The meaning is: they believe in those who establish prayer, and they are the angels. Others said: Rather, it refers to the prophets who came before. They said: Then He returned with His saying "wa-al-mu'tūna," so it is joined to His saying "wa-al-mu'minūna." Some people said: "wa-al-muqīmīna" is joined to "mā unzila" and what is meant by them is the believers in Muḥammad, i.e., those firmly rooted believe in them and in what they are upon; and His saying "wa-al-mu'tūna" means: and they are the givers of zakat. Some people said: "wa-al-muqīmīna" is joined to the pronoun in "minhum." Others said: Rather, it is joined to the kāf in His saying "min qablika," and it means the prophets. One group recited "sa-nu'tīhim" with the nūn, and one group recited "sa-yu'tīhim" with the yā'.

[p-67]

**His statement, exalted is He:**

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and We gave David the Zabur.﴾ ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And God spoke to Moses with direct speech.﴾

It is narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas that the reason for this verse was that Sukayn the rabbi and ʿAdiyy ibn Zayd said: "O Muhammad, we do not know that God sent down anything to a human after Moses, nor revealed to him." So this verse was revealed as a refutation of their statement.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said: When God revealed ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾ [al-Nisa: 153], up to the end of the verses, they were recited to them, and they heard the news of their own wicked deeds. They said: "God has not sent down anything to a human, nor to Moses, nor to Jesus," and they denied all of that. So God revealed: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything to a human."﴾ [al-Anʿam: 91].

Wahy (revelation) is the casting of meaning in concealment. It is made known to the prophets through the mediation of Gabriel, peace be upon him, and this is what is meant by His words "as We revealed," that is, through an angel descending from God. Noah was the first of the messengers on earth to a disbelieving nation. "Noah" is diptotic despite being non-Arabic and definite, due to its lightness. Abraham, peace be upon him, is the Khalil (Friend of God). Ishmael, peace be upon him, is his eldest son and is the one sacrificed, according to the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun). He is the father of the Arabs. Isaac is his youngest son. Jacob is the son of Isaac, and he is Israel. The tribes (al-asbat) are the sons of Jacob: Joseph and his brothers. Jesus is the Messiah. Job is the one tested who endured patiently. Jonah is the son of Matta. Ibn Jammaz narrated from Nafiʿ "Yunis" with a kasra on the nun, while Ibn Waththab and al-Nakhaʿi read it with a fatha. All of these are dialectal variants. Aaron is the son of ʿImran. Solomon is the prophet-king, and David is his father.

Most people read "Zaburan" (*zaburan*) with a fatha on the zay, and it is the name of the Book of David by specification (takhsis). Every written book in the language is a *zabur*, from your saying "I wrote the book" (*zabartu al-kitab*) when you wrote it. Hamza alone read *zubur* (*zuburan*) with a damma on the zay. Abu ʿAli said: It may be the plural of *zabr*, with the name *zabr* applied to the thing written, as they say "the striking of the commander" (*darb al-amir*) and "the weaving of Yemen" (*nasj al-Yaman*), and as the written is called *kitab*. It may also be the plural of *zabur*, with the extra letter removed, as they say *zarif* and *zurouf*, *karawan* and *kirwan*, *warashan* and *wirshan*, and similar forms pluralized by removing the extra letter. This view is strengthened by the fact that broken plural (al-taksir) is like diminutive (al-tasghir), and this meaning is consistent in the diminutive of truncation (tarkhim), as in *azhar* and *zuhayr*, *harith* and *huraith*, and *thabit* and *thubayt*. So the plural is like it analogically, if it is less common in usage.

As for His words, ﴿And messengers We have related to you before﴾, up to the end of the verse: "Rusulan" is in the accusative on the basis of meaning, because the meaning is "We sent you as We sent Noah." It may also be accusative by a hidden verb, whose estimate is "We sent messengers," because the refutation of the Jews concerns their denial of the sending of messengers and the continuity of revelation. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, "wa-rusulun" is in the nominative in both places, on the estimate "they are messengers." "Qasasnahum" means: We mentioned their names and their reports. His words, ﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾, imply the great number of prophets without specifying a number. God has said: ﴿There was no nation but a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24], and He said: ﴿And many generations between them﴾ [al-Furqan: 38]. What is mentioned about the number of prophets is not sound. God knows their number, may the blessings of God be upon them.

[p-69]

His words, ﴿"And God spoke to Moses with direct speech"﴾, are information about Moses' particular status, and that God the Exalted honored him with His speech. Then He emphasized the verb with a verbal noun (masdar), and this generally indicates the confirmation of the act and its occurrence, and that it is outside the forms of metaphor (majaz) and figurative usage (istiʿara). The Arabs cannot say "the basin filled and my cord said a saying." Verbal nouns are only used to emphasize literal meanings. Among the rare usages is the saying of Hind bint al-Numan ibn Bashir:

*... and the cloaks of Judham cried out a cry*

God's speech to the prophet Moses, peace be upon him, is without modality (takyif), without limitation (tahdid), without admitting of occurrence (tajwiz huduth), without letters, and without sounds. What those firmly grounded in knowledge hold is that speech is the meaning subsisting in the soul, and God creates for Moses, or for Gabriel, a perception through hearing by which speech is obtained. [p-70] Just as God the Exalted exists unlike existing things, and is known unlike known things, so His speech is unlike speech. What is narrated from Kaʿb al-Ahbar, from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, and similar figures, that what Moses heard was like the most intense of thunderclaps, and in another narration like still thunder, is all unacceptable to the usul scholars (al-usuliyyun, theorists of the foundations of religion).

The majority of the Muslim community read "And God spoke to Moses with direct speech" with a raised *ḍamma* on the name of God. Yahya ibn Waththab and Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi read "wa-kallama Allaha" with a fatha, on the basis that Moses is the speaker. This is a weak recitation (qira'a) in terms of its fame, but it is admissible under several interpretations.

"Rusulan" (messengers): a badal (substitute/apposition) of the first (mentioned earlier); "mubashshirina wa-mundhirina" (bearers of good tidings and warners): two ḥāl (circumstantial accusatives); meaning: they give good tidings of Paradise to whoever believes and obeys, and warn of the Fire to whoever disbelieves and disobeys. Allah, exalted is He, intended by the messengers to cut off the argument of one who says: "If He had sent a messenger to me, I would have believed." Allah is ʿAzīz (Mighty), nothing overcomes Him, and no one has any argument against Him; and He is, despite that, Ḥakīm (Wise), whose acts proceed from wisdom. Thus He cut off the argument by the messengers as a wisdom from Him, exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He has sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness. And sufficient is Allah as a Witness﴾. The occasion of its revelation was the saying of the Jews: ﴿Allah did not send down anything upon a human being﴾ [al-Anʿām: 91]. Some of them also said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "We do not know, O Muhammad, that Allah has sent you, nor that He has sent down anything to you." Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and al-Jarrāḥ al-Ḥakamī read "Lakinna Allāha yashhadu" with the nun of "lakinna" doubled and the word following it (Allāh) in the accusative as the subject of "lakinna."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾. This verse is among the strongest proofs relied upon by the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) in establishing the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, contrary to the Muʿtazila, who say "knowing without knowledge" (ʿālim bi-lā ʿilm). The meaning according to the People of the Sunnah is: He sent it down while knowing its sending down and its descent. The position of the Muʿtazila on this verse is that He sent it down accompanied by His knowledge, i.e., His knowledge of unseen matters, commands and the like is in it. So "knowledge" is an expression for the known matters that are in the Qur'an, as in the saying of al-Khiḍr: "My knowledge and your knowledge have not diminished the knowledge of Allah except as much as this sparrow has diminished from this sea," meaning: from the knowledge of Allah that He scattered among His servants. al-Jumhūr read "anzala" with the verb in the active voice; al-Ḥasan read "unzila" with a ḍamma on the hamza, with the verb in the passive voice.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the angels bear witness﴾. This is a strengthening of the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and a refutation of the Jews. Qatāda said: "Witnesses, by Allah, who are not accused of partiality." His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a Witness﴾; its original form is: "And Allah is sufficient as a Witness," but the bāʾ (ba) entered so as to indicate that the meaning is: be content with Allah.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about the disbelievers who turn people away from the path of Allah, exalted is He, that they have indeed strayed far from the truth and gone astray with a far-reaching straying, from which their return is unlikely and their escape from it is improbable. ʿIkrima and Ibn Humrūz read "waṣuddū" with a ḍamma on the ṣād.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about the disbelievers who are wrongdoers in that they placed a thing in other than its proper place, namely disbelief in Allah, whereas Allah, exalted is He, deserves from them other than that, because of His manifest and hidden blessings. Indeed they are in such a state that He would not forgive them. This expression is stronger than a bare report that He does not forgive. An example of that: when you say, "I do not sell this thing," it is understood that you value it highly; but when you say, "I would never sell this thing," your valuing of it is greater. This is the meaning conveyed by this expression.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor would He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell﴾. This is guidance to roads, not guidance in the absolute sense (of guidance to faith). The remainder of the verse is clear, and it includes belittling the matter of the disbelievers and that Allah does not care for them in the least, as occurs in the hadith: "The righteous will pass away, one after another, until there remains a worthless residue like the residue of dates; Allah will not care for them in the least." Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and al-Jarrāḥ al-Ḥakamī read "Lakinna Allāha yashhadu" with the nun of "lakinna" doubled and the word following it (Allāh) in the accusative as the subject of "lakinna."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾. This verse is among the strongest proofs relied upon by the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) in establishing the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, contrary to the Muʿtazila, who say "knowing without knowledge" (ʿālim bi-lā ʿilm). The meaning according to the People of the Sunnah is: He sent it down while knowing its sending down and its descent. The position of the Muʿtazila on this verse is that He sent it down accompanied by His knowledge, i.e., His knowledge of unseen matters, commands and the like is in it. So "knowledge" is an expression for the known matters that are in the Qur'an, as in the saying of al-Khiḍr: "My knowledge and your knowledge have not diminished the knowledge of Allah except as much as this sparrow has diminished from this sea," meaning: from the knowledge of Allah that He scattered among His servants. al-Jumhūr read "anzala" with the verb in the active voice; al-Ḥasan read "unzila" with a ḍamma on the hamza, with the verb in the passive voice.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the angels bear witness﴾. This is a strengthening of the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and a refutation of the Jews. Qatāda said: "Witnesses, by Allah, who are not accused of partiality." His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a Witness﴾; its original form is: "And Allah is sufficient as a Witness," but the bāʾ (ba) entered so as to indicate that the meaning is: be content with Allah.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about the disbelievers who turn people away from the path of Allah, exalted is He, that they have indeed strayed far from the truth and gone astray with a far-reaching straying, from which their return is unlikely and their escape from it is improbable. ʿIkrima and Ibn Humrūz read "waṣuddū" with a ḍamma on the ṣād.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about the disbelievers who are wrongdoers in that they placed a thing in other than its proper place, namely disbelief in Allah, whereas Allah, exalted is He, deserves from them other than that, because of His manifest and hidden blessings. Indeed they are in such a state that He would not forgive them. This expression is stronger than a bare report that He does not forgive. An example of that: when you say, "I do not sell this thing," it is understood that you value it highly; but when you say, "I would never sell this thing," your valuing of it is greater. This is the meaning conveyed by this expression.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor would He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell﴾. This is guidance to roads, not guidance in the absolute sense (of guidance to faith). The remainder of the verse is clear, and it includes belittling the matter of the disbelievers and that Allah does not care for them in the least, as occurs in the hadith: "The righteous will pass away, one after another, until there remains a worthless residue like the residue of dates; Allah will not care for them in the least." The meaning: since they are disbelievers at the end of time, and upon them the Hour will be established.

Allah is ʿAzīz (Mighty), nothing overcomes Him, and no one has any argument against Him; and He is, despite that, Ḥakīm (Wise), whose acts proceed from wisdom. Thus He cut off the argument by the messengers as a wisdom from Him, exalted is He.

(p-72) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess (ghuluww) in your religion, and do not say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, 'Isa, son of Maryam, was only a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Maryam and a spirit from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not say, "Three"; desist, it is better for you. Allah is but one God; exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾

The address with His saying ﴿O mankind﴾ is addressed to all of mankind. The surah is Medinan, so this is among what was addressed to all people after the Hijra, because the verse is a call to the Law (al-shar'). Had it been in a command of the legal rulings or the like, it would have been "O you who believe." The Messenger in this verse is Muhammad (ﷺ), and "the truth" is his Law.

As for His saying ﴿better for you﴾ (khayran lakum), it is in the accusative (mansub) by an elided verb; its estimate is "come with what is better for you" or "take hold of what is better for you." And His saying "believe" (fa-amminu), and His saying after that "desist" (intahu), are a command to abandon one thing and enter upon another; therefore the comparative form which is "khayran" is appropriate. This is the position of Sibawayh regarding the accusative of "khayran," and its parallel from poetry is the saying of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a:

Then make an appointment with her at the two trees of Malik, or at the hills between them, make it easy.

That is: let him come to the easier one. Abu 'Ubayda said: the estimate is: let belief be better, and desisting better; so its accusative is on the predicate of "kana." Al-Farra' said: the estimate is: "believe with a belief better for you," so its accusative is as a qualifier (na't) of an elided verbal noun (masdar).

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿But if you disbelieve, then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾. This is a report of His independence (from them), and that the harm of disbelief descends only upon them. To Allah, the Exalted, belong knowledge and wisdom.

Then the Exalted addressed the People of the Scripture among the Christians, bidding them to leave off excess (al-ghuluww), which is going beyond the limit; (p-73) and from it comes the high price (ghala') of goods, and from it the range (ghalwat) of an arrow.

As for His saying, the Exalted, "in your religion," its meaning is only: in the religion for which you are held accountable. So it is as if it were a generic noun (ism jins), and He attributed it to them to make clear that they are taken to account for it. The reference is not to their misguided religion, nor were they commanded to remain upon it without excess; rather they were commanded to abandon excess in the religion of Allah absolutely, and to affirm the oneness (of Allah), and not to say about Allah except the truth. And if they follow what they were commanded, that is what will lead them to Islam.

Then the Exalted explained the matter of the Messiah, that he is the messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and His word; that is, he was brought into being by His word, which is "Be" (kun). His saying "He directed it" (alqaha) is an expression for bringing this occurrence into being in Maryam. Al-Tabari said: "and His word He directed" means the glad tidings which He sent the angel with to her. His saying, the Exalted: "and a spirit from Him," that is, from among His creatures; so "min" (from) is for the beginning of the extent, when the consideration of it is verified. Al-Tabari said: "and a spirit from Him" means a breath from Him, since it was from Jibril by His command; and he recited the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

I said to him: draw her to you and revive her with your spirit, and make for her a fire-vessel of measured size.

He describes the spark of fire. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: the spirit of 'Isa, peace be upon him, is among the spirits of Allah which He created and made to speak by His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said, "Yes"﴾ (Al-A'raf: 172). Then Allah sent him to Maryam, and he entered into her; then He commanded them to believe in Allah and His messengers, that is, those of whom 'Isa is one, and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not say, "Three"﴾. The meaning is: "Allah is the third of three." So the subject and the attributive noun (al-mudaf) were elided; thus Abu 'Ali estimated it. It is possible that the estimate is: "the worshipped is three"; or "the god is three"; or "the gods are three"; or "the hypostases (aqanim) are three." And however the expressions of the Christians branch out in their disagreement, it differs according to that estimate. The discussion of the meaning of ﴿desist, it is better for you﴾ has already preceded.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 172–173:

(p-74) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Indeed, Allah is but one God. Exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ [An-Nisa: 171] ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels who are near [to Him]. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant – He will gather them to Himself all together.﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty.﴾

"Innama" (indeed, only) in this verse is restrictive (ḥāṣira). The meaning under discussion requires this restriction by reason ('aql), but the form "innama" does not by itself necessitate restriction. Rather, it is suitable for restriction and for emphasis of the attribute, even if there is no restriction, as in the example: "Innama al-shujā'u 'Antara" (the brave one is only 'Antara), and other uses. "Subhanahu" means: glorifying Him and magnifying Him, [exalting Him] above having a son, as you (O Christians) claim concerning the matter of 'Isa, when you transferred the fatherhood of compassion and tenderness to the fatherhood of begetting. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "in yakūnu lahu waladun" with a kasra on the alif of "an," and it is negative, meaning: "mā yakūnu lahu waladun" (it is not for Him to have a son). His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [An-Nisa: 171]; the verse is a statement that encompasses the servitude of 'Isa and other matters.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, cleared the Messiah's side of their statements and purified him for what befits him, so He said: ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be...﴾; the verse. Al-istinkaf is refusal out of pride (ibaya bi-anafa). His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿nor the angels who are near﴾ is an addition to the argument and a bringing closer to minds; that is: nor do those who are at the highest ranks of created beings disdain that; so how about others? In this verse there is clear evidence for the excellence of the angels over the prophets.

(p-75) Then Allah, may He be exalted, informed about those who disdain, that is, who refuse ('ya'nafu') the worship of Allah and are arrogant, that they will be reached by gathering on the Day of Resurrection and return to Allah. His saying "fa-sayaḥshuruhum" is an expression of warning. The majority of people read "fa-sayaḥshuruhum" with a yā'; al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "fa-sanaḥshuruhum" with the nūn of the plural; "fa-nuwaffīhim," "wa-nazīduhum," "fa-nu'adhdhibuhum," all with nūn. Abu al-Fath said: Maslama read "fa-sayaḥshurhum" and "fa-yu'adhdhibhum" with a sukūn on the rā' and the bā', as a lightening.

Allah, may He be exalted, explained the condition of those gathered: He informed concerning the believers who did righteous deeds that He will give them their rewards in full, so that He does not diminish anything for anyone, little or much; and that He will increase them from His bounty. This increase may be what was reported concerning the good deed being multiplied by ten up to seven hundred times; and it may be that the multiplication is that which is not limited and not counted, and it is what is referred to in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 261].

The majority of people read "fa-sayaḥshuruhum" with a yā'; al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "fa-sanaḥshuruhum" with the nūn of the plural; "fa-nuwaffīhim," "wa-nazīduhum," "fa-nu'adhdhibuhum," all with nūn. Allah, may He be exalted, explained the condition of those gathered: He informed concerning the believers who did righteous deeds that He will give them their rewards in full, so that He does not diminish anything for anyone, little or much; and that He will increase them from His bounty. This increase may be what was reported concerning the good deed being multiplied by ten up to seven hundred times; and it may be that the multiplication is that which is not limited and not counted, and it is what is referred to in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 261].

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verses 174–175:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿As for those who scorned [to worship Him] and grew arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will find for themselves, besides Allah, no protector and no helper.﴾ [al-Nisa': 173] ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a conclusive proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a manifest light.﴾ ﴿As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty, and guide them to Himself on a straight path.﴾

This is a warning to those who scorn [worship], who abandon the worship of Allah out of disdain and arrogance. This scorning only occurs among the disbelievers, in refusing to follow the prophets and what is similar to that, such as the act of Huyayy ibn Akhtab and his brother Abu Yasir toward Muhammad (ﷺ), and the act of Abu Jahl and others. Otherwise, if you suppose any human being who has come to know Allah the Exalted, it is impossible that you would find him disbelieving in Him out of arrogance toward Him. The obstinacy that is permitted only drives a person to it through arrogance toward other humans, and along with the closeness of their ranks in the estimation of the arrogant one.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a conclusive proof from your Lord﴾ to the end of the verse, refer to Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "Burhan" (conclusive proof) is the clear, bright argument that gives complete certainty. The meaning is: there has come to you, accompanying Muhammad (ﷺ), a proof from Allah the Exalted confirming the correctness of what he calls you to, and the falsehood of the sects (nihal) you are upon. The words of the Exalted: ﴿and We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ mean the Qur'an. In it is a clarification of everything; it is the admonisher and restrainer, the one who enjoins and forbids.

Then the Blessed and Exalted One promised the believers in Allah, those who hold fast to Him. The pronoun in "bihi" (in Him/it) may refer to Allah the Exalted, and it may refer to the Qur'an, which is implied in the words of the Exalted: ﴿"a manifest light"﴾. Holding fast to it (i'tisam) means clinging to its cause and seeking salvation and protection through it. It protects just as fortresses (ma'aqil) protect. This is explained by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Qur'an is the strong rope of Allah; whoever holds fast to it is protected." Al-fadl (bounty) is Paradise and its blessings. "Yahdihim" (He will guide them) means: to the bounty. This is the guidance to the path of the gardens, as the Exalted said: ﴿He will guide them and set right their affairs﴾ [Muhammad: 5], because the guidance of direction (hidayat al-irshad) had already preceded and was attained when they believed in Allah the Exalted and held fast to His Book.

"Sirat" (path) is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by "yahdihim"; its estimated form is: "fa-yu'arrifuhum" (so He will make them know). It may be in the accusative as the second object, since "wa-yahdihim" carries the meaning of "yu'arrifuhum." It may be in the accusative as an adverb of place in some sense. It may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "ilayhi" (to Him). It has also been said that it is from "wa-fadl" (and bounty). "Al-sirat" means the road, and its explanation has been given more than once before.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 4, verse 176:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning al-kalala (the one who leaves no direct heir). If a man dies leaving no child but has a sister, she receives half of what he left; and he inherits from her if she has no child. If there are two sisters, they receive two-thirds of what he left. If there are brothers and sisters, men and women, the male receives the equivalent of the share of two females. Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray. And Allah is Knowing of all things."﴾

The discussion of the meaning of "al-kalala" has already been given at the beginning of the surah, and that the more preferred view is that it is the inheritance from which a father, a son and a daughter are absent, there being no line of ascent or descent, and in which there remains someone who "yatakallalu" (surrounds), i.e., encircles from the sides, as a crown (iklil) encircles.

The matter of al-kalala was problematic for 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, so he said: "I never went back and forth with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about anything as much as my going back and forth with him about al-kalala, and I wished that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had not died until he had explained it." And he said on the pulpit: "There are three things which, had the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained them, would have been dearer to me than the world: al-jidd (grandfather's inheritance), al-kalala, and the caliphate, and doors of usury (riba)." It is narrated from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he wrote a document concerning it, then remained seeking Allah's guidance regarding it, saying: "O Allah, if You know good in it, then carry it out." When he was stabbed, he asked for the document, and it was erased, so no one knew what was in it. Al-A'mash narrated from Ibrahim and the rest of his teachers, who said: They mentioned that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "That I should know al-kalala is dearer to me than the poll-tax of the palaces of Syria." Tariq ibn Shihab said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab took a shoulder-blade and gathered the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), then said: "I will certainly decide concerning al-kalala a judgment that women will speak of in their chambers." Then a snake came out to them from the house, and they scattered. 'Umar said: "If Allah had willed to complete this matter, He would have completed it." Ma'dan ibn Abi Talha said: "'Umar addressed the people on Friday, saying: 'By Allah, I leave after me nothing more important to me than the matter of al-kalala. I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he was never harsher with me about anything than about it, until he struck my chest and said: (The verse of summer will suffice you, the one revealed at the end of Surat al-Nisa'. If I live, I will decide about it with a ruling over which no two people who recite the Qur'an will differ.)'" 'Uqba ibn 'Amir was asked about al-kalala and said: "Are you not amazed at this? He asks me about al-kalala, and nothing has perplexed the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as much as al-kalala has perplexed them."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The apparent meaning of 'Umar's words, may Allah be pleased with him, is that the verse of summer is this one. Abu Salama narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about al-kalala, and he said: "Did you not hear the verse that was revealed in summer: ﴿And if a man leaves an inheritance as kalala...﴾ [al-Nisa': 12]?"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the apparent meaning, because al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: The last verse revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) was: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning al-kalala﴾. Many of the companions said: it is among the last of what was revealed. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: It was revealed because of me. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited me while I was ill, so I said: "O Messenger of Allah, how should I dispose of my property? I had nine sisters, and I had neither father nor child," and then the verse was revealed.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The verse of summer suffices you concerning it" is a clarification that is sufficient and manifest. I do not know what in it was problematic for al-Faruq, may Allah's pleasure be upon him, unless the indication of the word did not apply consistently to it, since the Quraysh used it rarely; and there is no doubt that the indication of the word was confused for many people. Therefore some said: al-kalala is the deceased himself; others said: al-kalala is the property; and other differences besides these. When there is in the estate neither father nor child, and the deceased leaves a sister, she has half as a fixed share (fard musamma) by this verse. If the deceased leaves a daughter and a sister, then the daughter has half and the sister has half by way of 'asaba (residuary), not by the fixed share. There is a difference of opinion among people on this issue from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas. It is mentioned from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said in his sermon: "Verily, the verse at the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' Allah revealed concerning the child and the parent; the second verse Allah revealed concerning the spouse, the wife, and the brothers and sisters from the mother; and the verse with which Allah concluded Surat al-Nisa' He revealed concerning the brothers and sisters from the father and the mother; and the verse with which He concluded Surat al-Anfal He revealed concerning the relatives (ulu al-arham)."

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "fa-inna lil-dhakari mithla hazzi" (with the particle inna and the accusative of hazz).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"an tadillu"﴾ means: "out of dislike that you go astray; and out of caution that you go astray." So the estimate is: "lest you go astray." Among this is the saying of al-Qutami, describing a she-camel:

"We saw what the discerning see in her, so we swore an oath upon her that she be sold."

When 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾, he would say: "O Allah, whomever You have made the kalala clear to, yet it has not become clear to me..."
